title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
1. What is the stereocentre?
Locate it in CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list its four substituents.






Check your answer





The CH(OH) carbon bears OH, H, CH₃ and COOH. They are different, so it is a tetrahedral stereocentre.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
2. Does proton loss invert it?
For hydroxide removing the carboxyl OH proton of lactic acid, does that step invert the alcohol-bearing centre?






Check your answer





No. The drawn proton transfer does not change the bonds or spatial arrangement at that centre. It produces lactate and water.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
3. What does oxidation change?
Oxidise lactic acid’s secondary alcohol to a ketone. Is the original centre still R/S?






Check your answer





The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The former centre is trigonal planar, so it is not assigned R/S.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
4. Which mechanism returns C=O?
Compare an aldehyde addition product with an acyl substitution product.






Check your answer





Addition opens the carbonyl pi bond and produces a tetrahedral product after appropriate protonation. Acyl substitution first adds, then eliminates a viable leaving group to reform C=O.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
section: 5. What does a large mass prove?
text:
5. What does a large mass prove?
A plausible high isolated yield conflicts with major unexpected NMR signals. Which observation should be ignored?






Check your answer





Neither. The apparent yield depends on the identity/purity assumption, while unexpected NMR signals call that assumption into question. Investigate the discrepancy before claiming pure product.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
6. What makes a conclusion inspectable?
Give the ingredients of an evidence-based conclusion and a reproducible report.






Check your answer





State a chemical claim, observations, a reason connecting them, a limitation and a next test. Save raw inputs and code so a fresh R session can recreate tables and plots; separately check chemical validity.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Connect structure, stereochemistry, reaction mechanisms and experimental evidence in each case.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Working refresher
Use the same checks on every case: identify functional groups, draw explicit atoms and charges at the changing site, follow electron pairs, and test a proposed structure against observations. In wedge/dash drawings, solid wedge points toward the observer and dashed wedge away. For a tetrahedral centre rank CIP priorities by atomic number, break ties with next attached atoms and treat multiple bonds by duplicated-atom bookkeeping; with priority 4 away, clockwise 1→2→3 is R and anticlockwise S. For the simple C/H/O spectra use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2 and the supplied first-order n +1 rule. Amount=n=m/M; theoretical product comes from balanced limiting extent; apparent yield=100×isolated/theoretical mass. The local lecture provides the chemical drawings used in these exercises.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 1. Read lactic acid without a pathway
text:
1. Read lactic acid without a pathway
For CH₃CH(OH)COOH, identify both oxygen-containing functional groups, alcohol type and the possible stereocentre. Supply the four groups attached to that centre.






Hint





The CH(OH) carbon, rather than the carbonyl carbon, is tetrahedral.









Worked explanation





The molecule has a secondary alcohol and carboxylic acid. CH(OH) bears OH,H,CH₃ and COOH, four different groups, so it is a stereocentre. No metabolic knowledge is needed to infer those features.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
2. Rank the carbon substituents
At the lactic acid centre, compare COOH with CH₃ using supplied CIP multiple-bond bookkeeping: duplicate a doubly bonded atom in the attached-atom comparison. Give the complete priority order.






Hint





The directly attached atoms tie at C; compare their next atoms.









Worked explanation





COOH carbon compares as O,O,O while methyl compares H,H,H, so COOH outranks CH₃. Complete order is OH>COOH>CH₃>H. Atomic identities, not group size or drawn length, determine priority.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 3. Assign a view with lowest priority away
text:
3. Assign a view with lowest priority away
In a tetrahedral drawing H(4) points away. OH(1) is at upper left, COOH(2) upper right and CH₃(3) lower left. Determine R/S and explain what reverses if H points toward you instead.






Hint





Read 1→2→3 with the lowest-priority group away.









Worked explanation





The sequence is clockwise in this stated view, so R. If the same apparent sequence is viewed with H toward the observer, invert the result to S or reorient a model. A page rotation alone does not change configuration.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
4. Distinguish mirror and rotation
Two lactic-acid drawings have identical connectivity but opposite tetrahedral arrangement at their sole stereocentre. State their relationship and whether R/S predicts the sign of optical rotation.






Hint





Configuration and a measured optical property are distinct labels.









Worked explanation





They are enantiomers and cannot be superimposed by rigid rotation. R/S does not determine positive or negative optical rotation; that sign must be measured or otherwise supplied.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
5. Draw one acid–base mechanism
For lactic acid plus OH⁻, draw removal of the carboxyl OH proton with both curved arrows. Give products and state whether that step inverts the alcohol-bearing centre.






Hint





Start an arrow at the base pair and the other at the acid O–H bond.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻ and H₂O form. The proton-transfer step does not break or rearrange the bonds at CH(OH), so it does not itself invert that centre. Other conditions could cause other chemistry, but that is not this drawn event.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
6. Check atom conservation quantitatively
For CH₃CH(OH)COOH+OH⁻→CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻+H₂O, count C,H,O and total charge on each side. Explain why dropping the water product would fail the audit.






Hint





Lactic acid is C₃H₆O₃ and lactate is C₃H₅O₃⁻.









Worked explanation





Each complete side has C₃H₇O₄ and total charge −1. Omitting water loses H₂O from the inventory and hides the proton recipient; electron-flow bookkeeping alone cannot permit atoms to disappear.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
7. Use a supplied ionisation model
For a dilute monoprotic acid with pKa 3.86, use fraction_Aminus=1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)). Calculate fractions at pH3.86 and 4.86 and interpret the population.






Hint





At one pH unit above pKa the ratio A⁻/HA is 10.









Worked explanation





Fractions are 0.5 and 10/11≈0.909. They describe relative populations of acid and conjugate-base species, not molecules each losing half or 90.9% of a proton.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
8. Predict oxidation and geometry
Oxidise the secondary alcohol in CH₃CH(OH)COOH to a ketone while retaining the carbon skeleton. Write the product and explain what happens to the original stereocentre.






Hint





A secondary alcohol becomes a ketone at its OH-bearing carbon.









Worked explanation





The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The changing carbon becomes trigonal planar, so the original tetrahedral R/S centre no longer exists.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
9. Check the oxidation-state change
At the changing carbon of lactic acid assign +1 per C–O bond order,−1 per C–H and 0 per C–C. Compare the ketone product carbonyl.






Hint





The alcohol centre has one C–O and one C–H; ketone has C=O and no C–H.









Worked explanation





The alcohol centre is +1−1=0; the ketone carbon is +2. The increase by 2 confirms oxidation. This conclusion does not require adding an oxygen atom to the molecular formula.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
10. Choose a target ester site
The selected target from lactic acid and ethanol is CH₃CH(OH)COOCH₂CH₃. Identify the functional-group change and state a condition-related limitation of this target drawing.






Hint





The drawn secondary OH remains; the carboxylic acid becomes ester.









Worked explanation





Acid-group esterification is the intended net change. The drawing does not guarantee selective reaction under arbitrary conditions, since the starting molecule has more than one reactive oxygen function. Actual conditions and competing pathways must be assessed.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
11. Track the alcohol oxygen
In standard esterification, ethanol is labelled at oxygen as CH₃CH₂OH. Write the labelled ethyl-lactate target and identify the two atoms directly bonded to O.






Hint





The incoming alcohol O forms the new bond to acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH(OH)C(=O)OCH₂CH₃. O is bonded to the acid-derived carbonyl carbon and the ethyl CH₂ carbon. Atom identities follow the pathway rather than being inferred from final drawing positions.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
12. Choose addition versus substitution
Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃ reacting with a suitable nucleophile. State the shared first bond changes and the key reason their later pathways can differ.






Hint





Both initial attacks move the carbonyl pi pair, but the ester has an oxygen-based substituent at acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





Both form C–Nu and move C=O pi electrons to O. The ester can undergo a viable leaving-group step to restore C=O; ordinary aldehydes lack the corresponding group, since H⁻ is not a normal leaving group here.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
13. Read amino-acid charges
For H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, identify individual formal charges and net charge. Does net zero make it equivalent to an entirely uncharged hydrocarbon in water?






Hint





Sum the charges without deleting their local presence.









Worked explanation





N is +1 and carboxylate −1, net 0. The molecule is zwitterionic and contains strongly polar charged sites, so net neutrality does not make its interactions hydrocarbon-like.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
14. Predict high-pH deprotonation
Starting from H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, draw OH⁻ accepting one ammonium proton. Give the product formula, N bond count and net charge.






Hint





The N–H bonding pair returns to N.









Worked explanation





H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻ and water form. N has three bonds and a lone pair, neutral; carboxylate remains −1. Net −1 on each complete side is conserved.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
15. Assign a complete unknown dataset
U1 has C₄H₈O₂, carbonyl IR without broad OH, proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. Assign CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and link each observation to a structural part.






Hint





Join the ethyl quartet/triplet, then place the acetyl singlet and carbonyl.









Worked explanation





O–CH₂ gives 4.12 q 2H and terminal ethyl CH₃ gives 1.25 t 3H. Acetyl CH₃ gives 2.05 s 3H because adjacent carbonyl C has no H. Ester carbonyl explains IR and lack of acid/alcohol OH; all atoms fit the formula.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
16. Test a hydroxyketone alternative
For the same U1 dataset, compare CH₃COCH(OH)CH₃. Explain two predicted differences without using filenames or expected reaction products as evidence.






Hint





The proposed O-bearing carbon is CH, not CH₂.









Worked explanation





The hydroxyketone predicts an OH-bearing 1H environment and a methyl adjacent to CH, commonly a doublet in the simple model. It also predicts OH functionality. U1 instead has O–CH₂2H quartet and ethyl 3H triplet, favouring the ester among these candidates.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 17. Calculate yield while stating its assumption
text:
17. Calculate yield while stating its assumption
A1:1 teaching reaction has 0.0100 mol limiting reagent, product M180.16 g/mol and isolate 1.70 g. Calculate theoretical mass and apparent yield, then state why neither number proves purity.






Hint





Theoretical amount comes from starting reagents; isolated mass enters separately.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g and apparent yield 94.4%. The calculation assumes isolated mass is product; impurities, residual solvent or wrong identity can invalidate that interpretation. Purity requires separate evidence.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
18. Resolve contradictory observations
A sample gives 94% apparent yield and one TLC (thin-layer chromatography) spot, but full NMR has an unexpected major signal group. Give a defensible interpretation and two possible explanations without identifying a unique impurity.






Hint





A single separation feature can hide co-migration, and mass can include other components.









Worked explanation





The sample may not be pure despite its plausible mass. Residual solvent or another organic component could contribute; incorrect assignment is also possible. Investigate with complete spectral assignments or a discriminating separation rather than ignoring the contradiction.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
section: 19. Critique a reproducible but invalid calculation
text:
19. Critique a reproducible but invalid calculation
An Rmd file always reproduces 100×isolated_mass/starting_reagent_mass and calls the result percent yield. Explain why reproducibility alone does not make this formula chemically correct.






Hint





Mass yield must use theoretical product mass from balanced stoichiometry and molar masses.









Worked explanation





The denominator is generally wrong because starting and product molar masses and coefficients can differ. Correctly compute theoretical product amount from limiting extent, convert using product molar mass, then compare isolated product mass. Repeating an invalid formula is reproducibly wrong.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
20. Write a final evidence-based conclusion
You have a formula-consistent ester candidate, matching simulated IR/NMR, an apparent 66.6% yield from teaching masses and no actual measured isolate spectra. Write a supported claim, limitation and useful next observation for a real sample.






Hint





Keep model demonstration and real measurement separate.









Worked explanation





The supplied simulated evidence supports the ester candidate and the teaching mass calculation gives 66.6% apparent yield under its assumptions. It does not identify or establish purity of a real isolate. Appropriate measured sample spectra and independent purity assessment would test that real-sample claim.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry
text:
Explore
Question: can you reach a target while justifying each functional-group change and accounting for the extra reacting molecules?
Allow 10 minutes: plan for 2, build and revise for 5, then explain one accepted and one rejected step for 3. This is a reasoning tool, not a laboratory protocol.

Enable JavaScript to select a target, propose transformations and inspect accepted bond changes.




Predict
Starting with ethanol, propose a route to ethyl ethanoate through ethanoic acid. The acid-derived and alcohol-derived fragments cannot both arise from one two-carbon molecule without another carbon source. Identify the needed separate ethanol portion before building the route.


Explore

Select a transformation and press Apply. A rejected step leaves the current structure unchanged and explains the mismatch.
Reach the acid, then esterify using a separate ethanol portion. Inspect the explicit ethanol reactant and water product.
Undo a step and try oxidation via the aldehyde instead.
Hydrolyse the ester in base. Why does the current structure become carboxylate rather than neutral acid? Apply acid work-up separately.
Reset and try the shorter acid target.



Worked route and accounting
One accepted route is ethanol → ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate. Esterification uses the balanced net comparison
\[\mathrm{CH_3COOH+CH_3CH_2OH\rightleftharpoons CH_3COOCH_2CH_3+H_2O}.\]
It therefore supplies the added two-carbon fragment explicitly. A longer route can go through ethanal before further oxidation. Base-promoted ester hydrolysis gives ethanoate and ethanol; a later hydronium transfer gives the neutral acid and water.


Model limits
Only the listed small toolkit is implemented. An unsupported choice means that it is not justified by this supplied toolkit, not that chemistry can never achieve any related change. [O] is a net oxidation equivalent, not an identified reagent. H:⁻ represents hydride-equivalent delivery from a suitable reagent, not free hydride persisting in water; proton donation is explicitly included afterward. Actual selectivity, conversion, equilibrium and isolated yield need suitable conditions and observations. Review local synthesis reasoning.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
About this lecture
Acetylsalicylic acid was first made in 1853, as a crude product that nobody could sell. In 1897 chemists at Bayer made it clean and reproducibly, and two years later it went on sale as aspirin. Same reaction; the difference was evidence of identity and purity.
In the practical you’ll make aspirin yourself. Today we learn to answer three separate questions about the white solid on your filter paper:

Planning: a route is a sequence of functional-group changes
Amounts: moles, the limiting reagent, and coefficients
Yield: the theoretical maximum versus what you weighed
TLC (thin-layer chromatography): what Rf measures, and what one spot can’t prove
Spectra: IR and NMR as checks on identity and purity

Yesterday you read structures from spectra; today those spectra become evidence about a reaction you ran.

Open with the aspirin story. Charles Gerhardt made acetylsalicylic acid in 1853 but his material was impure and he didn’t pursue it; Felix Hoffmann’s 1897 preparation at Bayer was clean enough to become a medicine, sold as Aspirin from 1899. The chemistry hadn’t really changed; what changed was being able to make a pure product reliably and show that it was pure. That’s exactly the gap students meet in the lab: a mass on a balance isn’t the same as a pure compound. Name the three questions explicitly and keep coming back to them: how much (yield), is it the right molecule (identity), and is anything else in there (purity). Most marks lost on practical reports come from letting one of those answers stand in for another.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: Plan a route by functional-group changes
text:
Plan a route by functional-group changes

Ethanol to ethanoic acid to ethyl ethanoateWork backwards from the target: an ester comes from an acid plus an alcohol, and the acid comes from oxidising an alcohol (Day 13). Each arrow changes one functional group.

Try it: where does the O–CH₂CH₃ part of ethyl ethanoate come from?

From a second portion of ethanol. The first portion is oxidised to the acid; a fresh portion supplies the alkoxy group in the acid-catalysed esterification.



Planning is just functional-group bookkeeping. Ask: what bond did the last step make? In an ester it’s the C(=O)–O bond, so the last step joins an acid and an alcohol. That’s the Fischer esterification from Week 4 (acyl chemistry, Day 17). The common confusion is thinking the same ethanol molecule somehow becomes both halves. Draw two separate flasks if needed. Stress that a route on paper says nothing about conditions, work-up or yield; it’s a plan, not a protocol.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Choose where the oxidation stops

Ethanol to ethanal to ethanoic acidA primary alcohol oxidises to an aldehyde and then on to an acid. If ethanal is the target, a bare “[O]” isn’t enough: the conditions must stop at the aldehyde and let you isolate it.
Stopping early doesn’t prove you have pure ethanal either. You still need evidence that it’s there and that the acid isn’t.

Link back to alcohols and redox on Day 13. In practice, aldehyde-selective conditions or distilling the aldehyde out as it forms (ethanal boils at about 20 °C) are ways to avoid over-oxidation; we don’t need the reagent details today. The key reasoning point is the second sentence: a target label on a reaction scheme is a hope. Ask the room what evidence would distinguish ethanal from ethanoic acid. Good answers: IR (broad acid O–H, aldehyde C–H near 2700–2800), NMR (aldehyde H near 9.8 ppm versus acid H near 11–12). That’s yesterday’s content applied.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: The aspirin reaction: one oxygen changes
text:
The aspirin reaction: one oxygen changes

Salicylic acid plus acetic anhydride gives aspirinThe phenol O–H becomes an ester; the carboxylic acid is untouched, so aspirin is an acid and an ester. All coefficients are 1: 138.12 + 102.09 = 180.16 + 60.05.
It’s an acyl substitution (Day 17): the phenol oxygen attacks one C=O of the anhydride, and acetate leaves as acetic acid.

This is an acyl substitution from Day 17: the phenol oxygen attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, and acetate leaves, ending up as acetic acid. Make students point at the shaded atoms: the acetyl group comes from the anhydride, the oxygen comes from salicylic acid. Ask why we bother writing acetic acid in the equation if we only want aspirin: it balances the atoms, and it’s a real by-product that can contaminate the crude solid. Have them check the molar masses add up; it’s a quick way to catch a wrong formula.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Grams don’t react; moles do

n = \frac{m}{M} \qquad \frac{\text{g}}{\text{g mol}^{-1}} = \text{mol} \qquad 1\ \text{mol} = 1000\ \text{mmol}
Write the units every time and let them cancel.

Try it: you weigh out 1.00 g of each reagent. Is either in excess?

Yes, the anhydride. 1.00 / 138.12 = 7.24 mmol acid, but 1.00 / 102.09 = 9.80 mmol anhydride. Equal masses aren’t equal amounts.



This is Day 1 arithmetic, but now it’s load-bearing. Give students 60 seconds to do the anhydride row on paper before revealing it. Watch for two slips: dividing the wrong way round (M/m), and mixing mmol and mol later when multiplying by a molar mass in g/mol. Here the anhydride really is in excess, but you can only say that after converting both to moles. The next slide makes the comparison properly.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: The limiting reagent sets the ceiling
text:
The limiting reagent sets the ceiling

Reaction extent bars for two scenariosDivide each amount by its coefficient. The smallest n / coefficient is the limiting reagent; the rest is left over and can’t make extra product.

Try it: keep 10.00 mmol salicylic acid but use only 0.51045 g anhydride. What limits, and what’s the maximum aspirin mass?

0.51045 / 102.09 = 5.00 mmol anhydride, which now limits. 0.00500 mol × 180.16 g/mol = 0.9008 g aspirin.



The point of the second panel is that “salicylic acid is the limiting reagent” is not a fact about aspirin chemistry; it’s a fact about the amounts you weighed. Recompute every time an input changes. In the planned case, the 5 mmol of excess anhydride is deliberate: it’s cheap, it pushes the reaction along, and it’s easy to remove (it hydrolyses to acetic acid during work-up). Ask: does using 30 mmol of anhydride raise the theoretical yield? No, the acid still caps it at 10 mmol.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Coefficients change the comparison

2 A + B gives P: raw amounts and amounts divided by coefficientFor 2 A + B → P with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, A looks plentiful but limits: 10/2 = 5 versus 8/1 = 8. At most 5 mmol P.

Try it: same amounts, but the equation is 2 A + B → 2 P. How much P can form?

10 mmol. The limiting extent is still 5 mmol; multiply it by the product coefficient, 2.



The aspirin reaction is 1:1:1:1, which hides this step. Taking min(10, 8) and declaring B limiting is the classic error. Separate two numbers: the reaction extent (how many times the balanced equation can run, 5 mmol here) and the product amount (extent times product coefficient). They’re only equal when the product coefficient is 1. This exact pair of problems appears in the exercises and the self-check.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: Theoretical mass is an upper bound
text:
Theoretical mass is an upper bound



step
calculation

aspirin amount

theoretical mass

It’s a prediction from the starting masses, never a measurement of what you made. It assumes:

only the desired reaction happens, with no side products;
every bit of the limiting reagent reacts;
nothing is lost in filtering, washing or recrystallising.

Real isolated masses are lower, and the gap tells you about losses, not about purity.

Keep full precision (1.8016 g) until the end and round only when reporting. Emphasise where this number comes from: the starting-material masses and the balanced equation, nothing else. That will matter on the report slide, where students who change the isolated mass sometimes also change the theoretical mass. Ask: does calculating 1.8016 g tell you the reaction went to completion? No; it tells you the most you could possibly get.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: Isolated yield compares the balance with the ceiling
text:
Isolated yield compares the balance with the ceiling

Apparent yield against isolated mass\text{apparent isolated yield} = 100 \times \frac{\text{isolated mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}} = 100 \times \frac{1.20}{1.8016} = 66.6\ \%

Try it: you recover 1.10 g instead. What’s the yield, and what else changes?

61.1 %. Only the numerator changed; the theoretical mass stays 1.8016 g.



Call it “apparent” deliberately: the formula treats every milligram on the balance as product. The line is straight because theoretical mass is a constant; that’s a property of the arithmetic, not evidence about the chemistry. Point at the red region: you can’t make more aspirin than the limiting reagent allows, so a value above 100 % tells you the assumption failed, which is the next slide.

text:

Yield measures how much you weighed. It says nothing about what you weighed. Sample A is probably the better product.

Try it: give two kinds of explanation for B’s yield above 100 %.

Extra mass that isn’t product (residual solvent or water, leftover reagents, by-product) or an error (weighing, molar mass, stoichiometry). Not extra aspirin.



This is the central idea of the lecture. Students instinctively rank isolates by yield. Turn it around: a high yield with dirty spectra is worse than a modest yield of clean material. Don’t let students diagnose a single cause for sample B without evidence; “residual solvent” is a hypothesis to test, for example by drying to constant mass or checking the NMR for solvent peaks. In the aspirin prep, wet crystals that weren’t dried properly are the most common culprit.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
TLC separates before you judge

TLC plate with starting material, product reference and crude lanesCompounds that stick more strongly to the polar silica travel less. The crude lane shows at least two detected components, matching the references. Spot darkness isn’t a measure of amount.

Run lanes side by side on the same plate: starting material, product reference, crude. Matching heights on the same plate are much more meaningful than comparing to a number from a book. Two spots in the crude means the reaction is incomplete or starting material survived work-up, at least under this detection method. Resist “the product spot is darker, so 80 % conversion”: the eye isn’t a calibrated detector. These are teaching data; with a real eluent the order of the spots depends on the conditions.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: Rf: two distances from the same origin
text:
Rf: two distances from the same origin

Measuring Rf, and a plate without a marked frontRf = distance to spot centre ÷ distance to solvent front, both from the origin. Mark the front as soon as the plate comes out: without it there’s no denominator, and you can’t invent one.

Try it: the starting-material spot is 1.2 cm up, front 5.0 cm. What’s its Rf, with units?

0.24, no units. Centimetres cancel. The value only holds for that plate, eluent and conditions.



Both distances start at the origin line, not the bottom of the plate. Measure to the centre of the spot. The right panel is a real lab-report problem: someone records a spot at 3.0 cm but forgot to mark the front, which evaporates within seconds. The honest answer is “Rf cannot be determined”, not “assume the front went to 5 cm”. Ask why an Rf from another eluent can’t confirm identity: retention depends on the conditions, and even identical values aren’t unique to one molecule.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: One spot can hide a mixture
text:
One spot can hide a mixture

Co-migrating compounds and an undetected componentDifferent compounds can co-migrate at the same Rf, and some components are invisible under UV or the chosen stain. One spot means one detected component under these conditions, not proof of purity.

Try it: your product shows a single spot. What evidence would test whether it’s pure?

A different eluent or stain, or an independent method such as NMR, where a second compound would add its own signals.



Students love “one spot, therefore pure”. Ask them to explain how the A + B lane could happen: the two compounds simply interact with silica and solvent in the same way. Two follow-ups that genuinely test the claim: rerun in a different solvent system (co-migration rarely survives a change of eluent) and look with a technique that sees the whole sample, like NMR. A melting point is another classic purity check in the aspirin practical: impurities lower and broaden it.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: IR: what should change, what should stay
text:
IR: what should change, what should stay

Schematic IR of salicylic acid and aspirinPredict from the structures before you look: the phenol O–H should go and an ester C=O near 1750 cm⁻¹ should appear. The broad acid O–H stays, because aspirin is still a carboxylic acid.
So an acid O–H band is not evidence of unreacted salicylic acid. These traces are schematic, not measured.

This is Day 2 and Day 21 IR reading applied to a reaction. The logic is “what’s lost, what’s gained, what’s retained”. The new ester carbonyl is the most useful positive evidence, appearing next to the acid carbonyl as two bands. The trap is over-interpreting the broad O–H: students see it and write “starting material still present”, but the target has an acid O–H too. Be explicit that IR here supports “functional groups consistent with aspirin”; it doesn’t measure purity, and a schematic trace documents nothing about a real sample.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
NMR: count every signal

Schematic proton NMR of an aspirin sample with an extra signalAspirin predicts 1 + 4 + 3 = 8 H: acid H, four aromatic H, one CH₃ singlet. Anything else needs explaining.

Try it: this sample gave a good yield and one TLC spot. Should the extra signal be ignored?

No. The yield assumed the solid was product; the NMR tests that. Residual solvent, starting material or a by-product are all possible; check integrations and references before naming one.



NMR sees everything with hydrogens in it, so it’s the strongest purity check students will meet. Walk through the prediction from the structure first, as on Day 21, then compare. The extra singlet is deliberately left unassigned. Acetic acid, a by-product of this very reaction, would give a CH3 singlet near 2.1 ppm, but it’s a hypothesis until you check it against a reference. The principle: contradictory evidence beats a convenient number. Never discard a spectrum because the yield looks nice.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: Three claims, three kinds of evidence
text:
Three claims, three kinds of evidence








claim
supported by
can’t show




how much
mass, theoretical mass, yield
what the solid is


reaction happened
new TLC spot, starting spot shrinks
exact conversion


identity
IR and NMR match the predicted structure
purity, on IR alone


purity
clean NMR, one spot in several eluents
– (never absolute)



A good conclusion keeps these apart: “Apparent yield 66.6 %; crude TLC shows two components; IR consistent with an aryl ester and an acid.”

Use this as the template for the practical report. Read out the example sentence and point out what it doesn’t claim: it doesn’t say “pure aspirin”. Ask students to add the limitation that belongs in the next sentence, for example “the crude still contains starting material, so the isolated mass may overstate the product” or “the IR trace was simulated”. This is the reasoning the integration day (tomorrow) builds on.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
A report that recomputes itself
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
theoretical_mass_g <- min(amounts$extent_mol) * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g



change isolated_mass_g to 1.10
should change
should not change




after Knit
yield → 61.1 %
amounts, extent, 1.8016 g



Compute every number from saved raw inputs and put results in the text with inline R, never retyped. Then one edited input updates exactly what depends on it.

Every number in the report should come from saved raw inputs, and every value in the text should be inline R, not retyped. Then a single change propagates. The dependency rule mirrors the chemistry: theoretical mass depends on the starting masses only; isolated mass only enters the yield. A student who edits the isolated mass and sees the theoretical mass move has a bug. Also warn about min(): it’s only right if the table contains just the starting reagents. Automatic updating guarantees consistency, not correctness; wrong stoichiometry recomputes beautifully.

text:
Mistakes we see every year

Read each mistake aloud and ask the room for the fix before you point at the right-hand column. Each row maps to an exercise: limiting reagent (3–7), yield above 100 % (11), yield versus purity (12), Rf and missing fronts (13–15), one spot (16), aspirin IR (17).

Next: putting the whole course together (Day 23). Practice: exercises · self-check

Close the loop with the opening story: the difference between 1853 and 1897 was not the reaction but the evidence. Recite the three questions once more: how much, is it the right molecule, is it clean. Tomorrow’s integration day combines mechanism, spectra and these calculations in single problems. Point students to the exercises: 1–10 are the core calculations and planning, 11–20 the evidence reasoning, and the R task builds the report that the practical needs.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
1. What does C₄H₈O₂ imply?
Calculate degree of unsaturation for an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule and state one limitation.






Check your answer





(2×4+2−8)/2 = 1. A carbonyl, another double bond or a ring could account for it; formula alone does not establish an ester.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
2. Which IR direction means absorption?
In a transmittance plot, do stronger absorptions point up or down?






Check your answer





They are dips to lower transmittance. An absorbance plot uses a different ordinate. Always inspect the axis label.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
text:
3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
For O–CH₂–CH₃ in the simple first-order model, give the two multiplicities and integrations.






Check your answer





CH₂ is a quartet integrating to 2H because it sees three adjacent equivalent H. CH₃ is a triplet integrating to 3H because it sees two adjacent H.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
text:
4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
In CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, explain the 3H signal near 2 ppm using neighbouring atoms.






Check your answer





The carbonyl carbon directly adjacent to that methyl has no H. The distant O–CH₂ hydrogens are not vicinal neighbours of the acetyl methyl in this introductory splitting model.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
5. Can NMR height replace integral?
A schematic triplet is taller than a singlet. Can you conclude that the triplet represents more H?






Check your answer





No. Integral is area over the whole signal, not the tallest line. Use supplied integration or measured integrated area; schematic heights are not quantitative proton counts.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
6. What rejects the acid candidate?
State two observations in U1 supporting ethyl ethanoate over butanoic acid.






Check your answer





No evident broad acid O–H in a suitable complete IR trace, and a 2H O–CH₂ quartet with matching terminal CH₃ triplet. The acetyl CH₃ singlet supplies additional support.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Use molecular formulas, IR observations and NMR patterns to test proposed structures.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Working refresher
All numerical spectra below are simulated teaching examples. For ordinary closed-shell C/H/O formulas use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2; O is omitted from this simple count. IR transmittance dips indicate absorption: broad alcohol O–H is often near 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, acid O–H can extend broadly around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ and carbonyls occupy roughly 1650–1800 cm⁻¹ depending on structure. In our simple first-order proton NMR model, n equivalent adjacent H give n +1 lines; integral gives relative total H area. A singlet/triplet/quartet has 1/3/4 lines. These shortcuts do not describe all real coupling or exchange. Chemical shifts are in ppm; supplied values are illustrative. Candidate tests and drawings are available in the lecture.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
1. Calculate one formula constraint
For an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule C₄H₈O₂, calculate DBE=(2C+2−H)/2. State two structural possibilities consistent with that degree without claiming a unique structure.






Hint





O does not enter this simplified expression.









Worked explanation





DBE=1. One double bond, such as C=O, or one saturated ring could supply it. The formula alone does not establish ester, acid or any unique connectivity.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
2. Check two proposed formulas
Count the atoms in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. Verify whether both can be U1 with C₄H₈O₂ and name their functional-group difference.






Hint





Write the carbonyl explicitly before counting.









Worked explanation





Each is C₄H₈O₂. Ethyl ethanoate is an ester, while butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid. Both include one C=O, satisfying DBE1, but the oxygen/hydrogen connectivity differs.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
3. Reject a formula mismatch
A proposed candidate for C₄H₈O₂ is ethanol CH₃CH₂OH. Count its atoms and explain why a plausible-looking O–H IR band would not rescue it as the whole U1 structure.






Hint





A matched functional group does not replace the molecular formula constraint.









Worked explanation





Ethanol is C₂H₆O, not C₄H₈O₂. Even if it shared an OH feature with some spectrum, it would not account for U1’s total composition. A full candidate must satisfy all supplied constraints.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
4. Read a transmittance trace
A simulated IR trace falls from 95% to 30% transmittance near 1740 cm⁻¹. Which position indicates stronger absorption, and why must you inspect the y-axis label?






Hint





Transmittance measures the fraction of incident light passing through.









Worked explanation





30% transmittance means less light transmitted and therefore stronger absorption than 95% at the comparison region. In an absorbance plot stronger absorption would normally be higher; the same curve direction cannot be assumed without reading the axis.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
5. Use an acid-region prediction
Candidate A is ethyl ethanoate and B is butanoic acid. The supplied complete simulated IR has C=O but no broad O–H envelope across the usual acid region. Which candidate is challenged, and what experimental limitation could weaken that argument?






Hint





Ask what each candidate predicts in a measured, sufficiently sensitive region.









Worked explanation





Butanoic acid predicts broad acid O–H, so its absence challenges B. Missing spectral coverage, weak signal or obscuration would weaken absence evidence. Ester A fits this functional-group comparison but still needs other evidence.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
6. Compare alcohol and carbonyl evidence
A teaching trace has broad O–H near 3300 cm⁻¹ and no evident C=O region band. Compare ethanol and ethanal as candidates, assuming adequate coverage and sensitivity.






Hint





Ethanol contains OH; ethanal contains C=O but no OH.









Worked explanation





The trace supports ethanol over ethanal for this pair. It does not uniquely prove ethanol against all possible alcohols; the carbon skeleton still requires further constraints.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
7. Avoid a unique-peak claim
A student assigns a whole molecule solely because its IR has a band near 1740 cm⁻¹. Explain why this is too strong and name two independent kinds of additional information used here.






Hint





Functional-group regions occur in many related molecules.









Worked explanation





A carbonyl-region band constrains a functional group rather than uniquely specifying connectivity. Molecular formula and proton/carbon NMR supply independent information about composition and atom environments.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
8. Interpret a quartet and integral
A simulated signal at 4.12 ppm is a quartet integrating to 2H. Under the supplied simple first-order n +1 model, give the number of neighbouring equivalent H and a plausible fragment.






Hint





Line count and integral describe different things.









Worked explanation





Four lines imply three neighbouring equivalent H. The 2H integral supports CH₂ beside CH₃; a downfield O–CH₂–CH₃ environment is consistent with the shift. That fragment still needs to fit the whole formula.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
9. Interpret a triplet and integral
A simulated signal at 1.25 ppm is a triplet integrating to 3H. Under the same simple model, state adjacent-H count and how it can pair with a 2H quartet.






Hint





A triplet has n +1=3, so n=2.









Worked explanation





A CH₃ next to CH₂ can give three lines and 3H integration. Paired with a 2H quartet, it supports an ethyl fragment. The triplet alone does not say whether the remote atom is O, C or another group.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
10. Explain a singlet structurally
For CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, explain why the acetyl CH₃ can be a 3H singlet near 2 ppm while the ethyl CH₃ is a triplet. Ignore small long-range couplings.






Hint





Identify the atom directly adjacent to each methyl.









Worked explanation





Acetyl CH₃ is adjacent to carbonyl carbon with no attached H, so no ordinary vicinal splitting is expected. Ethyl CH₃ is adjacent to CH₂ with two H, giving a triplet in this simple model.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
11. Normalise integrals
A spectrum reports integral areas 6, 6 and 4 for the three signal groups of a candidate with eight H. Normalise the ratio and explain why quartet line count is not a hydrogen count.






Hint





Divide by a common factor and compare the total.









Worked explanation





The ratio reduces to 3:3:2, totalling eight H. Splitting distributes a signal’s area across lines; a quartet can represent two equivalent H. Its four lines do not mean four H.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 12. Avoid using peak heights as areas
text:
12. Avoid using peak heights as areas
One line of a singlet is twice as tall as one line of a triplet. Can you infer relative H counts? State what quantitative information is required.






Hint





A multiplet spreads total area over several lines.









Worked explanation





No. Use integrated area over the full signal group, with a consistent integration scale. Individual line heights are not proton counts, especially when signal shapes or widths differ.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 13. Assign all proton environments in U1
text:
13. Assign all proton environments in U1
U1 is C₄H₈O₂ with 1.25 ppm triplet 3H, 2.05 ppm singlet 3H and 4.12 ppm quartet 2H. Assign every group to CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, explicitly connecting multiplicity and integral.






Hint





Start with the linked CH₂–CH₃ pair, then place the remaining methyl.









Worked explanation





The terminal ethyl CH₃ is 1.25 t 3H; O–CH₂ is 4.12 q 2H. The acetyl CH₃ is 2.05 s 3H, with no H on adjacent carbonyl carbon. The groups account for all eight H and the ester connectivity.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
14. Assign four carbon environments
A simulated decoupled ¹³C spectrum for CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ gives 14,21,60 and 171 ppm. Assign them and state why line height is not normally a quantitative carbon count.






Hint





Separate carbonyl, O-bound methylene and the two methyl environments.









Worked explanation





171 is ester C=O, 60 is O–CH₂, 14 terminal ethyl CH₃ and 21 acetyl CH₃. Routine ¹³C intensities depend on measurement/relaxation effects, so do not count atoms from heights.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
15. Interpret signal count with symmetry
A candidate has six total carbons but only four ¹³C environments. Is that automatically impossible? Explain using the distinction between atoms and equivalent environments.






Hint





Equivalent carbons can share a resonance.









Worked explanation





No. Symmetry or equivalence can make several carbon atoms share one signal. Four environments do not always mean four total carbons. The formula, structure and measurement conditions determine whether that equivalence is plausible.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: 16. Reject butanoic acid with two clues
text:
16. Reject butanoic acid with two clues
Use U1’s complete simulated IR (C=O, no broad OH) and proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. State two observations conflicting with CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, rather than citing the sample name.






Hint





An acid lacks O–CH₂ and predicts acid OH.









Worked explanation





The acid predicts broad carboxylic O–H and no O–CH₂ quartet. It also lacks the isolated acetyl methyl singlet arrangement. A terminal methyl triplet could fit both structures, so that feature alone does not reject the acid.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
17. Reject a hydroxyketone alternative
Candidate CH₃C(=O)CH(OH)CH₃ also has C₄H₈O₂. Compare its predicted OH-bearing proton count and adjacent methyl multiplicity with U1’s 4.12 q 2H and 1.25 t 3H.






Hint





The oxygen-bearing carbon is CH, not CH₂.









Worked explanation





The hydroxyketone has a one-H OH-bearing CH and a methyl adjacent to one H, commonly giving a doublet. It does not give the supplied two-H O–CH₂ quartet/three-H ethyl triplet pattern. Its OH adds another predicted difference.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
18. Distinguish support from proof
A supplied candidate fits formula, IR and simple NMR while two alternatives fail. Write an appropriately restrained identity conclusion and one remaining limitation.






Hint





Specify the compared candidates and the nature of the observations.









Worked explanation





The candidate best fits the supplied evidence among the tested structures. A finite comparison does not exclude every imaginable alternative, and real confidence depends on spectrum quality, assignment completeness and sample context.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
19. Check spectral provenance
An IR file is numerically generated for teaching and named ethyl_ethanoate.csv. Which claims can the plot support, and which claims about an actual laboratory isolate would be unjustified?






Hint





Separate a model demonstration from measured sample evidence.









Worked explanation





It can demonstrate a labelled functional-group pattern and plotting workflow. It cannot establish that a real isolate was measured, identified or pure. The filename records the intended teaching label, not independent experimental identity proof.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
20. Plan an independent next check
An unknown’s carbonyl IR fits both an ester and another carbonyl candidate. You can request either a molecular formula or repeat the same isolated peak label. Which is more informative here, and why?






Hint





Seek an observation that tests a different prediction.









Worked explanation





The formula adds an independent composition/unsaturation constraint. Repeating the same peak label without new data adds little. A full proton NMR could likewise test distinct connectivity predictions; choose evidence that discriminates the remaining alternatives.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
section: R task: present an IR comparison
text:
R task: present an IR comparison
Open the student project. The supplied data/ir.csv contains sample_id, wavenumber_cm1 and transmittance_percent. Plot the simulated ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid traces. Keep their sample labels so the plotted evidence can be traced back to the data.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ir <- read_csv("data/ir.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
comparison <- ir |>
  filter(sample_id %in% c("ethyl_ethanoate", "ethanoic_acid"))
ggplot(comparison,
       aes(wavenumber_cm1, transmittance_percent, colour = sample_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Wavenumber (cm−1)", y = "Transmittance (%)",
       colour = "Simulated sample") +
  theme_minimal()
Add a report caption explaining that these are simulated traces, that dips indicate absorption in a transmittance plot, and which region distinguishes the candidates. Use a descending wavenumber axis; it is conventional here and does not reverse the underlying physics. Check that transmittance values lie between 0 and 100. Do not fit a model or ask R to assign the unknown for you.






Interpretation check





The acid trace includes a very broad O–H region, while the ester trace lacks that broad feature. Both contain carbonyl absorption. The chemical comparison uses the functional groups expected from the candidate structures; the plot is a way to inspect and communicate the supplied observations. An exact carbonyl position is not a unique molecular fingerprint.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Leave with
A fully annotated structure, a rejected alternative, and a knitted Rmd section with a labelled IR comparison. Reading: Solomons chapters 2 and 9; see the reading guide.

title: Day 21: Exercises — Structure from spectra
text:
Explore
Question: what changes when a candidate must explain a complete set of observations rather than only its molecular formula?
Allow 10 minutes: predict for 2, inspect competing candidates for 5, then write an assignment and limitation for 3. All traces are fixed simulated teaching data, not measured sample spectra.

Enable JavaScript to compare a drawn candidate against supplied formula, IR and NMR clues.




Predict
Unknown U1 is C₄H₈O₂. Could both an ester and a carboxylic acid fit the formula? Which observation would make a stronger comparison than the formula alone?
For simple first-order proton NMR here, \(n\) equivalent neighbouring H give \(n+1\) lines. Integration counts relative H area; a quartet’s four lines do not mean four H. In an IR transmittance trace, absorption appears as a dip.


Explore

Compare ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid using Formula only.
Add the complete IR and identify which functional-group prediction changes.
Use all clues. Assign the 2H quartet, 3H triplet and remaining 3H singlet in U1 rather than merely selecting the green outcome.
Try Second unknown and test ethanol against dimethyl ether. Then reset.



Supplied data and worked check
U1 has carbonyl absorption without a broad O–H feature and proton signals 1.25 ppm triplet, 3H; 2.05 ppm singlet, 3H; 4.12 ppm quartet, 2H. Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, accounts for an ethyl pair and an acetyl methyl singlet. Butanoic acid predicts acid O–H and lacks the O–CH₂/acetyl pattern.
U2 is C₂H₆O, with broad O–H, no carbonyl, and 1.18 ppm triplet, 3H; 3.65 ppm quartet, 2H; an exchangeable broad OH signal, 1H in this illustrative model. Ethanol fits; dimethyl ether has the same formula but no OH and would not give that proton pattern.


Model limits
Peak positions, shapes and exchange depend on conditions. The listed patterns are introductory first-order examples, not a general spectral solver. Green means the candidate fits the selected supplied evidence, not that every possible alternative is excluded or the sample is pure. A filename is not identity evidence. See the local spectroscopy exercises.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
About this lecture
Old fish smells because bacteria turn a nitrogen compound into trimethylamine, a volatile amine. Squeeze lemon on it and the smell fades: citric acid hands a proton to the nitrogen, and the resulting ammonium salt can’t evaporate. That’s one lone pair taking one proton.
Today we follow the nitrogen lone pair:

Amines: classify them, and draw their protonation with curved arrows
Basicity: compare bases with conjugate-acid pKa values
Amides and aniline: when the pair is shared, the base gets weaker
Aromaticity: what makes benzene, pyridine and pyrrole special
Amino acids: glycine’s charge at different pH

Yesterday’s acyl chemistry made amides; today explains why their nitrogen hardly behaves like an amine.

Open with the fish. Fresh fish contains trimethylamine N-oxide, which bacteria reduce to trimethylamine as the fish ages; that’s the “fishy” smell. Lemon juice or vinegar protonates it to trimethylammonium, an ion that stays in the water instead of reaching your nose. The same trick explains why many drugs are sold as hydrochloride salts: the protonated amine is a stable, water-soluble solid. The thread through the whole lecture is one question: where is the nitrogen lone pair, and is it free to grab a proton? Amines, amides, aniline, pyridine and pyrrole are all answers to that one question.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Amines: count the carbons on nitrogen
text:
Amines: count the carbons on nitrogen

Primary, secondary and tertiary aminesA neutral amine N has three bonds and one lone pair, just like ammonia. Primary, secondary and tertiary count the carbons bonded to N, not the carbons in the molecule.

Try it: classify CH₃NHCH₂CH₃.

Secondary. Two carbon groups (methyl and ethyl) sit on N, plus one N–H. The total of three carbons doesn’t matter.



Amines are ammonia with carbon groups in place of hydrogens. Stress that the classification looks only at nitrogen’s neighbours. Students who learned “primary, secondary, tertiary” for alcohols on Day 13 often transfer the alcohol rule, which counts carbons on the carbinol carbon, not on oxygen. Here we count directly on N. Point at the lone pair in each drawing: all three are neutral, all three have one pair, and that pair is what makes them bases. Trimethylamine, on the right, is our fish molecule.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Protonation: the lone pair makes the new N–H bond
text:
Protonation: the lone pair makes the new N–H bond

Methylamine takes a proton from hydroniumTwo arrows: N pair → H, and H–O bond → O. Nitrogen goes from 3 bonds + 1 pair (neutral) to 4 bonds, no pair, +1. Net charge is +1 on both sides.

Try it: draw the reverse, CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻. What forms?

CH₃NH₂ + H₂O. Hydroxide’s pair takes the H, and the N–H bond pair goes back to N as its lone pair. Net charge is zero on both sides.



This is the Day 3 acid-base arrow pattern with nitrogen as the base. Insist on both arrows: one starts at the lone pair and ends at the H, the other starts at the H–O bond and ends on oxygen. A common error is drawing the arrow from H+ to nitrogen, which shows the proton carrying electrons; the arrow always follows the electrons. Also note that N doesn’t “lose an electron” to become positive. It shares its pair in a new bond, so it now owns one electron fewer by formal-charge bookkeeping. Ask: what happened to the positive charge of hydronium? It moved to nitrogen.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Charge and classification are separate questions
text:
Charge and classification are separate questions

Tertiary amine, its conjugate acid and a quaternary ammonium ionProtonating a tertiary amine gives a tertiary ammonium ion, not a quaternary one: it still has three carbons and now one N–H. Quaternary means four carbons on N. With no N–H to lose, it stays +1 at any pH.

Read across the three: carbons on N, N–H count, charge. 3/0/0, 3/1/+1, 4/0/+1. The middle one is what lemon juice makes from trimethylamine. Students often call it quaternary because N now has four bonds. Ask them what defines “quaternary”: four carbon groups. The practical difference matters: (CH3)3NH+ can give its proton back to a base and become volatile again, but (CH3)4N+ can’t, which is why quaternary ammonium ions show up in disinfectants and fabric softeners as permanently charged species.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Basicity: read the pKa of the conjugate acid
text:
Basicity: read the pKa of the conjugate acid

Conjugate-acid pKa values of five nitrogen basesWe rank bases by the pKa of BH⁺. A higher pKa means BH⁺ holds its proton tightly, so B is the stronger base. Ethylamine beats aniline by about six pKa units.

The single most important convention of the lecture: amine basicity is reported as the pKa of the protonated form. Students meet “the pKa of ethylamine” in sloppy sources and look up 35-ish, which is the N–H acidity of the neutral amine, a completely different equilibrium. Always ask “pKa of what?”. The chart sets up the rest of the lecture: alkyl amines and ammonia sit around 9–11, and the two green bars, pyridine and aniline, are about a hundred thousand times weaker as bases. By the end of today each bar should have a structural explanation.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Which way does a proton transfer go?
text:
Which way does a proton transfer go?

Anilinium gives its proton to ethylamineK \approx 10^{\,\text{pKa(product acid)} \;-\; \text{pKa(reactant acid)}}
The equilibrium favours the side with the weaker acid (higher pKa).

Try it: estimate K for anilinium + NH₃ ⇌ aniline + NH₄⁺ (pKa 4.6 and 9.2).

K ≈ 10^(9.2 − 4.6) = 10^4.6 ≈ 4 × 10⁴. Ammonia takes the proton, so the products win.



Walk through the formula with the figure: the product acid is ethylammonium, 10.7; the reactant acid is anilinium, 4.6; the exponent is 6.1, so K is about a million. Remind students that this works only when both pKa values come from the same solvent and conventions, here water. The rule in words: protons flow downhill to the stronger base, ending up on the weaker acid. This is the same tool students used on Day 3 for O–H acids; nitrogen changes nothing about the arithmetic.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Basicity is about equilibrium, not speed
text:
Basicity is about equilibrium, not speed







a pKa comparison tells you…
it doesn’t tell you…




which side of a proton transfer is favoured
how fast the proton transfer happens


which base holds a proton more tightly
which N attacks a carbon electrophile fastest


roughly how much of each form at a given pH
effects of solvent, sterics or the leaving group



A strong base is often a good nucleophile, but nucleophilicity is a rate, and pKa alone can’t rank rates.

Students tend to collapse “basic” and “nucleophilic” into one word. Basicity is thermodynamic: where the proton ends up at equilibrium. Nucleophilicity is kinetic: how fast a lone pair attacks carbon. They often trend together for similar nitrogens, which is why the shortcut is tempting, but a bulky tertiary amine can be a good base and a poor nucleophile because it can’t reach a crowded carbon. Connect back to substitution on Day 11, where solvent and sterics changed SN2 rates. If a question asks for a rate, pKa is at most one piece of evidence.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Amides: the pair is shared with C=O
text:
Amides: the pair is shared with C=O

The amide nitrogen pair is shared with the carbonylThe N pair delocalises into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character. Protonating N would cost that stabilisation, so amides are not basic like amines.

Try it: in CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺, check each charge. Is this a second molecule in equilibrium with ethanamide?

N has four bonds and no pair, so +1; O has one bond and three pairs, so −1; net 0. No: it’s a resonance contributor of the same molecule, with the same atoms in the same places.



This ties straight back to yesterday: amides are the least reactive acyl derivatives for exactly this reason, the nitrogen pair is feeding the carbonyl. Draw the two arrows slowly: the lone pair becomes the C=N pi bond, and the C=O pi bond becomes an oxygen lone pair. The double-headed resonance arrow is not an equilibrium arrow; nothing moves except our bookkeeping of electrons. The real molecule is a blend, and the evidence is that the amide C–N bond is shorter than a normal C–N single bond and doesn’t rotate freely, which is why peptide backbones are flat.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Two nitrogens, two behaviours

Two kinds of nitrogen in one moleculeBefore predicting protonation, look at what each N is bonded to. Is the next atom a carbonyl carbon? Here only the NH₂ end is a real amine, so acid protonates that nitrogen.

This is a dipeptide-like fragment: glycine’s amine end (drawn on the right) and a methyl amide (on the left). Both nitrogens are “an N with H on it”, and students who look only at the letter N will treat them identically. Make the habit explicit: follow each nitrogen’s bonds one atom out. The amide NH stays neutral in water at any ordinary pH, while the amine end is protonated near pH 7. That’s why the N-terminus of a protein is charged and the backbone NH groups are not.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Aniline: a ring can share the pair too
text:
Aniline: a ring can share the pair too

Aniline and benzylamineIn aniline the N sits directly on the ring, so its pair overlaps the ring’s π system and is less available. In benzylamine an sp³ CH₂ breaks that link, and the basicity is back near an ordinary amine.

Same atoms in the ring, same NH2 group, five pKa units apart, which is a factor of about a hundred thousand in basicity. The only difference is whether the nitrogen is attached directly to the pi system. The CH2 has no p orbital, so it’s an insulator. Be honest that other factors (solvation, inductive effects) also play a part; the structural argument explains the big gap, not every decimal. This is the same logic as the amide: a neighbouring pi system that can accept the pair makes a weaker base.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
What makes a ring aromatic

Benzene has six pi electronsAromatic rings are unusually stable: benzene resists the addition reactions that alkenes undergo easily. Check structure first, then count. We draw benzene with alternating double bonds, but the real π electrons are spread evenly around the ring.

Work through the checklist in order. It’s a ring; every carbon is sp2, so each has a p orbital; it’s flat, so the p orbitals overlap continuously all the way round; and 2+2+2 = 6, which fits 4n+2 with n = 1. The Kekulé drawing is one resonance contributor; all six C–C bonds are actually the same length. Mention the payoff from Day 12: bromine adds across cyclohexene instantly but leaves benzene alone without a catalyst. And a preview for spectroscopy next week: aromatic H atoms show up around 7 ppm in proton NMR, a fingerprint you’ll use constantly.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: A ring alone is not enough
text:
A ring alone is not enough

Aromatic, nonaromatic and antiaromatic ringsNonaromatic: the loop of p orbitals is broken or absent. Antiaromatic: a complete loop with 4n π electrons, which is destabilising.

Try it: cyclohexane fails the aromatic test. Is it antiaromatic?

No, it’s nonaromatic. It has no π system at all. Antiaromatic needs a closed loop of p orbitals with the wrong count.



The diene in the middle is the useful trap: it has two double bonds in a ring, but the two CH2 carbons are sp3 with no p orbital, so the loop is broken. Students see “ring plus double bonds” and say aromatic. Cyclobutadiene is the antiaromatic example: closed loop, 4 pi electrons, so unstable that it only exists at very low temperature. Keep antiaromaticity light today; the important distinction for the exam is that “not aromatic” usually means nonaromatic, not antiaromatic.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Pyridine: an extra pair, outside the ring
text:
Pyridine: an extra pair, outside the ring

Pyridine keeps its lone pair outside the aromatic sextetPyridine’s N gives one electron to the π system, through its double bond. Its lone pair points out of the ring, in the plane. Protonating that pair leaves the sextet intact, so pyridine is a real base (pKa 5.2).

Try it: a student counts pyridine’s lone pair in the π system. What total would they get, and why is that a red flag?

Eight, which is 4n, not 4n + 2. The pair sits in an sp² orbital at right angles to the p orbitals, so it never joins the ring count.



Pyridine looks like benzene with one CH replaced by N, and that’s exactly the right picture. The three double bonds give 6 pi electrons. The nitrogen still has a lone pair, but it lives in the plane of the ring, pointing outward like a C–H bond would. Protonation uses that pair, so the aromatic system is untouched and pyridinium is still aromatic. Why is pyridine weaker than an alkyl amine (5.2 vs about 10.7)? The pair is in an sp2 orbital, with more s character, held closer to N. Mention that pyridine is a common lab base, used to mop up HCl in acylations like yesterday’s.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Pyrrole: the pair is part of the sextet
text:
Pyrrole: the pair is part of the sextet

Pyrrole uses its nitrogen pair in the sextetPyrrole has only two C=C bonds, which supply four π electrons. The N lone pair supplies the other two. If N took a proton, that pair would leave the ring and the aromaticity would be lost.

Contrast with pyridine as sharply as you can. Both rings contain one nitrogen; in pyridine the pair is spare, in pyrrole it’s load-bearing. Count with the class: 2 + 2 from the double bonds, plus 2 from nitrogen, gives 6. Pyrrole’s conjugate acid has a pKa around −4, and when it is forced to protonate it does so on carbon, not nitrogen. Pyrrole rings appear in haem and chlorophyll, where the nitrogens bind metal ions rather than protons.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Imidazole: one nitrogen of each kind
text:
Imidazole: one nitrogen of each kind

Imidazole has one pyridine-like and one pyrrole-like nitrogenImidazole is the side chain of histidine. Its pKa near 7 makes it the proton shuttle in many enzyme active sites.

Try it: which nitrogen takes the proton, and why?

The pyridine-like N (top left). Its pair is outside the sextet; the NH’s pair is part of the six π electrons.



This is the worked example that combines the two previous slides. Count the pi electrons: two double bonds give 4, the NH nitrogen gives its pair, 2 more: 6, aromatic. The other nitrogen is pyridine-like: it contributes one electron through its double bond and keeps a spare pair in the plane. In imidazolium the two N–H nitrogens become equivalent by resonance, which is part of why it’s a better base than pyridine. Its pKa sits close to physiological pH, so histidine can be protonated or not with only a small pH change, ideal for passing protons around in enzymes.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Glycine: two sites, three charge states
text:
Glycine: two sites, three charge states

Glycine at low, middle and high pHTreat each site separately: below its pKa a site is mostly protonated, above it mostly deprotonated. Between 2.3 and 9.6 glycine is a zwitterion: net zero, but with +1 on N and −1 on O.

Try it: draw what happens when the pH 6 form meets OH⁻.

H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻ + OH⁻ → H₂NCH₂COO⁻ + H₂O. The ammonium loses its proton; net charge is −1 on both sides.



We met the glycine zwitterion on Day 1 as a formal-charge exercise; now we can explain when it exists. Go left to right along the pH axis. At pH 1, below both pKa values, both sites hold their protons: +1. Pass 2.3 and the carboxylic acid loses its H first: net 0. Pass 9.6 and the ammonium gives its proton up: −1. Emphasise that “net zero” doesn’t mean “uncharged”. The zwitterion has two full formal charges, which is why amino acids are high-melting solids that dissolve in water and not in hexane.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: How much is protonated? Use the ratio
text:
How much is protonated? Use the ratio

Fraction of an amine protonated, pKa 10At pH 9, [B]/[BH⁺] = 10⁻¹ = 0.1, so the protonated fraction is 1/(1 + 0.1) ≈ 0.91. Each pH unit changes the ratio tenfold.

Try it: at pH = pKa, half is BH⁺. Does every molecule carry a charge of +½?

No. Each molecule is either B or BH⁺; half the population is in each form. Charges on single molecules come in whole units.



The equation is Henderson–Hasselbalch rearranged: ratio = 10 to the (pH − pKa). Watch for the common slip of reporting the ratio as the fraction; 0.1 is the ratio of B to BH+, and the fraction protonated is 1/(1 + 0.1). Exercises 17 and 18 do exactly this calculation at pH 9, 10 and 11. The half-charge misconception is worth taking seriously, because it reappears in biochemistry when people talk about a residue being “half protonated”.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




counting all the carbons to classify an amine
count carbons on N


calling (CH₃)₃NH⁺ quaternary
quaternary means four carbons on N


quoting the amine’s N–H pKa for basicity
use the pKa of BH⁺


ranking reaction rates from pKa
pKa compares equilibria


treating an amide N like an amine N
check for a C=O next to N


counting pyridine’s lone pair in the sextet
its pair is in the plane, outside the π system


“a ring, so aromatic”
check the unbroken p-orbital loop first


“net zero, so no charges”
a zwitterion has +1 and −1




Read each mistake aloud and ask for the reason before revealing the fix. The amide and pyridine rows are the ones that cost the most marks. Point out that almost every row comes down to the same question as the title of the lecture: where is the nitrogen pair, and is it free?

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Summary







concept
key fact




amine N
3 bonds + 1 pair; protonated: 4 bonds, +1


classification
count carbons on N


base strength
higher pKa of BH⁺ = stronger base


proton transfer
K ≈ 10^(pKa product acid − pKa reactant acid)


amide, aniline

aromatic

pyridine vs pyrrole
