Next: reading structures from IR and NMR spectra (Day 21). Practice: exercises · self-check

Close with the fish: trimethylamine’s free pair grabs a proton from citric acid, and the ammonium salt stays in the water. Every row of this table is a variation on that one event. Tomorrow and Day 20 are consolidation days, and Day 20 is specifically about nitrogen, resonance and charge, so the exercises from today feed straight into it. Spectroscopy on Day 21 will bring back aromatic rings, which give characteristic signals near 7 ppm in proton NMR.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
1. What is the attacked atom?
In ethyl ethanoate reacting with hydroxide, identify the initial attacked atom and the electron pair that moves at the same time.






Check your answer





The nucleophile attacks acyl carbon. The C=O pi pair moves onto carbonyl oxygen. Directly attaching OH while retaining every carbonyl bond would give five bonds at carbon.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
2. What is the intermediate charge?
Write the intermediate from OH⁻ addition to CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and locate its negative charge.






Check your answer





CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₂CH₃), net −1. Incoming hydroxide becomes a neutral OH substituent; original carbonyl O now carries the charge.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 3. What is the final acid/base pair?
text:
3. What is the final acid/base pair?
After collapse in basic ester hydrolysis, can carboxylic acid and ethoxide be treated as the final predominant products?






Check your answer





No. Ethoxide deprotonates the much stronger acid to give carboxylate and ethanol. Acid work-up can later protonate the carboxylate.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
text:
4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
Predict the initial predominant reaction between ethanoic acid and methylamine in water.






Check your answer





Proton transfer gives ethanoate and methylammonium. Suitable activation or conditions are needed to form an amide; simply losing OH⁻ from the unactivated acid is not an adequate mechanism.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
text:
5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
Connect amide resonance to its geometry without treating resonance contributors as separate molecules.






Check your answer





Nitrogen pair donation into the carbonyl gives partial C–N double-bond character. The charge-separated contributor has O− and N+; both contributors describe one delocalised amide.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
text:
6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
Why is a tetrahedral aldehyde intermediate not normally converted to an acyl-substitution product by ejecting its carbon-bound hydrogen?






Check your answer





That would require loss of hydride, a very poor leaving group in this setting. Aldehydes normally undergo carbonyl addition rather than this acyl-substitution analogy.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text: Compare acids, esters and amides by drawing their addition and leaving-group steps. Work through 1–10 for core work, 11–16 for transfer and 17–20 for deeper checks. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, taking longer for complete mechanisms. Attempt each problem before using its hint, then compare your revised drawing with the worked explanation.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Working refresher
An acyl carbon is carbonyl carbon in R–C(=O)–Y. An ester has Y=OR′ and an amide has Y=NR′R″. A nucleophile donates a pair to carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi pair moves to O, giving a four-single-bond tetrahedral species. A viable leaving-group step can then restore C=O. Draw proton transfers with explicit donors and acceptors. Formal-charge checks used here: ordinary O with two bonds is neutral, one bond/three pairs is −1, and three bond orders is +1. For compatible pKa estimates, proton-transfer K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). A worked mechanism is shown in the lecture; every problem below supplies its own necessary species and constants.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
1. Identify four oxygen-containing families
Draw CH₃COOH, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃CONH₂ and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ with explicit C=O bonds. Classify each, circle each acyl carbon and explain which one lacks an acyl group.






Hint





An acyl group contains a carbonyl carbon attached to the substituent being compared.









Worked explanation





The structures are acid, ester, amide and ether. The first three share CH₃C(=O)–Y; the ether has no C=O and therefore no acyl carbon. Oxygen alone does not establish an ester.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
2. Read a condensed formula carefully
Expand HCOOCH₃ and CH₃OCH₃. Count the bonds to the carbon next to the first oxygen. Which compound can undergo the elementary carbonyl-addition pattern?






Hint





In HCOOCH₃ the first carbon is H–C(=O)–, not H–C–O–O.









Worked explanation





HCOOCH₃ is methyl methanoate, H–C(=O)–O–CH₃, an ester. CH₃OCH₃ is an ether. Only the ester contains the required carbonyl carbon for that addition pattern.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
3. Write the two addition arrows
For OH⁻ attacking CH₃C(=O)OCH₃, draw the hydroxide lone pair and both curved arrows. Show a valid intermediate with all charges and count carbon bond orders.






Hint





As the new C–O bond forms, the C=O pi pair must move.









Worked explanation





Draw OH pair→acyl C and C=O π→carbonyl O. The intermediate is CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃), with four single bonds at C and net −1. Incoming O is neutral OH; original carbonyl O is O⁻.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
4. Track three oxygen identities
Label ester carbonyl O as A, ester single-bond O as B and incoming hydroxide O as C. Draw the tetrahedral intermediate and identify which oxygen still bears a methyl group.






Hint





Carbon–oxygen bonds to substituents do not disappear during the addition step.









Worked explanation





The intermediate is CH₃C(O-A⁻)(O-CH₃-B)(OH-C). B remains attached to methyl. A bears the negative charge and C retains its original H. A label follows an atom, not a position on the page.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
5. Complete an elimination step
Starting from CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃), draw carbonyl re-formation and methoxide departure. Give the immediate acid and base products and their total charge.






Hint





One pair moves from O⁻ into C–O π; another moves from the C–OCH₃ bond to methoxy O.









Worked explanation





The immediate pair is CH₃COOH + CH₃O⁻. Total charge remains −1. Carbonyl is restored, and methyl stays bonded to its departing oxygen; the group is methoxide, not a free methyl carbanion.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
6. Add the missing acid–base step
After collapse gives CH₃COOH and CH₃O⁻, use approximate compatible aqueous pKa values 4.8 for CH₃COOH and 15.5 for CH₃OH. Draw proton transfer, state the favoured pair and estimate K = 10^(product-acid pKa − reactant-acid pKa).






Hint





The weaker acid has the larger pKa.









Worked explanation





Methoxide takes the acid proton to give CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃OH. K≈10^10.7≈5×10¹⁰ toward that pair. Stopping at neutral acid plus alkoxide misses a strongly favoured final proton transfer.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
7. Balance net base-promoted hydrolysis
Write the net equation for CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ with OH⁻. Include the protonation state present in a basic mixture and audit atoms and total charge.






Hint





Cancel intermediates, not final stoichiometric reagents.









Worked explanation





CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃CH₂OH. Both sides have C₄H₉O₃ and net −1. Hydroxide is consumed overall, unlike the regenerated OH⁻ in simple carbonyl hydration.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
8. Separate hydrolysis from acid work-up
The basic reaction mixture contains sodium ethanoate. Write its reacting anion with hydronium and give products. Does work-up form a new carbon skeleton?






Hint





A spectator sodium ion need not enter the proton-transfer step.









Worked explanation





CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. The acid carbon skeleton is retained. Work-up changes protonation state; it is not an unexplained deletion of the negative charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
9. Reject five-bonded carbon
A student draws CH₃C(=O)(OH)OCH₃ as the intermediate after OH⁻ attack. Count bond orders at carbon and repair the structure.






Hint





A carbonyl double bond contributes two to the bond-order count.









Worked explanation





That carbon has C–CH₃, C=O, C–OH and C–OCH₃: total five bond orders. Replace C=O with C–O⁻ to give CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃). The paired electron movement both restores carbon valence and locates charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
10. Compare ester and aldehyde
Compare OH⁻ addition to CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃. Draw both tetrahedral species and explain why an ordinary aldehyde does not normally undergo substitution by expelling H⁻.






Hint





Compare the substituent in the potential leaving-group position.









Worked explanation





The species are CH₃CH(OH)O⁻ and CH₃C(OH)(O⁻)(OCH₃). Methoxy can leave through an appropriate pathway; hydride is an extremely poor leaving group in these simple reactions. Similar first addition steps do not force the same later chemistry.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
11. Start acid-catalysed esterification
Use ethanoic acid, ethanol and hydronium. Draw carbonyl-oxygen protonation, then neutral ethanol attack with movement of the pi pair. Give the charge on each oxygen of CH₃C(OH)(OH)(OHEt).






Hint





The incoming ethanol oxygen gains a third bond; the protonated original carbonyl oxygen loses its pi bond.









Worked explanation





Protonation gives CH₃C(=OH⁺)OH plus water. Ethanol attack gives CH₃C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt). Original carbonyl O is now neutral OH, original acid OH is neutral and incoming oxygen is +1. Total charge is +1.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
12. Make the incoming oxygen neutral
For CH₃C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt), draw water removing the extra incoming-oxygen proton. Count bonds at that O after transfer and identify the catalyst-containing species produced.






Hint





The O–H bonding pair stays on the oxygen losing H⁺.









Worked explanation





Water pair→incoming-oxygen H; O–H pair→incoming O. Products include CH₃C(OH)(OH)(OEt) and H₃O⁺. Incoming O has two bonds and is neutral. Explicit proton donors/acceptors preserve both atoms and charge.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
section: 13. Create and remove a leaving group
text:
13. Create and remove a leaving group
From the neutral tetrahedral species, protonate an OH to OH₂⁺, then draw loss of water with carbonyl re-formation. Why is drawing direct OH⁻ loss inappropriate for this representative acidic pathway?






Hint





Protonation changes the identity and stability of the departing group.









Worked explanation





An OH₂⁺ substituent can depart as neutral H₂O while the other OH oxygen reforms C=O, initially giving a protonated ester. Deprotonation restores neutral ester and acid catalyst. Direct OH⁻ loss skips the activation central to this acid pathway.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
14. Distinguish catalyst from equilibrium change
For CH₃COOH + EtOH ⇌ CH₃COOEt + H₂O, predict the effect of removing water and separately the effect of adding an acid catalyst at fixed temperature.






Hint





One action changes composition; the other changes access to the reaction pathway.









Worked explanation





Removing water can shift the composition toward ester. A catalyst accelerates the forward and reverse approach without changing K for the same net reaction under fixed conditions. Faster equilibration does not imply a different equilibrium constant.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
section: 15. Check an oxygen label in the product
text:
15. Check an oxygen label in the product
In the standard esterification pathway, use ethanol labelled at oxygen as Et–O*H. Draw the labelled ester and say which bond links the labelled O to the acid-derived fragment.






Hint





The alcohol oxygen forms the new bond to acyl carbon.









Worked explanation





The ester is CH₃C(=O)OEt. O is the single-bond ester oxygen, directly attached to acyl carbon and ethyl. This follows the specified mechanism; do not track atoms solely by whether they are drawn above or beside carbon.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
16. Draw amide resonance correctly
Draw neutral CH₃CONH₂ and its C=N charge-separated contributor. Give all O/N charges, total charge and the correct connecting arrow type.






Hint





When N donates into C–N, the C=O pi pair moves onto O.









Worked explanation





CH₃C(=O)NH₂ ↔︎ CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. Total charge stays zero. Use a resonance double-headed arrow, not equilibrium arrows: these describe one delocalised amide with fixed nuclei.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
17. Explain restricted amide rotation
Compare CH₃CH₂NH₂ with CH₃CONH₂. Explain why their C–N bonds differ in rotational freedom and why their N basicities should not be assumed equal.






Hint





Connect the real bond to its resonance contributors rather than declaring the C–N bond literally always double.









Worked explanation





Amide donation gives partial C–N double-bond character, restricting rotation and delocalising the N pair into C=O. A simple alkylamine lacks that same neighbouring carbonyl conjugation. The different electron availability changes protonation behaviour.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
18. Predict acid plus amine
For CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ in water, use pKa 4.8 for the acid and 10.6 for methylammonium. Give the initially favoured acid–base products and explain why this is not already amide synthesis.






Hint





Compare the reactant and product acids.









Worked explanation





CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺ is favoured, with estimated K≈10^5.8. This is proton transfer. Forming CH₃CONHCH₃ would require suitable activation/conditions and a productive acyl-substitution pathway; the salt alone is not an amide.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
19. Read two biological linkages
A lipid fragment is R–C(=O)–O–glycerol and a peptide fragment is R–C(=O)–NH–R′. Identify each linkage, locate the electrophilic carbon and explain why their rates of hydrolysis need not match.






Hint





The carbonyl carbon is common; the substituent and stabilisation differ.









Worked explanation





The first is ester and the second amide. Nucleophilic acyl attack begins at carbonyl carbon. Amide resonance stabilisation, leaving-group behaviour, activation and reaction conditions differ, so a common motif does not imply equal reactivity.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
20. Audit an incomplete mechanism
A proposed ester hydrolysis drawing adds OH⁻, loses the ethoxy group, writes neutral acid as final product in base and omits every charge. List three independent repairs and explain one experimental claim this mechanism alone cannot establish.






Hint





Check valence, proton transfers and the difference between a model and observations.









Worked explanation





Move the C=O pi pair during addition; show O⁻ in the intermediate and ethoxide on collapse; include acid–base transfer giving carboxylate and ethanol in base. The mechanism alone cannot establish isolated yield, purity or the measured rate; those require observations.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 17: Exercises — Acyl chemistry
text:
Explore
Choose electron-pair steps for ester hydrolysis and follow the acid–base trap. Allow 7–10 minutes: predict first, change one input at a time and explain the result.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). For methyl ethanoate plus hydroxide in the supplied basic model, predict the first electron-pair operation. Which group at acyl carbon could leave after a tetrahedral intermediate forms?
Explore (4–5 minutes). Try addition, then inspect the tetrahedral intermediate. Test both plausible collapse directions: forward methoxide departure and reversal with hydroxide departure. Follow the forward route, then choose what happens to the transient acid–methoxide pair. Test a hydride or methyl leaving-group proposal and read why it fails.
Explain (2 minutes). Draw the accepted addition, collapse and acid–base steps. Use the supplied pKa values to explain why stopping with neutral acid plus methoxide misses the base-condition product. What additional operation would be needed to obtain neutral acid after the basic reaction?


Supplied model and its limits
The selected model is basic hydrolysis of CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Addition makes a tetrahedral O⁻ intermediate; collapse can expel methoxide or reverse by expelling hydroxide. Forward collapse gives a transient acid–methoxide pair. Compatible illustrative pKa values are 4.8 for ethanoic acid and 15.5 for methanol, so the proton-transfer equilibrium constant is approximately 10^(15.5−4.8)≈5×10¹⁰ toward carboxylate + methanol. Acid work-up is outside the interactive sequence. No rates, real operating protocol or universal leaving-group ranking is inferred.


Carry the explanation into practice
Return to the local exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
About this lecture
Glucose is drawn in every textbook as a six-carbon chain with an aldehyde at the end. Yet in your blood, well over 99 % of it is a ring, and only a trace is the open-chain aldehyde. The ring forms because the molecule’s own OH adds to its own C=O. That’s the reaction we study today.
Today we learn the one pattern behind it:

Why C=O reacts: a polar, flat carbonyl with an electron-poor carbon
The addition step: nucleophile in, π pair out, tetrahedral product
Base and acid routes: hydrates and hemiacetals, with every proton accounted for
Product classes: hydrate, hemiacetal, acetal, and how water controls the acetal equilibrium
Rings and stereocentres: cyclic hemiacetals, glucose, and new stereocentres

On Day 13 you reduced ketones with NaBH₄. That was already a carbonyl addition; today we see the general pattern.

Start with the glucose puzzle: the open-chain drawing is the one everyone memorises, but it barely exists in water. Ask the room why a molecule would “prefer” to be a ring. Don’t answer yet; tell them the answer is today’s reaction, and that by the end they’ll be able to draw how the ring forms, arrow by arrow. The link back to Day 13 matters: hydride reduction put H on the carbonyl carbon and O⁻ on oxygen before a proton finished the job. Today the nucleophiles are oxygen nucleophiles (water, alcohols), but the electron movement is exactly the same. Today’s tools come back tomorrow (Day 17), when the carbonyl carries a group that can leave.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: The carbonyl is polar and flat
text:
The carbonyl is polar and flat

Ethanal with partial charges and propanone with 120 degree anglesOxygen pulls the C=O electrons towards itself, so the carbonyl carbon is δ+ and attracts nucleophiles. The carbon is trigonal planar, so a nucleophile can approach from either face.

Two separate facts on one slide: polarity explains where nucleophiles attack, flatness explains how (from above or below the plane), which matters later for stereocentres. Probe the classic confusion: δ+ is not a formal charge. In the ordinary Lewis structure of ethanal every atom has formal charge zero. If someone writes C⁺ on a neutral aldehyde, ask them to count bonds: the carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs, so it’s neutral. Partial charge describes uneven electron sharing; formal charge is bookkeeping from the Lewis structure. Day 1’s formal charge rules still apply.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: One pattern: nucleophile in, π pair out
text:
One pattern: nucleophile in, π pair out

General nucleophilic addition with two curved arrowsArrow 1: a lone pair on the nucleophile forms the new C–Nu bond. Arrow 2: the π pair moves onto oxygen, which becomes O⁻. Carbon goes from planar to tetrahedral.

Try it: why can’t you draw only the first arrow and keep the C=O?

Carbon would have five bonds. The π bond must open as the new σ bond forms, so carbon stays at four.



This is the slide to come back to all day: every mechanism today is this pattern plus proton transfers. Insist on two arrows that start at electrons: the first from a lone pair (not from the atom letter or the minus sign), the second from the middle of the C=O double bond and ending on oxygen. Many students draw the first arrow and forget the second, producing a five-bonded carbon; the try-it targets exactly that. Mention the Day 1 “valence check” habit here.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Hydroxide adds to ethanal

Hydroxide oxygen B attacks ethanal; carbonyl oxygen A becomes the alkoxideLabel the oxygens so you can follow them: A was the carbonyl O, B came in with hydroxide. Total charge stays −1 on both sides.

Try it: after this step, which oxygen carries the negative charge, A or B?

A. It received the π pair. B arrived with its H and is now a neutral OH on carbon.



The oxygen labels are the core skill of today and of the Day 16 demo. Students often put the negative charge on the incoming oxygen because “it was the one with the minus sign”. Ask them to count: B started with one bond and three lone pairs (charge −1), and now has two bonds (to H and to C) and two lone pairs, so it’s neutral. A started with two bonds (the double bond) and two lone pairs, and now has one bond and three lone pairs, so it’s −1. The charge moved because the electrons moved. Also check that both sides show a total charge of −1.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Water finishes the hydrate

Water protonates the alkoxide to give the hydrate and regenerate hydroxideThe alkoxide takes H⁺ from water; the O–H bonding pair stays on water’s oxygen (C), which leaves as OH⁻. Hydroxide is used and then returned, so it’s a catalyst.
Net: CH₃CHO + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH(OH)₂, a hydrate (gem-diol).

Work through the arrows: lone pair on A to the H of water, and the H–O bond pair onto water’s oxygen. Point out that the hydroxide that comes out (oxygen C) is not the same hydroxide that went in (oxygen B). That’s fine: catalysts are regenerated as a species, not as the same atoms. Have students add the two steps and cancel OH⁻ to get the net equation; this is exercise 6. Also stress that a “proton” is never just floating: always name the donor and the acceptor.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: How much hydrate? It depends on the carbonyl
text:
How much hydrate? It depends on the carbonyl

Hydrate share for methanal, ethanal, propanone and chloralThe same mechanism works for all four. Where the equilibrium lies depends on structure: alkyl groups stabilise the C=O; electron-withdrawing groups (like CCl₃) favour the hydrate.

Try it: a student draws a correct hydration mechanism for propanone and concludes the flask is all hydrate. What’s missing?

Equilibrium data. A mechanism shows how species interconvert, not how much of each is present; propanone is about 99.9 % ketone.



This slide separates two questions students tend to merge: “can it happen?” (mechanism) and “how much is there at equilibrium?” (thermodynamics). Formaldehyde in water (formalin) is almost entirely the hydrate; acetone barely hydrates at all. Chloral is a nice story: its hydrate is so stable that chloral hydrate is a crystalline solid, and it was one of the first synthetic sedatives in the 19th century. Keep the explanation qualitative: alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilise the carbonyl; electron-withdrawing groups make the carbonyl carbon even more δ+ and favour addition. Exercise 20 is this exact argument.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: In acid, the oxygen is protonated first
text:
In acid, the oxygen is protonated first

Hydronium protonates ethanal’s carbonyl oxygenA lone pair on the carbonyl O takes H⁺ from H₃O⁺. The protonated carbonyl is far more electrophilic: its resonance form puts + on carbon. Now even a weak, neutral nucleophile can add.

Compare the two routes explicitly. In base, a strong nucleophile (OH⁻) attacks an ordinary carbonyl. In acid, the carbonyl is made more reactive so that a weak nucleophile (water or an alcohol) can attack. Both arrows matter: the lone pair to H, and the H–O bond of hydronium onto its oxygen. Ask what the charge on the product oxygen is: three bonds and one lone pair, so +1. The resonance form is the reason for activation; it’s the same resonance thinking from Day 3.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Base route vs acid route









base-catalysed
acid-catalysed




first step
nucleophile adds to C=O
carbonyl O is protonated


nucleophile
strong, anionic (OH⁻, RO⁻)
weak, neutral (H₂O, ROH)


intermediate
alkoxide, charge −1
oxonium, charge +1


last step
O⁻ takes H⁺ from water
O⁺–H gives H⁺ to water


catalyst
OH⁻ regenerated
H₃O⁺ regenerated




Try it: in methanol with plenty of acid, why don’t we draw CH₃O⁻ as the nucleophile?

It can’t survive there. Methoxide is a strong base and would be protonated at once; the nucleophile in acid is neutral CH₃OH.



This table is the map for the rest of the lecture. The key consistency rule: a mechanism has to respect the acid-base chemistry of the conditions. Strong bases and strong acids don’t coexist, so don’t draw OH⁻ or CH₃O⁻ in a strongly acidic flask, and don’t draw H₃O⁺ in a strongly basic one. Ask students which column the Day 13 NaBH₄ reduction belongs to (base-like: anionic nucleophile first, proton last). Exercise 8 is the try-it.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Methanol adds to the activated carbonyl
text:
Methanol adds to the activated carbonyl

Methanol attacks protonated ethanalSame two arrows as before. Now the incoming oxygen B ends with three bonds, so it carries the +1. Oxygen A becomes a neutral OH.

Try it: count the bonds and lone pairs on oxygen B after attack. What’s its formal charge?

+1. Three bonds (H, CH₃, C) and one lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.



This is the mirror image of the base route. In base, the incoming oxygen was neutral after attack and the old carbonyl oxygen took the negative charge. In acid, the old carbonyl oxygen was already protonated (+1) and becomes neutral once the π pair lands on it, while the incoming oxygen becomes +1. The overall charge is +1 throughout. Students often put the + on oxygen A out of habit. The formal charge formula from Day 1 settles it.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: A proton transfer gives the hemiacetal
text:
A proton transfer gives the hemiacetal

Water removes the proton from oxygen B to give the hemiacetalWater removes H⁺ from the three-bonded oxygen B, and H₃O⁺ is regenerated. The product, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃, is a hemiacetal: OH and OR on the same carbon.

Try it: in the hemiacetal, which labelled oxygen is the OH and which is in the OCH₃?

A is the OH, B is the OCH₃. Swapping them would need extra bond-breaking steps that we never drew.



The proton must come off the oxygen that has three bonds; taking it from oxygen A would leave an O⁻ next to an O⁺, which is the wrong product. Walk through the full acid sequence once more as “protonate, add, deprotonate” and count: H₃O⁺ in at the start, H₃O⁺ out at the end. The atom-tracking question is exercise 4 and quiz question 2 in a different form; the point is that atoms don’t silently swap places. A drawing in which the methanol oxygen ends up as the OH means something went wrong.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Hydrate, hemiacetal, acetal

Aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal with the key carbon shadedLook at the former carbonyl carbon and its two oxygen groups: OH + OH is a hydrate, OH + OR is a hemiacetal, and OR + OR is an acetal.

Try it: classify CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂.

Acetal. Two OCH₃ groups sit on the same carbon. An OCH₃ somewhere else in a molecule would just be an ether.



Classification is all about one carbon. A common error is to call any molecule with an OH and an OR a hemiacetal, even if they’re on different carbons; HOCH2CH2OCH3 is an alcohol plus an ether, not a hemiacetal. Run the four names quickly as an oral drill: point at a structure and have the room call out the class. This is exercise 11 and quiz question 4. Note that ketones give the same classes; you’ll sometimes see “hemiketal” and “ketal”, which are older names for the ketone versions.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
From hemiacetal to acetal

Protonation, loss of water and a second methanol give the acetalThe OH is a poor leaving group, so acid protonates it first. Water leaves, helped by the neighbouring OCH₃ lone pair, and a second CH₃OH adds to the oxocarbenium ion.
Net: CH₃CHO + 2 CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂ + H₂O

This is more steps than students need to reproduce in full today, but they must know that turning OH into OR is not a single arrow; that’s exercise 12. Point out the logic: OH⁻ is a terrible leaving group, but H₂O is a fine one, so protonation converts a bad leaving group into a good one. That idea returns in substitution and in tomorrow’s acyl chemistry. The oxocarbenium ion is just another strongly activated carbonyl, so the second methanol adds exactly like the first. Count atoms in the net equation: two methanols in, one water out. That balance is exercise 13.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Water decides the acetal equilibrium

Acetal equilibrium shifted by removing or adding waterAcid speeds up both directions but doesn’t change K. To make the acetal, remove water; to undo it, add excess water with a little acid. In base, acetals are stable.

Try it: you dissolve an acetal in dilute aqueous acid. Which way does the equilibrium move?

Back to aldehyde + alcohol. Water is a product of acetal formation, so a large excess of water pushes the reaction backwards (Le Chatelier).



Keep two operations separate: adding a catalyst changes how fast equilibrium is reached, while changing composition (removing or adding water) changes where it ends up. Students often say “acid makes the acetal”. Acid makes it possible, but water removal makes it favourable. A practical aside: chemists use this on/off switch to protect a carbonyl as an acetal, do chemistry elsewhere under basic conditions, then remove the acetal with aqueous acid. Sugars linked in starch and cellulose are acetals, which is why acid hydrolysis breaks them down. This is quiz question 6 and exercise 14.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Does addition create a stereocentre?

Hemiacetal from ethanal versus hemiketal from propanoneA tetrahedral carbon is a stereocentre only if its four groups differ. From ethanal: CH₃, H, OH, OCH₃, so yes. Attack on either face of the flat C=O is equally likely, giving a racemic mixture.

Try it: methanol adds to propanone to give (CH₃)₂C(OH)OCH₃. Is the former carbonyl carbon a stereocentre?

No. Two of its groups are identical CH₃ groups. Becoming tetrahedral isn’t enough.



Connect to Week 2. The flat carbonyl from the first slide is why both enantiomers form: the nucleophile is equally likely to approach from the top face and the bottom face. Assigning R or S is only meaningful once you draw a specific 3D product with wedges; a flat drawing of the hemiacetal is the racemate. Exercises 18 and 19 are this slide. Plant the seed for the next slides: in glucose, the new stereocentre at C1 is the origin of the α and β forms.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: A ring from inside one molecule
text:
A ring from inside one molecule

5-Hydroxypentanal closes to a six-membered cyclic hemiacetalWhen the OH and the C=O are in the same molecule, the addition closes a ring. Five- and six-membered rings form easily.

Try it: how many atoms are in the ring, and is any water lost?

Six (oxygen B and five carbons), and no water is lost. Both structures are C₅H₁₀O₂; addition only moves atoms around.



Draw the chain curled up so the OH is close to the carbonyl carbon; that’s how it actually reacts. Count the ring atoms aloud: O, C5, C4, C3, C2, C1. Students often leave the attacking oxygen outside the ring or remove water as if it were a condensation reaction. A hemiacetal forms by addition, so the formula can’t change; only acetal formation releases water. Also note that the old carbonyl oxygen, A, becomes the OH on C1, and the new ring oxygen is B. This is exercise 15, exercise 16 and quiz question 5.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Glucose is a cyclic hemiacetal

Open-chain D-glucose and β-D-glucopyranoseThe C5 OH adds to the C1 aldehyde, giving a six-membered ring. C1 becomes a new stereocentre, so there are two forms: β (about 64 %) and α (about 36 %) in water.

This answers the opening question. The ring is favoured because a six-membered ring is nearly strain-free (the chair you saw in conformations) and the reaction is intramolecular. Point out that this is exactly the previous slide with extra OH groups along the chain. The new stereocentre at C1 is called the anomeric carbon, and α and β are its two configurations; they interconvert through the open chain, which is why a fresh glucose solution slowly changes its optical rotation (mutarotation). Don’t expect students to draw glucose from memory; the goal is to recognise the hemiacetal carbon: the only carbon with two oxygens attached.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Same pattern, other nucleophiles

Hydride and cyanide add to propanoneHydride (from NaBH₄, Day 13) and cyanide add the same way: alkoxide first, then a proton. Only the new group on carbon changes.

Show how far the single pattern reaches. With NaBH₄ the “nucleophile” is a hydride delivered from boron; with cyanide a new C–C bond forms, which is how chemists extend a carbon chain. Keep the claims modest: we’re showing the electron pattern, not a full scope of reagents or conditions. Ask the room what product NaBH₄ gives from ethanal (ethanol) to check they can transfer the pattern. Hydride addition is effectively irreversible, whereas cyanohydrin formation is an equilibrium like hydration (cyanohydrins of ketones can fall back to ketone and HCN), which links back to the mechanism-versus-equilibrium slide.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Aldehydes keep the addition; esters can lose a group
text:
Aldehydes keep the addition; esters can lose a group

Tetrahedral intermediates from ethanal and from methyl ethanoateAsk what else is on the carbonyl carbon. An aldehyde or ketone has only H or C, which can’t leave. An ester has OR, so the C=O can re-form and push RO⁻ out: addition, then elimination.

This is the bridge to tomorrow (Day 17). The first step is identical: a nucleophile adds and gives a tetrahedral intermediate. What differs is the next step: in an aldehyde, H⁻ or CH₃⁻ are hopeless leaving groups, so the intermediate just picks up a proton. In an ester, the oxygen lone pair can push back down to re-form C=O and expel CH₃O⁻. Don’t over-claim: whether a group actually leaves depends on conditions and leaving-group ability, which is what Day 17 is about. Exercise 17 asks exactly this comparison.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake

the π pair must move to O

count bonds: the old C=O oxygen is O⁻

in acid, use neutral H₂O or CH₃OH

name the donor and acceptor every time

“a valid mechanism, so it’s all hydrate”

Read each mistake aloud and ask the room why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. Every row maps to an exercise: arrows (3, 9), charges (4, 9), conditions (8), proton accounting (5, 10), labels (4), ring formula (16), acetal steps (12) and pathway versus population (20). Students who still make one of these know exactly which exercise to redo.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Summary



concept
key fact




carbonyl
δ+ carbon, planar, attacked from either face


addition
Nu in, π pair to O, tetrahedral carbon


base route
add, then protonate O⁻ (OH⁻ catalyst)


acid route
protonate O, add, deprotonate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)


hydrate · hemiacetal · acetal

mechanism vs amount
a pathway doesn’t give the equilibrium mixture



Next: acyl chemistry, when a group can leave (Day 17). Practice: exercises · self-check

Recite the core sequence once: nucleophile in, π pair out, then fix the charges with proton transfers using real donors and acceptors. Close the loop on the opening: glucose is a ring because its own C5 OH adds to its own C1 aldehyde, and that ring is a hemiacetal. Point students to the exercises: problems 1–12 are the core, 13–20 are optional transfer. The Day 16 demo lets them step through the hydrate and hemiacetal routes and check each oxygen’s charge.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
text:
1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
Retain the carbon skeleton.






Check your answer





Propanone. The carbon bearing OH becomes a carbonyl carbon, while its two carbon substituents remain attached.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
text:
2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
Explain the missing bond at the carbon bearing OH.






Check your answer





It has no C–H bond at that carbon. Simple conversion to C=O while retaining all three C–C bonds would overbond carbon. Harsh oxidation can involve C–C cleavage, outside this selected pattern.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
text:
3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
A ketone receives H at carbon while its pi pair moves to oxygen. Name the species type before work-up.






Check your answer





An alkoxide. A subsequent proton transfer from an explicit donor produces the alcohol. Free hydride in water is not what the simplified H: minus drawing represents.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
text:
4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
State a limitation of functional-group IR evidence.






Check your answer





No. Many compounds share that functional group, bands can overlap, and samples can contain water or mixtures. Combine multiple observations with structural and purity evidence.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
text:
5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
Reactants are available as 10.0 and 15.0 mmol. Product coefficient is one.






Check your answer





The 10.0 mmol reactant limits product to 10.0 mmol. Compare amount divided by stoichiometric coefficient, rather than raw masses.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
text:
6. Does 66.6% isolated yield mean 66.6% conversion?
Explain one possible reason they differ.






Check your answer





No. Starting material may react but product may be lost during isolation; side products or impurities can also affect the relationship. Conversion, isolated yield and purity answer different questions.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
Track alcohol and carbonyl transformations, check oxidation states, and connect reagent amounts to the evidence for a product. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Selected primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehyde then acid; secondary alcohol gives ketone. Carbonyl reduction by a supplied suitable reagent gives an alkoxide then an alcohol after proton donation. For the carbon oxidation-state check, C–O bond order contributes+1, C–H−1, C–C0. For amounts use n=m/M and compare n/coefficient.
Worked starting example. Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH→ethanal CH₃CHO raises the changing carbon oxidation state from −1 to+1. In the reverse selected reduction, hydride-equivalent delivery forms CH₃CH₂O⁻ first; water can then donate H⁺ to give ethanol and OH⁻. Each stage has explicit atoms and charge.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
1. Classify the alcohol centre
Draw CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃COH. Classify the OH-bearing carbon and count its attached H.






Hint





Count carbon neighbours and H at that particular carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The centres are primary with two H, secondary with one H and tertiary with no H. These local differences determine whether the simple carbon-skeleton-retaining carbonyl oxidation pattern applies.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
2. Oxidise a primary alcohol once
Draw the selected net transformation ethanol → ethanal, preserving the carbon skeleton. Identify the changing C–O and C–H bond inventory.






Hint





Turn the alcohol-bearing carbon into a carbonyl carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





CH₃CH₂OH becomes CH₃CHO. The changing carbon loses a C–H bond overall and gains C–O bond order; O also loses its H. This is a net oxidation map, not an elementary one-step mechanism or a lab protocol.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
3. Oxidise the aldehyde further
Draw ethanal → ethanoic acid and explain why an aldehyde target requires controlled oxidation conditions.






Hint





Replace the aldehyde C–H with the acid C–OH in the net structure.









Worked answer and reasoning





CH₃CHO becomes CH₃COOH. Since the aldehyde can undergo further oxidation, an unspecified oxidation arrow does not guarantee that isolation stops there. Conditions and reagent scope matter.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
4. Oxidise a secondary alcohol
Predict the selected oxidation product of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. Name the functional group and give its condensed structure.






Hint





Retain both carbon substituents on the OH-bearing carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is butan-2-one, CH₃C(=O)CH₂CH₃, a ketone. Forming C=O while removing the appropriate H atoms retains the four-carbon skeleton.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
5. Explain the tertiary boundary
Why would drawing (CH₃)₃C=O as the direct simple oxidation product of (CH₃)₃COH be invalid?






Hint





Count bond orders at the central carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





Three C–C single bonds plus C=O give bond-order sum five. The starting tertiary centre has no C–H for the usual alcohol-to-carbonyl change. Oxidative C–C cleavage can occur under other conditions, but that is a different transformation.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
6. Assign a carbon oxidation state
Use +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H and zero per C–C to assign the changing carbon in ethanol, ethanal and ethanoic acid.






Hint





Double C=O contributes plus two.









Worked answer and reasoning





The values are −1, +1 and +3 respectively. Increasing oxidation state identifies oxidation even when simply counting oxygen atoms would miss the first change.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
7. Check a ketone carbon
Assign the carbonyl-carbon oxidation state in CH₃COCH₃ and the corresponding OH-carbon value in CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.






Hint





The ketone carbon has no attached H; the alcohol carbon has one.









Worked answer and reasoning





Propanone carbonyl C is +2 from C=O. Propan-2-ol carbinol C is 0 from +1 for C–O and −1 for C–H. The ketone-to-alcohol transformation lowers the carbon oxidation state by two.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
8. Reduce an aldehyde
Assume a suitable NaBH₄ reduction then proton-donor work-up of CH₃CH₂CHO. Predict the neutral organic product.






Hint





Carbonyl reduction preserves the carbon skeleton and adds H at carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





Propanal gives propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Hydride-equivalent delivery gives an alkoxide first; a proton donor supplies its O–H proton afterward.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
9. Reduce a ketone
Under the same selected reduction/work-up model, predict CH₃COCH₂CH₃ → product. Does the product have a stereocentre?






Hint





The former carbonyl carbon gains H and OH while retaining methyl and ethyl.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. Its OH-bearing carbon has OH, H, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, so it is a stereocentre. An achiral reagent/environment can allow both faces of the planar carbonyl to react.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
10. Draw the reduction arrows
For propanone, draw a simplified H:⁻ delivery step and the alkoxide. Explicitly state what H:⁻ represents.






Hint





Move the carbonyl pi pair onto oxygen as C–H forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is (CH₃)₂CHO⁻; one pair forms C–H and the C=O π pair returns to O. H:⁻ means hydride-equivalent delivery from a reagent such as borohydride, not a claim that free hydride persists in aqueous solution.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
11. Finish the work-up
Use water to turn (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ into alcohol. Draw the donor and conjugate base instead of writing unexplained H⁺.






Hint





Water loses one H⁺ when it protonates the alkoxide.









Worked answer and reasoning





Alkoxide O attacks water H; the water O–H pair returns to O. Products are propan-2-ol and OH⁻, with net charge −1 conserved.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
12. Test reagent scope
A student transfers the selected NaBH₄ aldehyde/ketone rule directly to an ordinary ester and an amide. Why is that unsupported by this course toolkit?






Hint





Carbonyl groups belong to different functional classes with different reactivity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The supplied rule establishes aldehyde/ketone reduction under appropriate conditions. Esters and amides have different electronic and leaving-group chemistry; their behaviour cannot be inferred just from the shared C=O drawing. More reagent/condition information is required.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
13. Read two IR observations
A supplied teaching sample loses a broad 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ alcohol feature and gains strong absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ after a proposed secondary-alcohol oxidation. Explain support and limitation.






Hint





Relate each observation to a functional group, then consider identity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The changes support loss of OH and formation of carbonyl, consistent with the proposed oxidation. They do not uniquely identify the ketone or establish purity; use additional structure and sample evidence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
14. Calculate amounts by hand
A balanced 1:1 aspirin teaching reaction uses 1.3812 g acid at 138.12 g/mol and 1.53135 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol. Calculate both mmol values and identify the limiting reagent.






Hint





Divide g by g/mol, multiply mol by1000, then compare amount/coefficient.









Worked answer and reasoning





The acid is 0.01000 mol=10.00 mmol and anhydride0.01500 mol=15.00 mmol. The acid limits the 1:1 reaction. Comparing raw grams would ignore the different molar masses.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: 15. Use a coefficient other than one
text:
15. Use a coefficient other than one
For the hypothetical balanced teaching stoichiometry 2 A + B → P, available amounts are 12 mmol A and8 mmol B. Calculate the maximum mmol P and identify the limit.






Hint





Compare n(A)/2 with n(B)/1.









Worked answer and reasoning





A permits 6 mmol reaction extent; B permits 8 mmol. A limits product to 6 mmol P. A larger molar amount can still limit when its stoichiometric coefficient is larger.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
16. Calculate theoretical mass
The aspirin teaching reaction can make10.00 mmol product with molar mass180.16 g/mol. Calculate theoretical mass in grams.






Hint





Convert mmol to mol before multiplying by g/mol.









Worked answer and reasoning





0.01000 mol×180.16 g/mol=1.8016 g. Using10 directly as mol would introduce a thousandfold error.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
17. Calculate isolated yield
Using theoretical mass1.8016 g and isolated mass1.20 g, calculate isolated yield. State a claim this value cannot establish.






Hint





Yield%=100×isolated/theoretical.









Worked answer and reasoning





The result is about 66.6%. It does not prove purity or conversion: isolation losses, unreacted material, side reactions and retained impurities require separate evidence.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: 18. Repair a yield over 100 percent claim
text:
18. Repair a yield over 100 percent claim
A wet isolated sample weighs 1.95 g although the theoretical pure-product maximum is 1.8016 g. Should this establish a 108% chemical yield? Give a better interpretation.






Hint





The balance measures all material present, not only intended product.









Worked answer and reasoning





The apparent mass-based percentage is about 108%, but a pure-product yield above the stoichiometric maximum is inconsistent with the assumptions. Residual solvent/water, impurities or input/measurement errors should be investigated before reporting an actual product yield.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
19. Plan a one-step interconversion
Given ethanal and a target of ethanol, choose oxidation or the supplied carbonyl reduction/work-up. Draw the target and explain why further oxidation is wrong.






Hint





The target carbon has more C–H and less C–O bond order.









Worked answer and reasoning





Use the selected reduction followed by proton donation to give CH₃CH₂OH. Oxidation moves toward ethanoic acid instead, increasing rather than decreasing the changing carbon oxidation state.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
20. Assemble an evidence statement
A proposed propan-2-ol→propanone experiment gives an IR carbonyl band, one visible TLC (thin-layer chromatography) spot and an isolated mass. Write two supported conclusions and two unresolved questions.






Hint





Separate functional-group evidence, chromatographic observation and chemical identity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The IR supports a carbonyl-containing sample; the TLC records one spot under its stated conditions. Neither alone proves pure propanone. Identity needs additional structural evidence, and purity/conversion require suitable separate checks; the isolated mass alone is not enough.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
section: R task: chemistry calculation in your report
text:
R task: chemistry calculation in your report
The balanced teaching equation is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid, with all coefficients one. The shared CSV supplies reagent masses and molar masses. This is a calculation context, not a synthesis protocol. Keep the raw data unchanged.
The amount in mol is mass in g divided by molar mass in g/mol. Divide each reactant amount by its stoichiometric coefficient. The smallest available reaction extent limits the maximum product amount. Here aspirin’s coefficient is one and its supplied molar mass is 180.16 g/mol.
Predict which of 10.0 and 15.0 mmol will limit a 1:1 reaction, then add this code to your report:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_product_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
theoretical_product_mass_g
Knit the report. Give the limiting reagent, theoretical product amount in mmol and mass in g. Change a copy of the acetic anhydride input to 0.51045 g and predict the new limiting reagent before recalculating. Do not overwrite the original CSV to make this alternative scenario.






Numerical and chemical check





The supplied amounts are 0.0100 mol acid and 0.0150 mol anhydride. Salicylic acid limits the product to 10.0 mmol, corresponding to 1.8016 g aspirin. With 0.51045 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, anhydride is 5.00 mmol and limits product to 5.00 mmol, or 0.9008 g. Comparing masses alone would be wrong because the reagents have different molar masses. In a different balanced reaction, coefficients other than one must also be included.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 13: Exercises — Alcohols and redox
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1–2 minutes). Assign the changing carbon in ethanol before checking. Use +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H bond and 0 per C–C bond. Is your answer a formal charge?
Explore (3–4 minutes). Check ethanol, then use the selected-next-oxidation button to move through ethanal to ethanoic acid. Compare propan-2-ol with propanone. Finally inspect 2-methylpropan-2-ol and explain why the simple next-oxidation button is unavailable.
Explain (2 minutes). Show one full bond-count calculation. Why can oxidation happen without adding a new oxygen atom? Why would retaining all three C–C bonds while converting the tertiary centre to C=O give an invalid ordinary carbon?


Supplied model and its limits
The displayed value is the oxidation state of the changing carbon, not its formal charge. C–O bond order contributes +1, C–H −1, C–C 0. The supplied selected net maps are primary alcohol→aldehyde→acid and secondary alcohol→ketone. The tertiary centre has no attached H, so the simple carbon-skeleton-retaining map cannot be used. Other harsh, C–C-cleaving chemistry is outside this model; no laboratory conditions are supplied.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
About this lecture
Every turn of the citric acid cycle, the enzyme aconitase pulls a water molecule out of citrate to make a C=C bond, then adds the water straight back on, the other way round. It’s an elimination followed by an addition, and it moves the OH to a carbon where your cells can oxidise it.
Today we learn the two reactions that make and consume a C=C bond:

α and β carbons: where the leaving group sits, and where the H comes from
E2: one step, three arrows, an anti-periplanar H
E1: carbocation first, then loss of a β-H, competing with SN1
Electrophilic addition: HBr through the more stable carbocation, Br₂ through a bromonium ion
Products: which alkene, E or Z, which face, which stereoisomer

Yesterday’s substitution reactions are the starting point: the same substrates, but now the reagent can grab a hydrogen instead of a carbon.

Open with aconitase. It’s a real enzyme in every mitochondrion: citrate to cis-aconitate is a dehydration (elimination of water), and cis-aconitate to isocitrate is a hydration (addition of water). The net effect is moving the OH from a tertiary carbon to a secondary one, which matters tomorrow: tertiary alcohols can’t be oxidised, secondary ones can, and the next enzyme in the cycle does exactly that. Don’t show the structures yet; we come back to them at the end once students can read the mechanism. Frame today as the second half of yesterday: an alkyl halide plus a base or nucleophile can substitute, or it can eliminate, and the alkenes we make can then add things back.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Two directions for one π bond
text:
Two directions for one π bond

Bromoethane loses HBr to give ethene; ethene adds HBr to give bromoethane
Elimination: lose H and a leaving group from neighbouring carbons; a new π bond forms.
Addition: a π bond is consumed and two new σ bonds form.
Bond audit for propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (C₃H₆ + HBr → C₃H₇Br): the C=C π bond and H–Br break; C–H and C–Br form; the C–C σ bond stays.


This is the bookkeeping slide. Get students to say out loud which bonds change, because every mechanism today is just a way of doing this bookkeeping with electron pairs. Point out that the formula of the product is just the sum of the formulas, so addition is atom-economical. Warn against one thing early: the two arrows look like an equilibrium, but in the lab the reagents and conditions that make each direction work are different. We return to that with cyclohexanol near the end.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
α and β carbons

2-Bromobutane with α and β carbons labelled, and bromomethaneThe α carbon carries the leaving group. A β carbon is directly bonded to it. β-Elimination removes an H from a β carbon, so CH₃Br, with no β carbon, can’t do it.

Try it: how many β hydrogens does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, have?

Nine. All three CH₃ groups are β, and all nine H give the same alkene, 2-methylpropene.



α and β are labels relative to the functional group, not permanent names; the same carbon can be α in one reaction and β in another. Ask students to point at the β carbons in 2-bromobutane before you reveal the labels: C1 and C3. C4 is γ and doesn’t take part. The methyl bromide case is the classic trick question: it can only substitute. The try-it shows that counting β-H is less important than asking how many different alkenes they lead to: nine H, one product.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
E2: three arrows, one step

E2 mechanism for 2-bromopropane with ethoxideThe base takes the β-H, the C–H pair becomes the π bond, and bromide leaves, all at once. There’s no intermediate, so the rate depends on both partners: rate = k[RBr][base].

Try it: a student draws base → H and C–Br → Br, but no third arrow. What’s wrong?

The C–H pair is lost. Without the C–H → C=C arrow, nothing forms the π bond and the electron count doesn’t balance.



Draw this on the board with the students, arrow by arrow, saying where each pair starts and ends. The first arrow starts at a lone pair on oxygen, not at the minus sign. The second arrow is the one people forget: when the base takes H as a proton, the two electrons of the C–H bond stay behind on carbon and swing into the C–C bond. Check charge: −1 on ethoxide on the left, −1 on bromide on the right. E2 means elimination, bimolecular, which is why the rate law has both concentrations. Note that I drew the H and Br pointing in opposite directions on purpose; that’s the next slide.

title: Elimination and addition
section: The H and the leaving group must be anti
text:
The H and the leaving group must be anti

Newman projection with the front-carbon H opposite the back-carbon BrIn E2 the reacting C–H and C–Br bonds lie in one plane on opposite sides: an H–C–C–Br dihedral of 180°, called anti-periplanar. The breaking C–H orbital then lines up with the back of the breaking C–Br bond.

Try it: rotate only the rear carbon by 60°. Is that H/Br pair still anti? Is it a different compound?

No, and no. The dihedral is now 60° or 300°, so that pair can’t react, but rotation only changes conformation, not connectivity. Another rotation brings an anti H back.



This is Week 2’s Newman projection put to work. Ask students to build this with a model kit if they have one: the front carbon is the dot, the back carbon the circle. Explain why anti: the electrons from the C–H bond flow into the C–Br σ* orbital, which points out the back of the C–Br bond. In open-chain molecules rotation is free, so some conformation always offers an anti H. In rings, especially cyclohexanes, the H and Br must both be axial, which can block elimination entirely. That’s a good extension question for strong students but not required today.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
One substrate, several alkenes

2-Bromobutane gives but-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene and (Z)-but-2-eneList the β carbons first; each gives its own alkene. With a small base the more substituted alkene usually dominates (Zaitsev). A bulky base such as t-BuO⁻ reaches the exposed CH₃ more easily and gives more of the terminal alkene.

Try it: which alkenes can 2-bromopentane give with ethoxide, and which is likely major?

Pent-1-ene, (E)-pent-2-ene and (Z)-pent-2-ene. The disubstituted pent-2-ene dominates, mostly as the E isomer.



The procedure is the point: find α, find every β, remove one H from each in turn, and draw the alkene without moving any carbons. Only then think about proportions. Students often skip straight to “the Zaitsev product” and miss the others. More substituted alkenes are more stable, and in E2 the transition state already has partial double-bond character, so it feels that stability. E over Z because the two methyl groups clash in Z. Don’t quote ratios as rules: they depend on base, solvent and temperature. For 2-bromobutane with ethoxide, roughly 80 % of the alkene is but-2-ene.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Can it be E or Z?
text:
Can it be E or Z?

But-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene and (Z)-but-2-ene with the H atoms on the alkene carbons drawnCheck both alkene carbons. Each needs two different groups. One end with two identical groups (like =CH₂) means there’s no E/Z, however the chain is drawn.

This is the stereochemistry habit from Week 2 applied to alkenes. Ask: in but-1-ene, what are the two groups on C1? Two H, so it fails the test immediately. The tempting mistake is calling a terminal alkene E because the zigzag chain looks stretched out. Drawing shape is never evidence; the substituent list is. Quick extra question: 2-methylbut-2-ene? No E/Z, because C2 carries two methyl groups. For E and Z with more complex groups, use the CIP priorities from Week 2.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Substitution or elimination?

Hydroxide attacking the alpha carbon or a beta hydrogen of 2-bromopropane






favours elimination
favours substitution




strong or bulky base (EtO⁻, t-BuO⁻)
good nucleophile, weak base (I⁻, CN⁻)


secondary or tertiary substrate

heat
lower temperature




This is the bridge from yesterday. The same reagent, hydroxide, can donate its pair to the carbon (SN2) or to a β hydrogen (E2). The first question is always which atom receives the pair. Then use the table to argue which wins, but stress that it’s a tendency, not a rule: a secondary bromide with hydroxide gives a mixture. Students should be able to state what extra information they’d need (base strength and size, substrate, temperature, solvent) before predicting a major product.

title: Elimination and addition
section: E1: lose the leaving group first
text:
E1: lose the leaving group first

E1 mechanism for tert-butyl bromide in waterStep 1 is the same slow ionisation as SN1. Step 2: even a weak base like water can pull off a β-H, because the C–H pair now flows into an empty p orbital. Rate = k[RBr]; the base doesn’t appear.

Contrast with E2 explicitly: in step 2 there is no C–Br arrow, because bromide left in step 1. Ask students to count the arrows in step 2 (two) and say why. E1 needs a substrate that ionises: tertiary, or secondary in a polar solvent. The rate law is first order because only the substrate is involved in the slow step, exactly as in SN1. The carbocation is the same species as yesterday, which is the point of the next slide.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
One carbocation, two products

The tert-butyl cation can be captured by water or lose a beta HAfter ionisation, water can bond to C⁺ (SN1) or remove a β-H (E1). Seeing a carbocation doesn’t tell you the product; the conditions do.

Try it: raising the temperature shifts the ratio toward the alkene. Why?

Entropy. Elimination turns one cation into two species (alkene + H₃O⁺), so its TΔS term grows with temperature.



Both branches release H3O+; the SN1 branch goes through an oxonium ion that loses a proton to water, so make sure students include that proton transfer. In water at room temperature, tert-butyl bromide gives mostly tert-butanol with some alkene. Heat, and a less nucleophilic medium, push toward the alkene. This branch point comes back in Week 4 whenever a carbocation appears, and it’s the same logic as acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols tomorrow.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
E1 or E2?

Energy profiles: one transition state for E2, two with a carbocation intermediate for E1



E2
E1

rate

base

weak is enough (H₂O, ROH)


geometry
anti-periplanar H needed

Read the energy profiles: E2 has one maximum, the transition state where all three pair movements are half done. E1 has a high first barrier for C–Br cleavage and a carbocation in the valley. Ask: which step is rate-limiting in E1 and why doesn’t the base appear in the rate law? Also: E1 can’t control stereochemistry tightly because the planar cation can lose any β-H, while E2’s anti requirement can force a particular alkene isomer. Strong base usually means E2; weak base, ionising solvent and a tertiary substrate mean E1.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Alkenes are nucleophiles: adding HBr

Two-step mechanism of HBr addition to propeneThe π electrons are exposed above and below the C=C plane, so the alkene acts as an electron-pair donor. Step 1: π pair → H, H–Br pair → Br. Step 2: Br⁻ lone pair → C⁺.

Turn the elimination around. Now the alkene is the nucleophile and HBr the electrophile. The first arrow starts in the middle of the double bond, not at an atom: that’s the π pair. Make sure the H ends up on C1 and the positive charge on C2; that choice is the next slide. Remind students this is the ionic mechanism, with no peroxides. With peroxides, HBr adds by a radical chain the other way round, which is outside this course. Ask what the carbon geometry is at each stage: trigonal planar alkene, planar carbocation, tetrahedral product.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Markovnikov: the more stable cation wins
text:
Markovnikov: the more stable cation wins

Protonation at C1 gives the secondary cation; protonation at C2 would give a primary cationH⁺ adds to the end that gives the more substituted carbocation, so Br ends up on the more substituted carbon. Ethene is symmetric: either way gives bromoethane.

Try it: what does 2-methylpropene give with HBr?

2-Bromo-2-methylpropane. H goes to the CH₂ end, giving the tertiary cation, which bromide then captures.



Teach the reason, not just the rule. Markovnikov’s rule (“H goes to the carbon that already has more H”) is a summary of carbocation stability: alkyl groups donate electron density to the empty p orbital, so tertiary beats secondary beats primary. The primary cation is so unstable that 1-bromopropane is essentially not formed by this route. Ethene is a good sanity check: swapping which equivalent carbon gets the H gives the same molecule, so there’s no regiochemistry to discuss. Students should name the product, not just say “Markovnikov”.

title: Elimination and addition
section: A planar cation has two faces
text:
A planar cation has two faces

But-1-ene and HBr give both enantiomers of 2-bromobutaneThe carbocation is flat, and bromide attacks the top and bottom faces equally. A new stereocentre made this way forms as a racemic mixture.

Try it: will 2-bromobutane made from but-1-ene and HBr rotate plane-polarised light?

No. It’s a 50:50 mixture of R and S, so the rotations cancel.



This links back to Week 2 and to SN1 yesterday: whenever a planar intermediate is attacked, both faces are available unless something chiral steers the reaction. Draw the empty p orbital with a lobe above and below to make it concrete. Enzymes are the exception, and that’s why aconitase makes only one stereoisomer of isocitrate. Check that students label R and S from the drawn wedges rather than guessing.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Br₂ adds through a bromonium ion
text:
Br₂ adds through a bromonium ion

Cyclohexene attacks Br2 to form a bridged bromonium ion and bromideBr₂ has no H to lose, but the alkene still donates its π pair to one Br as the other leaves as Br⁻. Instead of a free carbocation, the Br bridges both carbons: a three-membered bromonium ion.

Br2 is polarised as it approaches the electron-rich alkene, so one end behaves as the electrophile. A full mechanism has the bromine’s lone pair forming the second C–Br bond as the π bond attacks; at this level it’s enough to draw the result as a bridged cation with the positive charge on bromine. Ask what the formal charge on Br is: two bonds and two lone pairs on bromine gives +1. Also a practical note: the orange colour of bromine water disappearing is the classic test for C=C.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Back-side opening gives anti addition

Bromide opens the bromonium ion from the back face, giving the trans dibromide onlyThe bridge blocks one face, so Br⁻ attacks from the opposite face, like an SN2. The two Br end up anti: cyclohexene gives only trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

Try it: why can’t we just reuse the HBr carbocation mechanism for Br₂?

A free planar cation could be attacked from either face, giving cis and trans. Only trans forms, and only the bridged ion explains that.



This is where mechanism earns its keep: the product’s stereochemistry is the evidence for the intermediate. The opening step is an SN2 on the bromonium ion with Br+ as the leaving group, which is why it’s backside. Trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane is chiral and forms as a racemic pair, because bromide can open either carbon. The cis isomer is meso and is not formed. Students who have the SN2 picture from yesterday usually get this quickly; ask them to identify the nucleophile, electrophilic carbon and leaving group in the opening step.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Same bonds, opposite directions

Cyclohexanol dehydrates to cyclohexene; cyclohexene hydrates back to cyclohexanolAcid-catalysed dehydration (elimination) and hydration (addition) go through the same carbocation. Conditions pick the direction: remove the alkene to drive elimination, flood with water to drive addition.

Try it: in the lab prep, cyclohexene (bp 83 °C) distils out while cyclohexanol (bp 161 °C) stays. Why does that help?

Le Chatelier. Removing a product as it forms pulls the equilibrium toward the alkene.



This is a real undergraduate prep and a good place to correct the claim that “addition is just elimination backwards”. The net bonds are the reverse of each other, and for acid catalysis the intermediates are the same, but the useful conditions differ and many additions and eliminations use completely different reagents and mechanisms (E2 with base versus HBr addition, for instance). The protonated OH leaves as water, a much better leaving group than hydroxide; that idea is the start of tomorrow’s alcohol chemistry.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Back to the mitochondria: aconitase

Citrate loses water to give cis-aconitate, which adds water back to give isocitrateElimination: the OH leaves the central carbon and an H leaves a β CH₂. Addition: water adds back with OH on the other carbon. Net result: a tertiary alcohol becomes a secondary one.

Try it: why go to the trouble? (Hint: what happens to isocitrate next?)

A secondary alcohol can be oxidised to a ketone; a tertiary one can’t. The next enzyme, isocitrate dehydrogenase, does exactly that. That’s tomorrow’s topic.



Close the loop with the opening story. Have students identify the α carbon (the one bearing OH in citrate) and the β carbon that loses H. In the enzyme both steps are anti, and the enzyme’s chiral pocket means only one stereoisomer of isocitrate forms, unlike the racemic HBr addition we just saw. Don’t go into the iron-sulfur cluster; the chemistry students need is the elimination–addition pair. The oxidation question sets up Day 13: alcohols and redox.

Most of these come from skipping a step of the procedure: finding every β carbon, counting arrows, checking both ends of an alkene. Every row maps onto an exercise, so a student who recognises their own mistake knows where to practise.
