Run through the procedure once more: for an elimination, find α, find every β, decide E1 or E2 from the base and substrate, draw the arrows, then list the alkenes and check E/Z. For an addition, push the π pair to the electrophile, pick the more stable intermediate, then think about faces. Point to the exercises: problems 1 to 12 are the core, 13 to 20 are optional transfer. Tomorrow picks up exactly where aconitase left off.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
1. Which carbon is secondary?
Classify the carbon bearing Br in CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃.






Check your answer





It is secondary because it is directly bonded to two carbon atoms. The molecule containing four carbons does not make the reacting centre tertiary.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
2. What does SN2 leave behind?
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br, give products and net charge.






Check your answer





CH₃OH + Br⁻; total charge is minus one. The C–Br pair goes to Br while hydroxide makes C–O.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 3. What happens when both concentrations double?
text:
3. What happens when both concentrations double?
Use the supplied simple SN2 rate law k[RX][Nu]. Keep temperature and solvent fixed.






Check your answer





The initial rate becomes fourfold because each concentration contributes a factor of two. This does not by itself predict a fourfold isolated yield.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
text:
4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
Explain why priorities must still be checked after an SN2 replacement.






Check your answer





The reacting geometry inverts, but replacing one substituent can change CIP priorities. Assign the new priorities before translating geometry into an R/S label.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 5. What follows water capture in SN1?
text:
5. What follows water capture in SN1?
Water adds to a carbocation. Is the immediate product an ordinary neutral alcohol?






Check your answer





No. Oxygen has three bonds and formal charge plus one, giving a protonated alcohol. A base such as another water must remove a proton to give the neutral alcohol.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
text:
6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
A carbocation is planar. What does that suggest, and what qualification is needed?






Check your answer





Both faces can be accessible, giving both configurations when a stereocentre forms. Ion pairs and the molecular environment can bias attack, so exact 50:50 is not universal.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Classify reacting carbons, draw substitution mechanisms and explain how the conditions affect the pathway. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
A nucleophile donates a pair to saturated carbon; a leaving group takes the old bonding pair. SN2 couples these changes and inverts the reacting geometry. SN1 ionises first and then captures a carbocation. Methyl/primary/secondary/tertiary counts carbon neighbours at the reacting carbon. Conditions determine which model applies.
Worked starting example. For OH⁻+CH₃Br, oxygen gains a C–O bond and becomes neutral in CH₃OH; Br receives the C–Br pair as Br⁻. No carbocation appears in this concerted example. A neutral incoming water or ammonia instead acquires positive charge before a later proton transfer.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
1. Classify four centres
Draw CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃CBr. Classify each carbon bonded to Br and explain your counting rule.






Hint





Count carbon neighbours directly attached to the Br-bearing carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The classes are methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary, with zero, one, two and three carbon neighbours respectively. The total carbon count of the whole molecule is not the classification criterion.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
2. Same formula, different accessibility
Draw 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane. Circle the reaction centre and compare backside crowding under otherwise comparable SN2 conditions.






Hint





Their formulas match; the local carbon environment differs.









Worked answer and reasoning





The terminal reacting carbon in 1-bromobutane is primary and generally less hindered than the secondary carbon in 2-bromobutane. This favours SN2 access for the primary example, without establishing a universal rate ratio.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
3. Construct the methyl mechanism
Draw the concerted OH⁻ + CH₃Br SN2 step, showing the leaving pair and net charge.






Hint





Both bond changes occur in one elementary step.









Worked answer and reasoning





OH lone pair → C and C–Br pair → Br produce CH₃OH + Br⁻. Total charge is −1. A methyl carbocation is not an intermediate in this model.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
4. Change the incoming group
Assume an SN2 displacement of CH₃Br by I⁻ in a suitable medium. Draw the bond changes and products without claiming the equilibrium position.






Hint





Use iodine as pair donor and keep bromide as the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





The I pair forms C–I while C–Br breaks to Br⁻, producing CH₃I + Br⁻. The same electron-flow pattern applies. Conditions and relative activities are needed to discuss extent of reaction.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
5. Build an ether
Assume suitable dry SN2 conditions for CH₃CH₂O⁻ + CH₃CH₂Br. Draw the new bond and both products. Why is the organic product neutral?






Hint





The alkoxide oxygen changes from one bond to two.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ and Br⁻. Oxygen donates its pair to carbon and becomes a neutral two-bond ether oxygen. Net charge remains −1, now carried by bromide.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
6. Let ammonia attack
Draw the first SN2 step of NH₃ + CH₃Br. A proposed answer CH₃NH₂ + Br⁻ is missing something: identify it.






Hint





The attacking nitrogen initially carries three H atoms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The immediate product is CH₃NH₃⁺ + Br⁻. Nitrogen gains a fourth bond and positive charge. Neutral methylamine requires a separate proton-transfer step; it cannot lose H without a proton acceptor.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
7. Finish the amine proton transfer
Draw the possible equilibrium proton transfer from CH₃NH₃⁺ to another NH₃. Show both arrows and all products; do not assume quantitative deprotonation.






Hint





Ammonia is the base in this second event.









Worked answer and reasoning





An NH₃ lone pair takes H from methylammonium; the original N–H pair returns to methylamine N. Products are CH₃NH₂ and NH₄⁺. Charge +1 is conserved, and the nitrogen roles differ between attack and deprotonation. This is a valid proton-transfer possibility, not a claim that equilibrium intrinsically favours complete deprotonation. Amounts and reaction conditions, including excess ammonia, affect the resulting mixture.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
8. Use the SN2 rate model
For rate=k[RX][Nu], predict the initial-rate factor when [RX] is doubled and [Nu] tripled at fixed temperature and solvent.






Hint





Multiply the independent concentration factors.









Worked answer and reasoning





The rate increases sixfold in the supplied simple model. The calculation describes initial kinetics and does not imply a sixfold equilibrium conversion or yield.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
9. Hold the rate constant
In the same rate model, [RX] is halved while [Nu] is doubled. Predict the rate factor and state the assumptions.






Hint





One factor offsets the other if k is unchanged.









Worked answer and reasoning





The predicted initial rate is unchanged: 0.5×2=1. Temperature, solvent and the applicable mechanism must remain comparable; changing those can change k or the mechanism.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
10. Reject an obstructed pathway
Compare CH₃CH₂Br and (CH₃)₃CBr for direct backside substitution by the same nucleophile. Why should a tertiary substrate not be assigned SN2 merely because the nucleophile is strong?






Hint





Draw the carbon groups around the reaction centre.









Worked answer and reasoning





Three carbon substituents strongly obstruct backside approach at the tertiary centre. A strong donor cannot remove this geometric requirement; elimination or a stepwise route may compete depending on conditions. Primary ethyl is much more accessible.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
11. Begin a tertiary SN1 route
For (CH₃)₃CBr in an ionising aqueous medium, draw C–Br heterolysis and label the product charges.






Hint





The departing group receives the entire C–Br pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻. The tertiary carbocation is more stabilised than a methyl cation, and the medium can stabilise separated charge. Ionisation does not yet specify the final capture or elimination outcome.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
12. Capture with water
Draw H₂O attack on (CH₃)₃C⁺. Count oxygen bonds in the immediate product.






Hint





Use a water lone pair, not a hydrogen, to make the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The oxonium product is (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Oxygen has three bonds and charge +1. Writing the neutral alcohol at this stage would silently remove a proton.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
13. Obtain neutral alcohol
Use H₂O to deprotonate (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Include the species made from the base.






Hint





Water becomes hydronium after accepting H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are (CH₃)₃COH and H₃O⁺. The base pair forms O–H and the original oxonium O–H pair returns to its oxygen. The net charge is +1 before and after.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
14. Balance the overall aqueous route
Combine tertiary ionisation, water capture and water deprotonation into one net equation starting from (CH₃)₃CBr. Include bromide.






Hint





Two waters appear in the explicit overall accounting.









Worked answer and reasoning





(CH₃)₃CBr + 2 H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. This represents the selected substitution path; it does not exclude competing elimination. Atoms and overall zero charge balance.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
15. Assign a particular inversion
Start with (S)-2-bromobutane and assume stereospecific SN2 replacement of Br by OH. Assign the product configuration by checking priorities rather than just changing the letter.






Hint





For each structure, rank the heteroatom group, ethyl, methyl and H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Both Br and OH are highest priority in their respective structures; ethyl outranks methyl and H is lowest. Backside geometric inversion therefore gives (R)-butan-2-ol in this particular example. A different replacement could change the priority order and the letter relationship.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
16. Explain two-face access
A planar carbocation reacts in an achiral medium to form a stereocentre. Explain why both configurations may form and why an exactly 50:50 mixture is not guaranteed in every SN1 reaction.






Hint





Distinguish an isolated planar model from an actual ion pair and environment.









Worked answer and reasoning





Both faces of a planar intermediate may be accessible. Nearby leaving-group ions or other environmental constraints can bias capture, so the geometric argument supports both-face reaction without promising an exact racemic ratio in every experiment.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
17. Activate an alcohol
Draw CH₃CH₂OH protonation by H₃O⁺ and name the better departing group after protonation. Do not assume a primary carbocation forms.






Hint





Change the oxygen protonation state before discussing departure.









Worked answer and reasoning





The alcohol gives CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ plus H₂O. Neutral water is a better leaving group than hydroxide. That activation allows suitable substitution pathways, but a primary substrate still should not be forced into an unsupported SN1 carbocation model.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
18. Keep solvent claims controlled
A student predicts identical rates for CH₃Br + OH⁻ in every solvent because the two reactant formulas are unchanged. Give a chemically justified objection.






Hint





The medium can alter ion stabilisation and donor availability.









Worked answer and reasoning





Solvation changes the energies and effective reactivity of the charged nucleophile and transition state. Keeping formulas the same does not keep k unchanged. State solvent and temperature before transferring rate comparisons between experiments.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
19. Repair an atom-loss error
A proposed tertiary-water mechanism changes (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺ directly to (CH₃)₃COH and writes no other species. Add a valid missing step.






Hint





Supply a base and show where the departing proton goes.









Worked answer and reasoning





Another water takes H⁺ while the oxonium O–H pair returns to O, producing alcohol and H₃O⁺. The corrected step conserves H atoms and charge +1.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
20. Name the competing route
From (CH₃)₃C⁺ in water, draw removal of a β-H and the resulting alkene. How does this differ from water attack at carbon?






Hint





The C–H pair can form a C=C bond to the cationic centre.









Worked answer and reasoning





Water acting as base removes β-H, giving 2-methylpropene and hydronium through E1. Water acting as nucleophile at carbon instead starts the alcohol-forming SN1 path. The common intermediate permits competing outcomes.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 11: Exercises — Substitution
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1–2 minutes). With [RX]=0.050 mol/L and [Nu]=0.100 mol/L, use the supplied illustrative constants below to calculate both initial rates. Predict what happens when only [Nu] doubles.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Hold [RX] fixed while changing [Nu], then hold [Nu] fixed while changing [RX]. Set nucleophile to zero, and then substrate to zero. Find the nucleophile concentration where the two model lines cross. Use the reset to return to the named starting case.
Explain (2 minutes). Which model changes with nucleophile concentration and why? Why does a crossing of these assumed laws not identify the real mechanism of an arbitrary substrate? Report rates with units.


Supplied model and its limits
Supplied models: v₁=k₁[RX] with k₁=0.010 s⁻¹; v₂=k₂[RX][Nu] with k₂ = 0.100 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Concentrations are mol/L, and rates are mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. These constants are illustrative teaching inputs, not measured values for a named chemical. The two laws are compared as separate assumed pathways; this tool does not choose SN1/SN2 from substrate identity or calculate product competition.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
About this lecture
Every breath out carries CO₂ that your red blood cells first turned into bicarbonate. The enzyme that does it, carbonic anhydrase, holds a hydroxide on a zinc ion. That hydroxide pushes a lone pair onto the carbon of CO₂, and a C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. The enzyme makes this happen about ten million times faster, without changing where the equilibrium lies.
Today we learn the language that describes that event:

Curved arrows: each one moves a pair of electrons from a source to a sink
Bookkeeping: atoms, charges and four bonds to carbon after every step
Three core steps: proton transfer, one-step substitution, addition to C=O
Energy profiles: transition states, intermediates and barriers
Catalysts: a faster path between the same start and end

Yesterday’s stereochemistry comes back today: the SN2 step flips a carbon inside out.

Open with the carbonic anhydrase story because it contains the whole lecture in one reaction: a lone pair attacks an electron-poor carbon, a pi pair moves to oxygen, a proton gets shuffled around, and a catalyst speeds things up without moving the equilibrium. Don’t draw the mechanism yet; promise that by the end of the hour everyone can. Frame curved arrows as bookkeeping, not magic: they are the way chemists keep track of which electrons ended up where. Mention that mechanisms are the backbone of Weeks 3 and 4, so time spent getting the arrows right today pays back every single day after.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Curved arrows move pairs of electrons
text:
Curved arrows move pairs of electrons

Methanol gives its O–H proton to hydroxideThe tail sits on a lone pair or a bond. The head points to where that pair ends up: a new bond or a new lone pair.

Try it: in the products, which oxygen is in water and which is in methoxide?

B is in water, A stays in methoxide. Only the proton moves; oxygen atoms never hop between molecules in a proton transfer.



Walk through the two arrows slowly. Arrow one: a lone pair on hydroxide oxygen B becomes the new O–H bond. Arrow two: the old O–H bond pair in methanol collapses onto oxygen A, which now has three lone pairs and a negative charge. Stress that an arrow never shows an atom moving; it shows a pair of electrons moving, and the atoms follow. The labels A and B are the point of the try-it. Many students instinctively put oxygen A in the water because “the H went over there”. Count charges together: −1 on the left, −1 on the right. Mention that the double arrow just says this is an equilibrium; which side wins is an acid-strength question from Day 3, and arrows alone don’t answer it.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A neutral base becomes a cation
text:
A neutral base becomes a cation

Ammonia takes a proton from HClNitrogen’s lone pair becomes the new N–H bond. Nitrogen now has four bonds and no lone pair, so it carries +1. Chloride keeps the old bonding pair, so it carries −1.

Try it: a student draws an arrow from the H of H₃O⁺ to ammonia. What’s wrong?

The arrow runs backwards. A proton has no electrons to give, so the tail must start on nitrogen’s lone pair and point at H, with a second arrow from the O–H bond to O.



This is the same pattern as the last slide with a neutral base. Make the point that a neutral molecule can be the electron source. The most common arrow error of the whole course is drawing the arrow in the direction the proton travels. Say it plainly: arrows follow electrons, protons go the other way. Check the charge balance: 0 on the left, +1 and −1 on the right, so still 0 overall. Ammonium and chloride are the ions in ammonium chloride, the white smoke you see when bottles of ammonia and concentrated HCl are opened near each other.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Charges follow the electron count









atom
before the step
after the step
formal charge




N of NH₃ → NH₄⁺
3 bonds, 1 lone pair
4 bonds, 0 lone pairs
0 → +1


O of HO⁻ → H₂O
1 bond, 3 lone pairs
2 bonds, 2 lone pairs
−1 → 0


O of CH₃OH → CH₃O⁻
2 bonds, 2 lone pairs
1 bond, 3 lone pairs
0 → −1


Cl of HCl → Cl⁻
1 bond, 3 lone pairs
0 bonds, 4 lone pairs
0 → −1



An atom whose lone pair becomes a bond goes up by one. An atom that receives a bond pair goes down by one. The total charge never changes.

This is Day 1’s formal-charge rule applied to a moving picture. Ask students to read across each row and predict the charge before you reveal it. The rule of thumb in the last line makes most mechanisms self-checking: the atom at the tail of a lone-pair arrow becomes more positive, the atom at the head of a bond-breaking arrow becomes more negative. Warn against “fixing” a charge by moving it somewhere else at the end. If the totals don’t match, an arrow is wrong or missing.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Sources and sinks

Electron-pair sources and acceptorsA nucleophile gives a pair to an atom; an electrophile accepts it. Polar bonds tell you where the sink is.

Try it: the carbonyl C is δ+. Is acetaldehyde a carbocation?

No. δ+ is a partial charge from unequal sharing; every atom in CH₃CHO has formal charge 0.



Teach students to look for these two things before drawing anything: where is a lone pair (or later in the course, a pi bond) that could be given away, and where is an atom attached to something more electronegative. The electronegative partner, O or Br or Cl, pulls the shared pair and leaves its neighbour electron-poor. Point out water in the top row: neutral molecules are perfectly good sources. The try-it targets a very common confusion between δ+ and a formal +1; a carbocation has only three bonds, while the carbonyl carbon has four.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Same reagent, different role

Hydroxide as a nucleophile and as a baseBase and nucleophile aren’t fixed labels. They name what this pair is doing in this step: attacking H makes it a base, attacking another atom (usually C) makes it a nucleophile.

Students like to sort reagents into boxes: “hydroxide is a base”. Break that habit now. Both rows use the same lone pair; the difference is the atom it lands on. In Week 3 you’ll see the competition between these two roles directly: hydroxide meeting an alkyl halide can either substitute at carbon (SN2) or pull off a proton next door (E2). Which one wins depends on the substrate and conditions, and that’s exactly the question of Day 12. For today, just make students name the attacked atom before naming the role.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
SN2: two arrows, one step

Hydroxide substitutes bromide on bromomethaneThe new C–O bond forms as the C–Br bond breaks. Carbon never has five bonds and there’s no intermediate. Hydroxide attacks from the back, so the CH₃ umbrella flips.

Try it: the drawing has two arrows. Is it two steps?

No. The number of steps is the number of barriers, not arrows. Both pairs move in one concerted event.



Name it: substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular, SN2. Point out where the nucleophile comes from: directly opposite bromine, where the C–Br antibonding orbital sticks out, which is why the three hydrogens fold over like an umbrella in a gust of wind. On a methyl group the flip is invisible, but yesterday’s stereochemistry tells you what it means on a stereocentre: R becomes S (if priorities stay in the same order). That’s the headline of Day 11. Check the bookkeeping out loud: oxygen goes from −1 to 0, bromine from 0 to −1, total −1 both sides. If someone asks “why doesn’t the reverse happen?”, that’s the next slide but one.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A neutral nucleophile needs a second step
text:
A neutral nucleophile needs a second step

Ammonia substitutes bromide, then a second ammonia removes a protonThe first product is CH₃NH₃⁺: nitrogen has four bonds. Neutral methylamine only appears when another base takes a proton.

Try it: why is CH₃NH₃⁺ not drawn as neutral CH₃NH₂ straight away?

Nitrogen used its lone pair for the C–N bond and kept all three H. Losing an H⁺ needs a real proton acceptor, here a second NH₃.



This mirrors ammonia protonation from earlier, but now the lone pair lands on carbon instead of hydrogen. Students often draw methylamine as the direct product and then can’t balance the H count. Make them count: three N–H bonds before, three after step 1, two after step 2. The second ammonia is why chemists use a large excess of ammonia when making amines this way. Also note that each step is a pattern we already know: an SN2, then a proton transfer. Most mechanisms in this course are just a few of these patterns in a row.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Balanced on paper isn’t the same as real
text:
Balanced on paper isn’t the same as real

Heterolysis of bromomethane and of tert-butyl bromideGiving both bond electrons to Br is valid bookkeeping for both. Only the tert-butyl cation is stable enough to exist. Arrows check electrons; energies decide what happens.

Try it: Br⁻ attacking CH₃OH to kick out OH⁻ balances perfectly. Why doesn’t it happen?

OH⁻ is a poor leaving group. It’s a much stronger base than Br⁻, so the reverse SN2 is uphill; you’d need acid to turn OH into water first (Week 3).



This slide is about the limits of arrow-pushing. A charge-balanced drawing is necessary but not sufficient. The methyl cation is so unstable that bromomethane never ionises; it reacts by SN2 instead. Three methyl groups donate electron density to the cationic carbon, which is why tert-butyl bromide does ionise in water or alcohols. That’s the SN1 pathway of Day 11. The try-it comes from the exercises: same arrow logic, wrong direction energetically. Leaving-group ability tracks the weakness of the leaving base, which links straight back to pKa values from Day 3 (HBr is a far stronger acid than water).

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Addition to C=O: carbon keeps four bonds
text:
Addition to C=O: carbon keeps four bonds

Hydroxide adds to acetaldehydeWhen a nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon, the π pair must move to O. The product is a tetrahedral alkoxide, CH₃CH(OH)O⁻.

Try it: a student keeps C=O and adds the OH. What’s wrong, and what’s the product’s charge?

Carbon would have five bonds. Moving the π pair gives O⁻ with three lone pairs, so the product is CH₃CH(OH)O⁻, charge −1, with C at formal charge 0.



This is the single most important step of Week 4, so it’s worth getting right now. Use Day 1’s valence check: the carbonyl carbon already has four bonds (C=O counts two), so a new bond has to come at the cost of an old one. The weakest one is the pi bond, and its pair goes to the more electronegative atom. Watch for two errors: the five-bonded carbon, and the right atoms but no charge drawn on the oxygen. Some students then “fix” the charge by putting +1 on carbon, which neither the arrows nor the total charge support. The carbon also changes shape, from trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Two steps: add, then protonate

Hydride adds to acetone, then water protonates the alkoxideNaBH₄ delivers H⁻ to carbon. The alkoxide then takes H⁺ from water. Every new H must come from a named species.

Try it: a student converts (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ into (CH₃)₂CHOH with no other reagent. Complete the step.

Add water as the donor. The O⁻ lone pair takes a water H, the O–H pair goes to water’s O, and the products are propan-2-ol and HO⁻. The total charge stays −1.



Two caveats to say aloud. First, free hydride ions don’t float around in solution; H⁻ is shorthand for a hydride delivered from the B–H bond of borohydride. Second, the first product is the alkoxide, not the alcohol; the workup supplies the proton. This is exactly how a ketone is reduced to an alcohol, which is a Day 13 reaction. The habit we’re building is that protons don’t appear from nowhere: if an H shows up, point to where it came from and draw what is left behind.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Resonance is not a reaction

Acetate resonance contributors and acetic acid dissociation








resonance ↔︎
equilibrium ⇌




what moves
only electrons, on paper
nuclei: an H goes to another molecule


how many species
one real ion
two different species




Students meet curved arrows in resonance too, so they need to know the difference. In acetate, the two drawings are not two molecules flipping back and forth. The real ion is one hybrid with two identical C–O bonds of about 1.5 bond order, and the negative charge shared over both oxygens. That’s why acetic acid is more acidic than ethanol (Day 3). The bottom equation is a real chemical change: a proton leaves acetic acid and ends up on water. Use the right arrow for each: double-headed for resonance, equilibrium half-arrows for a reaction.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Energy profile of one step

A one-step profile with forward and reverse barriersThe top of the hill is the transition state (‡): it lasts for one bond vibration and can’t be isolated. ΔG‡ sets the rate; ΔG sets the equilibrium.

Try it: what’s the reverse barrier here?

65 kJ/mol. Measure from the products up to the same transition state: 45 − (−20) = 65.



Every elementary step has one transition state at a maximum. Emphasise that each barrier is measured from its own starting valley. Reverse barrier errors usually come from measuring from the reactants. For the SN2 we drew earlier, the transition state is the moment where C–O is half formed and C–Br half broken, with the three hydrogens flat. You can draw it in brackets with a double dagger. A useful rule of thumb: around 80 to 90 kJ/mol is the barrier that lets a reaction proceed at a convenient rate at room temperature.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Intermediates sit in valleys

A two-step profile with an intermediateAn intermediate is a real species with a lifetime. It sits in a minimum between two transition states. Count steps by counting maxima: two maxima and one valley means two elementary steps.

Contrast the two words carefully: an intermediate is a minimum and could in principle be observed or trapped; a transition state is a maximum and can’t. In the hydration reaction coming up, the alkoxide is the intermediate between the hydroxide-addition step and the protonation step. Point out that the SN2 profile from the previous slide has no valley, because it has no intermediate. The highest transition state in a multi-step path usually controls the overall rate.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Favourable is not the same as fast
text:
Favourable is not the same as fast

Favourable but slow versus fast but unfavourableSugar plus O₂ is hugely downhill, yet a sugar bowl doesn’t burst into flames: the barrier is high. Endpoints set K; barriers set the rate. Given paths with 15 and 25 kJ/mol barriers, the 15 one is faster.

This is a place where everyday intuition misleads. Knowing ΔG tells you where a reaction ends up if you wait long enough; it says nothing about how long that takes. Knowing a barrier tells you about speed, but nothing about the final ratio of products. The 15 versus 25 kJ/mol example is from the exercises: the lower barrier wins on rate, all else equal, but neither number tells you the equilibrium composition. Your body burns sugar, of course, but only through enzymes that offer lower-barrier paths, which is the bridge to the next slide.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Catalysts are regenerated

Base-catalysed hydration of acetaldehydeAdd the steps and cross out what appears on both sides: CH₃CHO + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH(OH)₂. Hydroxide is used in step 1 and returned in step 2, so it’s a catalyst; the alkoxide is an intermediate.

The two steps are things we already drew today: carbonyl addition, then a proton transfer from water. Sum them on the board and cancel species: OH− appears on the left of step 1 and the right of step 2; the alkoxide appears on the right of step 1 and the left of step 2. What’s left is the net hydration. The distinction to make crisp: a catalyst goes in first and comes out last; an intermediate is made first and consumed later. Carbonic anhydrase from the opening works the same way, with zinc-bound hydroxide doing step 1. Carbonyl hydration and its cousins return in Week 4.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A catalyst lowers the barrier, not ΔG
text:
A catalyst lowers the barrier, not ΔG

Catalysed and uncatalysed profiles between the same endpointsThe catalysed path is different, often with more steps, but it starts and ends at the same place. Both directions get faster, so equilibrium is reached sooner but K doesn’t change.

Return to carbonic anhydrase: the enzyme doesn’t make more bicarbonate at equilibrium; it gets there millions of times faster, in both directions. That matters because in your lungs the same enzyme runs the reaction backwards to release CO2. A catalyst that speeded only the forward reaction would be a perpetual-motion machine. Point out that the green path has two humps, so it also has an intermediate. A lower highest barrier doesn’t require fewer steps.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




arrow from H⁺ to the base

carbon with five bonds after an addition
move the π pair to O

recount: total charge is conserved


H appears from nowhere
name the proton donor and its conjugate base

it lowers barriers both ways; K is unchanged




Read out each mistake and ask the room to give the fix before you show it. Every row corresponds to at least one exercise: 2 for the reversed arrow, 6 and 17 for the five-bonded carbon and missing charge, 8 for the missing proton donor, 3 and 12 for counting steps, 4 and 11 for the balanced-but-wrong drawings, and 15 for catalysis.

Next: substitution, SN2 versus SN1 (Day 11). Practice: exercises · self-check

Run the checklist once more as the take-home habit: for each step, every arrow starts on a pair, carbon never exceeds four bonds, atoms and total charge balance, every new H has a donor. Then ask whether the step makes sense energetically. Close the loop with carbonic anhydrase: students can now draw its key step (zinc hydroxide adds to CO2, pi pair to oxygen) and explain why the enzyme speeds the reaction without changing its equilibrium. Days 9 and 10 are consolidation days; Day 11 builds directly on the SN2 and heterolysis slides.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?
text:
1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?






Check your answer





No: the two methyl substituents are identical. A simple tetrahedral stereocentre requires four different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.
text:
2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.






Check your answer





OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. Oxygen outranks carbon. For the carbon tie, the COOH carbon has O,O,O in the comparison, whereas CH₃ has H,H,H.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.
text:
3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.






Check your answer





S. The 1→2→3 trace appears clockwise, but the lowest-priority H is horizontal and points toward the viewer, so invert.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 4. Can propene have E and Z forms?
text:
4. Can propene have E and Z forms?






Check your answer





No. Its terminal alkene carbon bears two identical H substituents. Each alkene carbon needs two different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?
text:
5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?






Check your answer





No. A meso compound has stereocentres but is achiral because of its overall symmetry. Meso-tartaric acid is an example.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?
text:
6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?






Check your answer





40% ee in favour of R. The major enantiomer makes up 70%, not 40%, of the two-enantiomer mixture.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?
text:
7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?






Check your answer





No. R/S specifies configuration and (+)/(−) is a measured rotation sign; there is no universal mapping.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text: Draw and compare stereoisomers, assign R/S and E/Z, and explain each priority decision. Review the lecture when you need a drawing convention. Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when a practical session also includes R.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
1. Find a candidate centre
Draw CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list all four substituents at CH(OH). Is it a simple tetrahedral stereocentre?






Hint





Compare complete groups, not only their first atoms.









Worked check





It has OH, H, CH₃, COOH: four different groups. It is a tetrahedral stereocentre.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
2. Reject a false stereocentre
Compare CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and explain why a wedge on OH cannot make the central carbon stereogenic.






Hint





Two methyl groups remain identical regardless of drawing style.









Worked check





The central carbon has two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not a simple stereocentre. Wedges describe geometry but do not change group identity.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
3. Rank the first attachment atoms
For a centre attached directly to Br, Cl, OH, H, give CIP priority. Do not use total group size.






Hint





Atomic number decides the first shell.









Worked check





Br>Cl>O(in OH)>H. This compares directly attached atoms, not the number of atoms in each substituent.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
section: 4. Resolve the carbon tie in lactic acid
text:
4. Resolve the carbon tie in lactic acid
Rank OH, COOH, CH₃, H. Explain the duplicate-atom convention for C=O in this comparison.






Hint





OH attaches through O; COOH and CH₃ both attach through C.









Worked check





OH>COOH>CH₃>H. For the carbon tie, COOH compares as O, O, O and methyl as H, H, H. The duplicate entry is bookkeeping, not an extra real O atom.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
5. Read a Fischer depth convention
Draw a cross with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left, H right. Which bonds point toward and away from you?






Hint





Fischer is a convention, not an ordinary planar cross.









Worked check





Horizontal OH/H bonds point toward; vertical COOH/CH₃ bonds point away. The central crossing is the stereocentre carbon.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
6. Assign the left-OH Fischer
Use the preceding projection and priorities OH1, COOH2, CH₃3, H4. Trace 1→2→3 and assign R/S with justification.






Hint





The lowest-priority group is horizontal and therefore forward.









Worked check





The trace appears clockwise, but H4 points toward you, so reverse the apparent result. This configuration is S.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
7. Assign the mirror Fischer
Keep COOH top and CH₃ bottom, but put H left and OH right. Assign R/S and its relation to the preceding structure.






Hint





One interchange at a single stereocentre inverts configuration.









Worked check





The new projection is R. It is the nonsuperimposable mirror/enantiomer of the S-lactic-acid drawing, with unchanged connectivity.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
8. Rotate a Fischer by 180°
Rotate the entire S projection in the plane by 180°. State each new label position and whether configuration changes.






Hint





All four labels rotate together.









Worked check





CH₃ becomes top, COOH bottom, H left, OH right. The configuration stays S. A complete valid 180° Fischer rotation preserves configuration.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
9. Test a 90° Fischer rotation
Explain why simply rotating a Fischer cross 90° is unsafe as an identity operation.






Hint





It changes which group positions are interpreted as horizontal versus vertical.









Worked check





The implied toward/away pattern changes under the convention, so a 90° Fischer rotation changes the represented configuration. Redraw using a valid 3D transformation instead.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
10. Assign Z-but-2-ene
Draw CH₃CH=CHCH₃ with both methyl groups on the same side. Rank the groups at each end and assign E/Z.






Hint





Methyl carbon outranks H at each alkene carbon.









Worked check





The higher-priority groups are together, giving Z-but-2-ene. Rank each end independently rather than treating left-to-right page direction as a descriptor.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
11. Assign E-but-2-ene
Draw but-2-ene with methyls on opposite sides. Explain why ordinary single-bond rotation is not the relevant interconversion.






Hint





The arrangement is around a C=C bond.









Worked check





Opposite high-priority methyl groups give E. Interconversion requires changing the double-bond arrangement; it is not a freely rotating anti/gauche relationship.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
12. Check whether E/Z is defined
For CH₂=CHCH₃ and (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, test the two-different-substituents requirement at both ends.






Hint





One identical pair at either end is enough to fail.









Worked check





Neither qualifies. Propene has H/H at one end; the second molecule has CH₃/CH₃ at one end. No E/Z descriptor applies to those double bonds.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
13. Classify a four-pair set
Classify ethanol/ether, anti/gauche butane, R/S-lactic acid, and E/Z-but-2-ene by their structural relationship.






Hint





Ask connectivity, rotation, mirror relation in that order.









Worked check





Respectively: constitutional isomers; conformers; enantiomers; diastereomers. E/Z pairs are stereoisomers that are not mirror-related.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
14. Use a two-centre framework carefully
Use CH₃CH(Br)CH(Cl)CH₃ (2-bromo-3-chlorobutane), numbered from the Br end. Compare the supplied configurations (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) and (2R,3R)/(2R,3S). Classify their relationships; no new R/S assignment from a drawing is required.






Hint





Mirror inversion reverses every centre.









Worked check





RR/SS are enantiomers; RR/RS are diastereomers. The symmetry assumption prevents a hidden meso equivalence from invalidating the simple classification.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
15. Examine meso-tartaric acid
Draw a Fischer with COOH top/bottom and OH right/H left at both central carbons. Explain why two stereocentres do not force chirality.






Hint





Inspect the equivalence of its upper and lower halves.









Worked check





The whole structure has an internal symmetry relationship and is meso-tartaric acid, achiral despite stereocentres. Overall superimposability matters, not centre count alone.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
16. Reject an R, S shortcut
A student calls every molecule with one R and one S centre meso. Give the missing structural condition.






Hint





Descriptors do not establish equivalence of the two ends.









Worked check





The complete molecule must have appropriate symmetry/superimposability with its mirror. An unsymmetrical R, S molecule can be chiral.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
17. Calculate 70:30 excess
A pure two-enantiomer composition is 70 % R and 30 % S. Compute ee and explain why it is not 70%.






Hint





Subtract the two populations.









Worked check





ee=|70−30|=40% in favour of R. Major-enantiomer percentage and excess are different quantities; the excess is the imbalance after pairing equal R/S amounts.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
18. Recover composition from excess
Assume only R/S components. A sample has 80 % ee in favour of R. Solve for the two percentages.






Hint





Use R+S=100 and R−S=80.









Worked check





R=90% and S=10%. Adding equations gives 2R=180. Calling this 80 % R would give the wrong excess.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
19. Separate configuration and rotation
Does an R label establish positive optical rotation or a stronger receptor effect? State what each additional claim requires.






Hint





Configuration is assigned; rotation/effect is measured.









Worked check





No universal mapping connects R/S to(+)/(−) or biological magnitude. Optical rotation needs specified measurements; receptor effects require appropriate experimental evidence in a chiral environment.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
text:
20. Distinguish ee from total purity
R:S is 95:5 among the measured enantiomeric components. Compute ee and explain whether solvent contamination is excluded.






Hint





The measured ratio may describe only a subset of all material.









Worked check





The enantiomeric excess is 90 % R. The ratio does not exclude solvent or other molecular impurities; enantiomeric composition and total chemical purity are separate questions.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry
section: R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
text:
R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
Question: how unbalanced is each supplied two-enantiomer mixture? The simulated table data/enantiomers.csv contains sample identifiers and percentages of R and S. This model assumes R and S are the only components being counted and have no missing composition. First check that R% + S% = 100.
For this model, ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent). Report the major enantiomer too. Predict the ee for E1 (70% R, 30% S) before running the code.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
mixtures <- read_csv("data/enantiomers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(total_percent = R_percent + S_percent,
         ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent),
         excess = case_when(R_percent > S_percent ~ "R",
                            S_percent > R_percent ~ "S",
                            TRUE ~ "racemic"))
knitr::kable(mixtures, digits = 1)
ggplot(mixtures, aes(sample_id, ee_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Enantiomeric excess (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
Write one sentence about each sample, specifying both composition and ee. If a sample has 80% ee in favour of R, calculate R% and S% by solving R + S = 100 and R − S = 80. Explain why the graph alone does not establish sample purity or optical-rotation sign.






Numerical and chemical check





E1 has 40% ee in favour of R; E2 (50:50) is racemic, 0% ee; E3 (95:5) has 90% ee in favour of R. An 80% R ee corresponds to 90% R and 10% S. Enantiomeric composition does not establish the absence of other chemical contaminants. Without a validated composition measurement and suitable assumptions this is only a calculation on supplied data. R/S alone does not give optical-rotation sign or a biological effect.

Review your work
Choose one corrected mistake and explain the chemical rule that repairs it. Continue with the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 7: Exercises — Stereochemistry

Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Assign the initial configuration yourself using OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. State whether H points toward or away before interpreting the clockwise/counterclockwise trace.
Interchange one selected pair and reassign. Interchange a second pair and explain why two interchanges can restore the original configuration. Compare with the left/right mirror operation.

Take-away

Model and limits

A 180° in-plane Fischer rotation preserves configuration; a 90° layout rotation changes the implied configuration. R/S describes geometry, not measured (+)/(−) optical rotation.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Conformations
text:
About this lecture
Glucose is the most common sugar on Earth. It’s what cellulose, starch and your blood sugar are built from. Of the eight sugars in its family (the D-aldohexoses), it’s the only one whose ring can put every OH group in a relaxed, uncrowded position. That’s no coincidence, and by the end of today you’ll be able to see why.
Today we learn how molecules change shape without breaking bonds:

Conformers: shapes reached by turning a single bond
Newman projections: looking straight down a C–C bond
Energy profiles: why staggered beats eclipsed, and anti beats gauche
Populations: turning an energy gap into “how much of each”
Cyclohexane chairs: axial, equatorial and the ring flip

Last time (Day 3) we followed protons. Today we keep every bond and follow the shape.

Open with glucose. Ask: why would nature settle on this particular sugar? There are many reasons, but one is shape. In its chair, β-glucose has all five big substituents pointing outward around the rim, with nothing crowding anything else. We’ll draw that chair at the very end, so the opening question gets answered by the students themselves. Frame the day as “3D thinking”: a skeletal drawing tells you connectivity, but molecules are floppy 3D objects. Rotation about single bonds happens billions of times a second at room temperature. Today is about which shapes are preferred and by how much. Tomorrow (stereochemistry) is about 3D differences that can’t be undone by rotation.

title: Conformations
text:
Same molecule, many shapes

Conformers versus constitutional isomersTurning a C–C single bond changes the shape but keeps every bonded neighbour. Those shapes are conformers: one molecule, not isomers. Butane and 2-methylpropane have different neighbours, so they’re constitutional isomers.

The key test is connectivity. Trace the carbon chain in anti and gauche butane: C1–C2–C3–C4 in both, nothing broken. To get from butane to 2-methylpropane you’d have to break a C–C bond and make a new one, which is a chemical reaction. Conformers interconvert in a fraction of a nanosecond at room temperature, so you can’t put anti-butane in one bottle and gauche-butane in another. Probe the misconception “different drawing = different compound”. Ask: “If I rotate my model, have I made a new compound?” No.

title: Conformations
section: Pick a bond, then pick where your eye is
text:
Pick a bond, then pick where your eye is

Looking along the C2–C3 bond of butaneIn a Newman projection you look straight down one bond. The front carbon is the dot where its three bonds meet; the rear carbon is the circle, with bonds coming out from behind it.

Try it: you now look from C3 toward C2 instead. Which carbon is the dot?

C3. Whichever carbon is nearer your eye is the front carbon, so the roles swap and you have to redraw both groups of three.



Always say out loud which bond and which direction: “along C2 to C3”. Each carbon on that bond has three other groups: C2 has C1 (a methyl) and two H; C3 has C4 (a methyl) and two H. Students often forget the H atoms or draw all six groups on one carbon. Encourage a physical model here if you have them: hold the model so you look down the bond, and the Newman projection is literally what you see. In this drawing the methyls point in opposite directions, which is the anti conformer we’ll meet properly in a moment.

title: Conformations
text:
Staggered and eclipsed

Staggered and eclipsed ethane
Staggered: rear bonds sit between front bonds, 60° apart.
Eclipsed: rear bonds hide behind front bonds, 0° apart. We draw them slightly offset so you can see them.

The angle between a front bond and a rear bond is the dihedral angle.

Ethane is the simplest case because all six groups are H. Turning the rear carbon by 60° goes from staggered to eclipsed, another 60° gives staggered again. Point out that eclipsed H atoms only overlap on the page; they’re on different carbons, about 2.3 Å apart in space, and they don’t bond to each other. The dihedral angle is the angle you’d measure on the Newman face between a chosen front bond and a chosen rear bond. It’s the x-axis of every energy plot today.

title: Conformations
text:
Ethane’s energy as it turns

Ethane torsional energyEclipsed costs about 12 kJ/mol (torsional strain, roughly 4 per H/H pair). A full turn passes three identical staggered minima, at 60°, 180° and 300°.

Try it: is every single bond free to rotate?

No. There’s always some barrier, rings lock bonds in place, and some “single” bonds have partial double-bond character, like the C–N bond of amides (Week 4).



12 kJ/mol is small compared with thermal energy at room temperature, so ethane rotates billions of times per second. That’s why we call it “free rotation”, but free is relative. The staggered minima are equivalent because every substituent is H, so they’re identical in energy. Ask students to read the minima off the axis: 60, 180, 300. Students who have a curve with only one minimum have forgotten that the rear carbon has three equivalent bonds. The torsional strain is the extra energy from bonding electron pairs being lined up; the textbook explanation is electron repulsion plus loss of a stabilising orbital overlap, but the number is what matters today.

title: Conformations
text:
Butane: one full turn

Butane through one full turnHold the front CH₃ at 12 o’clock and turn the rear carbon. Track the two CH₃ groups: anti puts them at 180°, gauche at ±60°. Both are staggered.

Try it: how many gauche minima are there in one full turn?

Two, at +60° and −60° (300°). They’re mirror images with equal energy, but they’re distinct conformations.



Hold the front methyl at 12 o’clock and only turn the rear carbon, in 60-degree steps. This is the procedure for exercises 2 to 4. A common mistake is to think “staggered” means “anti”. Gauche is staggered too: no bonds eclipse, but the two methyls are only 60° apart. Count the eclipsed views: one has the methyls on top of each other (syn, 0°), and two have a methyl eclipsing an H (120° and 240°). The two gauche forms are mirror images, a little preview of tomorrow.

title: Conformations
text:
Butane: what each crowding costs

Butane torsional energy


interaction
cost (kJ/mol)




H/H eclipsed
4


CH₃/H eclipsed
6


CH₃/CH₃ eclipsed
11


CH₃/CH₃ gauche
3.8




The costs add up. At 0°: two H/H plus one CH3/CH3 eclipsed, 4 + 4 + 11 = 19. At 120°: one H/H plus two CH3/H, 4 + 6 + 6 = 16. Have students verify one of these themselves. Gauche costs 3.8 kJ/mol even though nothing is eclipsed. That’s steric strain: the two methyls are close enough to bump. Anti is the global minimum because it puts the two biggest groups as far apart as possible. In Week 3 (elimination) you’ll need the anti arrangement again: E2 eliminations need the H and the leaving group anti to each other.

section: Lower energy means more, not all
text:
Lower energy means more, not all
w = e^{-\Delta G/RT} \qquad \text{fraction} = \frac{w}{\sum w}

At 298.15 K, RT = 8.314 × 298.15 ≈ 2479 J/mol. ΔG and RT must use the same units, so ΔG/RT has none.

Try it: what’s the weight of the state with ΔG = 0?

exactly 1, because e⁰ = 1. The reference state always has weight 1. The weights don’t sum to 1 until you normalise them.



This is the calculation in the R task, done by hand once. Walk through the three steps: divide by RT, exponentiate the negative, divide by the sum. The classic unit error is using ΔG in kJ/mol with R in J/(mol K): 3.5/2479 gives a weight of practically 1 and a meaningless 50/50 answer. The other classic error is calling the weights “fractions” before normalising. These ΔG values are a supplied two-state teaching model and already include any degeneracy (both gauche forms are rolled into state B). So don’t multiply by two again. That’s exercise 20.

title: Conformations
section: How the energy gap shifts the balance
text:
How the energy gap shifts the balance

Populations from free-energy gapsEqual energies give 50/50. A bigger gap tilts the balance more, but a finite gap never makes the minor state zero.

Try it: add 1000 J/mol to both states. Do the fractions change?

No. Both weights get the same factor e^(−1000/RT), which cancels on normalising. Only the energy difference matters.



Read the three pairs left to right. Doubling the gap from 3500 to 7000 doesn’t double the minor fraction’s drop; it’s exponential. Every 5.7 kJ/mol at room temperature is a factor of ten. Stress that “disfavoured” isn’t “absent”: even at a 7000 J/mol gap there’s about 6% of B. The common-offset question tests whether students understand that energies are relative. Picking a different zero can’t change any physical prediction.

title: Conformations
section: Equilibrium and rate are different questions
text:
Equilibrium and rate are different questions

Equilibrium versus rateThe gap between A and B sets the equilibrium ratio. The barrier between them sets how fast they interconvert.

Try it: two molecules have the same ΔG between conformers but different barriers. Same rotation rate?

No. Same ratio at equilibrium, but the one with the higher barrier interconverts more slowly.



Point at the two curves: they start and finish at the same heights, so the equilibrium mixture is identical. Only the hill between them differs. A population calculation tells you nothing about speed. This distinction comes back in every kinetics discussion in Weeks 3 and 4, where reaction barriers (activation energies) decide what happens fast. Ask: “If I lower the barrier with a catalyst, does the ratio change?” No, only how fast it’s reached.

title: Conformations
section: Rings: a flat drawing isn’t a flat molecule
text:
Rings: a flat drawing isn’t a flat molecule

Flat ring drawing versus the chairRings stop full rotation. Cyclopropane has to be flat, so its 60° angles are badly strained. Cyclohexane puckers into a chair, where every angle is close to tetrahedral and every C–H is staggered.

The hexagon in a skeletal drawing only states connectivity: six carbons in a ring. If cyclohexane were really flat, its angles would be 120°, too wide for sp3 carbon, and every C–H would be eclipsed. By puckering, it gets roughly 111° angles and fully staggered bonds, so it’s essentially strain-free. That’s why six-membered rings are everywhere in nature: sugars, steroids, many drugs. Cyclopropane can’t pucker, so it carries large angle strain and is unusually reactive. No need to memorise strain energies.

title: Conformations
text:
The chair: axial and equatorial

Axial and equatorial positions in a chairEach carbon has one axial bond (vertical, alternating up and down around the ring) and one equatorial bond (out around the rim, tilted slightly the other way).

Try it: does “equatorial” mean “down”?

No. Equatorial bonds point up on some carbons and down on others. Axial/equatorial is the bond’s direction; up/down is which face of the ring it’s on.



Two separate labelling systems, and students mix them up every year. Axial/equatorial describes the bond direction in this particular chair. Up/down describes which face of the ring the group is on, and that’s fixed by the molecule’s configuration. On a carbon whose axial bond points up, the equatorial bond tilts slightly down, and vice versa. Practise drawing the chair: two parallel long bonds, then the tips; axial bonds are all vertical; equatorial bonds are parallel to the ring bond once removed. Have students try drawing one now.

title: Conformations
text:
The ring flip

A ring flip swaps axial and equatorialA chair can flip into the other chair by turning bonds only. Every axial group becomes equatorial (and back), but up stays up.

Try it: an axial-down group goes through a ring flip. Where does it end up?

Equatorial-down. The flip swaps axial and equatorial, never up and down.



The flip is a conformational change: no bonds break, and at room temperature cyclohexane flips about 100,000 times a second. Follow the same carbon through the flip. The ring tip that pointed up now points down, so its axial bond points down too; the methyl, which can’t change faces, moves into the equatorial slot that still points up. Students often “flip” by mirroring one bond on paper, which turns up into down. Insist they track the whole ring. Exercises 10 and 11 practise both directions.

title: Conformations
text:
Why big groups go equatorial

Why methyl prefers equatorialAn axial methyl crowds the axial H atoms on C3 and C5: 1,3-diaxial interactions. Equatorial is lower by about 7.3 kJ/mol, so w = e^(−7300/2479) ≈ 0.053, giving about 95 : 5 at 25 °C.

The axial methyl points straight up alongside two other axial H atoms on the same face. Each of those contacts is basically a gauche butane interaction, and 2 × 3.8 is about 7.6, close to the measured 7.3. That’s a nice link back to the butane slide. Then use today’s population formula: weight 0.053 relative to 1, so roughly 95% equatorial. Emphasise again: preferred, not exclusive. Bigger groups have bigger preferences: a tert-butyl group is so large that it is effectively locked equatorial.

title: Conformations
section: Cis and trans survive a ring flip
text:
Cis and trans survive a ring flip

cis and trans in a ringCis = both groups on the same face (up/up or down/down); trans = opposite faces. A ring flip changes axial and equatorial, but never the faces.

Try it: a pair of groups is cis in one chair. Can the ring flip make it trans?

No. Each group keeps its face, so cis stays cis. Turning cis into trans means breaking a bond: that’s a different stereoisomer, which is tomorrow’s topic.



In cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane one methyl is always axial and one equatorial; flipping just swaps which one. In the trans isomer the two chairs are diequatorial or diaxial, and the diequatorial one is strongly preferred. Note the wedge drawing on the left shows both methyls hashed (both down) while the chair shows both up. That’s the same molecule seen from the other side; cis just means “same side”. Use this to bridge to stereochemistry: cis/trans is configuration, which no rotation can change, while axial/equatorial is conformation.

title: Conformations
text:
Back to glucose

β-D-glucose in its chairIn β-D-glucose all five big groups, the four OH groups and the CH₂OH, sit equatorial. Every axial position holds a small H, so there are no 1,3-diaxial clashes.

Close the loop with the opening question. Point at each substituent and ask the room: axial or equatorial? All equatorial. The alternating up/down pattern of the OH groups in glucose is exactly what lets them all be equatorial at once. Other six-carbon sugars, such as galactose or mannose, have to put at least one OH axial. Biology builds cellulose, starch and glycogen from this low-strain building block. The detailed sugar chemistry comes later; today the point is that you can now read strain straight off a chair.

title: Conformations
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




calling anti and gauche butane isomers
same neighbours: they’re conformers


“staggered” taken to mean “anti”
gauche is staggered too


forgetting the H atoms on the rear carbon
each carbon has three groups


flipping a chair and turning up into down
a flip swaps axial/equatorial only


ΔG in kJ/mol divided by R in J/(mol K)
use the same units


calling weights “fractions”
divide by the sum first


“the axial conformer is absent”
lower population, not zero


using population to predict speed
rate depends on the barrier




Read each mistake and ask the room for the fix before revealing the row. Every row maps onto exercises: conformers versus isomers (exercise 8), the Newman problems (1 to 7), chair flips (10 to 13), and the population model (15 to 20 and the R task).

title: Conformations
text:
Summary



concept
key fact




conformer

Newman projection
front = dot, rear = circle


ethane

butane
