title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
About this lecture
Yesterday we left two bottles of C₂H₆O on the bench: ethanol boils at 78 °C, dimethyl ether at −24 °C. Same atoms, a 100-degree gap. Today we explain it. And the police breath test? It shines infrared light through your breath and measures how much ethanol absorbs.
Today we learn:

Polarity: why bonds and molecules carry partial charges
Hydrogen bonds: donors, acceptors and how to count them
Properties: boiling points and water solubility from structure
IR spectroscopy: reading the axes and a few key bands
Limits: what one observation can and can’t prove

Yesterday you learned to read a structure; today you use it to predict what a molecule does.

Open by reminding them of the cliffhanger from Day 1: ethanol and dimethyl ether are constitutional isomers, yet one is a drink and the other a spray-can gas. Ask the room for guesses before revealing anything; someone usually says “the OH”, which is exactly right, and today we make that guess precise. The breathalyzer is a nice second hook: evidential breath-alcohol instruments use IR absorption by ethanol’s C–H or C–O bonds, so the second half of the lecture is the physics inside that machine. Stress the theme of the day: structure in, observable property out.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Electronegativity makes bonds polar

Ethanol with partial charges, beside a Pauling electronegativity scaleThe more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons towards itself and gets a partial negative charge, δ−. O and N are the electron-greedy atoms in organic molecules; C–H bonds are close to nonpolar.

Electronegativity is the tug-of-war strength for bonding electrons. The numbers on the scale are Pauling values; students don’t need to memorise them, only the order H ≈ C < N < O. In ethanol the oxygen pulls electron density from both the carbon and the hydrogen, so both neighbours become δ+. Point out that the C–H bonds, which make up most of an organic molecule, are almost nonpolar: that’s why the hydrocarbon part of a molecule behaves like oil. That sentence comes back when we discuss solubility.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Partial charge is not formal charge
text:
Partial charge is not formal charge

Ethanol and ethoxide with oxygen lone pairs and charge bookkeepingδ− describes uneven sharing in a neutral molecule. Formal charge is Day 1’s integer electron count.

Try it: the O in ethanol is δ−. Does it carry a formal charge of −1?

No. Two bonds and two lone pairs give 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. The δ− is a fraction of an electron, not a whole extra one.



This is the most common confusion of the day. A partial charge is a shift of electron density; the molecule as a whole stays neutral. A formal charge is the bookkeeping from yesterday and only appears when an atom deviates from its normal bonding pattern, as in ethoxide, which is ethanol after losing its O–H proton. Ethoxide is a preview of Day 3: removing H+ from an O–H leaves the bonding pair on oxygen. Ask them to say out loud which numbers go into each formal-charge calculation.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Polar bonds, polar molecule? Add the vectors
text:
Polar bonds, polar molecule? Add the vectors

Carbon dioxide bond dipoles cancel; water bond dipoles addEach polar bond is an arrow pointing at its δ− end. The molecular dipole is their vector sum, so shape decides.

Try it: a friend says “CO₂ has two polar bonds, so it’s a polar molecule.” What did they forget?

Geometry. CO₂ is linear, so its two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. Bent water keeps a net dipole.



Draw the arrows on the board as tug-of-war ropes: two equal teams pulling in opposite directions go nowhere. Water is bent (about 104.5°), so its two arrows add to a net dipole pointing at oxygen. Link back to Day 1’s geometry slide: you needed the shapes to do this. CO2 will return in the IR section, where its lack of a permanent dipole turns out to be less important than you’d think. Another example if there’s time: CCl4 is nonpolar for the same reason.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Same size, very different boiling points
text:
Same size, very different boiling points

Butane, propanone and propan-1-ol with similar molar mass and rising boiling points
Dispersion: every molecule has it; grows with size and contact area.
Dipole–dipole: polar molecules line up δ+ to δ−.
Hydrogen bonds: an O–H or N–H meets a lone pair. The strongest of the three.


The trick of this slide is the controlled comparison: all three molecules weigh about the same, so dispersion forces are similar and the differences come from the polar groups. Butane only has dispersion and is a gas at room temperature; the C=O of propanone adds dipole–dipole attraction; propan-1-ol’s O–H can hydrogen-bond and boils almost 100 degrees above butane. Emphasise that these are forces between molecules. Nothing inside the molecule changes when it boils. Ask: which of the three would you expect to mix with water? That sets up the solubility slides.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: The hydrogen bond: a donor meets an acceptor
text:
The hydrogen bond: a donor meets an acceptor

Ethanol donating to water, and water donating to dimethyl etherThe donor brings an H on O or N. The acceptor brings a lone pair on O or N. The dashed contact is between molecules: no covalent bond forms or breaks.

Insist on the dashed line and on keeping both molecules intact. Students often draw a hydrogen bond as a solid line or move the H halfway across, which turns it into a proton transfer, a reaction for tomorrow. The H on a donor must be on O or N because only then is it δ+ enough; a C–H is not a donor. Show that water can play both roles: it accepts from ethanol on the left and donates to the ether on the right. That dual role is why water dissolves so many small polar molecules.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Count donors and acceptors

Donor and acceptor counts for ethanol, dimethyl ether, propanone and methyl acetateAsk two separate questions of every molecule: is there an O–H or N–H? and is there a lone pair on O or N?

Try it: can pure dimethyl ether form hydrogen bonds with itself?

No. Its O can accept, but it has no O–H to donate. Mixed with water, it can accept from water’s O–H.



This inventory habit is the tool for the rest of the day. “Contains oxygen” is not enough: every oxygen here can accept, but only the alcohol has a donor. The ester is a nice case: two oxygens, two acceptor sites, zero donors, so it’s not “an alcohol plus an ether”. Have students write the two numbers for each molecule before you reveal the labels. Pure ether molecules can’t hydrogen-bond to each other because a hydrogen bond needs a donor and an acceptor at the same time.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Amines: count the N–H, then the lone pair
text:
Amines: count the N–H, then the lone pair

Methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine and methylammoniumNeutral amines all accept at N. Only those with N–H can donate. Adding H⁺ uses up the lone pair.

Try it: CH₃NH₂ picks up a proton to become CH₃NH₃⁺. Can that N still accept a hydrogen bond?

No. The lone pair became the new N–H bond, so N has four bonds and no lone pair. It gained a donor and lost its acceptor.



Same inventory, now with nitrogen. Trimethylamine is the trap: it has three methyls on N and no N–H, so it can only accept. Its boiling point (about 3 °C) is actually lower than dimethylamine’s (about 7 °C) despite being bigger. The ammonium ion is the bridge to tomorrow: amines are bases precisely because that lone pair can grab a proton, and once it has, the inventory changes. Check that students count the formal charge on N in methylammonium: four bonds, no lone pairs, +1.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Back to the two bottles

Hydrogen-bonded ethanol molecules beside dimethyl ether moleculesEthanol molecules hold on to each other through O–H···O hydrogen bonds. To boil, they must be pulled apart. Dimethyl ether has no O–H, so its molecules let go easily.

Try it: which bonds break when ethanol boils?

None of the covalent ones. Boiling separates whole ethanol molecules by overcoming the attractions between them. Breaking C–O would be a chemical reaction.



This is the payoff for Day 1’s cliffhanger, so slow down. Same formula, same mass, same number of polar bonds; the only difference is whether a donor exists. Ethanol’s liquid is a constantly rearranging network of hydrogen bonds, and boiling means tearing every molecule out of that network. The try-it targets the misconception that boiling breaks the molecule: ethanol vapour condensed again is still ethanol, which is exactly why distillation works as a purification. Ask a student to restate the explanation in one sentence using the words donor and acceptor.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Size and shape: dispersion adds up
text:
Size and shape: dispersion adds up

Boiling points of straight-chain alcohols, and pentane versus 2,2-dimethylpropaneEvery extra CH₂ adds contact area and roughly 20 °C of boiling point. Branching makes a molecule more compact, so it touches its neighbours less and boils lower.

Hydrogen bonding isn’t the whole story. In the alcohol series every member has exactly one O–H, yet the boiling point keeps climbing: that’s dispersion growing with chain length. On the right, pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are constitutional isomers with no polar groups at all, and the compact one boils 26 degrees lower. A good image: long chains are like spaghetti that tangles; a ball is like a marble that rolls away. Yesterday’s butane versus 2-methylpropane comparison is the same effect.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Will it dissolve in water?

Methanol, butan-1-ol and hexan-1-ol with the OH shaded and their water solubilityWater welcomes the polar head that can hydrogen-bond, but the hydrocarbon tail gets in the way. The longer the tail per OH, the lower the solubility.

Try it: which mixes better with water, methanol or hexan-1-ol? And what does “it has an OH, so it dissolves” miss?

Methanol. Hexan-1-ol has six carbons per OH; the big nonpolar tail outweighs one polar head. A single OH doesn’t settle the question.



“Like dissolves like” in a more useful form: count polar heads against carbons. A rough rule is that one O–H can carry three or four carbons into water. The numbers are approximate room-temperature solubilities and the exact values depend on temperature, so keep the claims qualitative. Biology link: soaps, membrane lipids and many drugs are exactly this kind of molecule, with a polar head and a long tail, and that balance decides whether a drug dissolves in blood or crosses a membrane.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
A charge changes everything

Benzoic acid and sodium benzoate with the carboxyl group shadedAn ion is surrounded by water dipoles (ion–dipole hydration), far more strongly than a neutral molecule. Add base, and an acid that barely dissolves becomes very soluble.

Try it: your benzoic acid is mostly ionised in a basic water layer. Is that enough to predict how many grams you recover in an extraction?

No. You also need how the neutral form partitions between the two solvents, the phase volumes, the starting amount and losses. Speciation alone gives ratios, not grams.



Sodium benzoate is the preservative E211 in soft drinks, so its high water solubility is something students have drunk. This slide is the bridge to tomorrow: whether the acid is ionised depends on pH and pKa, which is Day 3’s whole topic. The try-it heads off a shortcut we see in lab reports: knowing the species ratio in water doesn’t give you a recovered mass. Extraction needs a partition model too. Keep it qualitative today.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
IR: bonds vibrate like springs

Symmetric and asymmetric stretches of carbon dioxideInfrared light makes bonds stretch and bend. A vibration absorbs only if it changes the dipole. Positions are given as wavenumbers (cm⁻¹): higher means stiffer bonds or lighter atoms.

The spring picture is good enough for this course: a stiff spring with light masses vibrates fast, so O–H, N–H and C–H (light hydrogen) and C=O (a stiff double bond) sit at high wavenumbers. CO2 is the lovely example: it has no permanent dipole, but its asymmetric stretch and its bend change the dipole while vibrating, so it absorbs IR. That’s precisely why CO2 is a greenhouse gas, while N2 and O2 are not. Nothing breaks: the bond just oscillates more. Wavenumber is 1 divided by the wavelength in cm; students only need “bigger number, more energy”.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Read the axes before the peaks
text:
Read the axes before the peaks

The same carbonyl band plotted as transmittance and as absorbanceThe x-axis runs backwards, from 4000 down to about 500 cm⁻¹. On a transmittance plot absorption is a dip; on an absorbance plot it’s a peak.

Try it: a classmate’s spectrum has tall upward bands and they think it’s wrong. What do you check?

The y-axis label. If it says absorbance, upward bands are correct: it’s the same absorption drawn the other way up.



Make reading axes a ritual: x first (units, direction), then y (transmittance or absorbance), then the bands. Most textbook and lab spectra are transmittance, so students learn “peaks point down” and are then confused by absorbance data from other instruments. These two traces are schematic, not measured, which is why they’re labelled as such. Also mention that “less light got through” and “more light was absorbed” are the same statement.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
The regions worth knowing

Bars showing approximate IR ranges for O–H, N–H, C–H and C=O
Above 2500: bonds to H. Hydrogen bonding makes O–H bands broad.
1650–1800: C=O, strong and sharp. Its exact position depends on the neighbours.
Below 1500: the fingerprint region. Compare whole patterns; don’t assign single bands.


These are teaching ranges, not exact values, and the same numbers appear on the exercise sheet. Connect the broadness of O–H to today’s first half: in a liquid, every O–H sits in a slightly different hydrogen-bonded environment, so the band smears out. The carboxylic-acid O–H is even broader because acids form strongly hydrogen-bonded pairs. C–H appears in nearly every organic molecule, so it’s rarely informative. Don’t ask students to memorise the fingerprint region; it matters again in Week 4’s spectroscopy unit.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Three spectra side by side

Schematic IR traces of ethanol, propanone and acetic acidRead each one with two questions: is there a broad O–H? and is there a strong C=O? The two answers already separate an alcohol, a ketone and an acid.

These are schematic traces drawn to show the key bands, not real measured spectra. Walk through them as a detective. Ethanol: broad O–H, no C=O. Propanone: C=O, nothing above 3000 except C–H. Acetic acid: both, and the O–H is so broad it swallows the C–H region. Ask which band tells the alcohol from the acid when both have O–H: the C=O and the shape of the O–H. Remind them that this is presence-and-absence reasoning, which is exactly what the exercise asks.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Using IR to choose between candidates
text:
Using IR to choose between candidates

Four C3 and C2 candidates with their predicted O–H and C=O bandsPredict the bands for each candidate first, then compare with the data. Both presence and absence count as evidence.

Try it: a strong band at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no O–H. Does that prove the sample is propanone?

No. It supports a C=O and no O–H, but propanal and many other carbonyl compounds fit too. You need more evidence to name one structure.



This is the reasoning pattern of the whole spectroscopy week, in miniature. Write the candidate list first; then for each one predict “O–H? C=O?”; then cross out what contradicts the data. Two candidates survive here, and that’s an honest result. An aldehyde also has a characteristic C–H stretch around 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹, which could separate propanal from propanone; mention it only as a teaser for Week 4. The worst habit to avoid is reasoning backwards from one band to one favourite molecule.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: What one spectrum can and can’t tell you
text:
What one spectrum can and can’t tell you








observation
supports
doesn’t prove




strong band near 1715 cm⁻¹
a C=O is present
which carbonyl compound


broad band near 3300 cm⁻¹
an O–H somewhere in the sample
that the target has O–H (water?)


no band at 1650–1800
no C=O in the sample
anything about the rest of the molecule


it absorbs IR at all
some vibrations change the dipole
that it dissolves in water



A wet sample shows water’s broad O–H even if your compound has none. Check the sample before you blame the structure.

Keep the claims sized to the evidence. The wet-sample row is the one students meet in the lab: a broad O–H in a supposed ether or ketone often means water or an alcohol impurity, or the target assignment is wrong, and one spectrum can’t tell those apart. The last row targets an odd shortcut that turns up in exam answers, linking IR absorption to solubility. They answer different questions: IR probes vibrations, solubility depends on intermolecular interactions with water. Ask students to suggest one extra observation that would separate the wet-sample explanations (a dried sample, a reference spectrum, a boiling point).

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




“O is δ−, so it’s O⁻”
δ is partial; formal charge comes from bonds and lone pairs


“two polar bonds, so a polar molecule”
add the vectors: geometry decides


“it has oxygen, so it hydrogen-bonds with itself”
a donor needs O–H or N–H


“boiling breaks the C–O bond”
boiling separates intact molecules


“it has an OH, so it dissolves in water”
weigh the polar head against the tail


“the IR peaks point the wrong way”
check transmittance vs absorbance


“1715 cm⁻¹, so it’s propanone”
one band supports a group, not an identity




Read each mistake aloud and let the room explain why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. Every row corresponds to an exercise: partial versus formal charge is exercise 1, geometry is 2, donors are 4 and 5, boiling is 8, solubility is 9, axes are 11 and the carbonyl claim is 13. Students who still make one of these should redo that exercise.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Summary







concept
key fact




bond polarity
O and N pull electrons: δ−


partial vs formal charge
uneven sharing vs integer bookkeeping


molecular dipole
vector sum of bond dipoles; shape decides


hydrogen bond
donor O–H/N–H + acceptor lone pair


boiling point
H-bonds, then size and shape; molecules stay intact


water solubility
polar head vs hydrocarbon tail; ions dissolve best


IR absorption
a vibration that changes the dipole; check the y-axis


key bands
O–H 3200–3600 broad · C=O 1650–1800 strong



Next: what happens when that O–H gives away its proton: acids and bases (Day 3). Practice: exercises · self-check

Close the loop with the opening question: ethanol boils 100 degrees higher because its O–H can donate a hydrogen bond and the ether’s oxygen can only accept, and the breathalyzer works because ethanol’s bonds absorb infrared light. Tomorrow we stop treating the O–H proton as fixed: acids give it away, bases take it, and the charges we met today (ethoxide, ammonium, benzoate) are the products. Point students to the exercises: problems 1 to 12 are core, 13 to 20 optional transfer.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 1. How many carbons are in a zigzag with four line segments and no branches?
text:
1. How many carbons are in a zigzag with four line segments and no branches?






Check your answer





Five: one at each of the two endpoints and three internal vertices. Saturated acyclic neutral pentane is C₅H₁₂.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 2. Does C₂H₆O establish that a sample is ethanol?
text:
2. Does C₂H₆O establish that a sample is ethanol?






Check your answer





No. Dimethyl ether shares that molecular formula. Connectivity or suitable experimental evidence is needed.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 3. How many oxygen atoms are in CH₃C(=O)OH?
text:
3. How many oxygen atoms are in CH₃C(=O)OH?






Check your answer





Two. One is double-bonded to carbon; the other is single-bonded to carbon and H.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 4. What charge has oxygen with one single bond and three lone pairs?
text:
4. What charge has oxygen with one single bond and three lone pairs?






Check your answer





Formal charge −1: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Hydroxide is an example.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 5. Does a wedge add a fifth bond to carbon?
text:
5. Does a wedge add a fifth bond to carbon?






Check your answer





No. It describes one bond pointing toward the viewer. Carbon still obeys its valence requirements.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 6. Convert 1.3812 g using molar mass 138.12 g/mol.
text:
6. Convert 1.3812 g using molar mass 138.12 g/mol.






Check your answer





The amount is 0.01000 mol = 10.00 mmol. Dividing grams by grams per mole gives moles.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
Draw each structure and check its atoms, bonds and charges. Use the lecture and the refresher below when needed.
Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when the session also includes R.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
1. Recover a five-carbon line
Draw an unbranched four-segment skeletal zigzag with only single bonds. Label each carbon CH₃ or CH₂ and obtain its molecular formula.






Hint





Segments are bonds; corners and endpoints are atoms.









Worked check





Five carbons give CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. The H count is 3+2+2+2+3=12, so the formula is C₅H₁₂.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
2. Read a branch
Expand (CH₃)₃CH. Draw its three C–C bonds, count atoms and explain whether it has the same connectivity as CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃.






Hint





The subscript three repeats the complete parenthesised methyl group.









Worked check





There are four C and ten H. A central CH connects to three methyl carbons. This is 2-methylpropane, a constitutional isomer of unbranched butane, not simply another view.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
3. Introduce a double bond
Draw CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃ with explicit H at both alkene carbons. Compare its formula with the saturated five-carbon chain.






Hint





Each end of C=C uses two bond orders in that connection.









Worked check





The structure is C₅H₁₀. Each alkene carbon has one H; the extra bond order replaces one H at each end relative to pentane.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
4. Read a terminal triple bond
Expand CH₃C≡CH and give the H count at all three carbons. Is its middle carbon CH or C?






Hint





Single plus triple already totals four bond orders.









Worked check





The counts are 3,0,1 and the formula is C₃H₄. The middle carbon is C with no H. The terminal alkyne carbon bears one H.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
5. Distinguish oxygen neighbours
Draw ethanol CH₃CH₂OH and dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃ with oxygen lone pairs. State formula and O neighbours for each.






Hint





Count H after drawing the connectivity.









Worked check





Both are C₂H₆O. Ethanol O connects to C and H; ether O to two C atoms. Each neutral O has two bonds/two lone pairs, but the molecules are constitutional isomers.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
6. Audit an oxygen series
Draw H₂O, OH⁻ and H₃O⁺ with all O lone pairs. Calculate charge using FC=6−nonbonding electrons−half the bonding electrons.






Hint





A lone pair contains two electrons.









Worked check





Water has two bonds/two pairs/FC0; hydroxide one bond/three pairs/FC−1; hydronium three bonds/one pair/FC+1. Show each charge explicitly.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
7. Audit nitrogen protonation
Draw CH₃NH₂ and CH₃NH₃⁺ with relevant nitrogen lone pairs. Use five valence electrons for N to explain the charge change.






Hint





Compare three bonds/one pair with four bonds/no pair.









Worked check





Methylamine N has FC5−2−3=0. Methylammonium N has FC5−0−4=+1. The original pair forms the new N–H bond.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
8. Read carbonyl parentheses
Expand CH₃C(=O)OH. Count atoms and carbonyl-carbon neighbours; distinguish neighbour count from bond-order sum.






Hint





The double bond connects the carbon to one O atom twice.









Worked check





The formula is C₂H₄O₂. Carbonyl C has three atom neighbours: methyl C, carbonyl O and hydroxyl O. The bond-order sum is 1+2+1=4.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
9. Classify five local patterns
Draw CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃OCH₃, CH₃CHO, CH₃COCH₃ and CH₃COOCH₃. Identify each functional group and circle all carbonyl carbons.






Hint





Rewrite CO as C(=O) where the indicated condensed carbonyl notation requires it.









Worked check





The groups are alcohol, ether, aldehyde, ketone and ester. The last three contain carbonyls; only the alcohol in this list has an O–H bond.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
10. Name two alcohol positions
Draw CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Name each by a three-carbon parent chain and give the OH locant.






Hint





Number to identify the OH-bearing carbon consistently.









Worked check





They are propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol. They are constitutional isomers: in the second, OH is attached to the central rather than terminal carbon.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
11. Repair a carbon valence error
A neutral proposed carbon has C=O, C–C and three C–H bonds. Count its bond orders and repair it to an aldehyde carbon.






Hint





Ordinary second-row carbon cannot keep six bond orders.









Worked check





The proposed sum is 2+1+3=6. In CH₃C(=O)H, the carbonyl carbon instead has C=O, C–C and one C–H, summing to four.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
12. Connect geometry with bonding
For CH₄, H₂C=CH₂ and HC≡CH, state local carbon geometry and approximate bond angles. Which drawing needs a depth convention?






Hint





Use tetrahedral, trigonal planar and linear.









Worked check





Methane is tetrahedral (~109.5°), ethene carbons trigonal planar (~120°), and ethyne carbons linear(180°). A full methane 3D drawing needs wedge/dash or another depth convention.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
section: 13. Do not create an isomer by reversing text
text:
13. Do not create an isomer by reversing text
Compare CH₃CH₂CH₂OH with HOCH₂CH₂CH₃. List neighbours of O and the OH-bearing carbon. Are they distinct?






Hint





Trace connectivity rather than left/right order.









Worked check





They are the same propan-1-ol. O attaches to H and terminal CH₂; that carbon attaches to O, the next C and two H in either notation.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
14. Find two groups in glycine
Expand neutral H₂NCH₂COOH, draw lone pairs and give the molecular formula. Do not assume any biological pathway knowledge.






Hint





Count N–H, C–H and O–H separately.









Worked check





Glycine contains an amine and carboxylic acid. Its neutral drawn form is C₂H₅NO₂:2 N–H+2 C–H+1 O–H. Other protonation forms will be considered later.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
15. Read lactic acid completely
Expand CH₃CH(OH)COOH. Count atoms, classify both oxygen-containing groups and identify the carbon with four different substituents.






Hint





The parenthesised OH is a branch on CH.









Worked check





The formula is C₃H₆O₃, with alcohol and carboxylic acid groups. The middle carbon connects to OH, H, CH₃, COOH: four different groups.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
section: 16. Distinguish a diol from an acid
text:
16. Distinguish a diol from an acid
Compare HOCH₂CH₂OH and CH₃COOH. Both contain two O atoms. Explain why counting O alone cannot assign the group.






Hint





Draw all C–O bond orders.









Worked check





The first is a diol with two single-bonded OH groups and no carbonyl. The second is a carboxylic acid with one C=O and one O–H. Connectivity and bond orders distinguish them.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
section: 17. Find all H atoms in an ester
text:
17. Find all H atoms in an ester
Draw CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃. Give its molecular formula and the number of H on the carbonyl carbon.






Hint





The carbonyl C already has two single bonds plus its double bond.









Worked check





Ethyl ethanoate is C₄H₈O₂. Its H counts are 3,0,2,3 on the four carbons. The carbonyl carbon has no H.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
18. Compare two skeletal naming choices
For CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, explain why numbering OH at 3 is unnecessary and give the preferred simple alcohol name.






Hint





Number the same chain from the opposite end.









Worked check





Butan-2-ol gives the OH the lower locant. Butan-3-ol describes the same connectivity with an inappropriate numbering direction, not a different isomer.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
19. Calculate an amount manually
A teaching sample has mass 0.6906 g and supplied molar mass 138.12 g/mol. Use n=m/M and report mol and mmol.






Hint





Divide grams by grams per mole.









Worked check





n=0.005000 mol=5.000 mmol. The gram units cancel. This amount is half that represented by 1.3812 g at the same molar mass.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
20. Explain a formula-only limitation
Give two distinct connected structures consistent with C₃H₈O, name their groups and state one additional kind of evidence that could distinguish them.






Hint





Consider moving OH or replacing an alcohol by an ether.









Worked check





Examples include propan-1-ol and methoxyethane CH₃OCH₂CH₃, an alcohol and ether. Structural or suitable spectral evidence is needed; a molecular formula alone does not decide.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
section: R task: what amount did the balance give us?
text:
R task: what amount did the balance give us?
Chemical question: how many moles are represented by a measured mass? Use the supplied relationship amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol. The molar mass has units g/mol; the division leaves mol. Multiply mol by 1000 to obtain mmol. Molar masses are supplied, not memorised.
Download and extract the student project. Open its RStudio project, then open report.Rmd. Keep input CSV files in data/. The table data/amounts.csv is a simulated teaching amount table; it is not a reaction protocol. First work the salicylic-acid row by hand: 1.3812 g at 138.12 g/mol should give 0.01000 mol.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
Predict whether doubling a mass at fixed molar mass doubles the amount. Change an input in a copied R object, not in the raw CSV, and check. Add a sentence explaining what mmol measures. Knit the report from a fresh R session; an unrun object in the console should not be required.






Numerical and chemical check





Salicylic acid gives 10.00 mmol. With the supplied second row, 1.53135 g of acetic anhydride at 102.09 g/mol gives 15.00 mmol. Doubling either mass doubles its amount. These amounts alone do not select the limiting reagent: that requires the balanced reaction’s stoichiometric coefficients, introduced later. The unit mmol counts chemical amount, not volume, concentration or number of independent experiments.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
Review your work
Choose one corrected mistake and explain the chemical rule that repairs it. Continue with the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 1: Exercises — Reading organic structures
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
Before revealing H counts, predict the complete formula of propanone. How does its C=O bond change the H count compared with propane?
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Select ethanol and trace the skeletal endpoints and vertices. Switch to labelled atoms without revealing carbon H counts; explain what changed in the representation and what stayed identical.
Reveal H counts and check each carbon against a bond-order sum of four. Switch to propanone and explain why its central carbon has no H.
Compare ethanol and dimethyl ether in condensed and skeletal modes. Both share a formula, but list the neighbours of oxygen in each. Reset and reconstruct the starting molecule without the reveal.



Take-away
Choose one molecule and justify every hidden carbon-bound H using the actual bonds. What information does its molecular formula leave undecided?


Model and limits
These are neutral, ordinary-valence C/H/O examples. Carbon uses four bond orders and oxygen two. O-bound H is drawn explicitly; the reveal concerns implicit carbon-bound H. No charges, radicals or unusual valences are inferred.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
Compare the spectral evidence, test a proposed structure and check the associated synthesis calculations.
Allow 150 minutes: 10 minutes for retrieval, 48 for exercises 1–6, 48 for 7–10, 34 for 11–12 and 10 to review your solutions. Drawing and comparison are included in that time. Finish remaining problems independently rather than rushing a mechanism.
Local explanations: Spectroscopy and synthesis evidence.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
Working definitions
Use full-headed arrows for electron pairs: start at a lone pair or bond and end at its acceptor. Keep ordinary carbon to four bond orders and conserve atoms and net charge. For compatible proton-transfer data, K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For amounts use n=m/M and 1 mol=1000 mmol; compare n/coefficient before predicting theoretical product. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated/theoretical product mass. TLC (thin-layer chromatography) uses Rf=spot/front distances from the same origin. For simple first-order NMR, n adjacent equivalent H give n +1 lines while integration counts H area. Any further structure, constant or observation you need is given in the problem.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
1. Constrain an unknown formula
Unknown V has C₄H₈O₂. Use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2 and draw one ester and one acid compatible with its value.






Hint





O is omitted in this simple C/H/O count.









Worked explanation





DBE=1. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH both fit. The formula constrains composition but does not choose connectivity.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
2. Read functional-group evidence
V has a complete simulated IR trace with strong carbonyl near 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H. Which of those two candidates is challenged, assuming adequate coverage?






Hint





A carboxylic acid predicts a broad OH envelope.









Worked explanation





Butanoic acid is challenged; the ester remains consistent. Absence evidence depends on detection and coverage, and one carbonyl feature does not uniquely prove the ester.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
3. Join two proton environments
V has 1.25 ppm triplet 3H and 4.12 ppm quartet 2H. Use the simple n +1 rule to explain both linesets and propose a connected fragment.






Hint





Triplet sees 2H; quartet sees 3H.









Worked explanation





The pair fits O–CH₂–CH₃: CH₂ is split by 3H and methyl by 2H, with 2:3 integration. The downfield CH₂ shift helps place O; multiplicity alone would not locate that atom.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
4. Place a third environment
A remaining 2.05 ppm singlet integrates 3H. Assign it in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and explain why the distant O–CH₂ does not give ordinary vicinal splitting.






Hint





The acetyl methyl’s adjacent carbon is the carbonyl carbon.









Worked explanation





CH₃–C(=O) gives the singlet because adjacent carbonyl C has no H. The O–CH₂ protons are not vicinal neighbours of that methyl in this simple model.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
5. Use carbon evidence
V has simulated ¹³C signals 14,21,60,171 ppm. Assign them to the proposed ester and explain whether peak heights count carbons.






Hint





Separate ester carbonyl, O-bound CH₂ and two methyls.









Worked explanation





171=C=O,60=O–CH₂,14=terminal ethyl CH₃,21=acetyl CH₃. Routine carbon intensities are not reliable quantitative carbon counts; environment count and formula must be checked together.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
6. Test a competing structure
Compare V with CH₃COCH(OH)CH₃, also C₄H₈O₂. Give two differences predicted by that hydroxyketone.






Hint





Its oxygen-bearing carbon is CH rather than CH₂.









Worked explanation





It predicts an OH-bearing 1H environment and a methyl beside one H, commonly a doublet, unlike V’s 2H quartet/3H triplet pair. It also predicts OH functionality in suitable conditions.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
7. Calculate reagent amounts
A supplied 1:1 reaction uses 0.750 g reagent A at 150.0 g/mol and 0.900 g reagent B at 100.0 g/mol, giving one product P per reaction extent. Calculate mmol and limiting reagent.






Hint





Use n=m/M and compare n/coefficient.









Worked explanation





A=0.00500 mol=5.00 mmol; B=0.00900 mol=9.00 mmol. A limits the desired reaction to 5.00 mmol product.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
8. Predict and compare product mass
For that reaction, P has M=200.0 g/mol and isolate mass 0.720 g. Calculate theoretical mass and apparent isolated yield and state the purity assumption.






Hint





Theoretical product amount is 5.00 mmol from the supplied limiter.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mass=0.00500×200.0=1.000 g. Apparent yield=72.0%. This assumes weighed isolate is product; it does not establish purity or actual conversion.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
9. Interpret TLC references
Under one condition front distance is 6.0 cm, A reference 1.8 cm, P reference 3.6 cm and crude spots at both. Calculate Rf and state the strongest modest conclusion.






Hint





All distances start at the same origin.









Worked explanation





Rf A=0.30 and P=0.60. The crude has at least two detected components with matching retention to the references under those conditions, without unique identity proof or quantitative conversion.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
10. Recognise unresolved mixtures
An isolate shows one TLC spot atRf 0.60 but extra major NMR signals. Explain why the observations can coexist and propose a targeted next check.






Hint





Different compounds may co-migrate or evade the detection method.









Worked explanation





The single retention feature can hide a mixture. Compare full spectral assignments or use a suitable second separation condition that tests the extra component. Do not overrule NMR using the spot count.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
11. Check independent mass inputs
A report recomputes theoretical mass from isolated mass rather than starting reagents. Explain why this makes the yield circular and give the correct calculation chain.






Hint





The denominator must be predicted independently of recovered mass.









Worked explanation





Starting masses→mol→limiting extent→theoretical P mol→theoretical P mass. Independently measured isolated mass enters only the yield numerator. Reusing it to define the theoretical denominator destroys the intended comparison.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
12. Write one supported conclusion
For V, all spectral observations are simulated and fit the ester candidate; the separate reaction data give 72% apparent yield. Can you claim these spectra identify that reaction’s real isolate?






Hint





Do not merge unrelated teaching datasets into one experimental story.









Worked explanation





No. The V model supports a candidate assignment for its supplied data, and the amount exercise gives 72% under its product-mass assumption. Real-isolate identity requires appropriately measured and linked sample evidence, not an unrelated simulated trace.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
Review your reasoning
Choose two corrected errors: one in a drawing/calculation and one in an interpretation. Explain why the corrected answer follows from the supplied inputs. Keep the first attempt so you can see the change in your reasoning.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 24: Exercises — Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations
text:
Explore
Question: is an unmeasured spectral region the same as an observed absence, and can partial peak information justify a complete assignment?
Allow 9 minutes: predict for 2, mask and restore evidence for 4, then audit two contrasting claims for 3. The molecule does not change when observations are hidden; all data are fixed simulated U1 teaching observations.

Enable JavaScript to change available evidence and inspect which claims remain justified.




Predict
The supplied formula is C₄H₈O₂. If an IR measurement covers only the carbonyl window, can you claim that a broad O–H feature was absent? If NMR supplies only relative integrated areas 3:3:2, can you place an O–CH₂ group without shifts or splitting?
In the simple NMR model, integration gives H-area ratios while chemical shifts and multiplicities provide different clues. Missing observations are not negative observations.


Explore

Begin with the missing-region preset and audit The O–H absence is observed.
Restore full IR coverage. Identify what new observation now supports or challenges the acid candidate.
Change NMR from relative areas only to splitting only, then to full evidence. Compare Integrals account for eight H with O–CH₂–CH₃ is assigned.
Try the purity and unique-structure claims, even with complete evidence.



Explain and check
A carbonyl-only window cannot establish O–H absence; the grey area explicitly marks unmeasured data. Reliable relative areas can normalise to 3:3:2 and account for eight H using the formula, but they do not by themselves locate those H in the molecule. A 2H quartet near 4.12 ppm with the corresponding 3H triplet provides additional support for O–CH₂–CH₃ in the stated candidate comparison.
Complete U1 observations favour ethyl ethanoate over the supplied acid and hydroxyketone alternatives. They do not establish purity or exclude every conceivable molecular structure.


Model limits
The coverage choices stipulate which observations are available and whether O–H detection is adequate. They do not simulate instrumental noise or compute quantitative confidence probabilities. Use the local spectroscopy explanations to connect each observation to a structural prediction.
crumbs: Day 24: Spectral evidence and synthesis calculations

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
Compare carbonyl addition and acyl substitution by drawing mechanisms and tracking atoms, charge and amounts. Allow 150 minutes: 10 minutes to recall the key steps, 48 minutes for problems 1–6, 48 minutes for 7–10, 34 minutes for 11–12, and 10 minutes to review. These timings include drawing and comparison; continue unfinished problems later rather than rushing a mechanism.
Local explanations: Acyl chemistry and carbonyl addition.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
Working definitions
Use full-headed arrows for electron pairs: start at a lone pair or bond and end at its acceptor. Keep ordinary carbon to four bond orders and conserve atoms and net charge. For compatible proton-transfer data, K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For amounts use n=m/M and 1 mol=1000 mmol; compare n/coefficient before predicting theoretical product. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated/theoretical product mass. TLC (thin-layer chromatography) uses Rf=spot/front distances from the same origin. For simple first-order NMR, n adjacent equivalent H give n +1 lines while integration counts H area.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
1. Classify the reactive motif
Draw CH₃CH₂C(=O)OCH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂OCH₃. Identify ester versus ether and circle the carbonyl carbon where present.






Hint





Look for C=O directly next to single-bond O.









Worked explanation





The first is methyl propanoate, an ester with acyl carbon. The second is an ether without carbonyl; an oxygen atom alone does not supply an acyl-addition site.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
2. Predict hydroxide addition
Draw OH⁻ addition to CH₃CH₂C(=O)OCH₃ with both arrows and all intermediate charges.






Hint





Move the C=O pi pair to O while forming the new bond.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH₂C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃) forms. Carbon has four single bonds; incoming OH is neutral and original carbonyl O is negative. Net charge remains −1.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
3. Collapse with atom labels
Label the ester carbonyl O as A and methoxy O as B. On collapse of the hydroxide-addition intermediate, which labelled oxygen remains carbonyl and which leaves attached to methyl?






Hint





Follow the original atoms rather than redrawing unlabelled products.









Worked explanation





O-A reforms the carbonyl; O-B leaves as CH₃O-B⁻. The immediate acid is CH₃CH₂C(=O-A)OH. B remains attached to methyl; that C–O bond is not the bond broken.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
4. Complete proton transfer
The collapse gives CH₃CH₂COOH and CH₃O⁻. Use supplied pKa 4.9 for the acid and 15.5 for methanol to predict the favoured pair and estimate K.






Hint





Use 10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa).









Worked explanation





Propanoate and methanol are favoured. K≈10^(15.5−4.9)≈4×10¹⁰. The basic mixture should not be represented as neutral acid coexisting predominantly with methoxide.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
5. Write the net equation
Write complete net base-promoted hydrolysis of CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ by OH⁻, then a separate hydronium work-up equation.






Hint





Hydrolysis consumes hydroxide overall; work-up protonates the carboxylate.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH₂COOCH₃+OH⁻→CH₃CH₂COO⁻+CH₃OH. Then CH₃CH₂COO⁻+H₃O⁺→CH₃CH₂COOH+H₂O. The protonation change is a separate chemical event.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
6. Distinguish addition
For CH₃CH₂CHO, draw hydroxide addition and proton transfer from water. Does the carbon-bound H ordinarily leave as H⁻ by the ester analogy?






Hint





An aldehyde lacks the methoxy leaving group present in the ester.









Worked explanation





Addition gives CH₃CH₂CH(OH)O⁻ and water protonation gives CH₃CH₂CH(OH)₂ with OH⁻ regenerated. H⁻ loss is not the normal pathway here; a common first step does not imply identical later chemistry.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
7. Audit five bonds
A student writes CH₃CH₂C(=O)(OH)OCH₃ as the tetrahedral intermediate. Count carbon bond orders, repair it and place the missing negative charge.






Hint





Two bond orders belong to C=O.









Worked explanation





The proposed carbon has five bond orders. Opening C=O to C–O⁻ gives four single bonds and retains net −1. Correct electron flow and correct valence are linked checks.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
8. Activate an acid carbonyl
Draw protonation of CH₃CH₂C(=O)OH by hydronium. Give the oxygen charge and the water product, then identify the atom ethanol attacks next.






Hint





Carbonyl O accepts a proton; carbon becomes a better electron-pair acceptor.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH₂C(=OH⁺)OH+H₂O forms. Ethanol subsequently attacks acyl carbon, moving the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen; it does not need to exist as ethoxide in the acidic pathway.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
9. Audit neutral-alcohol attack
After ethanol attacks that activated carbonyl, write the tetrahedral species and locate the +1 charge. What transfer makes the incoming oxygen neutral?






Hint





The incoming alcohol oxygen now has three single bonds.









Worked explanation





CH₃CH₂C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt) has positive charge on incoming O. Water can remove its H, giving neutral OEt and hydronium. Each oxygen charge follows its bond count.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
10. Make water the leaving group
From CH₃CH₂C(OH)(OH)(OEt), explain the activation and elimination needed to form ester rather than simply drawing OH⁻ loss.






Hint





Protonate an OH before elimination under the representative acidic conditions.









Worked explanation





An OH₂⁺ substituent can leave as H₂O as the other O pair reforms C=O. The initially protonated ester is then deprotonated. These steps conserve charge and regenerate acid catalyst.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
11. Compare amide and ester
Draw CH₃CH₂CONH₂ and its charge-separated contributor. Explain one rotational and one reactivity consequence compared with the ester.






Hint





Use N pair donation and C=O pi-pair movement.









Worked explanation





Contributor CH₃CH₂C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺ gives partial C–N double-bond character, restricting rotation. It also stabilises the amide and reduces N-pair availability; comparable amide acyl substitution is generally less facile than ester substitution under ordinary analogous conditions.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
12. Critique a synthesis claim
A student mixes propanoic acid and methylamine in water and labels the immediate product an amide. Supplied acid pKa is 4.9; methylammonium pKa 10.6. Predict the initial acid–base outcome and explain the missing synthetic requirement.






Hint





The product acid in proton transfer is the ammonium ion.









Worked explanation





Propanoate+methylammonium are favoured, K≈10^5.7. Proton transfer is not amide formation. A productive coupling requires suitable activation or conditions; a salt drawing does not establish a new acyl C–N bond.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
Review your reasoning
Choose two corrected errors: one in a drawing/calculation and one in an interpretation. Explain why the corrected answer follows from the supplied inputs. Keep the first attempt so you can see the change in your reasoning.

title: Day 19: Exercises — Carbonyl and acyl chemistry
text:
Explore
Question: can you predict a favoured proton-transfer direction from the reactant and product acids, without confusing equilibrium with reaction speed?
Allow 8 minutes: predict for 2, compare cases for 4, and explain for 2. All numerical inputs and reacting species are supplied in the workbench.

Enable JavaScript to select a proton donor and base and inspect the complete conjugate-pair reaction.




Predict
For the reaction HA + B ⇌ A + BH, compare the conjugate-pair pKa values using
\[K\approx10^{pK_a(BH)-pK_a(HA)}.\]
Charges depend on the chosen pair; the actual charged formulas are displayed. The supplied approximate aqueous acid pKa values are ethanoic acid 4.8, methylammonium 10.6, phenol 10.0 and pyridinium 5.2. A lower pKa means a stronger acid within this compatible comparison.
Predict the result of ethanoic acid with methylamine before using the controls.


Explore

Inspect all four species, not only the numerical constant.
Try Equal pair. Why does swapping a proton within the same conjugate-pair bookkeeping give K = 1?
Try Reactant-favoured case and identify the weaker acid on each side.
Make your own product-favoured comparison and check the net charge.



Explain and check
Ethanoic acid plus methylamine gives a pKa difference of \(10.6-4.8=5.8\), so \(K\approx6.3\times10^5\) toward ethanoate plus methylammonium. Phenol plus pyridine gives \(5.2-10.0=-4.8\), so \(K\approx1.6\times10^{-5}\) and reactants are favoured. Neither value specifies how rapidly equilibrium is approached.


Model limits
The values are approximate and used under a common aqueous comparison. Standard-state, activity, solvent and temperature conventions must be compatible when transferring this calculation to other datasets. K alone also does not give the final composition without starting amounts and an appropriate equilibrium model. No equilibrium solver or laboratory protocol is implied. Review the acid–base exercises.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
Choose, draw and audit substitution and elimination mechanisms, then explain how competing pathways differ. Revisit the substitution and elimination and addition lectures, or inspect the SN1 demo.
Core 1–8: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 9–12: an optional 30–45 minutes. Draw before opening a check; compare reasoning with a partner and keep your own corrected drawing.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
Refresher and worked start
Full-headed arrows move pairs from bonds/lone pairs; ordinary carbon has total bond order four. Alpha is the leaving-group carbon; beta is its neighbour. E2 uses an appropriate anti geometry and three linked pair movements. Selected carbonyl reduction gives alkoxide then alcohol after proton transfer.
For the worked starting example OH⁻+CH₃Br→CH₃OH+Br⁻, draw OH pair→C and C–Br pair→Br. Both sides have net charge −1; the concerted step contains no carbocation. Use the same atom/charge audit in the problems below.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
1. Find two reacting centres
Draw CH₃CH₂Br and CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃. Mark the Br-bearing carbon and every beta carbon. Which substrate has the more accessible SN2 centre?






Hint





Compare local neighbours rather than whole-molecule carbon totals.









Worked answer and reasoning





Ethyl bromide has a primary reaction centre and one beta carbon;2-bromobutane has a secondary centre and two beta carbons. The primary centre is less sterically obstructed for backside attack, all else comparable.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
2. Build a carbon–oxygen bond
Assume suitable dry SN2 conditions for CH₃O⁻+CH₃CH₂Br. Draw both arrows and products, including charge.






Hint





Oxygen donates the pair; Br takes the old C–Br pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are CH₃OCH₂CH₃ and Br⁻. Oxygen becomes a neutral two-bond ether oxygen. Net charge is −1 before and after. The new bond is to the substrate carbon, not to bromine.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
3. Keep the nitrogen proton count
Draw the first step of NH₃ attack on CH₃CH₂Br in the selected SN2 model. Then draw a possible equilibrium proton transfer to another NH₃ molecule.






Hint





Separate bond formation from a later proton transfer.









Worked answer and reasoning





First obtain CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺+Br⁻. Another ammonia takes H⁺ to give CH₃CH₂NH₂+NH₄⁺. Neutral ethylamine is not the immediate attack product, because nitrogen initially retains all three H atoms. No quantitative equilibrium extent is asserted by these formal steps; excess ammonia and the actual conditions matter.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
4. Repair a charge-inconsistent mechanism
A drawing shows H₂O adding to (CH₃)₃C⁺ and immediately labels the product(CH₃)₃COH. Supply the missing intermediate and proton-transfer step.






Hint





Water oxygen has two H atoms when it first bonds to carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The immediate product is(CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Water then removes H⁺, giving (CH₃)₃COH+H₃O⁺. This preserves the original H atoms and positive charge through the steps.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
5. Draw one anti view
Look from a beta carbon toward the Br-bearing alpha carbon of an alkyl bromide. Put reacting beta-H at twelve o’clock and rear Br at six. Draw a Newman view and name the angle.






Hint





Front bonds start at the dot; rear bonds at the circle.









Worked answer and reasoning





The H–C–C–Br dihedral is 180°, anti-periplanar. Add the remaining substituents consistently to each carbon; the selected H and Br are on opposite sides of the viewed bond.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
6. Turn that view into E2
Using that anti arrangement and B⁻, draw the E2 step and account for all three pairs.






Hint





Do not leave the C–H pair without a destination.









Worked answer and reasoning





B pair→H forms BH; C–H pair→C–C forms the pi bond; C–Br pair→Br gives Br⁻. The step is concerted and has no carbocation intermediate.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
7. Choose possible alkene positions
Draw all constitutional alkenes from formal HBr loss from 2-bromobutane. State which has E/Z forms and one reason products need not be equally abundant.






Hint





Test each beta site and then apply the two-different-groups rule at each double-bond carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The constitutional products are but-1-ene and but-2-ene. But-2-ene has E/Z forms; but-1-ene does not. Geometry, base sterics and other conditions can make pathways unequally favoured.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
8. Map the SN1/E1 branch
From(CH₃)₃C⁺ in water, draw carbon capture and beta-H loss as separate branches, keeping charges visible.






Hint





Water can donate a pair to carbon or to H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Carbon capture gives oxonium and then alcohol after deprotonation; beta-H loss gives2-methylpropene+H₃O⁺. These are the SN1 and E1 branches after ionisation. A common cation does not imply a unique final product.









Note



Optional transfer problems 9–12. Select for revision; they are not additional required contact hours.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
9. Invert and reassign
Assume SN2 replacement of Br by OH in(R)-2-bromobutane. Draw the inverted geometry and independently assign the product descriptor.






Hint





For this case, Br/OH rank first, ethyl second, methyl third and H fourth.









Worked answer and reasoning





Inversion produces(S)-butan-2-ol for this particular priority ordering. The geometric inversion is the mechanism rule; the R/S change follows only after checking the actual replacement priorities.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
10. Add HBr with a reason
For ionic HBr addition to propene without peroxides, draw protonation and capture. Explain the major connectivity using the two possible carbocations.






Hint





Compare secondary and primary cation formation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Protonation giving CH₃CH⁺CH₃ is favoured over CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ in the selected model. Br⁻ capture gives2-bromopropane. Move the alkene pi pair to H and the H–Br pair to Br before drawing capture.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
11. Distinguish a bridged intermediate
Sketch bromonium opening by Br⁻ and explain why the relative addition is anti.






Hint





Show opposite-side carbon attack plus return of the bridge-bond pair to Br.









Worked answer and reasoning





Backside attack opens the corresponding C–Br bridge bond, placing the new bromine opposite the bridging bromine. This is a different intermediate and stereochemical account from the free-carbocation HBr model.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
12. Write a justified pathway comparison
Compare methyl bromide+OH⁻ with tertiary bromide in an ionising aqueous medium. Give a plausible pathway for each and identify one unsupported claim to avoid.






Hint





Use steric access and cation stability, then remember competing elimination.









Worked answer and reasoning





Methyl supports the concerted SN2 example and has no beta carbon for ordinary elimination. Tertiary bromide can ionise and undergo water capture or E1. Avoid promising an exact substitution/elimination ratio without actual conditions or data.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
Revisit the relevant lesson
Use the substitution, elimination/addition and alcohol/redox explanations when a correction needs more context.

title: Day 14: Exercises — Reaction-mechanism review
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). Draw the first electron-pair operation for a tertiary bromide in the selected aqueous SN1 route. Which ion receives the old C–Br pair?
Explore (3–5 minutes). Choose an operation, try it and read the feedback. Work from tertiary bromide through carbocation and oxonium to neutral alcohol. Deliberately try the neutral-alcohol shortcut or deletion of an H. Find the precise atom/charge problem. Watch bromide and both explicit waters through the sequence.
Explain (2 minutes). Write the complete net equation including water, hydronium and bromide. Explain why the positive charge moves from carbon to oxygen before the final proton transfer, and why an explicit proton acceptor is essential.


Supplied model and its limits
The substrate is (CH₃)₃CBr, and the selected branch is ionisation→water capture→water deprotonation. Start with two waters: one becomes the alcohol oxygen and the other receives the extra proton. Br⁻ remains after ionisation. Total charge of all displayed species is zero. E1 can compete in real conditions, but its proportion is not calculated here. The choices test a stated mechanistic model, not a universal reaction selector.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text: Compare Newman and Fischer drawings, follow a chair flip, and distinguish conformation from configuration. Core 1–8: about 75–95 minutes including comparison and correction. Extension 9–12: about 30–45 minutes for optional independent work. Revisit the hints after an attempt; each worked check explains the rule, not just the label.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
1. Specify an eye position
Draw butane, number C1–C4, and look C3→C2. List front/rear methyl labels.






Hint





Front is nearest your eye in the stated direction.









Worked check





C3 is front, with C4 methyl; C2 is rear, with C1 methyl. Each also bears two H. Reversing the view swaps front/rear but does not alter connectivity.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
2. Build staggered anti
Along C2→C3, place front CH₃ at 12 and rear CH₃ at 6. Complete the four H positions.






Hint





Separate each carbon’s set by 120°.









Worked check





Front H at 4/8 and rear H at 2/10 make a staggered projection. The methyl dihedral is 180°, so it is anti.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
3. Generate both gauche arrangements
Hold front methyl at 12. Draw rear methyl at 2 and 10, completing both projections.






Hint





The methyl groups are ±60° apart.









Worked check





Both are gauche and staggered. They preserve the butane framework and are equivalent in energy for ordinary butane in an achiral environment.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
4. Repair a false isomer claim
A student calls anti and gauche constitutional isomers. Name the unchanged atom relationships.






Hint





Connectivity tests constitutional difference.









Worked check





Every carbon keeps the same neighbouring atoms. Bond rotation changes conformation, not constitution. The student confused spatial view with bonded framework.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
5. Follow an up group
Carry axial-up methyl through a cyclohexane chair flip. Mark its side and local position afterward.






Hint





Use two separate labels.









Worked check





It becomes equatorial-up. Changing it to equatorial-down would alter the up/down configuration, not simply flip a chair.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
6. Check cis/trans persistence
Two ring substituents start up/up. A third example has up/down. State each relation before/after a flip.






Hint





Same side is cis; opposite sides trans.









Worked check





Up/up is cis and stays cis. Up/down is trans and stays trans. Axial/equatorial labels may exchange in both.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
7. Find a tetrahedral centre
Compare CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and CH₃CH(OH)COOH. List groups and identify which qualifies.






Hint





One repeated group prevents this simple stereocentre.









Worked check





Propan-2-ol has two methyl groups and does not qualify. Lactic acid has OH, H, CH₃, COOH and qualifies.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
8. Assign a complete Fischer
Draw COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left, H right. Assign S/R with priorities and the viewing correction.






Hint





H is horizontal and forward.









Worked check





PriorityOH1, COOH2, CH₃3, H4. The trace is clockwise but4 toward requires inversion, so S.




Optional extension
Use these after the core or during later revision.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
9. Mirror without changing connectivity
Mirror the previous Fischer. Assign its descriptor independently and classify the pair.






Hint





Swap left/right groups while keeping the vertical labels.









Worked check





The mirror has OH right, H left and is R. The pair is enantiomeric, with matching connectivity and opposite one-centre configuration.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
10. Classify an alkene pair
Draw same-side and opposite-side methyl groups around but-2-ene C=C. Assign E/Z and isomer relationship.






Hint





Methyl outranks H at both ends.









Worked check





Same-side is Z, opposite E. These are diastereomers, not conformers related by ordinary free single-bond rotation.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
11. Test a nonexample
Can CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ have E/Z? Give the failed requirement at each end.






Hint





Inspect duplicated substituents rather than geometry alone.









Worked check





No. One end has H/H and the other CH₃/CH₃. Each alkene carbon must have two different substituents.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
12. Separate centre count from chirality
Draw meso-tartaric-acid Fischer with COOH top/bottom, OH right at both centres. Explain its symmetry in words.






Hint





Inspect equivalent upper/lower halves.









Worked check





The complete structure has an internal symmetry relationship and is achiral despite two stereocentres. Counting centres alone does not establish chirality.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
Review your solutions
Choose one corrected drawing and one corrected explanation. State the observation or rule that made you change your answer. Save these beside your course notes; extra R tasks belong to their separate unit practice pages.

title: Day 9: Exercises — Models, rotations and configurations
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
With G(B) − G(A) = 3500 J/mol at 298.15 K, which state should be more populated? Would adding the same free-energy constant to both states change the fractions?
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Inspect the starting prediction and verify that fractions A and B sum to one. Compare the relative B/A weight with B’s normalised population fraction.
Set equal-state free energies, then make B lower in free energy by moving ΔG below zero. Explain the reversal without assigning a new molecular identity to A or B.
Hold the energy gap fixed and vary temperature. Then change only the common reference offset. Explain why the raw state weights can change while normalised fractions do not.



Take-away
Separate three quantities: relative free-energy difference, normalised equilibrium population and interconversion barrier. Which one is missing for a rate prediction?


Model and limits
This is a supplied two-effective-state equilibrium model; the state free energies already include degeneracy. Use consistent J/mol, R = 8.314462618 J/(mol K) and kelvin. A and B are abstract conformer states, not an asserted complete inventory of butane conformers. No activation barrier or rate constant is supplied.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
Read each structure, explain its properties and check the acid–base predictions.
Core 1–8: about 75–95 minutes including comparison and correction. Extension 9–12: about 30–45 minutes for optional independent work. Try each problem before opening its hint, then use the worked answer to check your reasoning.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
1. Recover two chains
Draw unbranched four-carbon and five-carbon saturated skeletal chains. Label all terminal H counts and give formulas.






Hint





Count vertices, not line segments.









Worked check





Butane has C₄H₁₀ and pentane C₅H₁₂. Terminal C carries3H; each internal chain C has 2H.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
2. Show a genuine constitutional difference
Draw propan-1-ol and methoxyethane CH₃OCH₂CH₃. Verify their shared formula and explain an oxygen-neighbour difference.






Hint





One has an O–H bond; the other has two O–C bonds.









Worked check





Both are C₃H₈O. The alcohol O neighbours C/H; ether O neighbours C/C. Their connectivity differs.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
section: 3. Audit all oxygens in an acid
text:
3. Audit all oxygens in an acid
Draw CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻. Assign relevant O bonds, lone pairs and net charges using one valid contributor for the anion.






Hint





Negative O with one bond has three lone pairs.









Worked check





Neutral acid has carbonyl O with two lone pairs and OH O with two. One ethanoate contributor has singly bonded O⁻ with three pairs; the other O is double-bonded. Net charges0 and−1.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
4. Predict a donor/acceptor contrast
Compare ethanol, dimethyl ether and propanone. Draw each and mark donor/acceptor sites.






Hint





A carbonyl oxygen can accept even without OH.









Worked check





Ethanol donates/accepts. Ether and propanone accept but lack O–H/N–H donor bonds. Do not invent H atoms on their oxygens.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
section: 5. Explain boiling rather than bond breaking
text:
5. Explain boiling rather than bond breaking
Use approximate normal boiling points ethanol78 ° C and dimethyl ether−24 ° C. Give a controlled interaction comparison and state what ordinary boiling preserves.






Hint





They share a molecular formula and similar size.









Worked check





Ethanol can form an OH hydrogen-bond network; ether lacks an OH donor. Ordinary boiling separates largely intact molecules, preserving C–O connectivity.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
6. Test two spectral candidates
A suitable complete IR has strong C=O near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no alcohol OH feature. Candidates are propanone and propan-1-ol. Give predictions and conclusion.






Hint





Compare expected bonds before naming the unknown.









Worked check





Propanone predicts C=O and no OH; alcohol predicts OH and no C=O. The observations support propanone within this pair, not unique identity among all compounds.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
7. Draw a proton-transfer pair
Draw CH₃COOH+CH₃NH₂⇌CH₃COO⁻+CH₃NH₃⁺ using two arrows. Check net charge.






Hint





Start at N lone pair and acid O–H bond.









Worked check





N pair→H; O–H pair→O. Reactant charge0 equals product−1+1=0. Both conjugate pairs differ by H⁺.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
section: 8. Calculate a midpoint and a nearby fraction
text:
8. Calculate a midpoint and a nearby fraction
Use pKa 4.8. Obtain A⁻/HA and ionised fraction at pH 4.8 and 5.8.






Hint





Convert ratio to fraction with its full denominator.









Worked check





Ratios1 and 10 give fractions0.5 and 10/11≈0.9091. A ratio of 10 is not a fraction of 10.




Optional extension
Use these after the core or during later revision.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
9. Repair a misleading functional-group label
A student calls CH₃COOCH₃ an ether because it contains C–O–C. Explain what they omitted.






Hint





Draw the adjacent C=O explicitly.









Worked check





The single-bonded O attaches to a carbonyl carbon, forming an ester motif. Local connectivity includes the carbonyl; it is not an ordinary simple ether.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
section: 10. Check a substitution effect on acidity
text:
10. Check a substitution effect on acidity
Supplied comparable aqueous pKa values:ethanoic acid4.8, chloroethanoic acid2.9. Explain which acid is stronger using conjugate-base stabilisation.






Hint





Cl withdraws electron density through sigma bonds.









Worked check





Chloroethanoic acid is stronger. Inductive withdrawal stabilises its conjugate base. The inference concerns compatible equilibrium data, not reaction rate.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
11. Distinguish three charges
Explain formal charge on hydroxide, partial negative charge on ethanol O, and net charge of water.






Hint





These labels describe different levels of bookkeeping.









Worked check





Hydroxide O has formal−1; ethanol O is formally0 but δ− in polar bonds; water has net0. Net neutrality does not prevent polar bonds or a molecular dipole.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
section: 12. Use a measured mass without a spreadsheet
text:
12. Use a measured mass without a spreadsheet
Using supplied molar mass138.12 g/mol, calculate amount for 0.27624 g. Give mol/mmol and show unit cancellation.






Hint





n=m/M.









Worked check





0.002000 mol=2.000 mmol. Dividing g by g/mol cancels grams and leaves moles. This is not a concentration without a solution volume.

title: Day 4: Exercises — Structure and property review
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
In lactic acid, should selecting “alcohol” highlight every O atom? Predict which O belongs to the alcohol and which atoms belong to the carboxylic acid.
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Inspect lactic acid with the highlight hidden. Locate its two oxygen-containing motifs, then reveal alcohol and acid separately.
Select ethanoic acid and ask for alcohol. Explain the absence of an alcohol match even though an O–H bond exists.
Compare ether with ketone, then inspect the neutral drawn glycine form for an amine and acid. Change the selected group before revealing so each attempt starts with your own prediction.



Take-away
Choose two molecules with oxygen and explain why one local O–H or C–O bond does not classify all their functional groups.


Model and limits
The workbench recognises the complete motifs supplied in these particular structures; it is not an automatic general chemical classifier. Highlighted atoms identify the chosen local site. Neutral drawn glycine is used to inspect connectivity; actual aqueous protonation depends on pH.
Continue with the exercises.
