title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text: Allow 30–60 minutes if you need a refresher. The goal is to reopen a project, read a table, calculate one result and Knit a report. You do not need to learn a new programming language or molecular modelling system for this course.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
1. Open an ordinary project folder
Download the student ZIP, locate it in your file manager and extract it. Open the extracted organic-chemistry.Rproj in RStudio. Work inside the extracted folder rather than opening files inside the ZIP.
The project root contains report.Rmd, the project file and data/. The report refers to data/amounts.csv: that is a relative path starting from the report’s folder. Keep the report there. Save derived files in output/ and leave the original CSVs unchanged.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
2. Check the software once
Use the R/RStudio environment supported by your programme. The course uses readr, dplyr, ggplot2, knitr and rmarkdown, the same report workflow as the introductory computing materials. If these packages are absent from your own installation, install them once from the R console:
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
Installation needs network access. In a managed teaching environment follow the provided setup instructions instead of changing its installation. RStudio normally supplies the Pandoc program used when knitting HTML reports.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
3. Read and inspect before calculating
Run the following in an R script or a code chunk, not the terminal:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
amounts
names(amounts)
Expect two reactant rows. Check the units in the column names and the data dictionary. A row is a reagent in a constructed reaction example, not an independent experiment.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
4. Check one calculation by hand
Amount in mol = mass in g / molar mass in g/mol. For salicylic acid, 1.3812 g / 138.12 g/mol = 0.0100 mol = 10.0 mmol.
amounts <- amounts |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = 1000 * amount_mol)
amounts
Explain why the result changes by a factor of 1000 when changing mol to mmol. A variable name is a reminder of units; R does not automatically enforce them.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
5. Knit from a fresh session
Open report.Rmd. Replace the author name, save, then click Knit to create the HTML report. The starter already creates every object it uses. Restart R and Knit again to check that saved code and data are sufficient.
In an Rmd, prose belongs outside code chunks. R belongs between the chunk’s opening and closing triple backticks. Use the editor’s Insert Chunk command if you lose track of those boundaries. The teaching website uses .qmd files; your student report remains .Rmd.

title: R and R Markdown: restart the familiar workflow
text:
Recover from common errors







Symptom
Check




“Cannot open file”
Is the ZIP extracted? Is report.Rmd beside the data/ folder? Is the filename exact, including its extension?


“Object not found”
Is the object created in an earlier chunk in the report? Running a command in the console does not add it to the report


“Could not find function”
Load the package in the report’s setup chunk; check spelling


A column contains text instead of numbers
Inspect the CSV, decimal marks and import messages; do not silently coerce errors away


The output did not change
Save the Rmd and Knit again; confirm you opened the new HTML file


A calculation is 1000 times too large
Check g/mg and mol/mmol conversions



Ask for setup help if you cannot open the project or Knit the supplied starter. Keep working on the paper chemistry questions while the software issue is resolved.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
text: A five-week course (5KE231, 7.5 credits, Umeå University) on how the structure of a molecule decides what it does: drawing structures, following electrons through reactions, and using spectra and lab data as evidence. R is used beside the lab notebook for calculations, plots and reports.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
text:
Before you start

Set up R and knit your first report, then download the student project.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
text:
Topics
Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Topic days have a lecture, exercises, a self-check and an interactive demo; review days have mixed problems and a demo.

Week 1: Structures, properties, acids and bases. Read a skeletal structure, explain boiling points and solubility, and predict where a proton goes.
Week 2: Shape and electron flow. Conformations, stereochemistry and the curved-arrow language of mechanisms.
Week 3: Reactions at saturated carbon. Substitution, elimination, addition, and alcohol oxidation and reduction.
Week 4: Carbonyls and nitrogen. Addition to C=O, esters and amides, and amines and aromatic rings.
Week 5: Evidence. IR and NMR, synthesis and yield, and a final case that brings it all together.

See Canvas for dates, lab arrangements and assessment.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text:
Read molecular representations and identify functional groups and charges.
Explain properties and reactivity using polarity, resonance and acid–base reasoning.
Distinguish conformations and configurations and interpret simple stereochemistry.
Draw valid elementary mechanisms that conserve atoms and charge.
Predict selected substitution, elimination, addition, redox and carbonyl reactions.
Propose a short synthesis and justify conditions and experimental checks.
Use simple IR and one-dimensional NMR evidence to distinguish structures.
Record, calculate and communicate laboratory results in a reproducible report.

The course syllabus on Canvas gives the formal outcomes and examination rules.

text:
How to study a day
Watch the lecture and pause to draw and predict when a “Try it” box appears. Then do the exercises before opening the hints and worked answers, try the interactive demo, and finish with the self-check. When you get something wrong, redraw it correctly and say what changed. The course is a foundation for biochemistry. Organic Chemistry II is a possible follow-on elective for deeper synthesis and reactivity.

Individual files



Data
Used for

title: Data and downloads
text:
Keep the raw inputs
Do not edit the original CSVs to make your result look better. Import them, record transformations in the Rmd, and save derived outputs separately. Keep labels and units. Missing or unexpected values are a reason to inspect the input, not to delete rows without explanation.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text: Use these prompts while drawing. Return to the unit for the worked explanation.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
section: Audit a charge before drawing a mechanism
text:
Audit a charge before drawing a mechanism
Formal charge = valence electrons of the neutral atom − nonbonding electrons − the number of bond orders attached to that atom. A double bond contributes two bond orders. This is electron bookkeeping, not a measurement of partial charge in a polar bond.








Atom
Neutral-atom valence electrons
Common closed-shell patterns in this course




C
4
Four bond orders, no lone pair: neutral; three bonds/no lone pair: +1; three bonds/one lone pair: −1


N
5
Three single bonds and one lone pair: neutral; four single bonds and no lone pair: +1


O
6
Two bond orders/two lone pairs: neutral; one single bond/three lone pairs: −1; three bond orders/one lone pair: +1


Cl or Br
7
One single bond/three lone pairs: neutral; unbonded ion with four lone pairs: −1



Worked check: hydroxide oxygen has six nonbonding electrons and one bond order, so its formal charge is 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. If its lone pair forms a bond to H⁺, the oxygen then has two bonds and four nonbonding electrons: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. The species is water. A curved arrow shows the movement of the pair; the proton does not carry that pair into the reaction.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Read a structure
In a skeletal structure, an unlabelled line end or corner normally represents carbon. Add hydrogens to give the appropriate valence; label heteroatoms and their hydrogens explicitly. Count bond orders, charges and implicit hydrogens before comparing two drawings. A changed viewing angle does not create a new molecule.








Group
Condensed pattern
First question




Alcohol
R–OH
What can hydrogen-bond or be protonated?


Ether
R–O–R′
Where are the oxygen lone pairs?


Aldehyde
R–C(=O)H
Where is the electrophilic carbonyl carbon?


Ketone
R–C(=O)–R′
How can a nucleophile add?


Carboxylic acid
R–C(=O)OH
What stabilises the conjugate base?


Ester
R–C(=O)OR′
What could leave after addition to the acyl carbon?


Amide
R–C(=O)NR′R″
How does nitrogen donation change the bonds and basicity?


Amine
RNH₂, R₂NH or R₃N
Is the lone pair available, or delocalised?



R symbols mean carbon-containing groups and do not necessarily mean the same group when marked with different primes. They are not the stereochemical R descriptor.
Common shorthand in the worked problems: Me = CH₃ (methyl), Et = CH₂CH₃ (ethyl), Ph = C₆H₅ (phenyl, a benzene ring attached through one carbon), Nu = a nucleophile and LG = a leaving group. A shorthand label stands for the stated atoms; count them when checking a formula or a reaction.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Draw an electron-pair mechanism

Locate the electron source: a lone pair, negative charge or pi bond.
Locate the electron-poor atom or a bond that can accept the pair.
Draw each curved arrow from the electron pair to its destination.
Redraw bonds, lone pairs and charges after the step.
Check atom conservation, charge conservation and valence.

A reaction arrow connects reactants and products. An equilibrium arrow shows opposing reaction directions. A resonance arrow connects contributors of one species. A curved arrow shows electron movement. These symbols have different jobs.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
section: Choose among a few reaction patterns
text:
Choose among a few reaction patterns








Pattern
What changes
What to inspect




Acid–base
A proton changes its bonded partner
Conjugate-base stabilisation and compatible pKa values


Substitution
One group replaces another
Substrate, nucleophile, leaving group, solvent and mechanism


Elimination
Two groups are lost as a pi bond forms
Base, accessible geometry, substrate and competition


Addition
A pi bond becomes two new sigma bonds
Electrophile/nucleophile roles and stereochemistry


Carbonyl addition
A nucleophile adds and C=O becomes tetrahedral
The oxygen’s electrons and proton transfer


Acyl substitution
Addition then loss reforms C=O
Leaving group and reaction conditions


Alcohol redox
The carbon’s bonds to H/O change
Oxidation level, reagent selectivity and conditions

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Read a stereochemical drawing
A normal line lies in the drawing plane; a solid wedge points toward you; a hashed wedge points away. Rotating the whole molecule in space preserves configuration. Exchanging two groups at a stereocentre reverses it.
For a simple R/S assignment, rank the directly attached atoms by atomic number: Br (35) > Cl (17) > O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1). Break a tie by comparing the next attached atoms in descending order until the first difference. For this comparison count a multiple bond using duplicate atoms. Point priority 4 away: 1→2→3 clockwise is R, counterclockwise is S. If 4 points toward you, invert that apparent result.
Worked check: for CH₃CH(OH)COOH, priority is OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. Oxygen wins at the first atom; the carboxyl carbon’s next-atom list O,O,O beats the methyl carbon’s H,H,H. In a Fischer projection with COOH at the top, CH₃ at the bottom, OH left and H right, the apparent 1→2→3 path is clockwise, but H points toward you under the Fischer convention. The configuration is S. Horizontal Fischer bonds point toward you and vertical bonds away.
For E/Z, rank the two substituents on each alkene carbon separately. Higher priority groups on the same side give Z; opposite sides give E. Each alkene carbon must have two different substituents for E/Z to apply. An R/S label does not specify the sign of measured optical rotation.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Calculate with units








Quantity
Relationship
Units/check




Chemical amount
\(n=m/M\)
g ÷ (g/mol) = mol


Reaction extent capacity
\(n_i/\nu_i\)
Compare balanced-equation coefficients; smallest reactant value limits


Theoretical product amount
\(n_P=\nu_P\min(n_i/\nu_i)\)
mol


Theoretical product mass
\(m_P=n_PM_P\)
mol × g/mol = g


Isolated yield
\(100m_{isolated}/m_{theoretical}\)
Percent; mass ratio does not establish purity


TLC (thin-layer chromatography) retention factor
\(R_f=d_{spot}/d_{front}\)
Dimensionless, from the same origin


Enantiomeric excess
\(ee=|\%R-\%S|\)
Percentage points expressed as % ee; specify major enantiomer



For a mixture containing only two enantiomers, 70% R and 30% S is 40% ee in favour of R. The major-enantiomer percentage is 70%, not 40%.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Ask what the evidence establishes
IR supports functional-group assignments. NMR reports chemical environments, integrations and coupling patterns. TLC compares behaviour under specified conditions. None is a universal identity or purity certificate on its own. Use several observations and explain the alternatives they rule out.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Decode the supplied spectra
In an IR transmittance plot, absorptions point downward. Wavenumber is normally shown decreasing from left to right. The local teaching examples use a broad alcohol O–H feature around 3350 cm⁻¹ and strong carbonyl features around 1710–1740 cm⁻¹. Carboxylic-acid O–H is much broader, extending across roughly 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. These are approximate clues; the full structure and measurement conditions affect band positions. The problem states its actual observations.
In the simple proton NMR examples, chemical shift is in ppm, integration is relative proton count, and multiplicity reports resolved coupling. For a first-order signal coupled to n equivalent neighbouring protons, the simple pattern has n + 1 lines. Do not apply that rule blindly to exchangeable O–H signals or complex nonequivalent neighbours. Peak height is not integration.
Worked check: a 3H triplet at 1.25 ppm and a 2H quartet at 4.12 ppm support an ethyl group with the CH₂ near oxygen. An additional 3H singlet at 2.05 ppm is consistent with CH₃–C(=O)–. Together with formula C₄H₈O₂ and ester-like IR, the supplied teaching unknown is consistent with CH₃COOCH₂CH₃. The singlet methyl has no neighbouring carbon-bound proton across the carbonyl. This interpretation combines several observations rather than treating one shift as unique proof.
When given a molecular formula containing ordinary C, H, N, O and halogens, the degree of unsaturation is \((2C+2+N-H-X)/2\), where X is the total number of halogen atoms. Oxygen does not change this count. For C₄H₈O₂ it is one: one ring or one double bond would account for it. The formula alone does not choose between those possibilities or establish connectivity.

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
Connect molecular representations, properties and acid–base behaviour in your answers.
Core 1–8: about 75–95 minutes including comparison and correction. Extension 9–12: about 30–45 minutes for optional independent work. Try each problem before opening its hint, then use the worked answer to check your reasoning.

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
section: 1. Build a formula from explicit groups
text:
1. Build a formula from explicit groups
Expand CH₃CH(OH)COOH and give its formula. Name its alcohol and acid patterns.






Hint





Count H on both OH groups.









Worked check





C₃H₆O₃. It contains a secondary alcohol and carboxylic acid. The middle CH has one H and four different substituents.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
2. Find an oxygen-placement isomer
Draw an alcohol and an ether satisfying C₄H₁₀O. State which has an O–H donor.






Hint





Unbranched butanol and diethyl ether are possible choices.









Worked check





Butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH and diethyl ether CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ both fit. Only the alcohol has OH; both have oxygen acceptor sites.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
3. Test a valence correction
A student draws neutral O with three single bonds and no charge. Supply the expected lone-pair count and formal charge for ordinary three-bonded O.






Hint





Use6 valence electrons and one remaining lone pair.









Worked check





With three bonds and one pair, O has FC6−2−3=+1. Add the+charge rather than claiming ordinary neutral oxygen has that pattern.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
section: 4. Give a solubility prediction with limits
text:
4. Give a solubility prediction with limits
Compare propan-1-ol and octan-1-ol CH₃(CH₂)₇OH in water. State a trend and why no exact g/L value follows.






Hint





The OH count is unchanged but hydrocarbon size changes.









Worked check





Propan-1-ol is more water compatible. The larger nonpolar region of octanol weighs against water compatibility; temperature and phase interactions are needed for exact solubility.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
5. Sketch two IR predictions
For propanone and propan-2-ol, sketch schematic transmission traces showing the key distinguishing feature. Label axes and simulated status.






Hint





Dip direction follows lower transmittance.









Worked check





The ketone has C=O without OH; the alcohol has broad OH without C=O. Use wavenumber in cm⁻¹, decreasing conventionally to the right, and transmittance vertically. These are predicted schematic traces.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
6. Protonate and conserve atoms
Draw CH₃CH₂NH₂+H–A⇌CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺+A⁻ with arrows and nitrogen charges.






Hint





The donor H becomes part of the ammonium product.









Worked check





N pair→H and H–A pair→A. Nitrogen goes from three bonds/neutral to four bonds/+1, with A⁻ balancing total charge.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
7. Predict equilibrium direction
Use supplied pKa 5 for HA and 9 for BH⁺. For HA+B⇌A⁻+BH⁺, calculate K and state the weaker acid.






Hint





Product-acid minus reactant-acid pKa.









Worked check





K≈10⁴. BH⁺ is the weaker acid with larger pKa; products are favoured under the compatible-data approximation.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
section: 8. Interpret an acid fraction in words
text:
8. Interpret an acid fraction in words
A supplied model gives0.80A⁻ and 0.20HA fractions. Give the ratio and explain what an individual molecule is.






Hint





Divide the two fractions; do not describe fractional proton charges.









Worked check





A⁻/HA=4. Individual species are HA or A⁻;80 % describes the population, not each molecule80 % deprotonated.




Optional extension
Use these after the core or during later revision.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
9. Construct a reversible comparison
Reverse the equilibrium with K=10⁴from problem7. Give the reverse K and explain why it changes.






Hint





Reverse exchanges numerator and denominator activities.









Worked check





Kreverse=10⁻⁴. A reaction and its reverse cannot both have the same strongly product-favoured constant under the same conventions.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
10. Separate resonance from a reaction
Draw two ethanoate contributors and a separate ethanoic-acid proton-loss equation. Label their different arrows.






Hint





Use one double-headed resonance arrow versus equilibrium notation.









Worked check





Contributors share nuclei/connectivity and describe one ion. Proton loss changes species by H⁺ transfer. Do not use a chemical-equilibrium interpretation for the resonance contributors.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
11. Critique a filename-based identity claim
An IR file is named alcohol.csv but has a strong carbonyl and no suitable OH feature. Give a cautious explanation and next check.






Hint





A supplied label is not experimental proof.









Worked check





The label, target or sample may be wrong, or data may be incomplete. Compare full spectra and independent evidence before calling it an alcohol. The filename alone cannot override observations.
crumbs: Day 5: Connecting structure, properties and acidity

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
12. Write a bounded conclusion
For a candidate ketone with suitable IR carbonyl evidence, write a claim, an observation, a chemical reason and one limitation.






Hint





Name what the observation actually tests.









Worked check





Example:“The sample is consistent with a carbonyl candidate because it absorbs strongly in the supplied C=O region. Several carbonyl structures remain possible; further evidence is needed for unique identity or purity.”

title: Day 5: Exercises — Connecting structure, properties and acidity
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
If only neutral HA enters the organic phase, will raising aqueous pH increase or decrease the total solute recovered there? What extra information beyond pH and pKa must the model use?
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Keep P = 10 and equal 50 mL phases. Compare the mostly neutral and mostly ionised acid presets. Explain why aqueous deprotonation changes the effective distribution ratio D.
Hold the aqueous pH fixed. Double the organic-phase volume, then double the aqueous-phase volume instead. Predict the direction of organic recovery before each change.
Change P while holding pH and volumes fixed. State which property P represents and why changing P is not the same operation as changing acid strength. Reset and compare all three total-solute fractions.



Take-away
Explain why an aqueous ionisation curve alone cannot predict extraction. Which additional assumptions would fail if ion pairing carried A⁻ into the organic phase?


Model and limits
Teaching extension: only neutral HA partitions, with P = [HA]organic/[HA]aqueous; A⁻ stays in water. Aqueous pH is externally fixed, equilibrium is reached, volumes remain constant and phases are immiscible. D = P/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)); organic fraction = D Vorg/(Vaq + D Vorg). Both volumes use the same units. The equal-height layer drawing is schematic; layer order does not predict solvent density. This is not an experimental extraction protocol.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text: Use molecular drawings and supplied observations to justify a stereochemical conclusion. Core 1–8: about 75–95 minutes including comparison and correction. Extension 9–12: about 30–45 minutes for optional independent work. Revisit the hints after an attempt; each worked check explains the rule, not just the label.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
section: 1. Recover identity behind a rotated drawing
text:
1. Recover identity behind a rotated drawing
Draw CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ twice with different bends in the chain. Do these establish different configurations? Identify any tetrahedral stereocentre or E/Z element that could justify that claim.






Hint





A drawn bend cannot create four different substituents or a double bond.









Worked check





Ordinary butane has no tetrahedral configurational stereocentre and no E/Z double-bond element. The bends are different views or conformations of the same connected molecule, not different configurations. Adding depth information cannot create a stereogenic element missing from the actual structure.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
2. Compare two constitutional frameworks
Draw CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and(CH₃)₃CH. Give formulas and explain why rotation cannot interconvert the connectivities.






Hint





Count carbon neighbours at the branching site.









Worked check





Both are C₄H₁₀. Branched central CH has three C neighbours; no carbon in unbranched butane has three. Bond rotation preserves neighbours and cannot create that branch.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
3. Read a torsional path
For a qualitative ethane curve with maxima at 0,120,240,360°, give minima positions and why they repeat.






Hint





Staggered lies halfway between adjacent eclipses.









Worked check





Minima at 60,180,300°. Equivalent H substituents make the three minima equivalent. The qualitative drawing does not give numerical free-energy populations.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
4. Use supplied numerical weights
Weights of states A/B are 1 and 0.10. Compute fractions and say whether B is absent.






Hint





Normalise by 1.10.









Worked check





A≈0.9091 andB≈0.0909. B has a smaller but finite equilibrium population, not zero. Weights are not fractions until normalised.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
5. Change only the energy reference
Two supplied state free energies are 0 and 3500 J/mol. Add2000 J/mol to both. Will the population ratio change?






Hint





The common exponential factor cancels.









Worked check





No. The difference stays3500 J/mol. Both weights gain the same multiplier and their normalised ratio remains unchanged.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
6. Distinguish a barrier claim
An equatorial methyl chair is favoured. Does that preference alone determine how many flips occur each second?






Hint





Equilibrium preference and activation barrier answer different questions.









Worked check





No. The state free-energy difference describes preference; the barrier affects the rate. Additional kinetic information is required.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
7. Do one direct-atom priority ranking
For a centre directly attached to I, Br, Cl, H, rank the groups. Supplied atomic numbers:I53, Br35, Cl17, H1.






Hint





Use atomic number, not page position.









Worked check





I>Br>Cl>H. The given atomic numbers resolve the first comparison without needing further substituent shells.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
8. Assign the opposite lactic projection
Draw COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH right, H left. Assign R/S, then rotate the entire Fischer180° and check identity.






Hint





H points toward; apply the final inversion.









Worked check





This is R. After180°, labels become CH₃ top, COOH bottom, OH left, H right, still R. The whole rotation is not a one-pair exchange.




Optional extension
Use these after the core or during later revision.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
9. Distinguish enantiomers from diastereomers
Use CH₃CH(Br)CH(Cl)CH₃, numbered from the Br end. Classify the supplied (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair and (2R,3R)/(2R,3S) pair; no new R/S assignment is required.






Hint





A mirror reverses both centres.









Worked check





RR/SS are enantiomers; RR/RS are diastereomers. The stated absence of special symmetry is necessary when using descriptors alone this way.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
10. Compute a different ee
A two-enantiomer mixture is 65 % S,35 % R. Give ee and recover the major percentage from the excess.






Hint





Subtract, then solve major=(100+ee)/2.









Worked check





30 % ee in favour of S. The major fraction is(100+30)/2=65%. An ee of 30 % does not mean30 % major enantiomer.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
11. Reject a rotation-sign shortcut
A student assigns R and writes “therefore rotates light clockwise and binds more strongly.” Identify both unsupported steps.






Hint





Configuration is not an optical or receptor measurement.









Worked check





R does not universally determine(+)/(−), and neither descriptor determines relative receptor affinity. Each claim needs the appropriate measured evidence and stated conditions.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
12. Design a bounded stereochemical conclusion
A sample’s measured enantiomer ratio is 90:10R:S but an unrelated solvent impurity remains. State ee and a conclusion that does not overclaim purity.






Hint





Separate the two kinds of composition.









Worked check





The measured enantiomeric components have80 % ee in favour of R. That result does not establish total chemical purity because the solvent is outside the R/S ratio.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
Review your solutions
Choose one corrected drawing and one corrected explanation. State the observation or rule that made you change your answer. Save these beside your course notes; extra R tasks belong to their separate unit practice pages.

title: Day 10: Exercises — Stereochemistry and mixtures
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). A mixture contains 70% R and 30% S among its measured enantiomeric components. Is its ee 70%, 40% or 30%? State which quantity each percentage describes.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Move the R slider toward 50%, then beyond it. Use the racemate and 95:5 presets. Find a composition giving 80% ee in favour of R, and another giving the same ee in favour of S. Record both full compositions.
Explain (2 minutes). Why is the major-enantiomer percentage (100+ee)/2 for a two-enantiomer mixture? Why does reversing the major enantiomer leave the magnitude of ee unchanged? Can any setting establish the sign of optical rotation?


Supplied model and its limits
The only counted components are R and S; their percentages total 100. ee=|R%−S%| gives the magnitude, and the major label gives its direction. Chemical impurities are outside this composition calculation. R/S describes configuration and does not predict (+)/(−) rotation or biological potency.


Carry the explanation into practice
Return to the local stereochemistry lesson. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved. The interactive works locally and needs no online account or additional software packages.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
Connect alcohol and carbonyl transformations to reagent amounts, isolated yield and experimental evidence. Revisit the alcohols and redox lecture, then explore the limiting-reagent and yield demo.
Core 1–8: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 9–12: an optional 30–45 minutes. Draw before opening a check; compare reasoning with a partner and keep your own corrected drawing.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
Refresher and worked start
Full-headed arrows move pairs from bonds/lone pairs; ordinary carbon has total bond order four. Alpha is the leaving-group carbon; beta is its neighbour. E2 uses an appropriate anti geometry and three linked pair movements. Selected carbonyl reduction gives alkoxide then alcohol after proton transfer.
For the worked starting example OH⁻+CH₃Br→CH₃OH+Br⁻, draw OH pair→C and C–Br pair→Br. Both sides have net charge −1; the concerted step contains no carbocation. Use the same atom/charge audit in the problems below.
Calculation conventions: n=m/M with g and g/mol gives mol;1000 mmol=1 mol. Compare n/coefficient for a balanced equation. Yield%=100×isolated/theoretical mass. TLC (thin-layer chromatography) Rf=spot/front distance using the same origin and matched plate conditions. All numerical observations below are constructed teaching data, not real experimental results.
For the local carbon oxidation-state comparison, assign +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H bond and 0 per C–C bond. Thus the OH-bearing carbon of ethanol has +1 − 2 = −1, while the carbonyl carbon of ethanal has +2 − 1 = +1. These supplied rules are sufficient for the C/H/O examples below.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
1. Map two directions
Draw ethanol→ethanal and ethanal→ethanol. Label oxidation and reduction and identify the changing carbon.






Hint





Compare local C–O bond orders and C–H bonds.









Worked answer and reasoning





Ethanol to ethanal is oxidation: the changing carbon rises from −1 to+1 in the supplied bond-count convention. Returning to ethanol is reduction. The same two-carbon skeleton is retained.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
2. Extend a secondary-alcohol map
Draw butan-2-ol and predict its selected carbon-skeleton-retaining oxidation product. Explain why butanal is not the corresponding product.






Hint





The OH-bearing carbon remains connected to methyl and ethyl groups.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is butan-2-one CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Butanal would place the carbonyl at an end, changing which carbon bears it rather than simply oxidising the original secondary centre.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
3. Detect impossible valence
A student oxidises(CH₃)₃COH to (CH₃)₃C=O with all C–C bonds retained. Draw and count the central bond orders.






Hint





Three single C–C bonds plus a double C=O are too many.









Worked answer and reasoning





The proposed carbon has bond-order sum five. A tertiary alcohol lacks the carbinol C–H required for the simple alcohol-to-carbonyl map. Harsh C–C-cleaving oxidation is a different process.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
4. Reduce then protonate
Use the selected NaBH₄-type model to reduce propanal, then use water for proton donation. Draw the alkoxide and neutral product.






Hint





Hydride delivery makes C–H while pi electrons go to oxygen.









Worked answer and reasoning





Propanal gives CH₃CH₂CH₂O⁻ first, then propan-1-ol plus OH⁻ after water protonation. H:⁻ is reagent-delivery shorthand, not free hydride persisting in water.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
section: 5. Prepare an amount table by hand
text:
5. Prepare an amount table by hand
For the supplied1:1 aspirin teaching equation, calculate mmol from 1.3812 g salicylic acid at 138.12 g/mol and1.53135 g acetic anhydride at 102.09 g/mol.






Hint





Use n=m/M; mmol=1000×mol.









Worked answer and reasoning





The values are 10.00 mmol acid and15.00 mmol anhydride. Acid limits the 1:1 reaction to 10.00 mmol product. The equation is a calculation context rather than a laboratory protocol.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
6. Change the limiting reagent
Keep the acid input but use0.51045 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol. Predict the limit before calculating the maximum product mass at 180.16 g/mol.






Hint





The changed anhydride input is 5.00 mmol.









Worked answer and reasoning





Anhydride now limits product to 5.00 mmol. Theoretical mass=0.00500 mol×180.16 g/mol=0.9008 g. Reusing the original acid-based theoretical mass would overstate the new maximum.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
7. Apply a nonunit coefficient
For the hypothetical balanced stoichiometry A+2B→P, amounts are 8 mmol A and12 mmol B. Calculate the maximum P.






Hint





Divide each amount by its coefficient.









Worked answer and reasoning





A permits 8 mmol extent; B permits 6 mmol. B limits the maximum P to 6 mmol. Raw amount alone would miss the stoichiometric demand.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
8. Compute and interpret yield
The original aspirin teaching case has theoretical mass1.8016 g and isolated mass1.20 g. Calculate yield and explain why it does not give conversion.






Hint





Use 100×isolated/theoretical, then think about isolation loss.









Worked answer and reasoning





Isolated yield is about 66.6%. Product can be lost during separation even if substantial starting material reacted; side reactions and contamination also complicate the relation. Conversion needs evidence about starting-material consumption.









Note



Optional transfer problems 9–12. Select for revision; they are not additional required contact hours.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
9. Keep every TLC spot
A matched normal-phase teaching plate has solvent front5.0 cm. Starting-material spot travels1.2 cm, reference product3.2 cm, and crude has both spots. Calculate each Rf and interpret the two crude spots.






Hint





Rf=spot distance/front distance; do not average two different compounds.









Worked answer and reasoning





The Rf values are 0.24 and0.64. Crude contains two resolved spots under these conditions, consistent with more than one detectable component. Co-migration supports comparison but does not prove identity; invisible impurities can remain.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
10. Interpret a functional-group change
A proposed secondary-alcohol oxidation loses broad alcohol OH absorption and gains strong C=O absorption. What is supported, and what does one visible TLC spot fail to establish?






Hint





Separate functional class from complete identity and purity.









Worked answer and reasoning





The IR supports formation of a carbonyl-containing material and loss of the alcohol feature. A single TLC spot does not prove pure intended ketone; co-migration or undetected components and other carbonyl structures remain possible.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
11. Check primary records
A report has a yield but no sample identifiers, no raw mass record and a spectrum labelled only unknown. Name three specific repairs and why each matters.






Hint





A later result needs to be tied to its actual observation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Restore sample IDs linking isolated material and spectrum; retain dated raw mass/amount records; label the spectrum axes, conditions and sample provenance. These make the chemical claim traceable instead of a disconnected number and picture.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
12. Assemble an evidence paragraph
Write four sentences using these teaching observations:1.20 g isolated, theoretical1.8016 g, crude TLC two spots, isolated sample one visible spot under matched conditions, carbonyl IR present. Include a justified limit.






Hint





Report observations first, then the conclusion they actually support.









Worked answer and reasoning





A defensible paragraph reports66.6% apparent isolated mass yield, records that crude had two visible TLC components and isolated material one under the stated conditions, and notes carbonyl evidence. It explicitly avoids equating one spot with purity or carbonyl presence with unique identity; more structure evidence is needed.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
Revisit the relevant lesson
Use the substitution, elimination/addition and alcohol/redox explanations when a correction needs more context.

title: Day 15: Exercises — Redox, amounts and evidence
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1–2 minutes). The starting masses represent 10.00 mmol salicylic acid and 15.00 mmol acetic anhydride in a 1:1 reaction. Predict the maximum aspirin amount and mass before changing a control.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Use the anhydride-limited preset and explain the new limit. Restore the default, then test zero acid, an empty field, a negative input and an isolate mass above the theoretical maximum. Distinguish an invalid input from a valid zero measurement.
Explain (2 minutes). Report the default theoretical mass and isolated yield. Why is yield undefined when theoretical product is zero? Why should an apparent yield above 100% trigger a check of composition/inputs instead of being clamped to 100% or celebrated as extra product?


Supplied model and its limits
Supplied balanced teaching equation: salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid; all coefficients are 1. Molar masses are 138.12 g/mol, 102.09 g/mol and 180.16 g/mol for the two reactants and aspirin respectively. Use n=m/M, minimum reactant amount/coefficient, and yield%=100×isolated/theoretical mass. The isolate mass can include impurities or solvent; mass yield does not establish purity or conversion. Inputs are constructed teaching quantities, not a protocol.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
Use nitrogen lone pairs, aromaticity and proton transfers to explain basicity and amino-acid charge. Allow 150 minutes: 10 minutes to recall the key ideas, 48 minutes for problems 1–6, 48 minutes for 7–10, 34 minutes for 11–12, and 10 minutes to review. These timings include drawing and comparison; continue unfinished problems later rather than rushing a mechanism.
Local explanations: Amines and aromatics and acyl chemistry.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
Working definitions
Use full-headed arrows for electron pairs: start at a lone pair or bond and end at its acceptor. Keep ordinary carbon to four bond orders and conserve atoms and net charge. For compatible proton-transfer data, K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For amounts use n=m/M and 1 mol=1000 mmol; compare n/coefficient before predicting theoretical product. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated/theoretical product mass. TLC (thin-layer chromatography) uses Rf=spot/front distances from the same origin. For simple first-order NMR, n adjacent equivalent H give n +1 lines while integration counts H area.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
1. Count N substituents
Classify EtNH₂, EtNHMe and EtNMe₂ as primary, secondary or tertiary, with Et=CH₂CH₃ and Me=CH₃. Count N–H bonds and neutral N lone pairs.






Hint





Classification counts carbon groups directly attached to N.









Worked explanation





They are primary with 2 N–H, secondary with 1 N–H and tertiary with 0 N–H. Each neutral ordinary amine has three bonds and one pair.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
2. Protonate explicitly
Draw EtNH₂+H₃O⁺ with both arrows and products. State the N bond count, N charge and total reacting charge after transfer.






Hint





The donor O–H pair returns to water oxygen.









Worked explanation





EtNH₃⁺+H₂O form. N has four bonds/+1; total +1 is conserved. A new bond uses the original N nonbonding pair.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
3. Compare base equilibria
Neutral bases B1 and B2 have supplied conjugate-acid pKa values 9.0 and 5.0. Which is stronger under comparable conditions? Predict BH2⁺+B1⇌B2+BH1⁺ and estimate K.






Hint





The weaker acid is the one with larger pKa.









Worked explanation





B1 is stronger. Products contain the weaker acid BH1⁺, so K≈10^(9−5)=10⁴ toward products. This does not alone determine every nucleophilic rate.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
4. Convert a ratio to fraction
For pKa(BH⁺)=9.0, use[B]/[BH⁺]=10^(pH−pKa). At pH8, find the ratio and protonated fraction.






Hint





The fraction BH⁺ is 1/(1+ratio).









Worked explanation





The ratio is 0.1 and the protonated fraction 1/1.1≈0.909, about 90.9%. The ratio 0.1 is not a 10% protonated fraction.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
5. Read an amide site
For MeC(=O)NHEt, draw the neutral and charge-separated contributors and identify why its N pair should not be treated like EtNH₂.






Hint





N donation shifts the carbonyl pi pair to O.









Worked explanation





MeC(O⁻)=N⁺HEt contributes with net 0. Delocalisation gives partial C–N double character and changes pair availability. A simple amine lacks this direct carbonyl conjugation.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
6. Check cyclic conjugation
Compare benzene with cyclohexane. For each state whether continuous cyclic pi overlap exists, and count benzene pi electrons using 4 n +2.






Hint





A ring of sigma bonds is insufficient.









Worked explanation





Benzene has continuous overlap and 6 pi electrons, n=1. Cyclohexane is nonaromatic because it lacks that network; it is not automatically antiaromatic.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
7. Compare aromatic nitrogens
Pyridine has an N pair outside its pi sextet; pyrrole supplies its N pair to the sextet. Which N is more readily protonated ordinarily, and why?






Hint





Ask whether the pair already supplies aromatic stabilisation.









Worked explanation





Pyridine is more basic at N in this comparison. Protonation uses its separate pair while retaining the sextet. Pyrrole pair participation makes ordinary N protonation much less favourable.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
section: 8. Draw an amino acid at low pH
text:
8. Draw an amino acid at low pH
Use the simple amino acid H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH with supplied pKa 2.4 for COOH and 9.7 for ammonium. Draw its predominant form at pH1 and net charge.






Hint





Both sites are mostly protonated well below their pKa values.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COOH predominates, net +1. The carbon skeleton and the stereocentre’s bonds are retained by those protonation changes.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
9. Draw the zwitterion
With the same pKa 2.4 and 9.7, draw the predominant amino-acid form at pH6. Mark individual and net charges.






Hint





pH lies above the acid pKa but below ammonium pKa.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻ predominates. N is +1 and carboxylate −1, net 0; charged sites remain even when the net charge is zero.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
10. Draw the high-pH form
At pH12 with supplied pKa 2.4 and 9.7, draw the dominant form and the reaction from its zwitterion with OH⁻.






Hint





Ammonium can lose H while carboxylate stays deprotonated.









Worked explanation





H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻ forms with water. Zwitterion+OH⁻→amino-acid anion+H₂O; total −1 is conserved and N returns to three bonds plus a pair.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
11. Explain a nonbasic peptide site
For H₂NCH₂C(=O)NHCH₃, identify which N is amide-like and explain why assigning one basicity to all N sites is unsound.






Hint





Trace each N’s direct attachment to C=O.









Worked explanation





The right NH is directly bound to acyl carbon and has amide delocalisation. The left H₂N is not directly bound to carbonyl. They are different local environments, so pair availability and protonation behaviour differ.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
12. Critique a universal rate rule
A student ranks two amines by conjugate-acid pKa and claims the stronger base must attack all carbon electrophiles faster. State the supported conclusion and two missing rate factors.






Hint





Equilibrium and kinetics ask different questions.









Worked explanation





Compatible pKa values compare proton-transfer basicity. Substrate structure, steric access, solvent, leaving group and nucleophile solvation can alter nucleophilic rates. The pKa comparison is useful but is not a universal kinetic law.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
Review your reasoning
Choose two corrected errors: one in a drawing/calculation and one in an interpretation. Explain why the corrected answer follows from the supplied inputs. Keep the first attempt so you can see the change in your reasoning.

title: Day 20: Exercises — Nitrogen, aromaticity and charge
text:
Explore
Question: which proposed arrow actually explains amide electron availability while conserving atoms, charge and ordinary valence?
Allow 10 minutes: predict for 2, audit several moves for 5, then draw and explain your corrected result for 3.

Enable JavaScript to choose an electron source and destination and inspect charge feedback.




Predict
Compare ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂, with ethanamide, CH₃C(=O)NH₂. For the amide, a nitrogen pair can form C=N only if the C=O pi pair moves to O at the same time. Predict the O and N charges and the net charge in that contributor.
A full-headed arrow starts at a lone pair or bond. A positive-charge symbol is not a pair source. Ordinary carbon must retain a total bond order of four.


Explore

Select Nitrogen lone pair → C–N pi bond for the amide. Omit the coupled carbonyl move, inspect the feedback, and then include it.
Compare the same proposed move for ethylamine. Identify the missing neighbouring structural feature.
Try Carbonyl pi pair → oxygen. Distinguish this polar contributor from the coupled N-donation contributor.
Compare formal amine protonation. Explain why adding H⁺ changes a molecular species whereas drawing resonance contributors does not.



Explain and check
The coupled amide contributor has N⁺ and O⁻, net zero: CH₃C(=O)NH₂ ↔︎ CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. The double-headed resonance link connects representations of one delocalised molecule, not two species switching at equilibrium. Partial C–N double-bond character helps explain restricted rotation and altered N-pair availability.
Moving only the carbonyl pi pair gives a minor C⁺/O⁻ polar contributor; it preserves net charge but does not alone show N donation. The tool distinguishes formally valid accounting from the most useful or most stabilised contributor.


Model limits
H⁺ abbreviates an actual proton donor; a complete reaction mechanism also shows the donor bond breaking. Amide N protonation is possible as a formal reaction but is much less favourable than ordinary alkylamine protonation; under common strong-acid conditions amide O protonation can be preferred. This tool does not compute site populations or energies. Use the local amide exercises and nitrogen exercises for further practice.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
Combine reaction amounts, stereochemical drawings and spectral observations into justified chemical conclusions.
Allow 150 minutes: 10 minutes for retrieval, 48 for exercises 1–6, 48 for 7–10, 34 for 11–12 and 10 to review your solutions. Drawing and comparison are included in that time. Finish remaining problems independently rather than rushing a mechanism.
See also: integrated chemistry and spectroscopy.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
Working definitions
Use full-headed arrows for electron pairs: start at a lone pair or bond and end at its acceptor. Keep ordinary carbon to four bond orders and conserve atoms and net charge. For compatible proton-transfer data, K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For amounts use n=m/M and 1 mol=1000 mmol; compare n/coefficient before predicting theoretical product. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated/theoretical product mass. TLC (thin-layer chromatography) uses Rf=spot/front distances from the same origin. For simple first-order NMR, n adjacent equivalent H give n +1 lines while integration counts H area. Any further structure, constant or observation you need is given in the problem.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
1. Read a new secondary alcohol
For CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COOH, identify the alcohol type, acid and possible tetrahedral stereocentre. List four groups at the OH-bearing carbon.






Hint





The changing centre is bonded to CH₃ and CH₂COOH, not directly to carbonyl carbon.









Worked explanation





It is a secondary alcohol and carboxylic acid with substituents OH,H,CH₃,CH₂COOH at the tetrahedral carbon. Those groups differ, so that carbon is a stereocentre.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
2. Rank the new carbon branches
At that centre compare CH₂COOH with CH₃ using attached-atom lists C,H,H versus H,H,H. Give full priorities with O and H included.






Hint





Break the first C/C tie at the next attached atoms.









Worked explanation





CH₂COOH outranks CH₃ because C outranks H at the first difference. Full order is OH>CH₂COOH>CH₃>H. Priority follows atomic comparison, not a memorised lactic-acid label.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
3. Transfer acid–base reasoning
Draw hydroxide removal of the COOH proton from CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COOH with both arrows. Does that elementary transfer invert the OH-bearing stereocentre?






Hint





Follow the acidic H and the original O–H bonding pair.









Worked explanation





The product is CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COO⁻+H₂O. Base pair→H and acid O–H pair→acid O. Bonds at the stereocentre are not rearranged by this step, so it does not itself invert.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
4. Transfer oxidation reasoning
Oxidise the secondary alcohol of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂COOH to a ketone while retaining skeleton. Give product and identify whether the former centre remains stereogenic.






Hint





The OH-bearing CH becomes C=O.









Worked explanation





CH₃C(=O)CH₂COOH forms as the selected target. The former centre is trigonal planar and no longer the tetrahedral stereocentre. Conditions/selectivity still matter in an actual reaction.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
5. Distinguish ester from amide
Compare CH₃C(=O)OCH₃ and CH₃C(=O)NHCH₃. Identify common electrophilic site and explain a structural reason their chemistry differs.






Hint





Both have an acyl carbon; only the amide has N-pair donation into it.









Worked explanation





Both initially accept a suitable nucleophile at carbonyl carbon. Amide resonance stabilisation and leaving-group behaviour differ from ester, so common carbonyl shape does not imply equal reactivity or conditions.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
6. Repair an acid–amine shortcut
For CH₃COOH+CH₃CH₂NH₂, use pKa 4.8 for acid and 10.7 for ethylammonium. Predict the initial favoured pair and explain why the result is not an amide bond.






Hint





Compare acid strengths in the proton-transfer equation.









Worked explanation





CH₃COO⁻+CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ are favoured, with K≈10^5.9. This transfers H, not an acyl group. Amide formation needs suitable activation/conditions and a valid addition–elimination pathway.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
7. Resolve a formula-compatible unknown
U has C₄H₈O₂, C=O IR without broadOH, and proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. Assign the ester candidate and reject the acid with two independent clues.






Hint





Use the full ethyl/acetyl pattern, not just one triplet.









Worked explanation





CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ fits O–CH₂ quartet, ethyl methyl triplet and acetyl methyl singlet. Butanoic acid predicts acid OH and lacks O–CH₂ plus isolated acetyl methyl; terminal triplet alone could occur in either.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
8. Keep model claims honest
The unknown spectra above are numerically simulated. A student uses the plot to claim their own unrelated isolate was measured and pure. Identify both unsupported parts of that claim.






Hint





Provenance and purity each need their own evidence.









Worked explanation





A generated teaching trace is not a measurement of the student’s isolate. Even an appropriate measured functional-group spectrum alone would not necessarily prove purity. Sample-linked measurements and suitable composition checks are needed.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
9. Calculate a new limiting case
A1:1 reaction has A=0.00400 mol, B=0.00600 mol and product coefficient 1. Product M=125.0 g/mol. Calculate limiter and theoretical mass.






Hint





Compare n/coefficient, then convert product mol to g.









Worked explanation





A limits at 0.00400 mol product. Theoretical mass=0.00400×125.0=0.500 g. Excess B does not increase that stoichiometric maximum.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
10. Interpret a high apparent yield
The previous theoretical mass is 0.500 g and isolate is 0.480 g. Calculate apparent yield. If NMR contains major extra signals, what should be investigated before stating pure product?






Hint





A plausible mass fraction does not establish the numerator’s composition.









Worked explanation





Apparent yield=96.0%, assuming product mass. Investigate residual solvent, another component, unreacted starting material or assignment error using appropriate full evidence; the problem does not identify a unique impurity.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
11. Audit a TLC conclusion
A reference and isolate each have one spot atRf 0.50 under one condition. Explain the supported comparison and two reasons it does not uniquely prove identity/purity.






Hint





Ask what separation and detection could fail to distinguish.









Worked explanation





Their detected retention matches under those conditions. Co-migration can hide distinct compounds, and some components may not be detected. A single matching spot is useful comparison evidence rather than a unique molecular proof.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
section: 12. Write a final conclusion and next test
text:
12. Write a final conclusion and next test
Combine the hypothetical reaction amounts,96% apparent yield and uncertain NMR from these exercises into a short claim with limitation and targeted next observation.






Hint





Include the quantity actually calculated and the evidence that challenges its interpretation.









Worked explanation





The mass calculation gives 96% apparent isolated yield under the product-mass assumption, but unexpected NMR makes purity/identity uncertain. A complete spectral assignment and suitable comparison or separation should test a specific remaining alternative before claiming successful pure-product isolation.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
Review your reasoning
Choose two corrected errors: one in a drawing/calculation and one in an interpretation. Explain why the corrected answer follows from the supplied inputs. Keep the first attempt so you can see the change in your reasoning.

title: Day 25: Exercises — Final synthesis and interpretation
text:
Explore
Question: which claims about amount, conversion, identity and purity follow from the supplied observations—and which remain unsupported?
Allow 10 minutes: predict for 2, change evidence for 5, then write a restrained conclusion for 3. All observations are hypothetical teaching scenarios; no actual isolate has been measured by this demo.

Enable JavaScript to vary isolated mass and evidence provenance and inspect the supported claims.




Predict
The hypothetical reaction is 1:1 with 10.00 mmol limiting reagent, one product per reaction extent, and product molar mass 180.16 g/mol. Calculate its theoretical product mass. Predict apparent isolated yield for 1.20 g of isolated material. Does that calculation alone provide conversion or purity?
The product is intentionally unnamed. The unassigned pattern comparison is schematic; it is neither an aspirin measurement nor the U1 spectrum from the other spectral demos.


Explore

Vary isolated mass and keep the starting-reagent amount fixed. Notice which derived quantities change and which stay fixed.
Try the Unrelated-spectrum trap. Why can an apparently matching pattern from another teaching sample not identify this isolate?
Link the pattern to this isolate, then introduce an extra unexpected signal group. Audit identity and purity separately.
Compare one versus two detected TLC (thin-layer chromatography) features.
Supply the optional quantitative same-batch assay: 2.00 mmol starting material remains from 10.00 mmol initially. Calculate conversion, then try the high-mass contradiction preset.



Explain and check
Theoretical mass is \(0.01000\times180.16=1.8016\) g. For 1.20 g isolated material, apparent isolated yield is about 66.6%, conditional on that mass representing product. It does not measure starting-material consumption.
The optional residual assay independently gives conversion \(100(10.00-2.00)/10.00=80.0\%\). An apparent product-mass yield above this same-batch conversion calls assumptions or records into question; retained solvent, impurities or incompatible records are possibilities to investigate.
A consistent, explicitly linked structural observation supports an identity claim; an unrelated trace does not. Contradictory signals require explanation. One TLC feature does not prove purity, and two resolved features support multiple detected components under the stated conditions.


Model limits
The conversion assay is stipulated quantitative and linked to the same batch. The qualitative pattern comparison supplies consistency/contradiction only; it does not measure purity percentages or generate actual molecular spectra. All plausible causes of a discrepancy are hypotheses, not diagnoses. Conclude with a supported claim, a limitation and a targeted next observation, as in integration exercises.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
About this lecture
Two bottles are both labelled C₂H₆O. One is the alcohol in beer and boils at 78 °C. The other is a spray-can propellant that boils at −24 °C. Same atoms, different molecules. Only the structure tells them apart.
Today we learn to read structures fluently:

Drawings: formula, condensed and skeletal, and what each one hides
Hidden atoms: every corner is a carbon; valence implies the H
Functional groups: the local patterns that decide behaviour
Formal charge: an electron count that keeps a drawing honest
Names and amounts: basic naming, and grams to moles

The rest of the course assumes you can read a structure at a glance.

Open with the two bottles. Ethanol and dimethyl ether really do share the formula C2H6O, yet one is a liquid you can drink (in moderation) and the other is a gas used in spray cans and as a diesel substitute. The 100-degree gap in boiling point is something we’ll explain tomorrow with hydrogen bonding; today the point is simply that the arrangement of atoms, not the list of atoms, is the molecule. Frame the lecture as learning a language: by the end, a skeletal drawing should read as fast as a sentence. Mention that most of this is review-plus-sharpening of general chemistry, but organic chemists use a shorthand that hides most atoms, and that shorthand is what trips people up.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
One formula, two molecules

Ethanol and dimethyl ether are constitutional isomersMolecules with the same formula but different connectivity are constitutional isomers.

Point at the oxygen in each. In ethanol, oxygen carries a hydrogen; in dimethyl ether, it sits between two carbons. That single difference in who is bonded to whom gives a liquid versus a gas at room temperature. Molecules with the same formula but different connectivity are constitutional isomers. The word “connectivity” is the key word of the whole lecture: a structure is a statement about which atoms are bonded to which. Everything else (left/right on the page, the angle you draw it at) is presentation.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Three ways to write the same molecule
text:
Three ways to write the same molecule

Ethanol as molecular formula, condensed structure and skeletal structure
Molecular formula C₂H₆O tells you what is there. It’s good for mass and amount, but useless for identity.
Condensed CH₃CH₂OH tells you the connectivity in a single line of text.
Skeletal is the drawing chemists actually use. It’s fast, and it puts the functional groups up front.


Each representation answers a different question. The molecular formula is what a mass spectrometer or an elemental analysis gives you; the condensed formula is convenient in text and in R code (you’ll type these into data frames); the skeletal structure is the working language of every paper and textbook. Stress that the condensed and skeletal forms contain identical information. Also stress that HOCH2CH3 and CH3CH2OH are the same molecule written in opposite directions. Writing a formula backwards does not create an isomer.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Skeletal structures hide most of the atoms
text:
Skeletal structures hide most of the atoms

Pentane as a skeletal zigzag and with every atom drawnRules: every end and corner is a carbon. Hydrogens on carbon are not drawn: add enough to give each carbon four bonds. Heteroatoms (O, N, …) and the H on them are drawn.

Try it: how many carbons are in an unbranched zigzag with four line segments?

Five. Segments are bonds, not atoms. The molecule is pentane, C₅H₁₂.



This is the single most important reading skill of the course. Walk along the pentane line: end, corner, corner, corner, end, five carbons. Then fill hydrogens: the ends have one carbon neighbour, so three H each; the inner carbons have two, so two H each. 3+2+2+2+3 = 12. Give students 20 seconds for the try-it before revealing. The classic error is counting the line segments (four) instead of the vertices (five). Heteroatoms are always written out, and so is any H attached to them. That’s why the skeletal ethanol on the previous slide shows “OH”.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Branches and rings: same counting rule
text:
Branches and rings: same counting rule

Butane, 2-methylpropane and cyclobutaneA branch point has three carbon neighbours, so it carries one H. A ring uses one more C–C bond and costs two H.

Try it: in 2-methylpropane, how many H are on the central carbon?

One. It has three carbon neighbours, so 4 − 3 = 1 H. The three CH₃ ends supply the other nine.



Extend the counting rule from chains to branches and rings. Draw butane and 2-methylpropane on the board side by side: both C4H10, but the branched one boils lower (about −12 °C versus about 0 °C). Shape matters even among hydrocarbons, which we’ll revisit tomorrow. The ring point is a preview: each ring, like each double bond, removes two hydrogens from the saturated formula. Students who internalise “H = 4 minus bonds to carbon” never need to memorise formulas.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Double and triple bonds change the hydrogen count
text:
Double and triple bonds change the hydrogen count

Ethane, ethene and ethyne with every hydrogen drawnA neutral carbon has a bond-order sum of four, not four neighbours. Each extra bond between two carbons removes one H from each.

Try it: start from butane, C₄H₁₀, and put in one C=C. What’s the formula?

C₄H₈. Each end of the new double bond loses one H.



Count bonds, not neighbours. An ethene carbon has three neighbours (one C and two H) but its bond-order sum is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Point out the pattern C2H6 → C2H4 → C2H2: every extra bond costs two hydrogens. This is the “degree of unsaturation” idea that will become a tool in spectroscopy week: from a formula alone you can count rings plus pi bonds. Notice that C4H8 is also the formula of cyclobutane from the previous slide, another case where a formula leaves a choice.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Bonding sets the shape

Tetrahedral, trigonal planar and linear carbon

This is why skeletal drawings use zigzags: they approximate the real 109.5° and 120° angles, and a triple bond is drawn as a straight line through the carbons. Shape matters for everything that follows: polarity and boiling point (Day 2), and stereochemistry and enzyme binding (Week 2). Keep it practical: students should be able to look at any carbon and say “tetrahedral”, “planar” or “linear” from its bonds. Hybridisation labels (sp3, sp2, sp) can be mentioned as names for these three cases without going into orbital theory today.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Functional groups: the parts that react
text:
Functional groups: the parts that react

Six functional groups in real moleculesA functional group is identified by its local connectivity, not just by which elements are present.

Most of a molecule is an inert carbon-hydrogen scaffold. The functional groups are where the chemistry happens, and each family has characteristic reactivity that the rest of the course is organised around. Ground each family in something students have smelled or used. The take-home message is in the last line: an ether, an acid and an ester all contain oxygen, but they’re recognised by what the oxygen is attached to. Teach students to look at the neighbours of each heteroatom.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Reading around a carbonyl

The neighbour of C=O decides the familyFind the C=O, then look at its other neighbour. An OH or OR with no C=O next to it is just an alcohol or ether.

Try it: is CH₃C(=O)NH₂ an amine or an amide?

Amide. The N sits directly on the carbonyl carbon, which makes it much less basic than an amine. That difference comes back in Week 4.



The carbonyl, C=O, is the most important functional group in biochemistry and the course. Read the condensed notation carefully: in CH3C(=O)OH the parentheses mean the oxygen hangs off the carbon with a double bond, so there are two different oxygens. A frequent mistake is calling HOCH2CH2OH (ethylene glycol, two OH groups) an acid because it has two oxygens. It’s a diol, because neither OH is on a carbonyl. Peptide bonds in proteins are amides, which is a good reason to care about the amine/amide distinction.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Formal charge: count the electrons each atom owns
text:
Formal charge: count the electrons each atom owns

Water, hydroxide and hydronium with bonds, lone pairs and charges\text{formal charge} = \text{valence electrons} - \text{lone-pair electrons} - \text{bonds}
Hydroxide O: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Hydronium O: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.

The formula is the usual V minus N minus B/2, written in a form students can apply by eye: count lone-pair electrons, count bonds. Emphasise that charges are part of the structure. Omitting a charge is a drawing error, not a simplification. Tomorrow’s acid-base unit lives entirely on this: when O–H loses a proton, the bonding pair stays on oxygen, so oxygen gains a lone pair and a negative charge.

title: Reading organic structures
section: The normal states, so charges jump out
text:
The normal states, so charges jump out









atom
neutral, “normal”
positive
negative




C
4 bonds, 0 lone pairs
3 bonds, 0 LP (carbocation)
3 bonds, 1 LP (carbanion)


N
3 bonds, 1 LP (amine)
4 bonds, 0 LP (ammonium)
2 bonds, 2 LP


O
2 bonds, 2 LP (alcohol)
3 bonds, 1 LP (oxonium)
1 bond, 3 LP (alkoxide)



Learn the neutral column. Any atom that doesn’t match it carries a charge.

Try it: amino acids in your cells exist as H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ (glycine). Which atoms carry the charges, and why?

N has four bonds, so it’s +1. One O has one bond and three lone pairs, so it’s −1. The molecule is neutral overall: a zwitterion.



Experienced chemists don’t calculate formal charges. They recognise deviations from the neutral pattern instantly, and this table is the shortcut. Carbocations and carbanions are previews of the mechanism unit. The glycine zwitterion connects to biochemistry and to acids and bases on Day 3: at physiological pH, amino acids are charged at both ends. Ask students to point at the exact atom, not just say “the molecule is charged”.

title: Reading organic structures
section: A valence audit catches impossible structures
text:
A valence audit catches impossible structures
Before you trust any drawing, including your own, check every atom:

Carbon: bond-order sum exactly 4 (unless a charge is shown).
N, O: compare with the neutral pattern, and write the charge if they differ.
Hydrogen: exactly one bond.


Try it: a proposed reaction intermediate keeps C=O and adds three single bonds at the same carbon. Is that possible?

No. 2 + 3 = 5 bonds to carbon. For a new group to attach, the C=O π bond must open first. That’s the key step of every carbonyl addition in Week 3.



This is the habit that saves the most marks on the exam. Students under time pressure draw five-bonded carbons, especially when adding a nucleophile to a carbonyl. Make the audit a reflex: after drawing anything, run a finger over each atom and count. The try-it deliberately previews mechanism: the reason a carbonyl’s pi bond breaks when a nucleophile adds is exactly this valence limit.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Naming: just enough to communicate

Butan-1-ol numbered from the OH end
Find the longest chain containing the group: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, …
Number from the end nearest the group.
Add the ending: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, …


Try it: name CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃.

Butan-2-ol. Numbering from the right puts OH on C2. “Butan-3-ol” is the same molecule, numbered the wrong way.



We teach naming only as far as needed to talk about molecules unambiguously; nobody will be asked to name a complex natural product. Propan-1-ol versus propan-2-ol is the essential contrast: the number says where the group sits, and moving it creates an isomer with a different name. Common names (acetic acid, acetone) will appear alongside systematic ones; the reading guide lists the ones we use.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Putting it together: two molecules from biology
text:
Putting it together: two molecules from biology

Glycine and lactic acidRead every atom, group by group: count each C–H, N–H and O–H separately, and don’t add an H to the carbonyl carbon.

Try it: write the molecular formulas of glycine and lactic acid.

Glycine C₂H₅NO₂ (2 N–H + 2 C–H + 1 O–H). Lactic acid C₃H₆O₃ (3 + 1 C–H on carbon, 1 + 1 O–H). Note the central carbon of lactic acid has only one H.



This slide combines everything: identify groups, count hidden hydrogens, respect the carbonyl carbon’s valence. The common error in lactic acid is giving the central carbon two hydrogens, forgetting that OH takes one of its four bonds. Lactic acid also has a carbon with four different groups, which is a teaser for stereochemistry in Week 2: there are two mirror-image lactic acids, and your muscles make only one of them.

title: Reading organic structures
section: From a structure to an amount
text:
From a structure to an amount

1.3812 g of salicylic acid divided by 138.12 g/mol gives 0.01000 moln = \frac{m}{M} \qquad \text{grams} \div \frac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}} = \text{mol}
The structure gives the formula, the formula gives M, and the balance gives m. In R: 1.3812 / 138.12 → 0.01.

The lab connection: every synthesis and titration in the practical starts from a weighed mass, and reactions happen in moles, not grams. The chain is structure → formula → molar mass → amount. Keep units visible so the grams cancel. Salicylic acid is the starting material for aspirin, which students will meet again. The R line is a deliberate nudge: today’s exercise has a short R task doing exactly this with a small data table, and the habit of keeping units in comments starts here.

Use this as a quick oral check: read out each mistake and ask the room why it’s wrong before showing the fix. Every row maps onto one or more exercises, so a student who still makes one of these knows exactly which exercise to redo.
