The summary is the revision sheet; recite the reading procedure once: find the vertices, fill hydrogens to four bonds, name the functional groups by their neighbours, check charges against the neutral patterns. Close the loop with the opening hook. Tomorrow answers the boiling-point question from the first slide, and the answer is hydrogen bonding, which only ethanol can do because only ethanol has O–H. Point students to the exercises: the core problems are required, and the transfer ones are optional.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
Use bond polarity, intermolecular interactions and IR observations to explain the structures below. Use the lecture and the refresher below when needed.
Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when the session also includes R.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
1. Assign two kinds of charge
Draw ethanol with O lone pairs. Mark C–O partial charges and calculate O formal charge. Explain why the two labels differ.






Hint





Unequal sharing differs from a Lewis integer count.









Worked check





C is δ+ and O δ− in the C–O bond. Ethanol O has formal charge zero with two bonds/two pairs. A partial charge is not a whole added electron.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
2. Combine dipoles geometrically
Sketch linear O=C=O and bent H₂O. Indicate bond-dipole directions toward O and predict each molecular sum.






Hint





Equal opposite vectors cancel; angled ones need not.









Worked check





CO₂ dipoles cancel by symmetry. Bent water has a nonzero net dipole. Polar bonds alone do not establish a polar molecule.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
3. Draw a donor–acceptor contact
Draw ethanol and water and mark one O–H···O hydrogen bond. Distinguish the covalent and intermolecular connections.






Hint





The donor supplies the H; the acceptor supplies a lone pair.









Worked check





Either molecule can donate OH to the other O. Covalent O–H stays within a molecule, while the H···O contact is dashed and does not change connectivity.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
4. Let ether accept
Draw CH₃OCH₃ with water as a hydrogen-bond partner. Which molecule supplies H? Can pure ether provide an O–H donor?






Hint





Ether O has two C neighbours and no attached H.









Worked check





Water donates an O–H hydrogen to ether O. Ether can accept but has no O–H donor; oxygen presence alone does not imply donor ability.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
section: 5. Compare amines by their actual bonds
text:
5. Compare amines by their actual bonds
For CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH and (CH₃)₃N, identify N–H donor bonds and the neutral N acceptor pair.






Hint





Count N–H before counting carbon substituents.









Worked check





All three neutral amines have a lone-pair acceptor. The first two have N–H donor bonds; trimethylamine lacks N–H and cannot donate at N.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
6. Test a protonated amine
Draw CH₃NH₃⁺ and compare its N donor/acceptor inventory with CH₃NH₂.






Hint





The original lone pair has become a bond.









Worked check





Methylammonium has N–H donors but no ordinary N lone-pair acceptor. It is not a neutral amine with the same available pair.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
7. Explain a controlled boiling comparison
Ethanol and dimethyl ether share C₂H₆O. Their approximate normal boiling temperatures are 78 ° C and−24 ° C. Explain a structural reason for the difference.






Hint





Keep molecular size and pressure comparable.









Worked check





Ethanol forms an OH donor/acceptor network; the ether lacks an OH donor. This supports stronger liquid intermolecular attractions in ethanol, not stronger covalent C–O bonds.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
8. Separate boiling from decomposition
A student says boiling ethanol breaks C–O bonds. Rewrite their claim to identify which interactions are normally overcome.






Hint





Ask whether vapour molecules still have the same connectivity.









Worked check





Boiling separates largely intact ethanol molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions. C–O cleavage would be a chemical transformation, not ordinary vapour formation.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
9. Compare related alcohols in water
Draw methanol and hexan-1-ol CH₃(CH₂)₅OH. Explain which is more water compatible and what a single-OH rule misses.






Hint





Balance the polar site against nonpolar size.









Worked check





Methanol is more water compatible. The longer alcohol has a much larger hydrocarbon region per OH group. The prediction is qualitative and depends on conditions.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
10. Read an IR transmission feature
A complete IR transmission trace dips strongly near 1715 cm⁻¹. Name the axes and explain what the dip means.






Hint





Less transmission corresponds to more absorption.









Worked check





The horizontal coordinate is wavenumber; the vertical coordinate is transmittance. The dip supports absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹, often a carbonyl feature, without uniquely identifying a molecule.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
11. Change the plotting convention
A second graph shows an upward band at the same wavenumber but labels its y-axis absorbance. Is it contradictory evidence?






Hint





The ordinate changes the feature direction.









Worked check





No. An absorbance band points upward while transmission decreases for the same absorption. Interpret axes before calling a plot wrong.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
12. Choose among three candidates
Unknown has strong C=O near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad alcohol OH region in suitable data. Candidates: ethanol, propanone, dimethyl ether. Choose and justify.






Hint





Draw the functional groups predicted by each.









Worked check





Propanone best fits this list: it has C=O and lacks OH. The other candidates lack carbonyl. This restricted comparison does not establish absolute identity or purity.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
13. Reject a unique-carbonyl claim
A student identifies propanone from one C=O band. Draw another three-carbon carbonyl compound and explain the limitation.






Hint





An aldehyde can contain the same total carbon count.









Worked check





Propanal CH₃CH₂CHO also contains C=O. One broad-region observation is shared by many structures; further spectral and other evidence is required.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
14. Inspect sample contamination
An intended ether sample has a broad OH feature. Give two explanations consistent with limited evidence without choosing one as certain.






Hint





A feature can belong to the target or another component.









Worked check





The sample could contain an OH-bearing impurity or water; the target assignment could also be wrong. More observations are needed to distinguish these explanations.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
15. Distinguish alcohol and acid OH
Draw ethanol and ethanoic acid. Which has a neighbouring carbonyl, and how can the expected broad IR regions differ?






Hint





Acid OH is part of C(=O)OH.









Worked check





Ethanoic acid has OH adjacent to carbonyl and often an especially broad acid-OH region around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Alcohol OH is commonly broad around 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; exact shapes depend on conditions.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
16. Check an ester inventory
For CH₃COOCH₃, identify the carbonyl and single-bonded O. Does the molecule have any O–H donor?






Hint





Write each oxygen bond explicitly.









Worked check





It has two oxygen environments able to accept hydrogen-bond contacts in this simple treatment, but no OH donor. It is an ester, not an alcohol plus an unrelated ether.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
17. Interpret ion hydration
Compare CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻ in water. Name an interaction made especially important by the latter charge.






Hint





Water is polar even though neutral overall.









Worked check





Carboxylate can engage in ion–dipole hydration. The neutral acid also interacts with water, but formal charge changes the interaction pattern. Exact solubility still needs conditions and additional thermodynamics.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
18. Repair an IR-to-solubility shortcut
Rewrite: “It absorbs IR, so it must dissolve in water.” Give separate valid claims about IR and solubility.






Hint





A changing vibrational dipole is not an entire solution free energy.









Worked check





IR absorption probes suitable vibrational transitions. Water solubility depends on the balance of interactions, size, charge, condensed-phase structure and conditions. A band alone does not establish it.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
19. Use two observations together
Unknown is one of propan-1-ol or propanal. Suitable IR has C=O and no broad alcohol OH. Give one prediction for each candidate and a restrained conclusion.






Hint





Test both presence and absence.









Worked check





The alcohol predicts OH and lacks C=O; the aldehyde predicts C=O and lacks alcohol OH. Propanal fits the two observations among this pair; further evidence would address identity beyond this list.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
20. Name the missing extraction inputs
A monoprotic acid becomes mostly ionised in water at high pH. Why can that fact alone not predict mass recovered into an organic solvent?






Hint





Two phases require a partition model and their quantities.









Worked check





Aqueous speciation supplies only species ratios. Partition coefficients, phase volumes, starting amount and losses affect recovered mass. More ionisation is not a complete recovery calculation.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
Review your work
Choose one corrected mistake and explain the chemical rule that repairs it. Continue with the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 2: Exercises — Properties and IR
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
Will ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same donor/acceptor inventory because they share C₂H₆O? Predict before looking at the highlights.
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Compare ethanol and ether with highlights hidden. Identify O–H bonds and available oxygen lone-pair sites, then reveal donors and acceptors separately.
Compare propanone with ethanol. Explain why carbonyl oxygen can accept even though propanone has no O–H donor.
Compare ethanoic acid with ether. Locate the complete carboxylic-acid pattern rather than counting O atoms alone. Return to the supplied alcohol/ether boiling values and explain what that comparison controls.



Take-away
Give a structural explanation for the supplied alcohol/ether boiling contrast. Why would site count alone fail as a universal boiling-point calculator?


Model and limits
Green circles mark donor sites; dashed blue squares mark acceptor sites. Site count differs from the number of donor H atoms. The protonated carboxylic-acid OH is not counted as a useful acceptor. Approximate normal boiling values are supplied teaching examples at comparable pressure, not predictions from a site-count formula.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 1. Can polar bonds give a molecule with zero net permanent dipole?
text:
1. Can polar bonds give a molecule with zero net permanent dipole?






Check your answer





Yes. Molecular symmetry can make bond dipoles cancel, as in linear CO₂. Geometry matters.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 2. Can dimethyl ether donate an O–H hydrogen bond?
text:
2. Can dimethyl ether donate an O–H hydrogen bond?






Check your answer





No: it has no O–H bond. Its oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from a suitable donor.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 3. Does boiling ethanol normally break its C–O bonds?
text:
3. Does boiling ethanol normally break its C–O bonds?






Check your answer





No. Boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions. Molecular connectivity is retained.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 4. Should every oxygen-containing compound dissolve readily in water?
text:
4. Should every oxygen-containing compound dissolve readily in water?






Check your answer





No. Hydrogen-bonding sites, nonpolar size, charge, temperature and condensed-phase effects all matter.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 5. What does a downward feature mean on an IR transmission plot?
text:
5. What does a downward feature mean on an IR transmission plot?






Check your answer





Less transmitted IR at that wavenumber, meaning absorption. Check the y-axis; an absorbance plot points the other way.

title: Self-check: properties and IR
section: 6. Can a strong carbonyl band alone prove a sample is a particular ketone?
text:
6. Can a strong carbonyl band alone prove a sample is a particular ketone?






Check your answer





No. Many carbonyl compounds absorb strongly in that broad region. Combine further IR features with other evidence and candidate structures.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
About this lecture
You swallow an aspirin tablet. In your stomach (pH ≈ 2) about 97 % of it is the neutral acid. A few minutes later, in your blood (pH 7.4), more than 99.9 % of it is the negatively charged ion. Same molecule, different form, and only the pH changed.
Today we learn to predict that kind of switch:

Proton transfer: curved arrows, and what happens to charges
Conjugate pairs: acid and base differ by exactly one H⁺
Acid strength: pKa, and why the conjugate base decides it
Equilibrium: which side of an acid–base reaction wins
Ionisation: how much is HA and how much is A⁻ at a given pH

Yesterday we used structure to predict boiling points; today the same reading skills predict acidity.

Open with the aspirin tablet, and keep the numbers on the board; we come back to them at the end and actually calculate them. Aspirin’s carboxylic acid has a pKa of about 3.5. The point of the hook: whether a drug carries a charge depends on the pH it’s sitting in, and that changes how it crosses membranes, dissolves and gets excreted. Ask the room which form they’d guess crosses a fatty cell membrane more easily, charged or neutral. Most will say neutral, which is right, and it sets up the extraction slide at the end. Remind them that Day 1’s formal-charge rules are exactly what we need today: every acid–base step changes one atom’s charge.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: An acid gives H⁺; a base gives an electron pair
text:
An acid gives H⁺; a base gives an electron pair

Ethanoic acid transfers a proton to hydroxide, shown with two curved arrowsA Brønsted acid donates H⁺; a base accepts it using a lone pair. Two arrows: the base’s lone pair → H, and the O–H bonding pair → O.

Try it: can a curved arrow start at the H⁺ and point to the base?

No. Curved arrows show where electrons go, and a bare proton has none. Start at a lone pair or a bond; H can only be where an arrow ends.



Draw this one slowly on the board alongside the slide. The hydroxide oxygen has three lone pairs; one of them reaches for the acidic hydrogen. At the same time the O–H bond of the acid breaks, and both electrons of that bond stay on the acid oxygen. That’s why ethanoate ends up with a negative charge: the oxygen keeps an extra lone pair. Students often draw a single arrow from H to OH⁻, which is backwards. The arrow notation tracks electrons, and this is the same notation we’ll use for every mechanism from Week 2 onward, so it’s worth getting right on the simplest possible reaction.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
A nitrogen base: methylamine

Methylamine’s lone pair takes a proton from a generic acid H–ASame two arrows. N goes from 3 bonds + 1 lone pair (neutral) to 4 bonds, no lone pair (+1). A keeps the bonding pair and becomes A⁻.
Total charge is conserved: 0 on the left, (+1) + (−1) = 0 on the right.

This is the nitrogen version of the previous slide. Use H–A as a placeholder for any acid, which is how the exercises write it. Ask: where did nitrogen’s lone pair go? It became the new N–H bond, so N now has four bonds and, by Day 1’s table, a +1 charge. Make students check total charge every time: if both products come out neutral, they’ve lost a charge somewhere. Amines as bases come back in a big way in Week 4 (amines and aromatics), and the ammonium ion is how most amine drugs are sold, as hydrochloride salts.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺
text:
Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺

Four acids above their conjugate basesRemoving H⁺ takes away one H and lowers the charge by one. The bonding pair stays behind as a new lone pair.

Try it: what is the conjugate base of CH₃NH₃⁺?

CH₃NH₂ (methylamine), neutral. N goes from four bonds to three bonds plus a lone pair, and +1 drops to 0.



One rule covers neutral and charged acids alike. Ethanoic acid (neutral) gives ethanoate (−1); methylammonium (+1) gives methylamine (0). A conjugate base is not necessarily negative, which surprises people. Point out the shaded atom in each pair: that’s where the lone pair appears. Common slip: students remove a hydrogen atom (H·) rather than a proton (H⁺) and end up with a neutral radical. The charge bookkeeping catches it.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Water can be either

Water accepting a proton from HCl and donating one to ammoniaWith a stronger acid, water is the base (→ H₃O⁺). With a stronger base, water is the acid (→ OH⁻). Being an acid or base is a role, not a fixed label.

Try it: a student draws neutral HA + neutral B → A⁻ + BH. What’s wrong?

BH must be BH⁺. Charge is 0 on the left, so A⁻ needs a +1 partner. A neutral BH would make a unit of charge disappear.



Water’s double role is why aqueous acid–base chemistry works at all: hydronium and hydroxide are the conjugates of water. Write the two pairs on the board: H₃O⁺/H₂O and H₂O/OH⁻. Water appears in both, once as the base and once as the acid. The try-it is a charge check written in generic letters; this is exactly the kind of error that shows up in exam mechanisms. Mention that HCl transfers its proton to water essentially completely, while ammonia in water is only slightly protonated, which is our cue for needing numbers: pKa.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: pKa: a logarithmic scale of acid strength
text:
pKa: a logarithmic scale of acid strength

pKa scale with five acids drawn at their positions\text{p}K_\text{a} = -\log_{10} K_\text{a}
Lower pKa = stronger acid. One pKa unit is a factor of 10 in Ka, so ethanoic acid (4.8) is about 10¹¹ times more acidic than ethanol (16).

Make sure everyone reads the scale in the right direction: small pKa, strong acid. Because it’s a log scale, the gap between 4.8 and 16 is not “a bit more than three times”; it’s eleven powers of ten. All the values here are approximate aqueous values and that’s the only kind we’ll compare; pKa values in DMSO or the gas phase are different and not interchangeable. Note that charged acids (ammonium, methylammonium) sit on the same scale as neutral ones. The pKa of methylammonium (10.6) is how we describe the basicity of methylamine. Ask: why is ethanoic acid so much more acidic than ethanol, when both lose H from an O–H? That’s the next slide.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Acid strength lives in the conjugate base
text:
Acid strength lives in the conjugate base

Ethoxide with charge on one oxygen, ethanoate with charge shared by twoBoth acids lose H⁺ from O–H. The difference is what’s left: in ethoxide the charge sits on one O, in ethanoate it’s spread over two equivalent O. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.

This is the central idea of the lecture: to compare two acids, compare their conjugate bases. A base that holds its negative charge comfortably has little drive to take the proton back, so the acid gives it up more readily. Ethanoate spreads its charge over two oxygens, ethoxide can’t. Students often try to explain acidity by looking at the acid itself (“the O–H bond is weaker”), which is a dead end here. Train them to draw the conjugate base first and ask where the charge goes. The two drawings of ethanoate need explaining, and that’s the next slide.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Resonance: one ion, two drawings

Two resonance contributors of ethanoate related by curved arrowsThe ↔︎ means “two drawings of the same thing”, not an equilibrium (⇌). The real ion is a blend: each O carries about −½ and the two C–O bonds are identical.

Try it: a classmate proposes a “second contributor” in which the H moves from one oxygen to the other. Is that resonance?

No. Moving an H moves a nucleus, which makes a different species (a proton transfer). Resonance contributors differ only in where the electrons are drawn.



Two classic misconceptions here. First, that ethanoate flips back and forth between the two forms. It doesn’t: there’s one ion, and neither drawing is the whole truth, a bit like describing a rhinoceros as part dragon, part unicorn. The evidence is that both C–O bonds have the same length, about 126 pm, between a normal C=O and C–O. Second, the equilibrium arrow and the resonance arrow get mixed up. Equilibrium (⇌) connects different species; resonance (↔︎) connects drawings of one species. Resonance comes back constantly: in amides in Week 4 and in aromatic rings in Week 4 too.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Induction: electronegative neighbours help

Ethanoic, chloroethanoic and trichloroethanoic acid with their pKa valuesCl pulls electron density through the σ bonds, which stabilises the carboxylate. More Cl, stronger acid. The effect fades quickly with distance.

Induction is a second, separate way to stabilise a conjugate base. Keep it distinct from resonance: chlorine does not get a share of the negative charge in any contributor; it just pulls on the bonding electrons along the chain. That’s why the effect drops off with distance: 3-chloropropanoic acid (pKa about 4.0) is only slightly stronger than propanoic acid (4.9), while 2-chloropropanoic is about 2.8. Quick check to ask aloud: which is the stronger acid, ClCH₂COOH or CH₃COOH, and why? Insist on a reason, not just the number. Then insist on fair comparisons: same functional group, same solvent, one change at a time. Comparing a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and calling it “induction” mixes up two effects.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Which way does an acid–base equilibrium lie?
text:
Which way does an acid–base equilibrium lie?

Ethanoic acid and methylamine reacting with pKa values under each acidFind the acid on each side and compare their pKa values. Equilibrium favours the side with the weaker acid (higher pKa):
K \approx 10^{\,\text{p}K_\text{a}(\text{product acid}) - \text{p}K_\text{a}(\text{reactant acid})}

Walk through it: on the left the acid is ethanoic acid, 4.8. On the right the acid is methylammonium, 10.6. The proton prefers to sit on the weaker acid’s base, i.e. methylamine holds it more tightly than ethanoate does. Subtract in the right order: product acid minus reactant acid gives +5.8, so K is about 6.3 × 10⁵ and the products win heavily. The most common mistake is comparing the wrong two numbers, for example the pKa of ethanoic acid with the pKa of methylamine’s N–H (which is about 40 and irrelevant here). Always compare HA on the left with BH⁺ on the right.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Reversing the equation, and what K doesn’t tell you
text:
Reversing the equation, and what K doesn’t tell you








direction
equation
K




forward
CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺
105.8 ≈ 6.3 × 10⁵


reverse
CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺ ⇌ CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂
10−5.8 ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁶



The reverse constant is the reciprocal. And K says where the equilibrium lies, never how fast it gets there.

Try it: a proton transfer has K = 10⁶. How many seconds does it take to reach equilibrium?

K can’t tell you. It compares the two states; speed depends on the pathway and its barrier. (Proton transfers between O and N happen to be very fast, but that’s extra information.)



Two short points that show up in the exercises. The reverse reaction uses 1/K, not the same big number; writing the same K for both directions would mean both sides are favoured, which is impossible. And K is a thermodynamic statement. Students conflate “favourable” with “fast” all the time, and it will matter a lot in Week 3 when we compare substitution and elimination, where a reaction can be favourable and still slow. Note for the curious: favourable O–H and N–H proton transfers really are near diffusion-limited, which is why we can treat acid–base steps as instant in mechanisms.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: From pKa and pH to a ratio
text:
From pKa and pH to a ratio
r = \frac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} = 10^{\,\text{pH} - \text{p}K_\text{a}} \qquad \text{fraction A}^- = \frac{r}{1 + r}

Try it: pKa 4.8, pH 3.8. Is the acid 10 % ionised?

No, about 9.1 %. r = 0.1, and the fraction is 0.1/(1 + 0.1) = 0.091. A ratio and a fraction have different denominators.



This is the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation rearranged, for a single acid in dilute water. Emphasise the two different quantities. The ratio compares A⁻ to HA and can be any positive number. The fraction compares A⁻ to the total and must lie between 0 and 1. If an R calculation gives a “fraction” of 10, the student has calculated the ratio. Learn the middle three columns by heart: one unit below pKa, about 9 %; at pKa, 50 %; one unit above, about 91 %. Two units either side, you’re at 99 % one way or the other, but never exactly 100 %.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
A fraction describes a population

Illustrative particles of HA and A⁻ at three pH valuesAt pH = pKa, half the molecules are HA and half are A⁻. No molecule is “half deprotonated”: each one is either HA or A⁻ at any instant.

The pictures are illustrative, not ten real molecules, but they make the ratio-to-fraction step concrete. In the left box, one A⁻ to ten HA is a ratio of 0.1, and one out of eleven is 9.1 %. Students who say “at the midpoint each molecule has lost half a proton” are mixing up a population average with a single molecule. Protons hop on and off constantly, so a given molecule spends part of its time in each form, but at any moment it is one or the other.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
The ionisation curve

Fraction A⁻ against pH for acids of pKa 4.8 and 6.0The fraction A⁻ rises with pH and crosses 0.5 exactly at pH = pKa. A higher pKa shifts the whole curve to the right.

Try it: at pH 4.8, how much of each acid is ionised?

pKa 4.8: 50 %. pKa 6.0: about 5.9 %, from 1/(1 + 101.2). At the same pH, the lower-pKa acid is more ionised.



This is the plot students build in today’s R task: 1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - pH)) over a pH grid. If their curve goes down with pH, the exponent sign is flipped and they’ve plotted the HA fraction instead. The curve is the same shape for every monoprotic acid; only the midpoint moves. Make sure nobody calls this a titration curve. Here pH is the input we choose; in a titration, pH is the result of adding a measured volume of base, which needs a different model.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Back to aspirin

Aspirin as the neutral acid in the stomach and as the carboxylate in blood



pH − pKa
ratio A⁻ : HA

Now we can do the opening calculation properly. Aspirin’s carboxylic acid has pKa about 3.5. In the stomach, pH minus pKa is −1.5, so the ratio is 10^−1.5 ≈ 0.032 and only about 3 % is ionised. In blood, the ratio is 10^3.9 ≈ 8000, so essentially all of it is the carboxylate. The neutral form crosses membranes more easily, which is part of why aspirin can irritate the stomach lining. Honest caveat: most aspirin is actually absorbed in the small intestine, despite being ionised there, because the surface area is enormous. pKa reasoning tells you which form dominates, not the whole pharmacology.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Two groups, two pKa values: glycine
text:
Two groups, two pKa values: glycine

Glycine drawn neutral and as the zwitterion that exists at pH 7.4Treat each group separately. COOH (pKa 2.3) at pH 7.4 is far above its pKa, so it’s COO⁻. NH₃⁺ (pKa 9.6) is below its pKa, so it stays NH₃⁺.

Try it: at pH 7.4, about what fraction of glycine’s amino groups are NH₂ rather than NH₃⁺?

About 0.6 %. pH − pKa = 7.4 − 9.6 = −2.2, so the ratio NH₂ : NH₃⁺ is 10−2.2 ≈ 0.006.



This links back to Day 1’s zwitterion try-it: we can now explain why amino acids exist as H₃N⁺–CH–COO⁻ in cells. For each ionisable group, compare pH with that group’s pKa. The neutral “textbook” form with NH₂ and COOH is almost absent in water at any pH, which surprises students. Remind them that the pKa of the ammonium group (9.6) describes the conjugate acid, so the amine is the base here. Proteins carry these charged groups on their side chains as well, which is why protein charge depends on pH.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Where this model stops

Two-layer extraction showing aqueous ionisation and partition between layersOur equation describes one acid in dilute water at a chosen pH. It doesn’t give the pH during a titration, and it doesn’t tell you how much ends up in an organic layer.

Try it: at high pH an acid is mostly A⁻. What else would you need to predict how much you recover from an organic extract?

Partition coefficients and the phase volumes, plus the starting amount and any losses. Aqueous ionisation is only one piece.



This is the lab connection. In a work-up you shake an organic solvent with aqueous acid or base, and the charged form stays in the water. So raising the pH pulls a carboxylic acid out of the organic layer, and lowering it pushes it back. That’s the principle, but the numbers need more: how strongly the neutral HA prefers the organic phase (the partition coefficient), how much of each solvent you use, and how much you started with. Being clear about what a model can and can’t predict is part of doing chemistry with R: the curve you plot today is a model consequence of an assumed pKa, not measured data.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




curved arrow starting at H⁺
start at a lone pair or a bond


conjugate base with the same charge as the acid
removing H⁺ lowers the charge by one


“lower pKa = weaker acid”
lower pKa = stronger acid


comparing pKa values of unrelated sites
compare HA on the left with BH⁺ on the right


resonance forms “switching back and forth”
one ion; ↔︎ is not ⇌


ratio 0.1 read as 10 % ionised
fraction = r/(1 + r) = 9.1 %


“half the molecule is deprotonated”
half the molecules are A⁻


a large K means a fast reaction
K gives position, not rate




Read each mistake aloud and ask the room why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. Every row maps to an exercise: arrows to 1 and 3, charges to 4 and 18, pKa direction and comparison to 5, 7 and 9, resonance to 6, ratio and fraction to 10 to 14, populations to 11, and K versus rate to 16.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
Summary



concept
key fact




proton transfer
two arrows: lone pair → H, bond pair → atom


conjugate pair
differ by one H⁺; charge changes by one


pKa
lower = stronger; 1 unit = factor of 10


acid strength
judged by conjugate-base stability


stabilisation
resonance (↔︎) and induction (σ bonds)


equilibrium
weaker acid side wins; K ≈ 10ΔpKa


ratio and fraction
r = 10pH − pKa, fraction = r/(1 + r)


midpoint
pH = pKa gives 50 % A⁻



Next: conformations, how molecules twist about single bonds (Day 6). Practice: exercises · self-check

Recite the procedure once: draw the conjugate base, find where the charge goes, compare pKa values on the same scale, and use pH minus pKa to get the ratio. Days 4 and 5 are consolidation days, and Day 5 puts structure, properties and acidity together, so today’s material comes straight back. Today’s R task plots the ionisation curve; encourage students to predict the fractions at pH 3.8, 4.8 and 5.8 before running the code. After the consolidation days we start Week 2 with conformations, where the question shifts from which atoms are bonded to how the molecule is shaped in 3D.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text: Draw Newman projections and cyclohexane chairs, then explain how a rotation changes the view and energy. Review the lecture when you need a drawing convention. Core 1–12: about 60–80 minutes with drawings and checks. Transfer 13–20: an optional 35–50 minutes for consolidation or later revision. Choose a smaller core subset when a practical session also includes R.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
1. Define the viewing bond
Number CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ C1–C4 and look C2→C3. Identify front/rear C and the three groups on each.






Hint





Nearest carbon is front.









Worked check





C2 is front, attached to C1 methyl and two H; C3 is rear, attached to C4 methyl and two H. Both carbon sets must be drawn.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
2. Draw anti-butane
Keep front CH₃ at 12 o’clock; place rear CH₃ at 6 o’clock and complete both H sets in a Newman projection. State methyl dihedral.






Hint





Each carbon has three projected bonds 120° apart.









Worked check





The methyl dihedral is 180°. Front H at 4/8 and rear H at 2/10 give a staggered arrangement. Anti names the methyl relationship.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
3. Draw one gauche arrangement
From anti, rotate only the rear set 120° while front stays fixed. State the resulting methyl dihedral and whether eclipsed.






Hint





A120° change from 180° reaches 60° modulo a full turn.









Worked check





Rear methyl reaches 2 or 10 o’clock depending direction, giving±60° to front methyl. The structure remains staggered and is gauche.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
4. Find both gauche minima
Draw the +60° and−60° methyl arrangements along C2→C3. Explain what stays identical.






Hint





Use rear methyl at 2 and 10 with front methyl at 12.









Worked check





Both preserve connectivity and are equivalent in energy in an achiral environment for ordinary butane. They are distinct conformations, not constitutional isomers.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
5. Draw an eclipsed view
Draw ethane along C–C with front/rear C–H bonds aligned. How does it differ from a staggered view?






Hint





Compare a 0° and 60° bond-set offset.









Worked check





Eclipsed projected bonds align; staggered bonds are offset 60°. The atoms do not form extra bonds just because their projected positions overlap.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
6. Count ethane energy minima
A qualitative full-turn ethane profile has eclipsed maxima every 120°. Locate the staggered minima between them.






Hint





Start with a maximum at 0°.









Worked check





Minima occur at 60°,180°,300°. The three are equivalent because the substituents are H. Numerical barriers cannot be extracted from an uncalibrated schematic.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
7. Compare butane minima
For ordinary butane, anti is lower than gauche. Explain the methyl-group arrangement and why lower does not mean exclusive.






Hint





Compare larger-group separation, then remember thermal populations.









Worked check





Anti separates the methyl groups more favourably. Gauche remains a possible populated conformation. A finite energy difference does not make the higher state mathematically absent.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
8. Separate conformer from constitutional isomer
Compare anti/gauche butane with butane/2-methylpropane. Identify which relationship changes bonded neighbours.






Hint





Trace carbon connectivity before reading the view.









Worked check





Anti/gauche retain one connected chain and differ by rotation. 2-methylpropane has a branched carbon framework, so it is a constitutional isomer of butane.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
9. Read a cyclohexane sketch
Explain why a regular hexagon for cyclohexane does not prove a flat molecular geometry. Name a common low-energy conformation.






Hint





A skeletal drawing first establishes connectivity.









Worked check





The polygon gives a six-carbon ring. Cyclohexane usually adopts nonplanar chair conformations; the flat drawing does not encode all 3D positions.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
10. Track axial-up through a flip
Draw/build methylcyclohexane with axial-up methyl. Perform a chair flip and label the same methyl both ways.






Hint





Axial/equatorial changes; up/down does not.









Worked check





It becomes equatorial-up. Follow the whole ring rather than reversing one drawn bond. The process changes conformation while preserving configuration.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
11. Track axial-down through a flip
Repeat with an axial-down substituent. Does down become up?






Hint





Use the same rule with the other side of the ring.









Worked check





Axial-down becomes equatorial-down. A ring flip exchanges axial/equatorial without changing the side of the ring.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
12. Preserve a cis relation
Two labelled substituents are both up before a chair flip. State their cis/trans relationship before and after.






Hint





Cis/trans describes sides, not axiality.









Worked check





They are cis before and remain cis after. Up/up remains up/up even though axial/equatorial occupancy changes.




Optional transfer and challenge
These extend the same concepts without assuming later reaction chemistry.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
13. Preserve a trans relation
One substituent is up and one down. Can choosing a different chair make this pair cis?






Hint





Track each substituent’s side through the motion.









Worked check





No. They are trans and remain trans. A conformation change cannot silently change the up/down configuration.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
14. Explain methylcyclohexane preference
Compare axial and equatorial methyl chairs. Name an unfavourable interaction reduced in the equatorial form.






Hint





Think of groups at the 1,3 positions relative to an axial substituent.









Worked check





Equatorial methyl avoids the unfavourable 1,3-diaxial interactions present for axial methyl. This explains a preference, not that the axial form is impossible.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
15. Check Boltzmann-model units
Use ΔG=3500 J/mol, R=8.314462618J/(molK), T=298.15 K. Compute RT and explain why ΔG/(RT) can appear in exp().






Hint





Both numerator and denominator must have the same units.









Worked check





RT≈2478.96 J/mol; ΔG/(RT)≈1.412 is dimensionless. Mixing kJ/mol with J/(molK) without conversion would produce a wrong exponent.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
16. Normalise a two-state model
Given weights wA=1 and wB=0.244, calculate fractions. Are these already percentages?






Hint





Divide each weight by their total 1.244.









Worked check





Fractions are about 0.804 and 0.196, or 80.4% and 19.6%. Relative weights need not sum to one; fractions do.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
17. Test zero energy difference
In a two-state model with degeneracy included, ΔG(A)=ΔG(B)=0. What equilibrium fractions result?






Hint





Both exponentials equal one.









Worked check





The two weights are 1 and 1; normalising gives 0.5 and 0.5. The qualification about degeneracy matters when grouping multiple conformations into one state.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
18. Shift the energy reference
Add 1000 J/mol to both supplied relative state energies. Explain whether normalised fractions change.






Hint





Both weights receive the same multiplicative factor.









Worked check





Fractions stay unchanged because exp(−1000/RT) multiplies every weight and cancels in their normalisation. Only the relative difference matters for the ratio.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
19. Distinguish equilibrium from rate
Two systems have the same state free-energy difference but different interconversion barriers. Must they have identical rotation rates?






Hint





A state difference and an activation barrier are distinct quantities.









Worked check





No. The equilibrium preference can match while rates differ because barriers differ. An equilibrium population does not by itself determine a time scale.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
text:
20. Identify a model boundary
A supplied two-state free-energy table already includes degeneracy. Should you independently multiply one weight by two because you remember two gauche views?






Hint





Avoid counting the same state multiplicity twice.









Worked check





No. The supplied convention already accounts for that effect. Adding it again changes the intended model. Distinguish a physical conformer inventory from an explicitly supplied effective-state model.

title: Day 6: Exercises — Conformations
section: R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
text:
R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
Question: in a deliberately simplified two-state model, how much of each conformer would be present at equilibrium? The file data/conformers.csv contains relative free energies, ΔG, in J/mol, for A and B: 0 and 3500. These values are supplied teaching values and already include any degeneracy; they are not measured energies for the qualitative butane curve above.
At temperature \(T=298.15\) K and \(R=8.314462618\) J/(mol K), use \(w_i=\exp[-\Delta G_i/(RT)]\) and \(p_i=w_i/\sum_jw_j\). The ratio in the exponent is dimensionless. A is the lower-free-energy state, so predict A will have more than half the population.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conformers <- read_csv("data/conformers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(weight = exp(-delta_G_J_mol / (8.314462618 * 298.15)),
         fraction = weight / sum(weight))
knitr::kable(conformers, digits = 4)
ggplot(conformers, aes(conformer, fraction)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Conformer", y = "Predicted equilibrium fraction") +
  theme_minimal()
sum(conformers$fraction)
Add the result to your Rmd report. Check the sum and the direction. As a transfer task, replace 3500 with 0 in a copied data object, predict the answer and recompute. Then set both input energies 1000 J/mol higher, keeping their difference unchanged. What happens to the normalised fractions?






Numerical and model check





At 298.15 K, A has fraction about 0.804 and B about 0.196 (rounding depends on constants). Equal free energies give equal fractions. Adding the same constant to both energies multiplies every weight by the same factor, which cancels on normalisation, leaving fractions unchanged. The calculation assumes the two states adequately describe the system at equilibrium. It does not predict the speed of rotation; an activation free energy would be needed for rates.

title: Self-check: conformations
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 1. What atom information is unchanged by rotating a C–C single bond?
text:
1. What atom information is unchanged by rotating a C–C single bond?






Check your answer





Connectivity: each atom retains its bonded neighbours. A different conformation is not a constitutional isomer.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 2. What does the circle represent in a Newman projection?
text:
2. What does the circle represent in a Newman projection?






Check your answer





The rear carbon viewed along a specified bond. The front carbon is shown as the central dot.

title: Self-check: conformations
text:
3. Is anti-butane staggered or eclipsed?






Check your answer





Staggered. Its terminal methyl groups have a 180° dihedral angle; gauche-butane is also staggered, with 60° between those groups.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 4. Does a chair flip turn an up substituent down?
text:
4. Does a chair flip turn an up substituent down?






Check your answer





No. Up stays up and down stays down; axial and equatorial exchange. Cis/trans configuration is preserved.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 5. At equilibrium, what does a positive ΔG for B relative to A predict?
text:
5. At equilibrium, what does a positive ΔG for B relative to A predict?






Check your answer





B has lower statistical weight than A at the same temperature. For the supplied two-state model, use exp(−ΔG/RT) then normalise.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 6. Do equilibrium populations determine how quickly a ring flips?
text:
6. Do equilibrium populations determine how quickly a ring flips?






Check your answer





No. Interconversion rates depend on activation barriers, while the equilibrium ratio depends on the free-energy difference of the states.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
About this lecture
Spearmint and caraway (the seeds in rye bread) owe their smell to the same molecule, carvone. Same formula, same bonds, same boiling point. The only difference is that one is the mirror image of the other, and the smell receptors in your nose can tell.
Today we learn to describe molecules in 3D:

Isomer types: constitutional, conformers, enantiomers, diastereomers
Stereocentres and how to name them R or S
Fischer projections and the moves you may make with them
Two centres, meso compounds and E/Z alkenes
Mixtures: enantiomeric excess, and what R/S does not tell you

Yesterday, anti and gauche butane turned into each other by rotation. Today’s isomers don’t.

Open with something students can smell: if you can, bring a pack of spearmint gum and a slice of rye bread. (R)-carvone smells of spearmint and (S)-carvone of caraway. Same atoms, same connectivity, same melting and boiling points; the only difference is handedness, and our olfactory receptors are themselves chiral proteins. That’s the theme of the day: a molecule’s 3D arrangement is part of its identity. Link to yesterday: conformers (anti/gauche, chair flips) interconvert by rotating single bonds, so they are one compound. Today’s stereoisomers can only be interconverted by breaking bonds. Ask the room: “Is your left hand a rotated version of your right?” Let them try to superimpose their hands.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Four ways two molecules can be related
text:
Four ways two molecules can be related

Constitutional isomers, enantiomers and diastereomersAsk in order: same connectivity? If no, constitutional isomers. If yes, same by bond rotation? Then conformers (Day 6). If not, they’re stereoisomers: mirror images are enantiomers; the rest are diastereomers.

This is the decision tree for the whole lecture; come back to it at the end. Walk through the three questions in order. Constitutional isomers we met on Day 1 (ethanol and dimethyl ether). Conformers were yesterday’s topic and are not drawn here: anti and gauche butane are the same compound. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but a different 3D arrangement that you can’t undo by rotating single bonds. Among stereoisomers, the mirror-image pairs are enantiomers and everything else is a diastereomer. Students often think “diastereomer” means something exotic. It just means “stereoisomer, not mirror image”, and E/Z alkenes are the simplest example.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: A stereocentre has four different groups
text:
A stereocentre has four different groups

Propan-2-ol and lactic acidA tetrahedral carbon with four different groups is a stereocentre: its mirror image can’t be laid on top of it. Two identical groups, and the mirror image is the same molecule.

Try it: someone draws a wedge on one of the H atoms of a CH₂ group. Is that carbon now a stereocentre?

No. A wedge shows direction; it can’t make two H atoms different.



Build a model if you have a kit: a carbon with four different coloured balls, and its mirror image. Try to superimpose them; you can’t. Then replace one ball so two are the same colour, and the mirror image now matches. Compare full groups, not only the first atom: in lactic acid both CH3 and COOH start with carbon but are clearly different groups. The try-it targets a very common belief that drawing a wedge “creates” a stereocentre. The drawing describes geometry; whether the carbon is a stereocentre depends only on what’s attached.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Spotting stereocentres in real molecules

Glycine, alanine, glycerol and ibuprofenCheck each sp³ carbon: does it carry four different groups? CH₂ and CH₃ carbons never do.

Try it: which of these four molecules have a stereocentre?

Alanine and ibuprofen, one each. Glycine’s carbon has two H; glycerol’s middle carbon carries two identical CH₂OH groups.



Give students 30 seconds. Teach the shortcut: skip every CH2, CH3, carbonyl carbon and alkene carbon, then look hard at what’s left. Glycerol is the trap: the middle carbon has H, OH and two CH2OH arms, and those arms are identical. Ibuprofen is sold as a racemic mixture of two enantiomers; only (S)-ibuprofen blocks the COX enzymes, and the body converts some of the (R) form into (S). Alanine is chiral like every amino acid except glycine; proteins use only the L forms, which is a good bridge to the Week 2 biology examples.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Enantiomers are mirror images

(S)- and (R)-lactic acidWedge = toward you, hash = away. Enantiomers have identical boiling points, solubilities and spectra. They differ only in a chiral setting: polarised light, an enzyme, a receptor.

Read the drawing out loud: OH and COOH in the plane, CH3 in the plane, H pointing back. The mirror flips left and right but keeps the H at the back. Your muscles make (S)-lactic acid (L-lactate) during hard exercise. Stress that the two enantiomers are not “two versions” chemically in a flask of achiral solvent: they boil, melt and dissolve identically, and you can’t separate them by distillation. That’s why the enzyme and receptor examples are so striking: biology is a chiral environment. Mention that swapping any two groups on a stereocentre gives the enantiomer; we’ll use that trick on Fischer projections.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Naming a stereocentre: rank by atomic number
text:
Naming a stereocentre: rank by atomic number

Priorities by atomic numberCahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) rule 1: rank the four groups by the atomic number of the atom attached to the stereocentre. Higher Z, higher priority. Size of the whole group doesn’t matter.

The names R and S come from a ranking system named after Cahn, Ingold and Prelog. Rule 1 looks only at the first atom of each group. Left: four different atoms, so it’s just a lookup of atomic numbers. Right: the deliberate trap. CH2Br contains bromine, but it’s attached through carbon, so it loses to OH, which is attached through oxygen. Ask: “What’s attached to the stereocentre?” and make students point at the atom. Many will want to rank CH2Br first because it “has Br in it”.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Breaking a tie: go out one atom
text:
Breaking a tie: go out one atom

Lactic acid prioritiesWhen two groups attach through the same atom, list what that atom carries and compare at the first difference. A double bond counts twice: C=O gives (O, O).

Try it: which ranks higher, –CH₂OH or –CH(CH₃)₂?

–CH₂OH. Its carbon carries (O, H, H); the other carries (C, C, H). Compare the highest first: O beats C.



In lactic acid, COOH and CH3 both attach through carbon, so we tie at rule 1. Go one atom further out: list the three atoms on each carbon, sorted from highest to lowest, and compare position by position. COOH carbon: O, O (counted twice for the double bond), O. Methyl: H, H, H. O beats H immediately. The duplicate O is bookkeeping, not an extra real atom. The try-it catches students who count atoms: isopropyl has more carbons, but you compare the highest atom in each set first, and O beats C.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: R or S: look with priority 4 away from you
text:
R or S: look with priority 4 away from you

Assigning (S)-lactic acidWith the lowest group pointing away, trace 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise = R (rectus), counterclockwise = S (sinister). This lactic acid is S.

Use the steering-wheel picture: hold the molecule so priority 4 points away from you like a steering column, then turn the wheel 1 to 2 to 3. Right turn is R, left turn is S. Do the trace live on the slide with your finger. Remind them that the arrow can skip past group 4; only 1, 2 and 3 matter. Then point back at the mirror image two slides ago: same procedure gives clockwise, so R. Every stereocentre in its enantiomer flips.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: When H points toward you, reverse it
text:
When H points toward you, reverse it

The same molecule drawn twiceIf priority 4 is on a wedge, trace 1 → 2 → 3 anyway and reverse the answer. Both drawings show the same (S)-lactic acid.

These two drawings are the same molecule viewed from opposite sides. Viewed from the front, the trace looks clockwise; but we’re looking at it from the wrong side, with H toward us, so the true answer is the opposite. Students who forget this get exactly the wrong answer, which is the worst kind of mistake because it looks confident. If priority 4 is in the plane, rotate the molecule in your head or swap two groups (which inverts), assign, and invert back. Encourage a quick model check whenever they’re unsure.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Fischer projections: a cross with depth
text:
Fischer projections: a cross with depth

Fischer projection and wedge drawingA Fischer projection is shorthand for one specific 3D shape: horizontal bonds come toward you, vertical bonds go away. The centre of the cross is the stereocentre carbon.

Fischer projections come from sugar and amino-acid chemistry, and you’ll see them again in biochemistry for D-glucose and L-amino acids. The cross is not a flat molecule. Make a “bow tie” with your arms: horizontal groups hug toward you, vertical groups lean back. Students who treat the cross as a flat drawing will rotate it freely and get the wrong answer, which is the next-but-one slide.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Reading R/S straight off a Fischer projection
text:
Reading R/S straight off a Fischer projection

Assigning R/S on a Fischer projectionIf H is on a horizontal bond, it points toward you: trace and reverse. If H is vertical, read the trace directly.

Try it: swap OH and H in this projection. Which configuration do you get?

R. One swap of two groups inverts a stereocentre. That’s D-lactic acid, the enantiomer.



This is the same reversal rule as the wedge drawing, applied to the convention. With H on the right, 1 (left) to 2 (top) to 3 (bottom) runs clockwise, H is toward us, so reverse: S. This is L-lactic acid, the muscle form. The try-it introduces the swap rule: exchanging any two groups gives the enantiomer. It’s also a handy trick to move H to a vertical position: swap, read, then reverse once more.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: What you may do to a Fischer projection
text:
What you may do to a Fischer projection

Rotating and swapping in a Fischer projection


move
result




rotate 180° in the page
same molecule


rotate 90°
enantiomer (toward/away swap)


swap two groups
enantiomer




Why does 180 degrees work and 90 not? A 180-degree turn keeps horizontal groups horizontal, so they still point toward you. A 90-degree turn moves the toward-you groups into vertical positions, which the convention reads as away from you, and that inverts the centre. Two swaps cancel, so swapping twice gives back the same molecule. Practise one example together: ask a student to rotate the starting projection 180 degrees aloud, naming each new position, then confirm S. The figure labels were checked by building each projection as a 3D model.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Two stereocentres: up to four stereoisomers
text:
Two stereocentres: up to four stereoisomers

The four stereoisomers of threonineWith n stereocentres there are at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers. An enantiomer inverts every centre; change only some and you get a diastereomer.

Try it: how are (2R,3R)- and (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane related?

Diastereomers. Only one centre changed, so they aren’t mirror images. (2S,3S) would be the enantiomer of (2R,3R).



Threonine is an essential amino acid, and your proteins use exactly one of these four: (2S,3R), L-threonine. Its enantiomer and the two allothreonines are not used. Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers have different physical properties: different melting points, solubilities and NMR spectra, so they can be separated by ordinary methods. The quick test for the relationship: compare descriptors centre by centre. All flipped means enantiomer; some flipped means diastereomer; none flipped means the same compound.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Meso: stereocentres but no chirality

Tartaric acid stereoisomersIf the two halves are built the same, (R,S) can be its own mirror image. That’s a meso compound: achiral, so tartaric acid has only three stereoisomers, not four.

Try it: is (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane meso?

No. The ends differ (Br vs Cl), so no internal mirror plane exists. It’s chiral.



Tartaric acid from grapes is the (2R,3R) form; Pasteur’s famous crystal-sorting experiment in 1848 was on tartrate salts. In the meso Fischer projection, both OH groups are on the same side, and a horizontal mirror plane maps the top half onto the bottom half. The descriptors are R at one centre and S at the other, because a mirror inverts. The key point: opposite descriptors are necessary but not sufficient for meso. You also need two identically substituted halves, as the try-it shows. Ask a student to rotate the meso drawing 180 degrees in the page and confirm it gives the same drawing.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: E and Z: stereoisomers at a double bond
text:
E and Z: stereoisomers at a double bond

(Z)- and (E)-but-2-eneA C=C can’t rotate, so the groups are fixed. Rank the two groups at each end separately with CIP rules. Higher priorities on the same side = Z, opposite = E.

Contrast with yesterday: a single bond rotates freely, so anti and gauche are conformers. Rotating around a double bond would break the pi bond, so (Z)- and (E)-but-2-ene are separate compounds with different boiling points, and they’re diastereomers (stereoisomers, not mirror images). For but-2-ene, E/Z matches the older cis/trans names, but E/Z works for any substitution pattern. Biology tie-in: natural fatty acids such as oleic acid have Z double bonds; “trans fats” have E double bonds, which pack differently and behave differently in the body.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Does this alkene have E and Z forms?
text:
Does this alkene have E and Z forms?

Testing alkenes for E/ZEach alkene carbon needs two different groups. One identical pair at either end, and E/Z doesn’t apply.

Try it: can pent-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, exist as E and Z forms?

Yes. Each alkene carbon carries one H and one carbon group, so both ends pass the test.



Do the test before any ranking. Propene fails because its terminal carbon has two H; 2-methylbut-2-ene fails because one carbon has two methyls. On the right, both ends pass, and the ranking matters: at C3, ethyl beats methyl at the second atom out (C,H,H versus H,H,H), and ethyl is opposite to the methyl on C2, so it’s E. This is the same tie-breaking we used for lactic acid, applied to an alkene.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: R/S is not the sign of rotation
text:
R/S is not the sign of rotation

(R)- and (S)-carvoneEnantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal and opposite angles: (+) or (−). That sign is measured, while R/S is assigned from a drawing. No rule connects them: (R)-carvone is (−).

Try it: (R)-carvone rotates light to the left, (−). What does (S)-carvone do?

Rotates it to the right, (+), by the same angle. That’s an experimental fact about this pair, not something R or S predicts.



Back to the opening hook. The two carvones have identical boiling points and IR spectra; a polarimeter shows the only physical difference you can measure in an achiral setting: equal and opposite rotation. Stress the independence of the two labels: you can find R compounds that are (+) and R compounds that are (−). Also, the size and even the sign of rotation depend on solvent, concentration, temperature and wavelength, so a rotation value always needs its conditions. The smell difference comes from chiral receptors, which leads to the next slide.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Chiral environments tell enantiomers apart








property
enantiomers
diastereomers




boiling point, solubility, IR
identical
different


optical rotation
equal and opposite
unrelated


reaction with an enzyme or receptor
often different
different


separated by distillation?
no
yes



A receptor is a chiral “glove”: only one hand fits well. Which enantiomer works better must be measured; R/S can’t predict it.

Use the hand-in-glove analogy: your two hands are identical in mass and shape, but only one fits a right glove. Enzymes and receptors are made of L-amino acids, so they’re chiral gloves. Examples: (S)-ibuprofen is the active painkiller; the carvones smell different; thalidomide is often quoted, but warn that its enantiomers interconvert in the body, so giving a single enantiomer would not have prevented the harm. The point for the exam: never claim that “R is the active form” or “S is toxic” as a rule. That requires biological data for each compound.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Enantiomeric excess: how lopsided is a mixture?
text:
Enantiomeric excess: how lopsided is a mixture?

Enantiomeric excess as bars\text{ee} = |\,\%R - \%S\,| \qquad 70{:}30 \rightarrow 40\%\ \text{ee, not } 70\%

Try it: a sample has 80% ee in favour of R. What are %R and %S?

90% R, 10% S. Solve R + S = 100 and R − S = 80, so 2R = 180.



A 50:50 mixture is racemic: its rotations cancel and ee is zero. Pair each S molecule with one R molecule; those pairs behave like a racemate, and the leftover R is the excess. So 70:30 is 40% ee, and the major enantiomer is 70%, not 40%. Drug companies report ee for every single-enantiomer drug. Today’s R exercise computes ee from a small data table. Caution: ee says nothing about other impurities such as solvent or water; a 95:5 sample (90% ee) can still be chemically impure.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Mistakes we see every year

Read each mistake aloud and ask the room why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. The reversal error and the 90-degree Fischer rotation are the two most common exam errors on this topic, and both give a confident wrong answer. Each row maps onto at least one exercise, so students can find the matching problem to redo.
