Next: curved arrows and how electrons move in reactions (Day 8). Practice: exercises · self-check

Recite the workflow once: is it a stereocentre? Rank the groups. Put 4 at the back. Trace and, if needed, reverse. Then go back to the decision tree on slide two and classify the opening pair: the two carvones are enantiomers, identical except in a chiral environment like your nose. Tomorrow we start mechanisms with curved arrows; stereochemistry returns in Week 3, when we ask whether a reaction keeps, inverts or scrambles a stereocentre. The exercises’ core problems are required; the transfer problems are optional.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text: Draw electron-pair movements and audit atoms, bond orders and formal charges at every step. Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target your mistakes.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Full-headed curved arrows move electron pairs. Start each tail on a lone pair or bond; end at an atom or new-bond location. Ordinary carbon has total bond order four. A transition state is a free-energy maximum and an intermediate a minimum. All drawings must conserve atoms and net charge.
Worked starting example. For OH⁻+CH₃Br, move an oxygen lone pair to methyl C and the C–Br pair to Br in one step. Products CH₃OH+Br⁻ have the same atoms and net charge −1. This is our worked SN2 electron-accounting pattern.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
1. Follow a proton transfer
Draw CH₃OH + OH⁻ ⇌ CH₃O⁻ + H₂O, including both curved arrows and every reacting oxygen lone pair. Audit all atoms and net charge.






Hint





Begin at a hydroxide lone pair; also move the methanol O–H bond pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The hydroxide pair forms its new O–H bond while the methanol O–H pair returns to methanol oxygen. Both sides contain C₁H₅O₂ and total charge −1. This draws a possible proton transfer; its equilibrium position needs compatible acid-strength data.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
2. Repair a proton arrow
A student draws an arrow from the H of H₃O⁺ to the oxygen of NH₃. Identify two errors and replace the step with a valid ammonia protonation drawing.






Hint





Which atom does ammonia contain, and which species supplies the electron pair?









Worked answer and reasoning





Ammonia contains nitrogen, not oxygen. The pair starts on nitrogen and points to a hydronium H; the donor O–H pair returns to O. Products are NH₄⁺ and H₂O, preserving charge +1. Arrows follow pairs, not the proton path.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
3. Construct a methyl substitution
Draw OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻ as one elementary SN2 step. Explain why two arrows do not imply two steps.






Hint





Pair donation to carbon and departure of Br occur together.









Worked answer and reasoning





The hydroxide lone pair forms C–O and the C–Br pair goes to Br in the same concerted event. There is one barrier and no intervening carbocation. Both sides have net charge −1.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
4. Draw the reverse bond changes
As a formal electron-accounting exercise, draw Br⁻ attacking the methyl carbon of CH₃OH with OH⁻ departing. Explain why balanced arrows do not establish that this reverse event is experimentally favourable.






Hint





Keep the bond-pair directions valid, then evaluate the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





A Br lone pair points to methyl C and the C–O bond pair points to O, producing CH₃Br and OH⁻. Atoms and charge balance, but hydroxide is a poor leaving group. Electron accounting is necessary; energies and conditions still determine plausibility.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
5. Locate the electrophile
Draw CH₃CHO with oxygen lone pairs and partial charges. Mark the usual attacked atom in hydroxide addition and distinguish partial from formal charge.






Hint





Unequal sharing in C=O leaves one atom relatively electron-poor.









Worked answer and reasoning





O is δ− and carbonyl C is δ+. Hydroxide attacks C while the π pair moves to O. The neutral starting Lewis structure has formal charge zero at both atoms; δ+ is not a carbocation formula.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
6. Repair five bond orders
A proposed product of OH⁻ addition to CH₃CHO retains C=O and adds C–OH while keeping C–H and C–CH₃. Count carbon bond order, then repair the step.






Hint





The carbonyl π pair cannot remain a bond if an extra sigma bond forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





The proposed carbon has bond-order sum five. Moving the C=O π pair to O gives CH₃CH(OH)O⁻, a four-single-bond carbon and net charge −1. Show both arrows in the addition step.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
7. Track hydride-equivalent addition
Represent a hydride equivalent from NaBH₄ as H:⁻ for a simplified step. Add it to CH₃COCH₃; draw both arrows and the immediate product, not the worked-up alcohol.






Hint





The incoming H makes C–H; the original carbonyl oxygen receives the π pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is (CH₃)₂CHO⁻. H-delivery forms C–H while C=O becomes C–O⁻. H:⁻ is a shorthand for delivery from the reagent, not free hydride present in water; protonation is a later step.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
8. Supply a missing proton donor
A drawing changes (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ directly to (CH₃)₂CHOH without another species. Complete it using water, including all products and arrows.






Hint





Water must become its conjugate base after losing H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





Alkoxide O donates a pair to water H; the water O–H pair returns to water O. Products are propan-2-ol and OH⁻. Net charge remains −1, and no H appears without a source.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
9. A neutral nucleophile gains charge
Draw NH₃ + CH₃Br → CH₃NH₃⁺ + Br⁻ as an SN2 electron-flow step. Count nitrogen bonds and lone pairs before and after.






Hint





Neutral ammonia has three bonds and one pair available for the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The N pair forms N–C as the C–Br pair moves to Br. Nitrogen now has four bonds, no lone pair and formal charge +1. Total charge is zero on both sides; neutral methylamine would require a later deprotonation.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 10. Base or nucleophile in this event?
text:
10. Base or nucleophile in this event?
Compare OH⁻ attacking CH₃Br at carbon with OH⁻ removing H⁺ from H₃O⁺. Draw each step and name the role in each.






Hint





Classify the particular attacked atom rather than permanently labelling OH⁻.









Worked answer and reasoning





Attack at methyl C forms methanol and bromide: OH⁻ acts as nucleophile. Attack at H of hydronium produces two waters: OH⁻ acts as base. Both use pair donation, but they ask different chemical questions.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
11. Heterolysis as bookkeeping
Draw formal C–Br heterolysis for CH₃Br and assign both product charges. Then explain why that picture alone is not a suitable SN1 proposal for methyl bromide.






Hint





Give the entire bond pair to Br, then consider the methyl cation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Formal products are CH₃⁺ and Br⁻. This conserves net charge zero, but the methyl carbocation is extremely poorly stabilised. A charge-balanced drawing does not establish a readily accessible intermediate; methyl SN2 avoids it.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
12. Count steps in a profile
Sketch a reaction profile containing two maxima separated by one minimum. Label every maximum and the intervening minimum. How many elementary steps are depicted?






Hint





A step goes from one minimum to the next through a maximum.









Worked answer and reasoning





Two transition states separate reactants, an intermediate and products, so two elementary steps are shown. The number of curved arrows within either step can be greater than one.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
13. Choose the higher barrier
Two alternative paths start from the same reactants and have activation free energies 15 and 25 kJ/mol at the same temperature. Which path is kinetically favoured, all else comparable? Is either final product proportion specified?






Hint





Compare barriers for rate; distinguish endpoint energies for equilibrium.









Worked answer and reasoning





The 15 kJ/mol path has the lower activation barrier and is faster under the stated comparison. The barrier values alone do not specify the relative equilibrium amounts of final products, which require their thermodynamic relationship.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
14. Calculate a reverse barrier
A one-step schematic has reactants at 0, transition state at +45 and products at −20 kJ/mol. Give forward barrier, reverse barrier and overall ΔG.






Hint





Measure each barrier upward from its own starting minimum.









Worked answer and reasoning





Forward ΔG‡ is 45 kJ/mol; reverse is 45−(−20)=65 kJ/mol; overall ΔG is −20 kJ/mol. A reaction can be thermodynamically favourable yet have a substantial forward barrier.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
15. Add a catalytic path
On the preceding profile, add a catalytic path with its highest relevant barrier at +25 kJ/mol while retaining the same endpoints. Explain what changes and what does not.






Hint





A different path need not alter reactant or product state energies.









Worked answer and reasoning





The catalysed path offers a lower barrier and can speed reaction. The endpoint ΔG remains −20 kJ/mol, so catalysis alone does not change the equilibrium constant for the same net reaction and conditions. A real catalytic path may have several steps.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
16. Separate equilibrium from time
A sample has not reached equilibrium after ten minutes, but its eventual equilibrium composition is known. Can that composition alone tell you the half-time? Explain using a profile.






Hint





An endpoint energy difference does not specify the height of the route between endpoints.









Worked answer and reasoning





No. Different barriers can connect the same reactant/product free energies. Equilibrium information constrains relative state stabilities; rates need kinetic information such as the relevant activation barriers and rate laws.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
17. Audit a missing charge
A student writes OH⁻ + CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)O with all atoms shown but no product charge. Repair the oxygen electron count and explain why assigning a +1 carbon would not solve it.






Hint





The original carbonyl oxygen now has only one bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The original carbonyl oxygen is O⁻ with three lone pairs, giving CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Carbon has four single bonds and formal charge zero. Placing +1 on carbon would not follow from the electron movement or preserve net charge −1.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
18. Resonance or reaction?
Draw the two equivalent ethanoate contributors, keeping all nuclei fixed. Contrast their relation with CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.






Hint





One comparison moves electrons only; the other removes a nucleus from the species.









Worked answer and reasoning





Ethanoate contributors differ in which C–O is drawn double and which O carries formal negative charge; they describe one delocalised ion. Acid dissociation changes which atoms belong to the acid species. Use a resonance double-headed arrow for contributors and an equilibrium arrow for dissociation.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
19. Preserve atom identity
Label methanol oxygen A and hydroxide oxygen B in methanol deprotonation. Which oxygen belongs to methoxide and which to the newly formed water?






Hint





A proton transfers; an oxygen atom does not move from one molecule to the other.









Worked answer and reasoning





A remains the oxygen of CH₃O⁻; B becomes the oxygen of H₂O. Assigning A to water would imply additional bond changes not present in a simple proton transfer.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
20. Build a two-step explanation
Using only CH₃CHO, OH⁻ and H₂O, draw base-catalysed formation of CH₃CH(OH)₂. Cross out the catalyst from the net equation and name the intermediate.






Hint





First add hydroxide, then use water to protonate the alkoxide.









Worked answer and reasoning





Addition gives CH₃CH(OH)O⁻; water then protonates that alkoxide and regenerates OH⁻. The net equation is CH₃CHO + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH(OH)₂. The alkoxide is an intermediate, while hydroxide is regenerated overall.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 8: Exercises — Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Explore
A 5–10 minute exploration, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

Predict first
Before choosing arrows, identify the electron source and the electron-poor destination in a supplied proton transfer. Can a full-headed electron-pair arrow begin at an isolated H⁺?
Loading interactive…This interactive needs JavaScript. The exploration instructions and linked exercises below remain available.




Explore

Repair the hydroxide/ethanoic-acid step. Choose both pair movements, set the total product charge and check. Follow the original acid O–H pair rather than treating an arrow as the proton’s path.
Select carbonyl addition. Compare moving the π pair to O with keeping C=O unchanged as OH⁻ makes a new bond. Check the carbon bond-order count.
Select amine protonation. Count N bonds before and after, then explain where hydronium’s original O–H pair goes. Use the valid-step preset only after making your own attempt.



Take-away
For one step, state both pair origins, both destinations and the total charge check. Which proposed intermediate would violate ordinary carbon valence?


Model and limits
Full-headed curved arrows represent electron pairs. Deliberately invalid proposals are included for repair and labelled as such; they are not proposed stable products. The carbonyl case isolates its initial elementary addition only, without claiming a final isolated hydrate yield. A valid ordinary tetrahedral carbon has four bond orders.
Continue with the exercises.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
text:
1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
Choose a lone pair, an ordinary atom label without a specified electron pair, or a positive charge. Explain the electron accounting.






Check your answer





Start at a lone pair or a bond containing the pair being moved. A positive charge is an acceptor cue, not an electron-pair source.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
text:
2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
OH⁻ forms a new bond to carbonyl carbon. What must happen to the C=O π pair?






Check your answer





It moves to oxygen in the same addition step. Otherwise the carbon would have total bond order five. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
3. Are two arrows two steps?
The methyl SN2 drawing has two curved arrows. Does it have two elementary steps?






Check your answer





No. Both pair movements occur in one concerted elementary step. Step counting depends on the mechanistic intermediates and barriers, not the number of arrows.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
4. What distinguishes an intermediate?
On a schematic free-energy profile, is an intermediate a maximum or a minimum? How does it differ from a transition state?






Check your answer





An intermediate is a minimum between elementary steps and has a finite lifetime. A transition state lies at a barrier maximum and is not an isolable species.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
text:
5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
An alkoxide takes a proton from water. Give both products and check charge.






Check your answer





The products are an alcohol and OH⁻. Net charge starts and ends at minus one. Writing only alcohol would omit the donor-derived conjugate base.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
text:
6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
A catalyst lowers a kinetically relevant barrier. Does that change the equilibrium constant for the same reaction and conditions?






Check your answer





No. It changes the pathway and can speed approach to equilibrium in both directions. The same reactant/product endpoint free-energy difference determines the same equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the exercises, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
About this lecture
In 1942, two Yale pharmacologists gave a nitrogen mustard, a chemical cousin of the mustard gas from the First World War, to a man dying of lymphoma. His tumours shrank. It was the start of cancer chemotherapy. The drug works by substitution: a nitrogen in DNA attacks a carbon, chloride leaves, and the drug staples the two DNA strands together.
Today we learn how one group pushes another off carbon:

SN2: one step, attack from the back, inversion of configuration
SN1: the leaving group goes first, a flat carbocation, two faces
What decides: the carbon, the leaving group, the nucleophile and the solvent
Bookkeeping: charges, extra proton transfers and net equations

Every step uses the curved arrows from Day 8, so have them ready.

Open with the nitrogen-mustard story; it’s true and it sticks. Goodman and Gilman treated their first patient in 1942, though the work was classified and only published in 1946. The real mechanism has a twist (the mustard first does an internal substitution to make a strained three-membered aziridinium ion, which the guanine N7 then opens), but every step is a substitution of the kind we’ll draw today. Mention that our own cells do the same chemistry on purpose: S-adenosylmethionine hands a methyl group to DNA and to hormones like adrenaline by an SN2 step. The link back to Day 8: students already know that an arrow starts at a lone pair or a bond and ends where the new bond forms. Today we just apply that to a carbon carrying a leaving group.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
One reaction, three parts

Ethoxide plus bromoethane gives diethyl ether plus bromide
The nucleophile brings a lone pair to carbon.
The electrophilic carbon is δ+ because Br pulls electron density away.
The leaving group takes the old C–Br bonding pair with it, as Br⁻.


This is the Williamson ether synthesis, and it’s a good first example because every part is easy to spot. Ask the room: which atom donates electrons? (the O⁻). Which bond breaks? (C–Br). Where does that pair go? (onto Br, which becomes bromide). Point out the charge bookkeeping: ethoxide’s oxygen has one bond and three lone pairs, so −1; in the ether it has two bonds and two lone pairs, so it’s neutral. The negative charge didn’t disappear, it moved to bromide. Total charge is −1 on both sides. That habit of checking total charge will catch half the errors today.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group
text:
Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group

Methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary bromidesCount the carbon neighbours of the carbon bonded to Br, not the carbons in the whole molecule.

Try it: classify the carbon bearing Br in CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃.

Secondary. It’s bonded to two carbons. The molecule has four carbons, but that doesn’t make the centre tertiary.



This classification decides almost everything that follows, so get it automatic. The trap is in the try-it: students see four carbons and say “tertiary”, or see a branch and say “tertiary”. Make them put a finger on the carbon that holds Br and count only the carbons touching it. The same counting comes back for carbocations later today (a tertiary cation has three carbons on C+) and for alcohols on Day 13 (primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols oxidise differently).

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
SN2: one step, two arrows

Hydroxide attacks bromomethane from the back as bromide leaves
The new C–O bond forms while the C–Br bond breaks.
Substitution, Nucleophilic, 2 molecules in the slow step.
Swap in I⁻ and the same two arrows give CH₃I + Br⁻.


Draw this on the board as well, slowly, and ask someone to redo it with iodide (exercise 4). Arrow one starts at a lone pair on oxygen and ends at carbon. Arrow two starts in the middle of the C–Br bond and ends on Br. Two arrows, one step. Point at the three H atoms: in the reactant they point left, away from Br; in the product they point right. The molecule has flipped inside out, like an umbrella in the wind. That flip is invisible here because methyl isn’t a stereocentre, but it’s the whole story two slides from now. Methyl bromide has no H on a neighbouring carbon, so elimination (tomorrow) can’t compete.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: The transition state sits at the top of one hill
text:
The transition state sits at the top of one hill

Single-step energy profile with the SN2 transition stateAt the top, C–O is half made and C–Br half broken. It’s a transition state, not an intermediate: it lasts one molecular vibration and can’t be isolated.

Students often draw the transition state as a real molecule with five bonds to carbon. Stress the dashed bonds and the double-dagger: this is the highest-energy arrangement on the path, not a stop along it. There’s no dip in the curve, so there’s no intermediate. Compare with the SN1 profile later, which has two dips. The three H atoms are flat in the transition state, which is the halfway point of the umbrella flip. The barrier height, Ea, is what the rate constant k depends on; anything that raises the transition-state energy (crowding, a poor nucleophile) slows the reaction.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: The SN2 rate depends on both partners
text:
The SN2 rate depends on both partners



change at fixed temperature and solvent

\text{rate} = k\,[\text{RX}]\,[\text{Nu}]
Both molecules are in the one step, so both concentrations appear. The factors multiply.

Try it: both concentrations double. What happens to the initial rate?

4×. 2 × 2 = 4, as long as k stays the same (same temperature and solvent).



This is the “2” in SN2: the rate law is second order overall. Keep it concrete with the factor table rather than algebra. Two warnings. First, this is about initial rate, not yield: a reaction that’s six times faster doesn’t give six times more product. Second, k is only constant if temperature and solvent stay the same; change the solvent and you change k. The Day 11 demo lets students compare this rate law with the SN1 one by changing concentrations and watching the predicted rates.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
Backside attack inverts a stereocentre

(S)-2-bromobutane gives (R)-butan-2-ol by SN2The nucleophile comes in opposite the leaving group, so the other three groups flip over. This is inversion of configuration, and it happens in every SN2 step.

Use a molecular model if you have one: hold the H, methyl and ethyl like the ribs of an umbrella and push the OH in from the back. The ribs flip. In the drawing, the H stays wedged but has moved from the left side of the carbon to the right, and the other two groups have swung across too. Walk through the priorities on both structures using the blue numbers: Br is 1, ethyl 2, methyl 3, H 4 in the reactant; OH is 1, ethyl 2, methyl 3, H 4 in the product. Because the new group takes the old group’s rank, the geometric flip shows up as S becoming R. The next slide shows why that’s not automatic.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: Inversion is geometry; R and S are labels
text:
Inversion is geometry; R and S are labels









(S)-2-bromobutane + OH⁻
(R)-2-bromopropan-1-ol + CN⁻




priorities before
Br > ethyl > methyl > H
Br > CH₂OH > CH₃ > H


priorities after
OH > ethyl > methyl > H
CH₂OH > CN > CH₃ > H


geometry
inverted
inverted


label
S → R
R → R




Try it: in the second example, why does the letter stay R even though SN2 inverted the centre?

Priorities 1 and 2 swapped. CH₂OH (O first) now outranks CN (N, N, N), so the relabelling cancels the geometric flip.



This is the slide that separates students who understand CIP from those who memorised “SN2 flips the letter”. The geometry always inverts. Whether the letter changes depends on whether the incoming group takes the same priority rank as the outgoing one. In the first example it does: Br and OH are both top priority. In the second, Br was 1 but cyanide is only 2, because at the first point of difference CH2OH has an O and the nitrile carbon only has N. Both labels here were checked with RDKit’s CIP labeller. Send students back to Day 7 if they’re shaky on how CIP counts the atoms of a triple bond.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: Crowding at the back stops SN2
text:
Crowding at the back stops SN2

Groups behind the carbon block the path of the nucleophileEach carbon group on the reacting carbon sits in the nucleophile’s path. Methyl > primary > secondary, and tertiary carbons don’t do SN2 at all.

The drawing shows the three groups on the attack side. For methyl they’re all small H atoms; for tertiary they’re three methyl groups, each with its own H atoms waving around, and there’s simply no room. A strong nucleophile can’t fix a geometric problem. That’s the point of exercise 10: students sometimes argue “strong nucleophile, so SN2” for tertiary bromides. What actually happens with a tertiary bromide and a strong base is elimination, which is tomorrow. Secondary is the grey zone: SN2 works, but slowly, and other paths compete.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: A good leaving group is a weak base
text:
A good leaving group is a weak base









leaving group

The leaving group has to hold the pair it takes. Strong acid, weak conjugate base, good leaving group.

This connects straight back to Day 3. A leaving group leaves with the bonding pair, so it ends up as an anion (or as a neutral molecule if it started positive). Anions that are happy holding a negative charge are the conjugate bases of strong acids. Bromide and iodide are great; hydroxide is terrible, because HO− is a strong base. So you can’t just push OH− off an alcohol. The table uses the classic value of 15.7 for water; some books quote 14, and the conclusion is the same either way. The next slide shows how to rescue alcohols.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
Activating an alcohol: protonate first

Ethanol is protonated by hydronium, then bromide displaces waterProtonating OH turns a terrible leaving group (HO⁻) into a good one (H₂O).

Try it: does protonating ethanol mean the reaction now goes SN1?

No. A primary carbocation is far too unstable. Bromide does an SN2 on the oxonium ion instead.



This is how HBr converts primary alcohols into alkyl bromides. Step one is the proton transfer from Day 3, drawn with two arrows. Step two is an ordinary SN2 with water as the leaving group. The common mistake is to write CH3CH2+ after water leaves. Activation fixes the leaving group; it doesn’t make a primary carbocation stable. With tertiary alcohols the same acid does give a carbocation, and that’s SN1, coming up. Alcohols get their own day on Day 13.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: Neutral nucleophiles leave a charge behind
text:
Neutral nucleophiles leave a charge behind

Ammonia attacks bromomethane, then a second ammonia takes a protonN goes from three bonds to four bonds and +1. The neutral amine needs a separate proton transfer to a base.

Try it: a student writes NH₃ + CH₃Br → CH₃NH₂ + Br⁻. What’s missing?

A step and a species. CH₃NH₃⁺ forms first; another NH₃ must take H⁺ and becomes NH₄⁺.



Count bonds at nitrogen after step 1: three to H, one to C, no lone pair, so +1. The tempting shortcut is to make the H “fall off”. Protons never just leave; something has to take them, and here that’s a second ammonia. Check the charge: step 2 starts at +1 and ends at +1. In practice you use excess ammonia, and the product mixture depends on amounts; the arrow-pushing is what we care about today. This neutral-nucleophile pattern repeats with water in SN1 in a few slides, and amines come back as nucleophiles in Week 4.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: SN1 step 1: the leaving group goes first
text:
SN1 step 1: the leaving group goes first

tert-Butyl bromide ionises to a carbocation; cation stability from methyl to tertiaryWith no room at the back, a tertiary bromide can ionise instead. The cation is flat, with three bonds and an empty orbital.

One arrow: the C–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. Nothing attacks yet. This is the slow step, because pulling charges apart costs a lot of energy, and it only happens when the cation is stabilised. Alkyl groups donate electron density into the empty orbital (hyperconjugation is the name if anyone asks), so tertiary is the most stable and methyl is hopeless. That’s the mirror image of SN2: SN2 needs an uncrowded carbon, SN1 needs a well-substituted one. A polar solvent like water helps by surrounding both ions.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: SN1 steps 2 and 3: capture, then lose H⁺
text:
SN1 steps 2 and 3: capture, then lose H⁺

Water bonds to the cation, then a second water removes a proton
Try it: add up all three steps, starting from (CH₃)₃CBr in water.

(CH₃)₃CBr + 2 H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. The cation and oxonium ion cancel out. Atoms and charge both balance.



After capture, oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, so it’s +1. Students love to write the neutral alcohol straight away, which silently deletes a proton. Insist on step 3 with a named base. It’s the same move as the ammonia case. For the net equation, two waters are consumed: one as nucleophile, one as base. A net equation is accounting, not mechanism: it hides the intermediates, and it doesn’t tell you how much alkene forms by the competing route on the last content slide.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
The SN1 energy profile

Three-step SN1 energy profile with two intermediatesOnly the substrate is in the slow step, so rate = k[R–Br]. The 1 in SN1 means one molecule in the slow step.

Try it: in an SN1 reaction you double the nucleophile concentration. What happens to the rate?

Nothing. The nucleophile only joins after the slow step, so it doesn’t appear in the rate law.



Compare with the SN2 profile: one hill there, three here, and two real dips. The dips are intermediates; you could in principle detect them. The peaks are transition states. Since the first hill is by far the highest, everything after it is fast and doesn’t affect the rate. This is the experimental test: change [Nu] and see if the rate changes. The demo for today does exactly that comparison with simulated data. Rate laws support a mechanism but don’t prove every detail of it.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: A flat cation has two faces
text:
A flat cation has two faces

A planar carbocation gives both enantiomers of 3-methylhexan-3-olWater can reach either face, so an optically pure starting material gives both enantiomers.

Try it: is an SN1 product always exactly 50 : 50?

Not exactly. The departing Br⁻ briefly shields one face, so there’s often a small excess of the inverted product.



Contrast with SN2, which is stereospecific: one enantiomer in, one out. Here the stereocentre is destroyed when the cation forms, because a flat carbon with three groups isn’t a stereocentre. Both products’ labels were checked with RDKit. Note the drawings show OH in the plane and the methyl wedged or hashed: same information, just a different way of placing the molecule on the page. The ion-pair point matters for honesty, not for exams: the textbook “racemic” is an idealisation. Day 7’s racemic mixtures and optical rotation are the link.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
Solvent changes the rate constant









solvent type
examples
what it does
favours




polar protic
water, methanol, ethanol
H-bonds stabilise both ions; also cage anions
SN1


polar aprotic
acetone, DMSO, DMF
dissolves salts but leaves anions free
SN2



Same reactants in a different solvent means a different k.

This is the content behind exercise 18. Protic solvents have O–H or N–H, so they can hydrogen bond. That’s great for SN1, where the slow step makes ions. But for SN2 with an anionic nucleophile, the H-bonds wrap the anion and make it less eager to attack. Aprotic polar solvents dissolve sodium or potassium salts by surrounding the cation, while the anion stays relatively free and reactive. Don’t oversell this: solvent is one factor among several, and the effect is on k, not on which atoms end up bonded.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
section: SN1 or SN2? Weigh the evidence
text:
SN1 or SN2? Weigh the evidence

Try it: CH₃CH₂Br + NaCN in DMSO, and (CH₃)₃CBr in water. Which mechanism for each?

SN2 for the primary bromide with a strong anion in an aprotic solvent. SN1 for the tertiary bromide in water.



Encourage students to argue from the table rather than from a flowchart. The carbon class is usually the strongest clue. Methyl and primary: SN2. Tertiary: SN1 (or elimination). Secondary is genuinely ambiguous and the conditions decide. In the try-it, the primary nitrile synthesis gives propanenitrile, and it makes a new C–C bond, which is why cyanide is so useful in synthesis. Practise saying “because” for each choice.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
Substitution has a competitor

Water can attack the carbocation or remove a beta-H from itThe same cation can gain a nucleophile (SN1) or lose a β-H (E1). Heat and strong bases push towards elimination.

This is the bridge to tomorrow. The carbocation is a shared intermediate, and water can play two roles: nucleophile at the positive carbon, or base at an H on the next carbon (the beta carbon). In the E1 arrows, the C–H bonding pair becomes the new pi bond. So a tertiary bromide in water gives a mixture of alcohol and alkene, and the net equation from three slides ago only described one branch. Tomorrow we’ll treat elimination properly, including the one-step E2 version that competes with SN2.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
text:
Mistakes we see every year

Read each mistake aloud and ask for the fix before revealing it. Every row is tied to an exercise: 1 and the quiz question on classification; 10; 17; 12 and 19; 6 and 7; 15; and 16. Students who still make one of these know which exercise to redo tonight.

Go back to the nitrogen mustard: a nitrogen nucleophile, a carbon with a chloride leaving group, an SN2 step. Students can now draw it. Tomorrow’s lecture picks up from the competition slide: the same reagents that act as nucleophiles can act as bases, and then we get alkenes. Core exercises 1 to 12 are the minimum; 13 to 20 are transfer problems, and 15, 16 and 20 are good preparation for tomorrow.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
Locate the reacting atoms, draw elimination and addition steps, and use geometry to explain the products. Use the lecture and demo to revisit a worked case.
Core 1–12: about 80–100 minutes. Transfer 13–20: an optional 45–65 minutes; choose problems that target the mistakes you want to resolve.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
Alpha means the carbon carrying the leaving group and beta an adjacent carbon. E2 couples base attack at β-H, C–H pair donation to C–C and leaving-group departure; a suitable anti-periplanar arrangement has180° H–C–C–leaving-group dihedral. Addition consumes an alkene pi bond. The ionic HBr cases here explicitly exclude peroxides.
Worked starting example. In a formal E2 step RCH₂CH₂Br+B⁻→RCH=CH₂+BH+Br⁻, three pairs move together: B→H, C–H→C–C and C–Br→Br. This balances atoms and charge, but a particular primary substrate may favour competing substitution under actual conditions.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
1. Find every beta carbon
Draw 2-bromobutane and mark α and all β carbons. Explain the local definition.






Hint





Alpha is the carbon carrying the leaving group.









Worked answer and reasoning





C2 is α; C1 and C3 are β because they are directly adjacent to C2. Alpha/beta labels are relative to this functional site, not permanent names for the molecule.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
2. List possible alkene connectivities
From formal HBr elimination of 2-bromobutane, draw but-1-ene and but-2-ene and show which β site produces each.






Hint





Remove H from either neighbouring carbon, without moving the carbon skeleton.









Worked answer and reasoning





Loss from C1 forms C1=C2, but-1-ene. Loss from C3 forms C2=C3, but-2-ene. This inventories possible connectivity, not product proportions in unspecified conditions.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
3. Test the E/Z prerequisite
Draw the preceding two alkene products and decide which can be E/Z.






Hint





Each end of a double bond needs two different substituents.









Worked answer and reasoning





But-2-ene can be E or Z because each alkene carbon bears CH₃ and H. But-1-ene has two H on one end, so it cannot have an E/Z descriptor.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
4. Construct an E2 electron-flow step
Assume a suitable anti conformation of 2-bromopropane and a strong base B⁻. Draw the three arrows and complete the products.






Hint





Base→β-H; C–H→C–C; C–Br→Br.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are propene, BH and Br⁻. All three pair movements are concerted in E2; no carbocation is inserted. Net charge remains −1. The conformation must support the reacting geometry.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
5. Reject methyl elimination
Explain why CH₃Br cannot undergo ordinary β-elimination to an alkene. Contrast it with CH₃CH₂Br as a formal bond inventory.






Hint





Count carbon atoms before searching for a β-H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Methyl bromide has no β-carbon. Ethyl bromide has one and can formally lose HBr to form ethene; however, a primary substrate with a strong nucleophile can favour SN2, so the inventory does not establish a dominant pathway.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
6. Read a Newman projection
Looking from the β-carbon toward the α-carbon, put the front reacting H at twelve o’clock and rear Br at six. Give the H–C–C–Br dihedral.






Hint





Opposing clock positions are separated by half a turn.









Worked answer and reasoning





The dihedral is 180°, an anti-periplanar arrangement. The front bond starts at the dot and the rear bond at the circle. Reversing which carbon is viewed first requires redrawing the projection consistently.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
7. Rotate without changing connectivity
Starting from that anti view, rotate only the rear carbon by 60°. Is the same H/Br pair still anti? Has the molecule become a constitutional isomer?






Hint





A torsion changes spatial arrangement around one bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The selected pair is no longer at 180°. Connectivity and substituent identities remain unchanged, so this is a conformational change, not a constitutional isomerisation.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
8. Fix a two-arrow E2 proposal
A drawing moves the base pair to β-H and the C–Br pair to Br, but never moves C–H electrons. What is missing?






Hint





Account for the pair left behind when H departs as H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





The C–H pair must form the new C–C π bond. Otherwise the proposed bond inventory and electron count do not describe the alkene. Draw all three arrows in the same elementary step.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
9. Separate accessible from favoured products
A student lists all β sites, then claims each gives equal alkene amounts. Give two reasons that conclusion is unsupported.






Hint





Consider geometry and the identities of base and substrate.









Worked answer and reasoning





Different sites can have different access to anti geometry and give differently substituted alkenes; steric properties of the base and other conditions also affect relative pathways. Possible products need not be equally probable.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
10. Draw E1 after ionisation
Use (CH₃)₃C⁺ and water to draw β-H loss, with both electron-pair arrows and all products.






Hint





Water supplies a pair to H while C–H supplies the alkene π pair.









Worked answer and reasoning





The products are (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ and H₃O⁺. This deprotonation follows prior ionisation in an E1 pathway. It is not the concerted C–Br-breaking E2 event.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
11. Contrast E1 with E2
Compare an E1 route from a tertiary bromide in water with an E2 model using a strong base. State the order of bond breaking and the presence or absence of a carbocation.






Hint





Ask whether loss of the leaving group is a separate elementary step.









Worked answer and reasoning





E1 ionises first to a carbocation, then loses β-H. E2 couples base attack, C–H cleavage and C–leaving-group cleavage in one step, without a carbocation intermediate. Conditions and competing routes must still be considered.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
12. Choose the attacked atom
For a secondary bromide with a reagent that can act as nucleophile and base, draw a carbon-attack possibility and a β-H-removal possibility.






Hint





The alternatives differ first in where the donated pair goes.









Worked answer and reasoning





Pair donation to saturated carbon with leaving-group departure gives substitution; donation to β-H with C–H electrons forming C=C gives elimination. A reagent label alone does not choose between them.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
13. Protonate propene in two ways
For ionic HBr addition without peroxides, draw both formal carbocation connectivities possible after protonating propene.






Hint





H can attach at either alkene carbon, leaving the positive site at the other.









Worked answer and reasoning





Terminal H addition gives secondary CH₃CH⁺CH₃; internal H addition gives primary CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺. The secondary route is favoured in the selected model because its intermediate is more stabilised.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
14. Complete bromide capture
Starting from CH₃CH⁺CH₃ and Br⁻, draw pair donation and name the organic product.






Hint





The cationic carbon needs the new bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





A bromide lone pair forms C–Br, giving 2-bromopropane. Carbon becomes tetrahedral and neutral. The HBr addition sequence is protonation followed by capture, not a single arbitrary placement of H and Br.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
15. Audit HBr addition
Balance propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane at the formula level and count the local bonds that change.






Hint





A pi bond is consumed while two sigma bonds are made.









Worked answer and reasoning





C₃H₆ + HBr gives C₃H₇Br. The C=C π bond and H–Br bond are consumed overall while C–H and C–Br form; the original C–C sigma bond remains.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
16. Recognise a symmetric alkene
Predict the connectivity of ionic HBr addition to ethene. Is there a distinct regioisomeric alternative?






Hint





The two alkene carbons are equivalent by symmetry.









Worked answer and reasoning





The product is bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. Exchanging which equivalent carbon receives H gives the same connectivity, so there is no distinct regioisomeric product in this example.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
17. Read bromonium opening
Draw a three-membered C–Br⁺–C bridge and Br⁻ approaching a carbon from the opposite side. Show which bridge bond pair returns to Br.






Hint





New C–Br formation opens the corresponding C–Br bridge bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





Bromide attacks carbon from the back of the bridge, and that carbon–bridge-Br pair returns to the bridging Br. This yields two C–Br bonds with anti addition in the representative mechanism.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
18. Compare HBr with Br₂
Why should the free-carbocation HBr picture not be copied unchanged when explaining anti Br₂ addition?






Hint





Compare the intermediates, not just the two letters Br in the reagents.









Worked answer and reasoning





The bromonium bridge changes access to the two faces and its backside opening explains anti addition. A freely planar carbocation picture omits this bridge and does not provide the same stereochemical explanation.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
19. Identify a false reverse reaction
A student calls every addition the reverse of the corresponding laboratory elimination under the same conditions. Rewrite the claim carefully.






Hint





Distinguish net bond inventory from microscopic path and operating conditions.









Worked answer and reasoning





Addition consumes a pi bond and elimination creates one, so some net transformations can be related. Their useful reagents, mechanisms, equilibrium conditions and competing processes may differ; the names alone do not establish an exact reverse under identical conditions.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
20. Explain a complete branch point
A tertiary carbocation is formed in water. Draw both capture leading to alcohol and deprotonation leading to alkene, including proton-transfer products.






Hint





Water can attack carbon or act as base at β-H.









Worked answer and reasoning





Carbon capture gives an oxonium ion, then water deprotonation gives alcohol plus H₃O⁺. β-H removal gives alkene plus H₃O⁺ directly from the cation. Both follow the same early ionisation, so seeing ionisation alone does not settle the product ratio.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 12: Exercises — Elimination and addition
text:
Explore
Use this explorer for about 7–10 minutes. Make a prediction first, change one input at a time, and record a chemical explanation rather than only a screenshot.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). Keep front H1 at twelve o’clock. At which rear-Br angle will H1–Cβ–Cα–Br be 180°? Repeat mentally for H2 at four o’clock.
Explore (3–4 minutes). Choose a reacting front hydrogen and rotate the rear carbon. Find anti alignment without the preset, then use “Align selected H anti” to check. Change the selected H without changing rotation. Does the same conformation remain eligible for that different H?
Explain (2–3 minutes). Draw one aligned Newman view on paper, then the three E2 electron-pair arrows and possible ethene product. Explain what stays unchanged during rotation and why alignment alone does not establish reaction speed or the dominant pathway.


Supplied model and its limits
The explicit substrate is bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br. View from its beta CH₃ (front) to alpha CH₂Br (rear). Front hydrogens stay fixed at 0°, 120° and 240°; rear Br and its two H atoms rotate together. A ±10° teaching window labels near 180° as near anti; it is not a kinetic threshold or reaction probability. This is a geometry model only: suitable nucleophiles can make primary bromoethane favour substitution instead of elimination.


Continue with the exercises
Continue with the exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
text:
1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
Draw the carbon skeleton before answering.






Check your answer





No. There is no beta carbon, and therefore no beta-H that could be removed to form an adjacent C=C bond.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
text:
2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
Identify the source and destination of each.






Check your answer





Three: base lone pair to beta-H; C–H bond pair into the C–C pi bond; C–leaving-group pair onto the leaving group. These describe one concerted elementary step.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text:
3. What is anti-periplanar?
State the H–C–C–Br dihedral angle in the preferred simple anti arrangement.






Check your answer





180 degrees. The reacting C–H and C–Br bonds lie in one plane on opposite sides of the viewed C–C bond. A Newman drawing must specify front and rear bonds.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
text:
4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
List constitutional possibilities and note the E/Z case.






Check your answer





But-1-ene and but-2-ene. The latter can be E or Z; but-1-ene has two H atoms at its terminal alkene carbon and cannot have E/Z configurations.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
text:
5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
Assume no peroxides and use the supplied carbocation model.






Check your answer





Protonation giving a secondary carbocation is favoured over the alternative primary carbocation. Bromide then captures that intermediate, giving the observed connectivity in this model.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
text:
6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
Name the key bridged intermediate and the relative opening geometry.






Check your answer





A bromonium intermediate can be opened by opposite-side bromide attack, giving anti addition. A free-carbocation HBr mechanism should not be copied unchanged for this process.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
About this lecture
After a drink, your liver turns ethanol into acetaldehyde and then into acetate. If the second step is slow, acetaldehyde piles up and you get the red face, racing heart and nausea of an “alcohol flush”. The drug disulfiram treats alcoholism by blocking that second step on purpose. Both steps are oxidations of one carbon.
Today we learn to follow that carbon:

Classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary, and predict what each oxidises to
Oxidation states of carbon, as a quick bookkeeping check
Reduction of aldehydes and ketones with NaBH₄, drawn as two steps
Activating OH so it can leave, and IR evidence for a redox change
Amounts and yield: limiting reagent, theoretical mass, what yield can’t tell you

Yesterday we made alcohols by adding water to alkenes. Today we change how oxidised the alcohol carbon is.

Open with the flush. Many students have seen it or felt it; the ALDH2 variant that slows acetaldehyde removal is common in East Asian populations. Disulfiram (Antabuse) blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase so that drinking makes people feel ill immediately. Methanol poisoning is the dark twin: the same enzymes turn methanol into formaldehyde and formic acid, which damages the optic nerve, and the antidote fomepizole blocks the first step. The point for today: these are ordinary organic oxidations, and the rules we learn for the lab apply in the liver. Link back to Day 12: hydration of an alkene gave an alcohol, but the carbon oxidation level didn’t change much there; today it does.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Your liver runs two oxidations in a row
text:
Your liver runs two oxidations in a row

Ethanol to ethanal to acetate in the liverLook at the shaded carbon. Each step removes a C–H bond and adds a C–O bond. The H leaves as a hydride, picked up by NAD⁺, which becomes NADH.

Point at the shaded carbon through all three structures: the carbon skeleton never changes, only what’s attached to that one carbon. Ethanol’s carbon has two H and one O; ethanal’s has one H and a double bond to O; acetate’s has no H and three bonds to oxygen. NAD+ is nature’s oxidising agent: it accepts a hydride (H with two electrons). Keep that in mind, because later today NaBH4 does the reverse and gives a hydride to a carbonyl carbon. Biology and the lab run the same chemistry in opposite directions. Students often say “oxidation means adding oxygen”; ask whether going from ethanol to ethanal adds any oxygen atom. It doesn’t, and that’s why we need a better definition on the next slides.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Primary, secondary, tertiary

Ethanol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-olClassify by the OH-bearing carbon (the carbinol carbon): count its carbon neighbours. That also tells you how many H it carries, which decides how far it can be oxidised.

This classification is the key to everything on oxidation. Primary means one carbon neighbour, so two H on the carbinol carbon; secondary, two carbon neighbours and one H; tertiary, three carbon neighbours and no H. The H are drawn explicitly here only on the carbinol carbon because those are the ones that matter today. A common slip: students classify by counting OH groups or by counting all the carbons in the molecule. Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol have the same number of carbons, but one is primary and one secondary. Same words as for carbocations on Day 11, same counting rule.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Oxidation state: a bookkeeping check for carbon
text:
Oxidation state: a bookkeeping check for carbon

Oxidation states of the changing carbonCount only bonds to the carbon you care about: C–O +1 per bond (C=O counts +2), C–H −1, C–C 0. Oxidation raises the number; reduction lowers it.

Try it: what’s the carbinol carbon in propan-2-ol, and the carbonyl carbon in propanone?

0 and +2. Propan-2-ol: +1 (C–O) − 1 (C–H) = 0. Propanone: +2 (C=O), no C–H. Up by two, so it’s an oxidation.



This is a bookkeeping tool, not a real charge. The rule comes from electronegativity: O pulls electrons from C, so each C–O bond counts as +1 for carbon; H is less electronegative than C, so each C–H counts as −1; a C–C bond is shared evenly. Walk through ethanol: one C–O (+1), two C–H (−2), one C–C (0), total −1. Ethanal: C=O is +2, one C–H −1, total +1. Ethanoic acid: C=O +2, C–OH +1, total +3. Each step is a change of two, which matches two electrons leaving with the hydride. Give 30 seconds for the try-it. Students who get +1 for propanone usually forgot that a double bond counts twice.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Primary alcohols: stop at the aldehyde, or go on to the acid
text:
Primary alcohols: stop at the aldehyde, or go on to the acid

Propan-1-ol oxidised by PCC or by aqueous dichromateA primary alcohol has two C–H to give up, so it has two oxidation targets. To stop at the aldehyde, use a reagent without water, such as PCC in CH₂Cl₂. In water, the aldehyde is oxidised again to the carboxylic acid.

Why does water matter? In water an aldehyde partly adds water to give a hydrate, which has a new C–H next to an OH and gets oxidised again; that’s a preview of carbonyl addition in Week 4, Day 16. PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in dichloromethane avoids that. The orange-to-green colour change of dichromate, Cr(VI) to Cr(III), is the chemistry of the old roadside breathalyser: ethanol in breath reduced the dichromate. Stress that “[O]” over an arrow is shorthand for some oxidant, not a free oxygen atom, and an arrow on a slide is not a lab protocol. The reagents here are examples to reason with; you won’t be examined on chromium mechanisms.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Secondary alcohols give ketones

Butan-2-ol oxidises to butan-2-oneThe C=O forms exactly where the OH was. Both carbon neighbours stay attached, so the product is a ketone. With no further C–H on that carbon, oxidation stops there.

Try it: a student writes butanal as the product. What went wrong?

The C=O moved. Butanal has its carbonyl on C1, but oxidation only changes the carbon that carried the OH, which is C2.



Numbering makes the point concrete: C2 carries the OH before, and C2 carries the O after. Oxidation doesn’t move functional groups along a chain and doesn’t break C–C bonds under these conditions. Ask why oxidation stops at the ketone: the carbonyl carbon has no H left, and making an acid would mean breaking a C–C bond. Everyday example: propan-2-ol (rubbing alcohol) oxidises to propanone (acetone, nail-polish remover). The exercises use butan-2-ol and butan-2-one, so make sure everyone can draw both.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Tertiary alcohols resist simple oxidation

Propan-2-ol versus 2-methylpropan-2-olOxidation to C=O needs a C–H on the carbinol carbon. A tertiary carbon has three C–C bonds and a C–O; drawing (CH₃)₃C=O would give it five bonds.
Harsh oxidants can break C–C bonds instead, but that’s a different reaction and outside our toolkit.

Run the valence check from Day 1 on the board: three C–C bonds plus a C=O is 3 + 2 = 5 bonds to carbon, which is impossible. So the simple alcohol-to-carbonyl pattern has nowhere to go. Be careful with the wording: don’t say “tertiary alcohols can never be oxidised”. Under forcing conditions C–C bonds break. What we can say is that the selected oxidations in this course leave tertiary alcohols alone. This is a useful test in practice: a mild oxidant distinguishes primary and secondary from tertiary alcohols.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Reduction runs the map backwards

NaBH₄ reduces an aldehyde and a ketoneSodium borohydride, NaBH₄, adds H to the carbonyl carbon; a proton source then puts H on oxygen. Aldehydes give primary alcohols, ketones give secondary alcohols. The carbon skeleton is unchanged.

This is the mirror image of the oxidation slides: one new C–H and one new O–H, oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon drops by two. The “1. 2.” numbering means two separate operations: first the reagent, then the water or acid work-up. NaBH4 is a mild, convenient reagent, often used in methanol or ethanol, and it’s selective, which we’ll come back to. In the body, NADH plays the same role as NaBH4: it delivers a hydride to a carbonyl carbon. Ask the room what a ketone reduction can never give: a primary alcohol, because the carbonyl carbon already has two carbon neighbours.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Step 1: a hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon
text:
Step 1: a hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon

Hydride delivery to propanoneTwo arrows: the H:⁻ pair forms the new C–H, and the C=O π pair moves onto O. The product is an alkoxide, with O⁻. “H:⁻” is shorthand for a hydride delivered by BH₄⁻; there’s no free hydride in solution.

Try it: why must the π bond break when the H adds?

Valence. The carbonyl carbon already has four bonds. A fifth is impossible, so the π pair has to leave, onto the more electronegative oxygen.



Draw this one on the board with the students. The first arrow starts at the electron pair (the H with its two electrons) and ends at the carbonyl carbon, which is electrophilic because O pulls electron density away from it. The second arrow starts at the middle of the C=O double bond and ends on O. Count charges: hydride −1 going in, alkoxide oxygen −1 coming out, so charge is conserved. This is the first example of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, which is the whole of Day 16. Probe the misconception that BH4- releases free H- ions into water; it doesn’t, and free hydride would react with water instantly to give H2.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Step 2: water protonates the alkoxide

Proton transfer from water to the alkoxideThe alkoxide is a strong base, so it takes H⁺ from water. Name the donor and write its conjugate base: charge is −1 on both sides, and every H is accounted for.

This is an acid-base step straight out of Day 3: an alkoxide (conjugate base of an alcohol, pKa about 16) and water (pKa about 15.7) are close, and with plenty of water the equilibrium gives the alcohol. The two arrows mirror each other: the O⁻ lone pair grabs the H, and the old O–H bond pair stays on the water oxygen, which becomes hydroxide. Students often write “+ H+” over the arrow and lose track of charge; insist on a named proton donor. The order matters: addition first, then proton transfer. The net product is the alcohol, but the steps don’t happen at once.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
A new stereocentre, both hands

Reduction of butan-2-one gives both enantiomersThe carbonyl is planar, so hydride can arrive from either face with equal ease. Butan-2-ol has a stereocentre, and an achiral reagent makes a racemic 50 : 50 mixture.

Try it: does the product solution rotate plane-polarised light?

No. Equal amounts of R and S cancel. A racemate is optically inactive even though each molecule is chiral.



Bridge to Week 2: the new carbon carries OH, H, CH3 and CH2CH3, four different groups, so it’s a stereocentre. NaBH4 is achiral and the two faces of butan-2-one are mirror images, so the rates are identical. Enzymes are different: the reductases in your cells and in baker’s yeast deliver NADH’s hydride to one face only, and give a single enantiomer. That’s why biocatalysis is used to make chiral drugs. Students sometimes assign the drawn wedge to R without checking; ask one of them to verify the R label with CIP priorities: OH > ethyl > methyl > H.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
NaBH₄ has a scope

What NaBH₄ reducesEsters and amides have a C=O too, but the O or N next to it donates electrons and makes the carbonyl less reactive. NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones; don’t stretch that rule to other carbonyl groups.

Same skill as Day 1: read the neighbours of the carbonyl, not just the C=O. In esters and amides, the lone pair on O or N is shared with the carbonyl by resonance, which makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic. Under ordinary conditions NaBH4 leaves them alone. A stronger reagent, LiAlH4, does reduce esters and amides; we meet that, and the reasons behind the reactivity order, in acyl chemistry on Day 17. The practical lesson for exam answers: state the reagent and the functional group it acts on, and don’t assume one reagent does everything.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Choose the direction from the target
text:
Choose the direction from the target

Ethanol and ethanal interconvertBefore naming a reagent, compare start and target: more C–O or fewer C–H means oxidation; more C–H means reduction. Then pick a reagent that does that and nothing else.

This is the planning habit that synthesis questions in Week 5 rely on. Give a quick oral drill: ethanal to ethanol? Reduction, NaBH4 then water. Ethanol to ethanal? Oxidation, and it has to be controlled, like PCC, or you overshoot to the acid. Ethanal to ethanoic acid? Oxidation. The oxidation-state numbers under each structure are the check: going up is oxidation, going down is reduction. A frequent wrong answer is “oxidise ethanal to get ethanol” because students pattern-match “ethanol and oxidation” from earlier slides; make them say which bonds change.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Activating OH: make it leave as water
text:
Activating OH: make it leave as water

Protonation of ethanol by hydroniumOH⁻ is a strong base, so it’s a poor leaving group. Protonate the OH first, and the group that leaves is neutral water, a weak base.

This connects the last three days. On Day 3 we learned that the weaker the base, the better the leaving group: compare the conjugate acids, water at pKa about 15.7 versus hydronium at about −1.7. On Days 11 and 12 this protonated alcohol was the starting point for SN1 with HBr and for E1 dehydration with sulfuric acid. Which one happens depends on the substrate and the conditions, so don’t assume SN1 for every alcohol. Ask why we can’t just do SN2 on ethanol with bromide: the hydroxide would have to leave, and it won’t. The curved arrow starts at the oxygen lone pair, not at the H, a mistake we see every year.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Evidence: did the alcohol really oxidise?
text:
Evidence: did the alcohol really oxidise?

Schematic IR traces before and after oxidationA broad O–H band (3200–3600 cm⁻¹) that disappears and a strong C=O band (about 1715 cm⁻¹) that appears both support oxidation to a ketone.

Try it: after oxidising propan-2-ol, the IR shows C=O and no O–H. What’s still unproved?

Identity and purity. IR shows which groups are present, not which ketone, and not whether the sample is pure.



These are schematic traces, not real spectra. The logic is what counts: the IR tells you which functional groups are present. Losing the O–H and gaining the C=O is consistent with oxidation, but many ketones absorb near 1715, and a mixture with a little leftover alcohol might show only a weak O–H. Water in the sample also gives an O–H band, so a wet product can look as if the alcohol is still there. Full identification combines IR with NMR and other evidence, which is the topic of Week 5 (Days 21 and 22).

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: From grams to the limiting reagent
text:
From grams to the limiting reagent

Amounts in the aspirin synthesisConvert each mass to moles, n = m/M, then compare n ÷ coefficient. The smallest value limits the product. Never compare grams directly.

Try it: for 2 A + B → P with 12 mmol A and 8 mmol B, which limits, and how much P?

A limits: 6 mmol P. A allows 12 ÷ 2 = 6, B allows 8 ÷ 1 = 8. The larger amount can still limit.



We switch from redox to the lab report for your synthesis practical. The reaction is aspirin from salicylic acid and acetic anhydride (acetic acid is the by-product); all coefficients are one. Work the numbers aloud: 1.3812 / 138.12 = 0.01000 mol = 10.00 mmol; 1.53135 / 102.09 = 0.01500 mol = 15.00 mmol. In the R task you’ll do the same with mutate() on the amounts CSV and then take min() of the extents. The 2A + B example is there because students who only ever see 1:1 reactions compare raw amounts and get the wrong answer once a coefficient isn’t one.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Theoretical mass and yield

Theoretical, isolated and wet massesTheoretical mass = 10.00 mmol × 180.16 g/mol = 1.8016 g. Isolated yield = 1.20 g ÷ 1.8016 g = 66.6%.

Try it: a wet sample weighs 1.95 g. Is the yield 108%?

No. You can’t make more pure product than the stoichiometry allows. The extra mass is water, solvent or impurity, so dry the sample and check your inputs.



Insist on unit conversion: 10.00 mmol is 0.01000 mol, and multiplying 10 by 180.16 gives a thousandfold error, which happens every year. The balance weighs everything in the vial, so a mass above the maximum is a measurement of your drying, not of your chemistry. The right response is to dry to constant mass, check for leftover solvent, and recheck the input masses and molar masses. A yield above 100% in a report should always trigger an explanation, never a celebration.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Conversion, yield and purity answer different questions
text:
Conversion, yield and purity answer different questions








quantity
question it answers
measured by




conversion
how much starting material reacted?
starting material left (e.g. TLC (thin-layer chromatography), NMR)


isolated yield
how much product did I recover?
product mass ÷ theoretical mass


purity
how much of my solid is the product?
melting point, NMR, chromatography




Try it: all the starting material is gone, but the isolated yield is only 40%. Give two reasons.

Side reactions made other products, and losses during work-up, filtering or recrystallisation. Full conversion doesn’t mean full yield.



These three numbers are often confused in lab reports. One spot on a TLC plate under one set of conditions is consistent with a pure sample but doesn’t prove it; one IR band doesn’t identify a compound; one mass doesn’t establish purity. A good evidence statement separates what’s supported from what’s still open: “IR shows a carbonyl; TLC shows one spot; identity needs NMR; purity needs a melting point.” That sentence structure is exactly what exercise 20 asks for, and it comes back in the synthesis-evidence day in Week 5.

Read out each mistake and ask the room why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. Every row matches one or more exercises: classification is exercise 1, the secondary and tertiary cases are 4 and 5, oxidation states are 6 and 7, the mechanism is 10 and 11, scope is 12, amounts and yield are 14 to 18.
