Next: nucleophiles adding to C=O, the general version of today’s hydride step (Day 16). Practice: exercises · self-check

Close the loop with the opening: ADH and ALDH are oxidations of a primary alcohol, first to the aldehyde and then to the acid (as acetate), and disulfiram stops the second one. You can now draw every step and assign the oxidation states. Recite the procedure once: find the carbinol carbon, classify it, decide the direction from the target, and check with oxidation states. Day 14 is a mechanism review and Day 15 practises redox, amounts and evidence. Then Day 16 generalises today’s hydride addition to other nucleophiles. The core exercises 1 to 12 are required; 13 to 20 and the R task are for the lab report.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text: Draw carbonyl-addition mechanisms, track oxygen atoms and check each proton transfer. Use problems 1–12 for core work (about 80–100 minutes); choose from 13–20 for optional transfer work (another 45–65 minutes), focusing on the steps you need to practise.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
section: Local refresher and worked starting example
text:
Local refresher and worked starting example
The polar C=O bond makes carbon electrophilic. Addition forms a new bond to carbon while the pi pair goes to oxygen, yielding a tetrahedral species. Proton transfers use actual donors/bases. Hydrate=two OH; hemiacetal=OH+OR; acetal=OR+OR at one carbon. Full-headed arrows move pairs, and R/S requires a defined 3D view.
Worked starting example. OH⁻ adds to CH₃CHO with OH pair→C and C=O pair→O, giving CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Water then donates H to that alkoxide and becomes OH⁻. The hydrate is neutral CH₃CH(OH)₂; net reaction is aldehyde+water⇌hydrate, not spontaneous loss of oxygen or creation of a proton.
Draw structures, identify the relevant atom and explain the reason. A name alone is insufficient where a mechanism or argument is requested.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
1. Separate partial and formal charge
Draw neutral CH₃CHO with oxygen lone pairs, δ labels and formal charges.






Hint





Unequal electron sharing need not create integer Lewis charges.









Worked answer and reasoning





O is δ− and carbonyl C δ+, while their ordinary neutral Lewis formal charges are both zero. Partial charge explains polarity; it is not a pre-existing carbocation formula.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
2. Count carbonyl geometry
Draw CH₃COCH₃ and count its carbonyl-carbon neighbours and bond orders. State the approximate geometry before addition.






Hint





There are three bonded atoms but one double bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





Carbonyl C has three atom neighbours and total bond order four, approximately trigonal planar. Confusing neighbour count with bond-order sum can produce an incorrect valence audit.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
3. Draw hydroxide addition
For CH₃CHO+OH⁻, draw two coupled arrows and the tetrahedral intermediate.






Hint





The carbonyl pi pair must move when the new bond forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





OH lone pair→C and C=O pair→O give CH₃CH(OH)O⁻. Carbon has four single bonds, and the original carbonyl oxygen bears the negative charge.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
4. Track oxygen labels
Label carbonyl O as A and incoming hydroxide O as B in the preceding step. Which becomes O⁻ and which is OH?






Hint





The incoming hydroxide keeps its H during C–O bond formation.









Worked answer and reasoning





A becomes O⁻ after receiving the π pair. B is the newly attached OH. Oxygen identities must not be exchanged without extra chemical steps.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
5. Complete hydration
Use water to protonate the preceding alkoxide, drawing all products.






Hint





Water becomes hydroxide when it loses H⁺.









Worked answer and reasoning





The alkoxide pair takes H from water while the water O–H pair returns to O. Products are CH₃CH(OH)₂ and OH⁻. Hydroxide used in the first step is regenerated overall.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
6. Write the net hydrated equation
Combine hydroxide addition and proton transfer, then cancel the regenerated catalyst.






Hint





OH⁻ occurs on both sides of the two-step sum.









Worked answer and reasoning





The net equation is CH₃CHO+H₂O⇌CH₃CH(OH)₂. The alkoxide is an intermediate and hydroxide a catalyst in this model. This does not specify which side dominates equilibrium.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
7. Activate with acid
Draw protonation of CH₃CHO oxygen by H₃O⁺ with both arrows and the charge on the product.






Hint





The carbonyl oxygen lone pair accepts a proton; hydronium loses it as water forms.









Worked answer and reasoning





Products are CH₃CH=OH⁺ and H₂O. The protonated oxygen has three bond orders and positive formal charge; carbon becomes more electrophilic. Do not assign an unexplained extra H to carbon.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
8. Choose a compatible nucleophile
For excess acidic methanol, should the selected elementary attack use neutral CH₃OH or freely persistent CH₃O⁻? Explain.






Hint





Check the strong base against the proton-rich medium.









Worked answer and reasoning





Neutral methanol is the suitable nucleophile for the selected acid-catalysed route. Methoxide is strongly basic and would be protonated in such a medium, so assuming it freely persists ignores acid–base chemistry.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
9. Attack the activated carbonyl
Draw methanol addition to CH₃CH=OH⁺, including movement of the carbonyl pi pair. Count incoming oxygen bonds afterward.






Hint





The formerly carbonyl oxygen becomes neutral OH; incoming methanol oxygen gains a bond.









Worked answer and reasoning





The intermediate is CH₃CH(OH)(O⁺HCH₃). Incoming oxygen has three single bonds and charge +1; original oxygen now has two single bonds and is neutral. Net charge +1 is retained.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
10. Finish the hemiacetal
Use water to deprotonate CH₃CH(OH)(O⁺HCH₃). Identify the group that loses H and all products.






Hint





Neutralise the oxygen that has three bonds.









Worked answer and reasoning





Water accepts H from the incoming methanol-derived oxonium group, giving CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ and H₃O⁺. The product is a neutral hemiacetal, and acid is regenerated.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
11. Classify four products
Classify CH₃CHO, CH₃CH(OH)₂, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ and CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂ by local functional pattern.






Hint





Count OH and OR groups attached to the same carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





They are aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal respectively. One OH plus one OR defines the hemiacetal; two OR groups define the acetal. An ether elsewhere in a molecule is not enough.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
12. Reject an unexplained acetal jump
A proposed arrow converts a hemiacetal OH directly into OCH₃ without another species or intermediate. Explain why it is incomplete.






Hint





A poor leaving group and a new incoming alcohol both need accounting.









Worked answer and reasoning





Acetal formation requires additional acid-mediated activation, loss of water, alcohol addition and proton transfers. Merely swapping labels omits bond changes, atom sources and charge bookkeeping.









Note



Optional transfer starts here. Choose problems that address your own gaps; the core route remains1–12.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
13. Balance acetal formation
Balance CH₃CHO+CH₃OH⇌CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂+H₂O by finding the required methanol coefficient.






Hint





The acetal contains two methoxy groups.









Worked answer and reasoning





Two methanol molecules are required: CH₃CHO+2CH₃OH⇌CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂+H₂O. Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen then balance. Acid catalyses the path and is not consumed in the net equation.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
14. Change water composition
For that acid-catalysed equilibrium, predict the direction favoured by excess water and explain the acid role separately.






Hint





Water is on the product side of acetal formation.









Worked answer and reasoning





Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward carbonyl plus methanol. Acid accelerates interconversion in both directions without changing K for the same net reaction and conditions. Changing composition and adding catalyst are different operations.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
15. Count a cyclic hemiacetal ring
Draw HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO and link its terminal alcohol O to aldehyde carbon through the hemiacetal pattern. Count ring atoms.






Hint





The attacking oxygen becomes part of the ring.









Worked answer and reasoning





The ring contains one oxygen and five carbons, six atoms total. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH at the former aldehyde carbon. Leaving the terminal oxygen outside the ring would lose the actual new C–O bond.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
16. Audit cyclisation formula
Compare the molecular formula before and after neutral cyclic hemiacetal formation from 5-hydroxypentanal. Is water lost overall?






Hint





Addition and proton transfer do not require removal of a whole molecule.









Worked answer and reasoning





The formula remains C₅H₁₀O₂. No net water is lost in hemiacetal cyclisation. Confusing this with later acetal formation would incorrectly subtract H₂O.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
17. Compare carbonyl substituents
Draw CH₃CHO and CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Which has an oxygen-based substituent at carbonyl C that can participate in a suitable addition–elimination route?






Hint





Inspect the group bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon.









Worked answer and reasoning





The ester has OCH₃; the aldehyde has H. Appropriate acyl substitution can involve departure of an oxygen-based group, whereas treating H⁻ as a normal leaving group is not a sound explanation for ordinary aqueous aldehyde addition.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
section: 18. Ask whether a new stereocentre forms
text:
18. Ask whether a new stereocentre forms
Methanol forms a hemiacetal from ethanal. List the four substituents at the former carbonyl carbon and test for a stereocentre.






Hint





The carbonyl carbon becomes tetrahedral.









Worked answer and reasoning





The groups are CH₃, H, OH and OCH₃, four different groups, so a stereocentre forms. Both faces of a planar aldehyde may react in an achiral environment; an R/S result needs an actual 3D product drawing.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
19. Contrast a symmetric ketone
Methanol adds to propanone to give(CH₃)₂C(OH)OCH₃. Does the former carbonyl carbon become a stereocentre?






Hint





Compare the identities of its two carbon groups.









Worked answer and reasoning





No. Its groups include two identical CH₃ groups, in addition to OH and OCH₃. Becoming tetrahedral is not alone sufficient for a simple stereocentre.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
20. Separate pathway from population
A student draws a valid hydrate mechanism and concludes the sample must be100% hydrate. Explain what evidence is missing.






Hint





A route describes how species interconvert; an equilibrium describes their relative amounts.









Worked answer and reasoning





A plausible mechanism does not supply the equilibrium constant or species concentrations. Structure, solvent, temperature and equilibrium evidence determine the mixture. The hydrate can be accessible without being the dominant form.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
Check your progress
Choose one corrected drawing and explain what changed in its atoms, charge, geometry or evidence. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 16: Exercises — Carbonyl addition
text:
Explore
Track oxygen labels and formal charges through hydrate and hemiacetal formation. Allow 7–10 minutes: predict first, change one input at a time and explain the result.

Explore the chemistry





Prediction, exploration and explanation
Predict (1 minute). Label aldehyde oxygen A and incoming nucleophile oxygen B. During initial hydroxide addition, which oxygen becomes negative? During methanol attack on a protonated aldehyde, which oxygen temporarily becomes positive?
Explore (4–5 minutes). Compare hydrate and hemiacetal routes. Step forward and backward, select each oxygen, and assign its formal charge plus the proton-transfer role entering that state. Use the check feedback. Pay special attention to oxygen C in water/hydronium and to the fact that addition itself is not a proton-transfer step.
Explain (2 minutes). Draw one labelled complete sequence. In base-catalysed hydration, why can the regenerated OH⁻ have oxygen C even though the incoming OH⁻ had oxygen B? In the acid route, which water accepts the final proton, and where is the catalyst at the end?


Supplied model and its limits
A always denotes the original carbonyl oxygen; B the incoming hydroxide or methanol oxygen; C the hydronium/water proton-transfer partner. The hydrate route has net charge −1 across all explicit species; the acid-catalysed hemiacetal route has net charge +1. Atom labels track identities, while catalyst regeneration means regeneration of a species, not necessarily the same individually labelled oxygen. These simplified paths do not predict equilibrium composition or supply operating instructions.


Carry the explanation into practice
Return to the local exercises. Keep your prediction, a corrected drawing or calculation, and two sentences stating what the model supports and what it leaves unresolved.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
text:
1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
Explain the labelled carbon in a neutral aldehyde.






Check your answer





No. Partial positive charge describes unequal electron density in the polar bond. The ordinary neutral Lewis structure assigns formal charge zero to the carbonyl carbon.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
text:
2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
Label carbonyl oxygen A and hydroxide oxygen B.






Check your answer





A becomes alkoxide after receiving the carbonyl pi pair. B becomes the newly bonded OH group. The intermediate is tetrahedral and has net charge minus one.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
text:
3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
Name the nucleophile in the methanol example and the purpose of O protonation.






Check your answer





Neutral methanol is the nucleophile. Protonating carbonyl oxygen increases carbonyl carbon electrophilicity. Drawing a strongly basic nucleophile freely present in excess strong acid would require reconsidering acid–base reactions.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text:
4. Which is the hemiacetal?
Choose CH₃CH(OH)₂, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ or CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂.






Check your answer





CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃: one OH and one OR group at the same carbon. The first is a hydrate and the third an acetal.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
text:
5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
Consider 5-hydroxypentanal closing by internal OH attack and proton transfers.






Check your answer





No net water is lost. The molecular formula is unchanged. Its six-membered ring contains the terminal alcohol oxygen and five carbon atoms; the original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
text:
6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
For aldehyde + two alcohols ⇌ acetal + water under acid catalysis, predict the direction favoured by excess water.






Check your answer





Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward aldehyde and alcohol. Acid catalyses the pathway in both directions and does not itself change the equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the exercises, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
About this lecture
Open an old bottle of aspirin and it often smells of vinegar. Aspirin is an ester. Moisture slowly splits it into salicylic acid and acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. Your body does the same kind of reaction thousands of times a second, and the proteins in your cells survive because amides do it very slowly.
Today we learn the reaction that links them:

The acyl family: acids, esters and amides share one carbonyl carbon
Addition, then elimination: a tetrahedral intermediate that can throw out a group
Ester hydrolysis in base: soap-making, step by step
Fischer esterification: how acid catalysis makes an ester, and why it’s an equilibrium
Amides: resonance, flat bonds, and why acid + amine gives a salt

Yesterday (Day 16) a nucleophile added to an aldehyde or ketone. Today the same first step has a second act.

Open with the smell. If you can, bring an old aspirin bottle (or just ask who has noticed it). The vinegar smell is acetic acid released by hydrolysis of the ester, and it’s a real quality-control issue: pharmacopoeias set a limit on free salicylic acid in aspirin tablets. We come back to aspirin as the last worked example. Then frame the lecture: on Day 16 a nucleophile added to C=O and stopped. Today the carbonyl carbon has a group attached that can leave, so after addition the carbonyl can reform and kick that group out. One extra step turns addition into substitution. Everything today is that pattern, plus careful proton bookkeeping.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
The acyl family

Acid, ester, amide and etherAn acyl carbon is a C=O carbon that also carries a heteroatom group Y. The Y on the carbonyl carbon names the family. An ether has O but no C=O, so no acyl carbon.

Try it: is HCOOCH₃ an aldehyde, an ether or an ester?

An ester (methyl methanoate), H–C(=O)–O–CH₃. The H on the acyl carbon doesn’t make it an aldehyde, because its other neighbour is OCH₃.



This is the Day 1 skill of reading the neighbours of C=O, applied to the three families we need today. Point at each Y. The ether is there on purpose: students see “O between two carbons” and call it an ester. Make them find the C=O first. Expanding condensed formulas is the other trap: HCOOCH3 is not H–C–O–O–CH3 (a peroxide); the first O after C in “COO” is the carbonyl oxygen. Also check CH3CONHCH3 orally: amide, because N sits on the carbonyl carbon.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Step 1: the nucleophile adds

Hydroxide adds to ethyl acetateExactly as on Day 16: the hydroxide lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Carbon goes from planar to tetrahedral.

Try it: a student draws CH₃C(=O)(OH)OCH₃ as the intermediate. What’s wrong?

Five bonds to carbon (C–CH₃, C=O counts 2, C–OH, C–OCH₃). The π bond must open: the correct structure is CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₃).



Insist on both arrows. The first arrow starts at a lone pair, not at the minus sign, and ends at the carbon. The second starts in the middle of the pi bond and ends on oxygen. Without that second arrow the carbon would have five bonds, which is the single most common error in this unit. Ask students to count bond orders at carbon in their own drawing before they move on. Ethyl acetate is a real solvent (nail-polish remover smell), so it’s a friendly example.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Track every oxygen

The tetrahedral intermediate with labelled oxygensLabel atoms and follow them, not positions on the page. The negative charge now sits on the old carbonyl oxygen, and the incoming OH is neutral. Oxygen b still carries the ethyl group: no bond to it has broken yet. Total charge: still −1.

Atom labels are a habit worth building now, because the acid mechanism later has three oxygens changing protonation state. The formal charges follow from the Day 1 patterns: a is one bond plus three lone pairs, so minus one; c has two bonds, so neutral. A quick conservation check catches many errors: the charge on the left of an arrow must equal the charge on the right. Point out that hydroxide gave its charge away when it donated its pair; the charge has moved to a, not disappeared.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Step 2: the carbonyl comes back and a group leaves
text:
Step 2: the carbonyl comes back and a group leaves

The tetrahedral intermediate collapsesThe O⁻ lone pair pushes back down to reform C=O, and the C–OEt bond pair leaves with its oxygen as ethoxide. Addition followed by elimination gives net substitution: OEt has been swapped for OH.
The intermediate could also throw out the OH it just gained. That simply reverses step 1. What pushes the reaction forward comes in step 3.

The two arrows mirror the two arrows of step 1. Carbon never has five bonds and there is never a free acyl cation. Stress that a tetrahedral intermediate has a choice: any group that can leave as a reasonably stable anion is a candidate. Here OH- and EtO- are comparable leaving groups, so this step alone is not strongly downhill. That sets up the question of what drives the reaction, which is the proton transfer two slides on.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: What can leave decides what happens
text:
What can leave decides what happens

Tetrahedral intermediates from an aldehyde and from an ester

This is the reason the Day 16 and Day 17 reactions differ. An aldehyde or ketone forms the same tetrahedral intermediate, but its only candidates for leaving are hydride or a carbanion, which are far too basic. So aldehydes and ketones stop at addition; acid derivatives go on to substitution. The rule of thumb: a weaker base (lower pKa of the conjugate acid) is a better leaving group. The same order explains why acid chlorides and anhydrides are the most reactive acyl compounds and amides the least, since NH2- (pKa of NH3 about 38) is a poor leaving group. We only need esters and amides today, but the table lets students predict the rest.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Step 3: a proton transfer drives it
text:
Step 3: a proton transfer drives it

Ethoxide removes the proton from acetic acidAcid and ethoxide can’t coexist in base. K ≈ 10^(pKa product acid − pKa reactant acid) = 10^(16 − 4.8) ≈ 10¹¹.

Try it: for methyl acetate the base is CH₃O⁻ (methanol pKa 15.5). Estimate K.

K ≈ 10^(15.5 − 4.8) = 10^10.7 ≈ 5 × 10¹⁰. Still hugely favourable, so carboxylate + alcohol is what you actually have.



This is the Day 3 acid-base rule at work: the equilibrium favours the side with the weaker acid, and the size of K comes from the pKa difference. Here ethanol (pKa about 16) is a much weaker acid than acetic acid (4.8), so K is around 10^11. Because this step is effectively irreversible, it pulls the whole sequence forward. That’s why base hydrolysis of esters goes to completion while acid hydrolysis does not. Students who stop at “acid + ethoxide” have drawn a mixture that cannot exist in base.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Saponification: the net reaction and work-up
text:
Saponification: the net reaction and work-up

Ester hydrolysis in base, then acid work-upHydroxide is used up, one per ester, so it’s base-promoted, not base-catalysed. Boil a fat with NaOH and you get glycerol plus fatty-acid carboxylates: soap. To isolate the acid, add acid at the end (work-up).

Two separate events: the reaction in base, which ends at the carboxylate, and the work-up, which is just a proton transfer from H3O+ to the carboxylate. Work-up does not change the carbon skeleton. Contrast with Day 16 hydration, where hydroxide was regenerated; here it ends up in the carboxylate, so you need a full equivalent. “Saponification” literally means soap-making: a triglyceride and three NaOH give glycerol and three sodium carboxylates. If time allows, ask why soap stays dissolved in basic water but greasy fatty acids separate when you acidify: the charged carboxylate is water-soluble, the neutral acid much less so.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Fischer esterification: acid activates the carbonyl
text:
Fischer esterification: acid activates the carbonyl

Hydronium protonates acetic acidEthanol is a neutral, weak nucleophile, and a base would just deprotonate the acid. So we make the carbonyl a better electrophile instead: protonate its oxygen.
The protonated O has three bonds and one lone pair, so it’s +1. The resonance form shows that charge shared onto carbon.

This is the same acid activation as acetal formation on Day 16. Explain why we can’t run esterification in base: a carboxylic acid plus a base just gives a carboxylate, and a carboxylate is a terrible electrophile (it’s negatively charged). In acid, the carbonyl oxygen picks up a proton and the resonance form with C+ shows why the carbon now pulls harder on a nucleophile. Make students draw the proton coming from a real donor (H3O+), not a bare H+ appearing from nowhere.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Ethanol adds

Ethanol adds to the protonated carbonylTwo arrows, as always. The incoming ethanol oxygen now has three bonds, so it carries the + charge. The old carbonyl oxygen has become a neutral OH.

Try it: give the charge on each oxygen in CH₃C(OH)(OH)(O⁺HEt) and the total charge.

Old C=O oxygen: 0. Original acid OH: 0. Ethanol O: +1. Total +1, the same as the protonated acid plus neutral ethanol.



Compare directly with hydroxide addition: same two arrows, but because the nucleophile is neutral, the charge ends up on the nucleophile’s oxygen rather than on the old carbonyl oxygen. Charge bookkeeping again: +1 in, +1 out. Many students put the plus charge on the wrong oxygen; ask them to count bonds at each O.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: A proton shuffle makes a leaving group
text:
A proton shuffle makes a leaving group

Proton transfers on the tetrahedral intermediateWater removes the extra proton from the ethyl oxygen. Then H₃O⁺ protonates one of the OH groups to give OH₂⁺, which can leave as neutral water.

Try it: why not just let OH⁻ leave directly, as in base?

In acid there’s essentially no OH⁻ around, and it’s a poor leaving group compared with H₂O. Protonating first turns a bad leaving group into a good one.



The rule for acid-catalysed mechanisms: every species should be neutral or positive; never draw OH- or alkoxide in strong acid. Proton transfers between oxygens go through water and hydronium, so draw those explicitly. Point out the leaving-group table again: water’s conjugate acid is H3O+ (pKa about −1.7), so water is a far better leaving group than hydroxide. Which OH gets protonated is a matter of statistics; protonating the OEt instead just leads back to starting materials, which is fine because the whole thing is an equilibrium.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Water leaves and the ester forms
text:
Water leaves and the ester forms

Loss of water and deprotonation give the esterAn OH lone pair reforms C=O and pushes out water, giving the protonated ester. Water takes that last proton, which regenerates H₃O⁺. The acid is a true catalyst.

This is the mirror image of the addition: lone pair down, leaving group out. The last deprotonation regenerates hydronium, which is the bookkeeping that makes acid catalytic, unlike hydroxide in saponification. A useful summary for students: protonate, add, deprotonate, protonate, eliminate, deprotonate. Six steps, every one of them either a proton transfer or one of the two arrow patterns they already know. Ask the room to count how many times H3O+ is consumed and regenerated.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: An equilibrium, and an isotope check
text:
An equilibrium, and an isotope check

Fischer esterification as an equilibrium with labelled oxygenK is only about 4: start with 1:1 acid and alcohol and you get about two-thirds ester. Excess alcohol or removing water pushes it further. The catalyst only gets you there faster.

Try it: you add more H₃O⁺ at the same temperature. Does K change?

No. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the composition is the same.



Two separate ideas. Equilibrium: with K = 4 and a 1:1 start, x²/(1 − x)² = 4 gives x = 2/3. Le Chatelier tells you to use the alcohol as solvent or to remove water (with a Dean–Stark trap or a drying agent). Catalysis: changes the rate, not K. The isotope experiment is the evidence for the mechanism: with 18O-labelled alcohol, the label ends up in the ester’s single-bonded oxygen, not in the water. So the C–O bond of the acid breaks, not the O–alkyl bond of the alcohol, exactly as the mechanism predicts. This is a nice example of how mechanisms are tested, which comes back in Week 5.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Amides are different: resonance

Amide resonance contributorsThe nitrogen lone pair is shared with the carbonyl. The real amide is a blend: the C–N bond has partial double-bond character and the carbonyl is less electrophilic.

Try it: in the right-hand contributor, what are the charges on O and N, and the total?

O is −1, N is +1, total 0. N has four bonds and no lone pair. The double-headed arrow means one molecule, not an equilibrium.



Resonance contributors are two drawings of one molecule; nothing flips back and forth. Use the double-headed arrow, never equilibrium arrows. The consequences are big: the amide C=O is less electrophilic because nitrogen is already feeding electrons into it, and the leaving group would be NH2- (or an amine anion), which is terrible. Together that makes amides the least reactive acyl compounds. Ask why an ester has a similar but weaker resonance: oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it shares its lone pair less willingly.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Amide nitrogen is not an amine
text:
Amide nitrogen is not an amine

Ethylamine and acetamide compared


property
ethylamine
acetamide




N lone pair

yes, pKaH 10.7

This is a preview of tomorrow (Day 18), where amine basicity is the main topic. Amides are protonated (weakly) on oxygen, not nitrogen, because protonating N would destroy the resonance. The restricted rotation is measurable: in N,N-dimethylformamide the two N-methyl groups are in different environments and give separate NMR signals at room temperature, which you’ll see in spectroscopy week. In proteins, the flat peptide bond is what makes the backbone stiff enough to form helices and sheets.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
section: Acid plus amine gives a salt, not an amide
text:
Acid plus amine gives a salt, not an amide

Acetic acid and methylamine transfer a protonMix an acid and an amine and the fastest thing is proton transfer. The carboxylate that forms is a poor electrophile, so no amide forms at room temperature.

Try it: use pKa 4.8 (CH₃COOH) and 10.6 (CH₃NH₃⁺) to estimate K.

K ≈ 10^(10.6 − 4.8) = 10^5.8 ≈ 6 × 10⁵. The salt is strongly favoured.



Students expect “acid + amine → amide + water” because that’s the net equation on paper. Show them it’s wrong as a first step. Industry gets round it by strong heating: nylon-6,6 is made by heating the salt of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid to drive off water. Labs and cells use activation instead: convert the acid into something with a better leaving group (an acid chloride, an activated ester or, in biology, an acyl phosphate or thioester). The next slide shows the biological version.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Esters and amides in biology

Acetylcholine and a dipeptide
Esters are built to be cut: acetylcholinesterase splits >10⁴ per second. Fats are glycerol esters.
Amides are built to last: a peptide bond survives for centuries in neutral water without a protease.
The ribosome makes amides from esters (aminoacyl-tRNA): downhill.


This is where the leaving-group logic pays off in biology. Esters are reactive enough to be used as on/off switches (acetylcholine) and as stores that can be mobilised (fats). Amides are stable enough to hold proteins together, but that same stability means the cell has to spend energy activating amino acids before linking them. The ribosome attaches each amino acid to its tRNA as an ester, then the amine of the growing chain attacks that ester: an acyl substitution where an alkoxide-type leaving group is replaced by nitrogen. Nerve agents and many insecticides work by blocking acetylcholinesterase, which shows how important fast ester hydrolysis is.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Back to aspirin

Aspirin hydrolysisAspirin’s acetyl ester is the reactive part. Water slowly hydrolyses it, which is why damp, old tablets smell of vinegar. The same acetyl group is what aspirin transfers to a serine in the COX enzyme, blocking it for good.

Try it: what would aspirin give with excess NaOH, before any work-up?

Acetate and the salicylate dianion. Saponification cuts the ester, then excess base removes the protons from both COOH groups and from the phenol OH.



Pull the whole lecture together on one real molecule. Ask students to point at the acyl carbon, say which oxygen leaves (the one bonded to the ring), and predict the products in acid and in base. In base, both carboxylic acids end up as carboxylates; the phenol of salicylic acid (pKa about 13) is also deprotonated by excess NaOH, so the product is the dianion. That’s why the answer says “excess”. Aspirin’s drug action is itself an acyl transfer: a serine OH in cyclooxygenase attacks the ester and gets acetylated, which permanently blocks the enzyme. Same mechanism, new nucleophile.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Mistakes we see every year

Read out each mistake and ask the room why it’s wrong before showing the fix. Every row maps onto a numbered exercise: five-bonded carbon is exercise 9, the missing proton transfer is 6 and 20, catalysis versus equilibrium is 14, resonance is 16, acid plus amine is 18.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and reactions
text:
Summary

Next: amines and aromatic rings, and why amine N is basic when amide N isn’t (Day 18). Practice: exercises · self-check

Recite the core pattern once more: add, then eliminate, with proton transfers wherever a charge needs to be fixed. Base hydrolysis is driven by the final proton transfer; acid esterification is an equilibrium pushed by excess alcohol or water removal. Amides resist all of this because of resonance. Tomorrow we look at the nitrogen from the other side: amines, where the lone pair is free, and aromatic rings, where resonance makes a whole ring unusually stable. Exercises 1 to 10 are core; 11 to 16 build the acid mechanism; 17 to 20 are deeper.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text: Use nitrogen lone pairs, conjugate-acid strengths and aromatic electron counts to explain the structures and reactions. Work through 1–10 for core work, 11–16 for transfer and 17–20 for deeper checks. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit. Attempt each problem before using its hint, then compare your revised reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Working refresher
A neutral ordinary amine N has three single bonds and a lone pair; ammonium N has four bonds and formal charge +1. Primary/secondary/tertiary amines have one/two/three carbon substituents on N. Proton-transfer arrows go from base pair to H and from donor H–A bond to A. A larger compatible conjugate-acid pKa means a stronger base; K≈10^(product-acid pKa−reactant-acid pKa). For simple aromatic rings first check planar cyclic conjugation, then count 4 n +2 pi electrons. Pyridine has a separate non-pi N pair; pyrrole uses its N pair in the sextet. In dominant-form pH reasoning, protonated forms predominate below a site’s pKa and deprotonated forms above it. See the local lecture for molecular drawings.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
1. Classify carbon substitution at N
Draw CH₃NH₂, CH₃NHCH₃ and (CH₃)₃N with lone pairs. Classify them as primary, secondary or tertiary and count N–H bonds.






Hint





Count carbon groups directly bonded to N, not the total molecular carbon count.









Worked explanation





They are primary with two N–H, secondary with one N–H and tertiary with zero N–H. Each neutral ordinary amine has three single bonds at N and one lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
2. Separate tertiary from quaternary
Compare (CH₃)₃N, (CH₃)₃NH⁺ and (CH₃)₄N⁺. Give carbon-substituent count, N–H count and formal charge for each.






Hint





A protonated tertiary amine still has three carbon groups; quaternary means four carbon groups.









Worked explanation





The three species have respectively 3/0/0, 3/1/+1 and 4/0/+1 for carbon groups/N–H/charge. Only the neutral first species has an available ordinary N lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
3. Draw protonation with a donor
Draw CH₃NH₂ + H₃O⁺ → products using both curved arrows. Count the N bond number before and after and audit net charge.






Hint





The N pair attacks H; the donor O–H pair returns to oxygen.









Worked explanation





Products are CH₃NH₃⁺ and H₂O. N changes from three bonds plus a pair to four bonds/+1. Net charge +1 is conserved; a positive proton is transferred rather than an electron being removed from N.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
4. Draw the reverse proton transfer
For CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻, draw deprotonation with both arrows and identify the conjugate acid/base pairs.






Hint





Hydroxide is the pair donor and the ammonium N–H bond is the pair returned to N.









Worked explanation





CH₃NH₂ + H₂O form. The pairs are methylammonium/methylamine and water/hydroxide. Net charge zero on each side; the newly neutral N regains its lone pair.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
5. Compare supplied conjugate-acid pKa values
Ethylammonium has approximate aqueous pKa 10.7 and anilinium 4.6. Rank the corresponding neutral bases and state what larger conjugate-acid pKa means.






Hint





A weaker conjugate acid has a stronger conjugate base under comparable conditions.









Worked explanation





Ethylamine is stronger than aniline. Ethylammonium loses H⁺ less readily, so its neutral base binds a proton more favourably in the corresponding comparison. These values do not alone determine all nucleophilic reaction rates.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
6. Estimate a nitrogen-to-nitrogen proton transfer
For PhNH₃⁺ + EtNH₂ ⇌ PhNH₂ + EtNH₃⁺, use pKa 4.6 and 10.7 for the acids. Estimate K and identify the favoured side. Ph means phenyl; Et means ethyl.






Hint





Use 10^(product-acid pKa − reactant-acid pKa).









Worked explanation





K≈10^6.1≈1.26×10⁶ toward aniline and ethylammonium. Approximate pKa values must be compatible in solvent and conventions. This equilibrium estimate is not a rate prediction.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
7. Distinguish amine from amide
Draw CH₃CH₂NH₂ and CH₃C(=O)NH₂. Identify the N directly connected to carbonyl and explain why its pair differs in availability.






Hint





Only one pair can overlap directly with the neighbouring C=O system.









Worked explanation





The second is an amide. Its N pair delocalises into the carbonyl, contributing partial C–N double-bond character. The first is a simple amine without this direct carbonyl conjugation; treating both as equally basic would ignore structure.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
8. Audit an amide contributor
Write CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺, count N bond orders and sum formal charges. Explain why this drawing is not an independently equilibrating isomer of neutral ethanamide.






Hint





N has a C=N double bond and two N–H single bonds.









Worked explanation





N has four bond orders and +1; O is −1, giving net zero. The neutral and charge-separated drawings are resonance contributors to one molecule with fixed nuclei, not two species undergoing a chemical equilibrium.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
9. Explain aniline conjugation
Compare PhNH₂ with PhCH₂NH₂, where Ph is a benzene ring. Which N pair can overlap directly with the aromatic pi system, and what structural interruption appears in the other?






Hint





The intervening CH₂ is an ordinary saturated carbon.









Worked explanation





Aniline PhNH₂ has N directly attached to the aromatic system. In PhCH₂NH₂, the sp³ CH₂ interrupts that direct conjugation. Other substituent and solvation effects can remain; the structural comparison does not claim that only one effect ever controls basicity.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
10. Check aromatic requirements
For benzene and cyclohexane, state whether a continuous cyclic pi system exists. For benzene count pi electrons and find n in 4 n + 2.






Hint





A ring of sigma bonds is not sufficient.









Worked explanation





Benzene has a planar continuous pi system and six electrons, giving n=1. Cyclohexane lacks continuous pi conjugation and is nonaromatic, not automatically antiaromatic.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
11. Avoid double-counting pyridine electrons
In pyridine, N supplies one electron to the ring pi system and has a separate lone pair outside it. Should the pair be included when counting the aromatic sextet? Predict the effect of protonating that pair.






Hint





Separate the electron in the p orbital from the two in the non-pi lone-pair orbital.









Worked explanation





Do not add the separate pair to the aromatic count. Its protonation makes pyridinium, and the sextet can remain. N becomes positive; the ring skeleton and pi electron count remain consistent with aromaticity.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
12. Count pyrrole electrons
A five-membered pyrrole ring has two C=C units and an NH whose pair joins the cyclic pi system. Count the contributions and explain why the N pair is less available than pyridine’s separate pair.






Hint





Each double bond contributes two pi electrons.









Worked explanation





Two C=C units supply four electrons, and N contributes its pair of two, giving six. Removing that pair from its aromatic role by ordinary N protonation costs stabilisation, so pyrrole N is much less basic than pyridine N in this comparison.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
13. Repair an aromaticity claim
A student says “Both pyridine and pyrrole contain one nitrogen, so they must have equal basicity.” Give a structural correction using the two lone-pair roles.






Hint





Atom count does not locate the pair’s orbital role.









Worked explanation





Pyridine keeps a non-pi pair available for N–H bond formation; pyrrole’s pair supplies part of the aromatic sextet. Their protonation equilibria differ because the pair environments differ, despite both molecules containing N.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
14. Draw glycine at low pH
Use supplied pKa 2.3 for COOH and 9.6 for NH₃⁺. Draw the predominant glycine form at pH 1 and give every formal charge and net charge.






Hint





At pH well below a pKa, the site’s protonated form predominates.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH₂COOH predominates: N is +1, carboxyl group neutral, net +1. Dominant-form drawings are approximations; minority forms still exist.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
section: 15. Draw glycine between its pKa values
text:
15. Draw glycine between its pKa values
Using the same supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6, draw predominant glycine at pH 6. Explain “zwitterion” and whether net zero implies no formal charges.






Hint





Apply the pH comparison separately to COOH and ammonium.









Worked explanation





H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻ predominates. COOH has mostly lost H while ammonium mostly retains it. Opposing formal charges sum to zero, so it is a zwitterion; it is not entirely uncharged at every site.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
16. Draw glycine at high pH
With pKa values 2.3 and 9.6, draw the predominant form at pH 12. Show the proton transfer from the pH 6 form to hydroxide and audit charge.






Hint





At sufficiently high pH, ammonium can lose a proton while carboxylate remains.









Worked explanation





H₂NCH₂COO⁻ predominates. Zwitterion + OH⁻ → H₂NCH₂COO⁻ + H₂O. N returns to neutral three-bonded form; total charge is −1 on both sides.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
section: 17. Calculate a simple amine protonation ratio
text:
17. Calculate a simple amine protonation ratio
For B + H⁺ ⇌ BH⁺, use pKa(BH⁺)=10.0 and [B]/[BH⁺]=10^(pH−pKa). At pH 9 and 11 calculate the ratios and fraction present as BH⁺.






Hint





Convert ratio r=B/BH⁺ to protonated fraction 1/(1+r).









Worked explanation





At pH9, r=0.1 and protonated fraction≈0.909. At pH11, r=10 and fraction≈0.0909. A higher pH reduces the protonated fraction; a ratio is not itself a population fraction.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
18. Explain coexistence near pKa
For the same simple amine with pKa(BH⁺)=10.0, predict fractions at pH10. Does every molecule carry half a positive charge?






Hint





At equal pH and pKa, the concentration ratio is one.









Worked explanation





The populations of B and BH⁺ are equal under the model, each about 50%. Individual molecules are in one protonation state or the other; the population average does not mean each N is half protonated.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
19. Separate equilibrium from kinetics
Two species have different conjugate-acid pKa values. A student infers which attacks every carbon electrophile fastest. State what the pKa comparison supports and name two missing factors for a rate prediction.






Hint





Basicity compares proton-transfer equilibrium; nucleophilicity is a kinetic property.









Worked explanation





The data compare basicity under compatible conditions. Substrate steric/electronic structure, solvent, leaving group and the particular nucleophile’s solvation can change rates. pKa alone cannot supply a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
20. Integrate a peptide-like fragment
For H₂NCH₂C(=O)NHCH₃, identify the simple amine-like N and the amide N. Explain which structural feature you would inspect first before predicting protonation and why the two sites should not be treated identically.






Hint





Follow each N’s directly attached atom: is it a carbonyl carbon?









Worked explanation





The left H₂N site is not directly attached to C=O; the right NH is the amide N. Carbonyl conjugation delocalises the amide pair and changes its basicity. The molecule can contain more than one chemically distinct nitrogen environment.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Consolidate your work
Choose one corrected error and explain what changed in your reasoning. Then complete the self-check. The reading guide lists the matching book chapters.

title: Day 18: Exercises — Amines and aromaticity
text:
Explore
Question: why can the same pH leave one nitrogen base mainly neutral and another mainly protonated?
Use this activity for about 8 minutes: predict for 2 minutes, explore for 4, then explain your result for 2.

Enable JavaScript to compare the supplied molecular species and aqueous ionisation model.




Predict
The supplied approximate aqueous conjugate-acid pKa values are methylammonium 10.6, anilinium 4.6, and pyridinium 5.2. For a base B and its conjugate acid BH⁺,
\[f_{BH^+}=\frac{1}{1+10^{pH-pK_a}}.\]
Before moving a control, predict the fraction BH⁺ at pH = pKa and at one pH unit below it. Predict which base is most protonated at pH 7.


Explore

Use At supplied pKa for each molecule. Explain the common midpoint.
Compare all three molecules at pH 7 while keeping the environmental pH fixed.
For one molecule, move pH two units upward. Follow both the curve and the drawn neutral/protonated molecular forms.
Use Reset to reconstruct the original state.



Explain and check
At pH = pKa, half the population is BH⁺. One unit below gives \(1/(1+0.1)=10/11\), about 90.9%. At pH 7, methylamine is much more protonated than aniline or pyridine under this model. Higher pH decreases BH⁺, because deprotonated B becomes favoured.
A 50% fraction describes two populations of molecular species; it does not mean that every nitrogen has half a proton. The ring drawings use implicit carbon/hydrogen conventions; the N–H count and charge are shown explicitly.


Model limits
These are supplied, approximate compatible aqueous pKa values in a dilute one-site model. Substituents, solvent, temperature and activities can alter behaviour. The plot predicts neither extraction recovery nor the rate of a nucleophilic reaction. See the local nitrogen exercises for lone-pair and charge explanations.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
1. Is a tertiary amine charged?
Trimethylamine has three methyl groups on N. State its charge before and after accepting one proton.






Check your answer





Neutral (CH₃)₃N has three N–C bonds and one lone pair. Its conjugate acid (CH₃)₃NH⁺ has four bonds and charge +1.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
text:
2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
Conjugate-acid pKa values are 10.7 for ethylammonium and 4.6 for anilinium. Which neutral base is stronger in comparable aqueous conditions?






Check your answer





Ethylamine. Its conjugate acid is the weaker acid with larger pKa. Basicity is an equilibrium property and is not a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
3. Is cyclohexane aromatic?
It is a six-membered ring. Explain why this is insufficient.






Check your answer





It has no continuous cyclic p-orbital network. It is nonaromatic; being cyclic does not imply aromaticity or antiaromaticity.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
text:
4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
Compare pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen lone pairs.






Check your answer





The pyridine lone pair lies outside its aromatic pi system. The pyrrole pair supplies two of the six aromatic pi electrons, making ordinary N protonation much less favourable.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 5. Does net zero mean no charge?
text:
5. Does net zero mean no charge?
Draw glycine in its predominant form near pH 6 with supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6.






Check your answer





H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ has N charge +1 and carboxylate charge −1, giving net zero. It is a zwitterion, not an entirely uncharged molecule.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
text:
6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
Identify the neighbouring structural feature that changes its electron availability.






Check your answer





Peptide nitrogen is directly attached to a carbonyl as part of an amide. Its pair delocalises into C=O, unlike the pair in a simple alkylamine.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
About this lecture
Two unlabelled bottles both contain C₄H₈O₂. One smells of pear drops and nail-polish remover. The other smells of rancid butter. You could sniff them, but a chemist would rather ask the molecules directly, with light and with magnets. The same physics, used on the water in your body, is an MRI scan.
Today we work one unknown, U1, from formula to structure:

Formula: count rings and π bonds before guessing anything
IR: which functional groups are there, and which aren’t
¹H NMR: shift, integral and splitting, one clue each
¹³C NMR: how many kinds of carbon
Testing candidates: a structure is a hypothesis that must explain every signal

Last time (Day 18) we read amines and aromatic rings by structure; today the structure is what we’re looking for.

Open with the two bottles: ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) is the solvent in nail-polish remover and gives pear-drop and fruity notes in wine; butanoic acid is the smell of rancid butter and, unfortunately, of vomit. Same molecular formula. Ask the room: “How would you tell them apart without smelling?” Collect answers, then say that this is exactly today’s problem. Mention MRI: the scanner detects the hydrogen nuclei in water and fat, the same nuclei we’ll read in a 1H NMR spectrum. Make clear that all spectra today are simulated teaching spectra with literature-typical values; the reasoning is the real thing. Tomorrow (Day 22) uses this evidence habit for synthesis.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Start with the formula

Four C4H8O2 candidatesDBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2 counts rings + π bonds. O doesn’t enter it. One DBE can be a C=O, a C=C or a ring.

Try it: what is the DBE of C₄H₈O₂, and does that prove there’s a C=O?

(8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1. No: 1,4-dioxane uses its one DBE as a ring. The formula narrows the field but doesn’t pick the structure.



This is the degree-of-unsaturation idea from Day 1, where every double bond or ring cost two hydrogens. A saturated acyclic C4 compound would have 2×4+2 = 10 H; we have 8, so one pair is missing. Walk across the four candidates: three spend the DBE on C=O, dioxane on a ring. Stress that oxygen is invisible to this formula because a divalent atom slots into a chain without changing the H count. A common slip is including O in the count. Another is assuming C4H8O2 “must be” an ester because that’s what the textbook example was. These four candidates will follow us through the lecture.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Three instruments, three questions








method
what it detects
what it tells you




formula
composition
DBE: rings + π bonds


IR
bond vibrations
which functional groups are present (C=O, O–H)


¹H NMR
each kind of H
shift: neighbourhood · integral: how many H · splitting: H next door


¹³C NMR
each kind of C
how many carbon types; C=O vs C–O vs alkyl



Each method tests a different prediction, which is why they’re stronger together than any one alone.

This is the map for the rest of the lecture. IR was introduced on Day 2 with boiling points and hydrogen bonding; here we use it as evidence. The key word is “independent”: the formula comes from mass and composition, IR from bond vibrations, NMR from nuclear spins in a magnetic field. If three independent methods agree on one structure, that’s far more convincing than any single peak. Don’t spend long here; the point is to give students a mental table they’ll fill in during the next slides.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Reading an IR trace

Simulated ester IR spectrum
The y-axis is transmittance: a dip means light was absorbed.
Wavenumber runs high to low, left to right, by convention.
Strong, sharp dip near 1740 cm⁻¹: C=O. Nothing broad at 2500–3600: no O–H.
On an absorbance plot the same band would point up, so read the y-axis label first.


Many students have only seen absorbance spectra from UV-vis in general chemistry, where peaks go up. IR is traditionally plotted as transmittance, so everything is upside down. Read the axes aloud: “per cent of light getting through” on the y-axis, wavenumber decreasing to the right. The two zones to look at first are 1650 to 1800 for C=O and 2500 to 3600 for O–H and N–H. The region below 1500 is the fingerprint region; we won’t assign it, but the 1240 band here is typical of the ester C–O.

title: Structure from spectra
section: Each functional group has its own band
text:
Each functional group has its own band

IR traces of an ester, an acid and an alcohol
C=O: 1650–1800 cm⁻¹, strong and sharp
Alcohol O–H: 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, broad. Acid O–H: 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, very broad, running into the C–H bands


Hydrogen bonding is why O–H bands are broad: each molecule has a slightly different H-bonding partner, so the vibration is smeared over a range. In carboxylic acids the dimers hold very tight hydrogen bonds, so the band is enormous and overlaps the C–H stretches near 3000. Point at the acid trace and let students see how much of the spectrum it eats. Then the alcohol: broad O–H, no C=O. If you had to choose between ethanol and ethanal from IR alone, the alcohol trace picks ethanol, but it says nothing about how many carbons there are.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Absence counts, if you looked

Unknown U1: simulated infrared traceU1 has a strong C=O and no broad O–H anywhere from 2500 to 3600 cm⁻¹.

Try it: which C₄H₈O₂ candidates does this challenge, and what would weaken that argument?

Butanoic acid (needs a huge acid O–H) and 3-hydroxybutan-2-one (needs an O–H). Dioxane has no C=O. The argument only holds if that region was measured and the signal wasn’t too weak.



This is the first real elimination. Students are comfortable with “a peak is there, so the group is there”; using absence is less natural. Absence is good evidence only when the method could have seen the feature: the region must be on the plot, the sample concentrated enough, and nothing else covering it. A C=O band near 1740 fits an ester, but plenty of other carbonyl compounds absorb nearby, so IR alone never names a molecule. Ask: “Is U1 definitely ethyl ethanoate now?” No: methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3, is another C4H8O2 ester with the same IR story. That’s why we need NMR.

title: Structure from spectra
section: ¹H NMR: one signal per kind of hydrogen
text:
¹H NMR: one signal per kind of hydrogen

Proton NMR of U1 mapped onto ethyl ethanoateEach signal carries three clues: where it is (shift), how big it is (integral), and how many lines (splitting).

This is the whole of U1’s proton spectrum, and the rest of the lecture unpacks it. Point at each coloured set of hydrogens: red O–CH2, green acetyl CH3, blue ethyl CH3. Don’t explain the shifts or splittings yet; just establish that each colour is one environment and gives one signal. Emphasise the vocabulary: chemical shift δ in ppm, integral, multiplicity (s, d, t, q). Students will see the same three-signal pattern on the next six slides, each time from a different angle.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Equivalent H share a signal

Counting proton environmentsH atoms are equivalent when symmetry or free rotation makes them indistinguishable. The three H of a CH₃ are always equivalent.

Try it: how many ¹H signals does butanoic acid give, and what are their integrals?

Four: CH₃ (3H), CH₂ (2H), CH₂ next to C=O (2H) and O–H (1H). That’s 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8 H.



Fast rotation about C–C single bonds (Week 2, conformations) is why the three methyl hydrogens look identical on the NMR timescale. Dioxane is a nice extreme: eight hydrogens, one signal, because every CH2 is related to every other by symmetry. Have students label the butanoic acid environments themselves before revealing. The usual mistake is to treat the two CH2 groups as one environment; they’re different because one sits next to C=O and the other next to CH3.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Chemical shift: what’s next door

Typical proton shift rangesElectronegative neighbours pull electron density away from H, which moves its signal downfield (to the left). U1’s three signals land in three zones: H–C–O at 4.12, H–C–C=O at 2.05 and plain alkyl at 1.25.

The physical picture: electrons around a proton shield it from the magnet. Pull electron density away, with oxygen or a carbonyl, and the proton feels a stronger field and resonates further left. That’s all the theory students need. Have them memorise four anchors rather than the whole chart: about 1 ppm for alkyl, about 2 for next to C=O, about 3.5 to 4 for on a carbon bearing O, and above 10 for COOH. Ask the room which ethyl ethanoate CH2 or CH3 should be furthest left, before pointing at the red line: the O–CH2, because it sits on the carbon bonded to oxygen.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Integrals count hydrogens

Integral curve over the U1 spectrumThe area under a signal, not its tallest line, is proportional to the number of H. The integrals give a ratio; the formula fixes the total.

Try it: the integrator reports 6, 6 and 4. Turn that into H counts for C₄H₈O₂. Is the singlet taller than the triplet because it has more H?

Divide by 2: 3 : 3 : 2 = 8 H. No: both have 3H. The singlet’s area sits in one line, while the triplet’s is spread over three.



The integration trace is the staircase drawn over the spectrum; each step’s height is the signal’s area. Instruments report arbitrary units, so students must reduce to the smallest whole-number ratio and check against the formula. Point out the trap in the figure: the green singlet towers over the blue triplet even though both are 3H. Line heights are never H counts. If the ratio doesn’t add up to the formula’s H, either an integral is wrong or the candidate is.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Splitting: count the neighbours’ H

An ethyl group gives a linked quartet and tripletn equivalent H on the neighbouring carbon(s) → n + 1 lines. A 2H quartet and a 3H triplet together are the signature of CH₃–CH₂–.

Try it: a CH₃ sits next to a CH carrying one H. What pattern does the CH₃ give?

A 3H doublet. One neighbouring H gives 1 + 1 = 2 lines; the integral is still 3H.



This is the simple first-order model: equivalent neighbours on adjacent carbons, equal coupling, no long-range coupling. Real spectra can be messier, but this rule explains every signal today. Stress the cross-over: the CH2 is a quartet because of the CH3’s three H, and the CH3 is a triplet because of the CH2’s two H. Each signal reports the neighbours, not itself. That’s why the integral and the line count answer different questions. The quartet’s four lines don’t mean four H. Spotting the quartet-triplet pair is the single most useful pattern in introductory NMR.

title: Structure from spectra
section: A singlet means nobody’s next door
text:
A singlet means nobody’s next door

Singlet versus doublet methylThe acetyl CH₃ of an ester sits on the C=O carbon, which has no H. So it’s a 3H singlet near 2 ppm. A CH₃ on a CH would be a doublet.

This is where the carbonyl earns its keep in NMR: it acts as a barrier with no hydrogens, so groups on either side of it don’t split each other. The O–CH2 hydrogens are four bonds away from the acetyl CH3, too far to couple in our model. The doublet panel is a deliberate setup for later: 3-hydroxybutan-2-one has a CH3 on a CH, so it must show a 3H doublet. Keep that prediction in mind when we test that candidate.

title: Structure from spectra
section: ¹³C NMR: one line per kind of carbon
text:
¹³C NMR: one line per kind of carbon

Carbon-13 NMR of U1 assigned to ethyl ethanoateU1 shows four carbon signals: C=O at 171, O–CH₂ at 60, and two CH₃ at 21 and 14. Routine ¹³C spectra show no splitting, and line heights are not carbon counts.

The carbon scale is about 20 times wider than the proton one: 0 to 220 ppm. The same logic applies: carbons on oxygen land around 50 to 80, carbonyl carbons above 160, plain alkyl carbons below 40. Routine carbon spectra are decoupled from hydrogen, so every signal is a single line, and intensities depend on relaxation, so you can’t integrate them. The carbonyl line is short here, which is typical for a carbon with no attached H. What 13C does give cleanly is the number of carbon environments: four for U1, matching four distinct carbons in ethyl ethanoate.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Symmetry hides carbons

Symmetry merges carbon signalsEquivalent carbons share one signal, so signals ≤ carbons. Fewer signals than carbons points to symmetry.

Try it: 3-methylpentane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, has six carbons. How many ¹³C signals?

Four: the two end CH₃, the two CH₂, the CH, and the branch CH₃. A mirror plane through the CH makes the two ethyl arms identical.



This guards against a common wrong rejection: “the formula has six carbons but the spectrum shows four, so it’s impossible.” It’s possible whenever there’s symmetry. Run through the three examples by finding the mirror plane in each. For U1, four signals and four carbons means no symmetry to worry about, which also argues against dioxane (one signal) once more. Symmetry and equivalence come back in Week 2 language: equivalent atoms are related by a symmetry operation of the molecule.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Putting U1 together

Every observation assigned to ethyl ethanoateFormula and IR give one C=O, no O–H. The q/t pair gives CH₃CH₂–, and its 4.12 shift puts it on O. The 2.05 singlet is CH₃ on C=O. Join them: CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, with nothing left over.

This is the deliverable students should be able to produce: every observation assigned to an atom or group, with nothing left over. Build it in order: formula and IR say “one C=O, no OH”; the quartet-triplet pair says “ethyl”; its shift at 4.12 says “on oxygen”; the singlet at 2.05 says “methyl on C=O”. Join the fragments: CH3–C(=O)–O–CH2–CH3. Then check it the other way round: does the structure predict anything we didn’t see? It doesn’t. That two-way check is what separates an assignment from a guess. Methyl propanoate would put a CH3 singlet near 3.7 (on O) and a CH2 quartet near 2.3 (on C=O), the opposite placement, so the shifts reject it.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Test the rival: butanoic acid

U1 against the butanoic acid predictionA candidate earns its place by predicting a spectrum. Butanoic acid predicts four signals; U1 has three.

Try it: give two observations that reject butanoic acid. Why doesn’t U1’s CH₃ triplet help?

No broad O–H (IR or ~11.5 ppm), and no O–CH₂ quartet or 3H singlet. Both structures end in CH₃–CH₂–, so a CH₃ triplet fits both.



Turn the candidate into a prediction first, then compare, rather than staring at U1 and hoping. Butanoic acid: CH3 triplet near 1, the middle CH2 as a six-line multiplet because it has five neighbouring H, the CH2 next to C=O as a triplet near 2.3, and the acid H as a broad singlet above 10. The good rejection uses observations the two candidates disagree about. The triplet is a nice trap: it’s real evidence for an ethyl end, but both candidates have one. Note that the name on a sample bottle is never evidence; the spectra are.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Test the rival: 3-hydroxybutan-2-one

U1 against the 3-hydroxybutan-2-one predictionThis candidate also has a quartet near 4.2 and a singlet near 2. Read the integrals and the methyl pattern.

Try it: which two features of this prediction contradict U1?

Its quartet is 1H (a CH on oxygen), not 2H, and its CH₃ is a doublet, not a triplet. It also has an O–H that IR didn’t see.



This is the best example of why one clue isn’t enough. Looking only at shifts and “is there a quartet?”, this hydroxyketone looks tempting. The integral says the quartet is 1H, so the carbon on oxygen is a CH, not a CH2. The methyl doublet follows from the previous slide: one neighbouring H gives two lines. Its OH adds an IR band U1 doesn’t have. 3-Hydroxybutan-2-one, also called acetoin, is a real molecule: it’s part of the buttery aroma of butter and some wines, made by yeast and bacteria, which is a nice link back to the smells we started with.
