✓
✗



“U1 is best explained by ethyl ethanoate among the candidates tested: it accounts for every observation and each rival fails at least one independent test.”

Try it: why not just write “U1 is ethyl ethanoate, proven”?

We tested a finite list, and these spectra are simulated. A real identification also depends on data quality, sample purity and a reference spectrum.



The table is the honest summary: every candidate fits the formula, so the formula alone was never going to decide. Point out that 13C alone doesn’t separate the first three either; it’s the combination that does. The wording of the conclusion matters and is what we ask for in exercises: say what was compared, what fits, and what remains open. In the R part of today’s exercise, students plot the simulated ester and acid IR traces from data/ir.csv; the caption must say they’re simulated, which is the same honesty applied to a figure. Tomorrow we use exactly this kind of evidence to decide whether a synthesis worked.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake
fix




including O in the DBE formula
DBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2; O drops out


“dip = less absorption” on an IR trace
in transmittance, a dip is absorption


“a quartet means 4 H”
lines count the neighbours’ H; the integral counts the H


comparing tallest lines as H counts
compare areas (integrals)


“6 carbons but 4 signals, so impossible”
symmetry makes carbons equivalent


naming a molecule from one IR band
C=O fits many molecules; add NMR and the formula


rejecting with a feature both candidates share
use an observation the candidates disagree about




Read each mistake aloud and ask for the fix before revealing the column. The quartet one is the most persistent, and the last one is the subtlest: using the ethyl triplet to reject butanoic acid feels right but isn’t, because the acid has an ethyl end too. Each row maps to a specific exercise, so students who still make a mistake know where to practise.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Summary



concept
key fact




DBE
(2C + 2 − H)/2 = rings + π bonds


IR
C=O 1650–1800 sharp; O–H broad; acid O–H very broad


¹H shift
further left near O or C=O


¹H integral
area ∝ number of H; formula fixes the total


¹H splitting
n neighbouring H → n + 1 lines


¹³C
one line per carbon environment; heights don’t count


symmetry
equivalent atoms share a signal


a structure
is a hypothesis: predict, compare, reject rivals



Next: using spectra as evidence in synthesis (Day 22). Practice: exercises · self-check

Recite the workflow once: formula and DBE, IR for groups, 1H for fragments (shift, integral, splitting), 13C for the carbon count, then build a candidate and test it against its rivals. Close the loop with the opening: the pear-drop bottle is ethyl ethanoate and the rancid-butter bottle is butanoic acid, and the spectra tell them apart on at least three independent counts. The exercises walk through U1 again step by step; the core problems 1 to 10 are required.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Plan short transformations, calculate the possible product amount and decide what the observations support.
Core exercises 1–10: begin here. Transfer 11–16: apply the same ideas to new cases. Further checks 17–20: use these to investigate mistakes and revise. Allow roughly 2–3 hours across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning with the worked explanation.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Working refresher
Keep these calculations distinct: amount n=m/M; reaction extent available from a reagent is n divided by its balanced coefficient; maximum product amount is limiting extent times the product coefficient.1 mol=1000 mmol. Theoretical product mass is product amount×product molar mass. Apparent isolated yield=100×isolated mass/theoretical product mass, interpreted as product yield only if the weighed mass is product. Yield does not measure purity or conversion. For TLC (thin-layer chromatography), Rf=spot-centre distance/front distance, both from the same origin; the ratio is dimensionless and depends on conditions. The lecture has worked examples.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
1. Plan a two-step functional-group route
Starting with ethanol, propose a route through ethanoic acid to ethyl ethanoate. Identify the separate ethanol portion needed in the second step and name each transformation.






Hint





The acid-derived and alcohol-derived fragments need not come from the same reacting molecule.









Worked explanation





Oxidise one ethanol portion to ethanoic acid, then use a separate ethanol portion in esterification. The first change is oxidation and the second acyl substitution. Conditions and work-up require suitable choices; this is a planning example, not a protocol.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
2. Choose an oxidation endpoint
Ethanol can give ethanal and then ethanoic acid under appropriate oxidation conditions. Explain why a target labelled ethanal needs more information than an unspecified [O] arrow.






Hint





Further oxidation is a possible competing transformation.









Worked explanation





Conditions must favour forming and isolating the aldehyde rather than proceeding to acid. A target name does not guarantee selectivity or purity, and product evidence is still needed after the reaction.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
3. Convert mass with visible units
A teaching amount table gives 1.3812 g salicylic acid and M=138.12 g/mol. Calculate mol and mmol, showing unit cancellation.






Hint





Divide mass by molar mass;1 mol=1000 mmol.









Worked explanation





1.3812 g/(138.12 g/mol)=0.01000 mol=10.00 mmol. Grams cancel. Converting mmol into mol requires dividing by 1000, which matters before multiplying by a molar mass in g/mol.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
4. Compare a second reagent
For 1.53135 g acetic anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, calculate amount. In a 1:1 reaction with 10.00 mmol acid, identify the limiting reagent and justify without comparing masses.






Hint





The balanced reaction has coefficients one for both starting reagents.









Worked explanation





Anhydride amount is 0.01500 mol=15.00 mmol. Acid has the smaller n/coefficient,10/1 versus 15/1, and limits theoretical product. A larger mass alone would not establish excess.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
5. Handle coefficients explicitly
For the illustrative equation 2A+B→P, starting amounts are 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B. Find limiting reagent and maximum P amount; explain why simply taking min(10,8) is wrong.






Hint





Compare n divided by reactant coefficient.









Worked explanation





A supplies 10/2=5 mmol reaction extent while B supplies 8/1=8 mmol. A limits and at most 5 mmol P forms. Taking the minimum raw amount ignores that two A units are required per product.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
6. Include a product coefficient
For 2A+B→2P with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, find maximum P amount. Compare with the previous equation 2A+B→P using the same inputs.






Hint





The limiting extent is multiplied by the product coefficient.









Worked explanation





A still limits extent to 5 mmol. With product coefficient 2, maximum P=10 mmol; with coefficient 1 it is 5 mmol. Extent and product amount are not universally the same number.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
7. Change the limiting reagent
In the 1:1 aspirin teaching reaction, acid stays 10.00 mmol but anhydride mass is 0.51045 g at 102.09 g/mol. Identify the new limiter and predict product mol and mass with M=180.16 g/mol.






Hint





Recompute the changed amount before reusing the original limiter label.









Worked explanation





Anhydride is 0.00500 mol=5.00 mmol and now limits. Theoretical aspirin is 0.00500 mol, giving 0.9008 g. The original 10 mmol acid is now in excess for the desired reaction.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
8. Calculate theoretical mass
A1:1 teaching reaction has 10.0 mmol limiting reagent and product M=180.16 g/mol. Calculate the theoretical mass and state what assumptions the upper bound contains.






Hint





Convert 10.0 mmol to 0.0100 mol before multiplying.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g before final rounding. It assumes the balanced desired transformation and complete use of limiting reagent toward that product; it does not establish actual conversion, recovery or purity.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
9. Calculate apparent isolated yield
For theoretical mass 1.8016 g and isolated material 1.20 g, calculate 100×isolated/theoretical. State the chemical assumption behind calling it product yield.






Hint





The numerator must represent product mass for the interpretation to hold.









Worked explanation





The apparent isolated yield is 66.6%. Interpreting this as product yield assumes the weighed material is product with appropriate identity/purity; solvent or impurities can inflate its mass.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
10. Predict a changed numerator
Theoretical mass remains 1.8016 g. Compare isolated masses 1.10 g and 1.20 g. Calculate both apparent yields and say which upstream quantities should remain unchanged.






Hint





Only isolated mass changes in the numerator.









Worked explanation





The yields are 61.1% and 66.6%. Starting-reagent amounts, limiting extent and theoretical mass should stay fixed. A report that changes those without changing the inputs has a dependency error.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
11. Critique a yield above 100 percent
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g but a sample weighs 1.95 g. Calculate the apparent yield and name two plausible classes of explanation without diagnosing a unique cause.






Hint





An apparent yield can expose a questionable mass or model assumption.









Worked explanation





The value is about 108.2%. Residual solvent/water or other impurities can add mass; a weighing, input or stoichiometry error is another possibility. It is not evidence of creating extra product atoms beyond the balanced maximum.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
12. Separate yield and purity
One isolate has low apparent yield but the supplied spectra are consistent with the target; another has high apparent yield and major extra NMR signals. Explain why yield cannot rank their purity.






Hint





Yield measures recovered amount relative to a theoretical amount, not composition.









Worked explanation





A small recovered amount can be relatively pure, while a large mass can include impurities. Purity needs composition evidence; yield and identity/purity are different claims. The facts do not give exact purities of either sample.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
13. Compute two Rf values
A TLC origin is 0 cm, solvent front 5.0 cm, starting-material spot 1.2 cm and product-reference spot 3.2 cm. Calculate both Rf values and give units.






Hint





Rf=distance from origin to spot centre divided by distance from origin to solvent front.









Worked explanation





The values are 0.24 and 0.64, dimensionless. Both distances must use the same baseline and units; the numbers are conditional on stationary phase, eluent and other conditions.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
14. Read a crude TLC lane
Under the same conditions, a crude lane has spots at 1.2 cm and 3.2 cm with front 5.0 cm; reference lanes match those positions. Write a restrained interpretation and one limitation.






Hint





Matching retention supports comparison but is not a unique molecular fingerprint.









Worked explanation





At least two detected components are present, with retention consistent with the references. Co-migration or invisible components remain possible; spot matching alone does not uniquely establish identity or quantitative conversion.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
15. Recognise missing information
A TLC image records a spot 3.0 cm above baseline but no solvent-front position. Can Rf be calculated? What observation is missing, and why should a typical front distance not be invented?






Hint





A ratio needs both numerator and denominator.









Worked explanation





Rf cannot be determined reliably. The actual front travel from the same baseline is missing. A presumed usual distance would substitute an invented observation and could give a false retention value.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
16. Test the single-spot purity claim
A and B each run at Rf 0.64 in one eluent, and their mixture shows one spot. Explain how this can happen and propose a useful follow-up kind of evidence.






Hint





The separation method may fail to resolve different compounds.









Worked explanation





Co-migration can give one retention feature for a mixture. A suitable changed separation condition or independent spectral assessment can test composition. One spot is not a guarantee of purity, and detection can miss some components.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
17. Track the aspirin functional-group change
Salicylic acid has adjacent aromatic COOH and OH groups. In the teaching aspirin target, the phenolic oxygen becomes O–C(=O)CH₃ while COOH remains. State which group changes and why acid O–H evidence may persist.






Hint





Not every oxygen-containing group is consumed by phenolic acetylation.









Worked explanation





Phenolic OH is converted to an acetate ester. The carboxylic acid remains, so acid-region features can persist in the target. Acid O–H alone does not uniquely establish unreacted salicylic acid.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
18. Interpret an extra NMR signal
An isolate has a plausible mass-based yield and one TLC spot but an extra major NMR signal group. Give two possibilities and a targeted next check without naming a definite impurity.






Hint





The identity/purity assumption should be tested against independent evidence.









Worked explanation





Residual solvent or another component, including starting material, could contribute; assignment error is also possible. Compare full integrations/assignments and suitable references or use a discriminating separation. Do not discard contradictory spectra because yield looks plausible.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
19. Audit a report dependency
A student changes isolated mass from 1.20 g to 1.10 g and the report also changes theoretical product mol from 0.0100 to 0.0090. Starting-reagent masses were unchanged. Identify the error and the correct dependency.






Hint





The theoretical maximum comes from starting materials, not from recovered mass.









Worked explanation





Theoretical mol must remain 0.0100 under the unchanged reaction inputs. Isolated mass only changes the apparent yield numerator. Reconstruct calculations from saved raw inputs and keep the independent measurements separate.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
20. Write a supported conclusion
Supplied teaching evidence gives theoretical mass 1.8016 g, isolate 1.20 g, crude TLC two spots and a product-like simulated IR comparison. Write a conclusion separating amount, reaction evidence and remaining identity/purity limits.






Hint





Avoid allowing one observation to answer every question.









Worked explanation





Apparent isolated yield is 66.6% under the product-mass assumption. Crude TLC shows at least two detected components, and the labelled teaching IR illustrates consistent functional groups. These observations do not uniquely prove a real isolate’s identity or purity, especially when the trace is simulated.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
section: R task: results that update when a mass changes
text:
R task: results that update when a mass changes
In the student project, save a results section containing the amount table, limiting-reagent reasoning, theoretical mass and isolated yield. Start from this calculation:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
theoretical_product_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_mass_g <- theoretical_product_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
knitr::kable(amounts)
isolated_yield_percent
The amounts.csv table contains the two starting reagents. If adding product or solvent rows later, select the relevant starting reagents before min(). Inspect the table and check the units. Write the numerical yield using inline R in the report, not by typing a second independent copy of the number. Add your TLC table and an interpretation distinguishing evidence for reaction, identity and purity. Change the isolated mass to 1.10 g, predict the direction of change, and Knit again before restoring the original teaching value.






Reproducibility check





At 1.10 g the apparent isolated yield becomes about 61.1%. Every dependent result should change when knitted. If a copied number remains 66.6%, it is no longer linked to the saved calculation. Correctness also requires the right stoichiometry and trustworthy primary observations; automatic updating alone cannot supply either.



Finish with two sentences stating what the observations support and what remains uncertain. Reading: Solomons chapters 8, 12 and 17; see the reading guide.

title: Day 22: Exercises — Synthesis and evidence
text:
Explore
Question: what does an Rf calculation tell you, and what information is lost if the solvent front was not recorded?
Allow 7 minutes: predict for 2, adjust the plate for 3, then explain the limits for 2. Distances are supplied hypothetical teaching measurements.

Enable JavaScript to vary distances from the origin and inspect the TLC ratio.




Predict
Rf is spot-centre distance divided by solvent-front distance, both measured from the same origin. Predict the value for 3.20 cm and 5.0 cm. Predict the value for a spot halfway to the front and state its units.


Explore

Change front and spot distances. Follow the geometrical plate as well as the reported ratio. The spot control stays between origin and front.
Use Spot halfway to front at more than one front distance.
Select Front unrecorded. Explain why spot height alone is insufficient.
Compare one known component with two components with the same retention. Can the visible plate distinguish those scenarios?



Explain and check
\(Rf=3.20/5.0=0.64\). A halfway spot gives 0.5, independent of the numerical front distance. The ratio is dimensionless. Without an actual recorded front, the denominator is unknown and the tool correctly declines to invent an Rf.
Two components can co-migrate and produce the same visible feature. The composition selector supplies a counterexample; the plate alone did not measure that component count. One spot therefore does not prove purity.


Model limits
Rf depends on stationary phase, eluent and other conditions, so matching retention is not a unique identity code. Detection can also miss components. Use matched conditions and appropriate independent structural/composition evidence. The geometric model does not simulate molecular adsorption or provide operating instructions.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
1. Which reagent limits?
A 1:1 reaction uses 10.0 mmol A and 15.0 mmol B. How much product can form stoichiometrically?






Check your answer





At most 10.0 mmol of the stated 1:1 product under the assumed desired transformation. A limits; leftover B does not increase that maximum.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
2. What if coefficients differ?
For 2A + B → P, with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, identify the limiting reagent and maximum P amount.






Check your answer





Compare 10/2 = 5 mmol with 8/1 = 8 mmol. A limits and at most 5 mmol P forms. Comparing amounts without coefficients would be misleading.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
3. What does 1.20 g mean?
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. Calculate apparent isolated yield and state its purity assumption.






Check your answer





100×1.20/1.8016 ≈ 66.6%. The calculation treats isolated mass as product mass; impurities or solvent can bias that assumption.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
4. What is Rf?
A spot travels 3.2 cm and solvent front 5.0 cm from the origin. Calculate Rf and give units.






Check your answer





Rf = 0.64, dimensionless. Both distances must be measured from the same origin; the ratio depends on separation conditions.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
5. Does one spot establish purity?
Give two reasons a mixture might show only one TLC (thin-layer chromatography) spot.






Check your answer





Distinct compounds can co-migrate, and a component may not be detected by the chosen visualisation. One spot under one condition does not uniquely identify or prove purity.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
6. What should change after Knit?
You change isolated mass from 1.20 to 1.10 g. Predict the effect and the approximate new yield.






Check your answer





The yield decreases to about 61.1%. Tables and inline computed values should update from saved inputs; manually copied numbers may not.



Return to the exercises for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
About this lecture
After a hard sprint your blood lactate can jump from about 1 to over 10 mmol/L. People call it “lactic acid”, but at blood pH almost none of it is the acid. The same three-carbon molecule makes yoghurt sour and is polymerised into compostable PLA cups. One small molecule, and every week of this course has something to say about it.
Today we read one molecule with every tool:

Structure and stereo: groups, CIP priorities, R/S, enantiomers
Acids and charge: proton transfer, atom audits, pKa and ionised fraction
Reactions: oxidation, esterification, addition versus substitution
Evidence: spectra, alternatives, yield and honest conclusions

Yesterday was about yield and evidence; today we use it alongside everything else.

Open with the sprint. Ask who has heard that “lactic acid” makes your legs burn, then promise that by slide eight we’ll show with one pKa that the blood is full of lactate, not lactic acid. Mention the yoghurt and the PLA cup to show this isn’t just a biochemistry molecule; the PLA link comes back on the esterification slide. Make clear that no metabolic pathways are needed: everything today is read from the atoms and bonds, using tools from Weeks 1 to 5. This is also a good model of how exam questions combine topics: one molecule, several questions in a row.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Read the molecule locally first

Lactic acid with its stereocentre and functional groupsBefore thinking about reactions, name what’s there: a secondary alcohol, a carboxylic acid, and one stereocentre carrying OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.

Try it: why is the alcohol secondary?

Answer. The OH-bearing carbon has two carbon neighbours (CH₃ and COOH) and one H.



This is the first move on any unfamiliar molecule, and it’s the habit from Day 1: look at the neighbours of each heteroatom. Point at the two OH groups and ask which one is an acid. Only the OH on the carbonyl carbon is a carboxylic acid; the other is an alcohol. Students sometimes call the C=O carbon the stereocentre; it’s trigonal planar with three neighbours, so it can’t be. The stereocentre is the CH(OH) carbon with four different groups. Formula C3H6O3, molar mass 90.08 g/mol: worth checking the H count, since the central carbon has only one H.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Rank the branches at the stereocentre
text:
Rank the branches at the stereocentre

CIP priorities at the lactic acid stereocentreO beats C beats H. The two carbons tie, so compare the next atoms: the C=O counts its O twice, so COOH is (O, O, O) against CH₃’s (H, H, H).

Try it: give the full priority order at this centre.

Answer. OH > COOH > CH₃ > H: oxygen first, then the two ranked carbons, then H.



This is the Week 2 CIP procedure applied to a real case. Stress the duplication rule: a double bond to O counts as two O substituents for comparison, which together with the OH gives O,O,O. The mistake to probe is ranking by group size or by “how big it looks” on the page. COOH wins because of what its first carbon is attached to, not because it’s drawn bigger. Ask a student to justify why the comparison stops at the first point of difference.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Assign R or S with H pointing away
text:
Assign R or S with H pointing away

Tracing 1 to 2 to 3 with H away and with H toward youWith H (4) hashed away, trace 1 → 2 → 3: clockwise is R, anticlockwise is S. On the left OH → COOH → CH₃ runs anticlockwise: (S)-lactic acid, the one your muscles make. With H on a wedge, reverse what you see.

Try it: in another drawing, H points toward you and 1 → 2 → 3 looks clockwise. What is the configuration?

Answer. S. With H toward you, reverse the apparent result (or rotate a model until H points away).



Trace the path with your finger on the screen: left (OH), right (COOH), up (CH3). That sweep goes anticlockwise, and since H is on the hashed bond, the answer stands: S. Then do exercise 3’s version orally: OH upper left, COOH upper right, CH3 lower left, H away gives clockwise, so R. The most common exam error is forgetting to reverse when H is on a wedge. Remind them that turning the page or rotating the drawing never changes the answer; only swapping two groups does.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Mirror images, not rotations

(S)- and (R)-lactic acid drawn as mirror imagesSame connectivity, opposite arrangement: enantiomers. No rotation turns one into the other. R/S is a naming rule; the sign of optical rotation has to be measured.

Try it: does rotating the whole drawing 180° on the page give the other enantiomer?

Answer. No. A rigid rotation keeps the configuration. Only swapping two groups at the centre (or reflecting) does.



(S)-lactic acid happens to be dextrorotatory, (+), but there is no rule linking S to plus. In fact its salts, the lactates, rotate the other way, which is a nice demonstration that the sign is a measured property. Biology cares about the difference: lactate dehydrogenase in muscle handles the S form, and some bacteria make the R form, which is why D-lactate is a clinical marker of certain gut infections. Connect back to Week 2: enantiomers share boiling point, IR and NMR in ordinary solvents, so these tools can’t tell them apart.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: The simplest reaction: a proton transfer
text:
The simplest reaction: a proton transfer

Hydroxide removes the carboxyl proton of lactic acidOne arrow from the base’s lone pair to H, one from the O–H bond onto O. The carboxyl O–H is the acidic one; the alcohol O–H is far less acidic.

Try it: does this step invert the stereocentre?

Answer. No. Only the carboxyl O–H bond changes. No bond to the stereocentre is made or broken.



Two arrows, both starting from electrons: this is the Day 8 rule. Ask students where each arrow starts and refuse an arrow that starts at the H. The carboxylic acid is the acidic site because its conjugate base is resonance-stabilised over two oxygens, which is the Day 3 argument; the alcohol has a pKa around 16, so hydroxide in water doesn’t remove it meaningfully. The stereocentre question is there because students sometimes assume any reaction “scrambles” stereo. A step can only change a configuration if it changes bonds at that carbon.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Audit every atom and the charge
text:
Audit every atom and the charge




lactic acid + OH⁻

lactate + H₂O




species
C₃H₆O₃ + HO⁻
→
C₃H₅O₃⁻ + H₂O


C, H, O total
C₃H₇O₄

C₃H₇O₄


net charge
−1

−1



The H isn’t lost; it moves to hydroxide. The bonding pair of the old O–H stays on oxygen, which is why that O now carries the −1.

Try it: what goes wrong if you write the products as just lactate?

Answer. You lose H₂O from the inventory: two H, one O. The equation no longer balances, and the proton’s new home is hidden.



This is the valence audit from Day 1 applied to a whole equation. Have students count with you: left side 3 C, 6 + 1 = 7 H, 3 + 1 = 4 O; right side 3 C, 5 + 2 = 7 H, 3 + 1 = 4 O. Charge −1 on both sides. The point is that arrows track electrons, but they don’t give permission to delete atoms. The audit is the fastest way to catch a dropped product in an exam answer.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: At blood pH it’s lactate, not lactic acid
text:
At blood pH it’s lactate, not lactic acid

Fraction of lactate against pH for pKa 3.86f_{\text{A}^-} = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{\,\text{p}K_a - \text{pH}}} \qquad \text{p}K_a = 3.86

Try it: what fraction is lactate at pH 4.86? And at blood pH 7.4?

Answer. At 4.86 the ratio A⁻/HA is 10, so 10/11 ≈ 0.91. At 7.4 it’s about 3500 : 1, so over 99.9 % lactate.



This answers the opening hook. At pH equal to pKa the fraction is exactly one half; every pH unit above multiplies the A-minus to HA ratio by ten. At 7.4 that’s 10 to the 3.54, about 3500. So “lactic acid in the blood” is really lactate, and the acidification during exercise is a more complicated story than the name suggests. Probe the population meaning: 0.91 means 91 % of molecules are ionised at any moment, not that each molecule has lost 91 % of a proton. Week 1 Day 3 introduced this curve; the dilute monoprotic model is what we assume.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Oxidation turns the stereocentre into a ketone
text:
Oxidation turns the stereocentre into a ketone

Lactic acid oxidised to pyruvic acidThe secondary alcohol becomes a ketone: pyruvic acid, CH₃C(=O)COOH. In your cells lactate dehydrogenase does this with NAD⁺.

Try it: does pyruvic acid still have an R/S centre?

Answer. No. C2 is now trigonal planar with three groups, so there’s no stereocentre left to label.



Week 3 redox: a secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone and stops there, because there’s no H left on the carbonyl carbon to remove. The formula changes from C3H6O3 to C3H4O3, a loss of two H, which is the classic signature of oxidation. Muscles run this reaction in both directions: pyruvate is reduced to lactate when oxygen is short, and lactate is oxidised back in the heart and liver. Emphasise geometry: the stereochemical information is destroyed, and reducing pyruvate back could in principle give either enantiomer. The enzyme is what makes it give only S.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Count the oxidation state at the changing carbon
text:
Count the oxidation state at the changing carbon

The carbon goes from 0 to +2: an oxidation, even though no O atom was added.

Try it: why does a C–C bond count zero?

Answer. The two atoms have the same electronegativity, so neither one is assigned the bonding electrons.



This is the bookkeeping from Day 13. The bond to O counts per bond order, so a C=O counts plus two. The take-home message is that oxidation is about electrons at the carbon, not about counting oxygen atoms in the formula; lactic and pyruvic acid have the same three oxygens. Ask the room what happens to the carboxyl carbon (nothing: plus three in both). The counting rule only works for the carbon that changes, which is why we focus on C2.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Esterification: track the alcohol oxygen

Lactic acid and ethanol give ethyl lactate, with the ethanol oxygen labelled O-starFischer esterification is an acyl substitution: ethanol’s O* attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the acid’s OH leaves as water. Ethyl lactate is a biodegradable solvent.

Try it: which two atoms is O* bonded to in the product?

Answer. The acid-derived carbonyl carbon and the ethyl CH₂. The water’s O comes from the acid.



Isotope labelling with oxygen-18 is the classic experiment that proved this: the label from the alcohol ends up in the ester, not in the water. That only makes sense if the alcohol is the nucleophile attacking the acyl carbon (Week 4). The bonds at the stereocentre aren’t touched, so (S)-lactic acid gives (S)-ethyl lactate. Now the limitation: lactic acid has its own OH, so one molecule’s OH can esterify another’s COOH. That’s exactly how lactide and PLA plastic are made. A target drawing doesn’t guarantee selectivity; the conditions do.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Addition or substitution? Look for a leaving group
text:
Addition or substitution? Look for a leaving group

Aldehyde plus cyanide stays tetrahedral; ester plus hydroxide expels methoxide and reforms C=OBoth start the same way: Nu adds, the C=O π pair moves onto O. An ester carries an OR that can leave, so C=O comes back. An aldehyde has only H or C there.

Try it: what’s the first elementary step both pathways share?

Answer. Nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide.



This is the Day 16 versus Day 17 decision in one picture. The question students should ask is: after the tetrahedral intermediate forms, is there a group that can leave and take a bonding pair with it? Methoxide can; hydride and methyl can’t, so aldehydes and ketones stop at addition. In base, the acetic acid at the end is immediately deprotonated to acetate, which is why ester hydrolysis in base (saponification) goes to completion. Probe the valence: keeping C=O and adding Nu at the same time would give a five-bonded carbon.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Amino acids carry two charges at pH 7
text:
Amino acids carry two charges at pH 7

L-alanine as a zwitterion with ammonium and carboxylate shadedRead the charges from the normal-state table (Day 1). The net charge is zero, but the molecule still has a + and a − end.

Try it: net zero, so does alanine behave like a hydrocarbon in water?

Answer. No. Both charged sites interact strongly with water, which is why amino acids are high-melting and water-soluble.



Alanine is lactic acid’s nitrogen cousin: swap the OH for NH3+. Ask the room to point at the exact charged atoms, not just “the molecule is charged”. At pH 7 the carboxylic acid (pKa about 2) has lost its proton and the amine (conjugate acid pKa about 10) has gained one, so both ends are charged. L-alanine is S, just like L-lactic acid, which is a nice coincidence of the CIP rules here (it isn’t true for every L amino acid; cysteine is R).

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Change the pH, keep the skeleton
text:
Change the pH, keep the skeleton

At high pH the ammonium group of alanine loses a proton to hydroxideHydroxide removes an N–H proton. The bonding pair goes back to N, which ends with three bonds and a lone pair. No C–C bond is touched.

Try it: is the N in a peptide bond (an amide) basic like this ammonium N?

Answer. No. The amide N’s lone pair is delocalised into the C=O, so it’s barely basic (Week 4).



Same move as the lactic acid deprotonation, at a different site. Check the charge audit: zwitterion plus hydroxide has net −1, anion plus water has net −1. Product formula H2NCH(CH3)COO−, C3H6NO2−. The peptide question links to Day 18: an amide N is planar and its lone pair is part of the amide resonance, which is why proteins don’t pick up a proton on every backbone nitrogen.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Identify an unknown: make the evidence agree
text:
Identify an unknown: make the evidence agree

Ethyl acetate with protons a, b and c matched to its NMR spectrumU1: C₄H₈O₂, IR C=O but no broad O–H, ¹H NMR 4.12 q 2H, 2.05 s 3H, 1.25 t 3H. The quartet and triplet are an ethyl on O; the singlet is a CH₃ next to C=O.

Try it: what does the molecular formula add to this argument?

Answer. DBE = 1, so one C=O and no ring. It also sets the atom budget: every C, H and O must be placed.



This is the Week 5 spectroscopy workflow from Day 21. Build the structure piece by piece: the quartet (2H) and triplet (3H) couple to each other, so they’re an ethyl group, and the 4.12 shift puts the CH2 on oxygen. The singlet at 2.05 has no neighbouring H, consistent with sitting next to the carbonyl. The IR rules out acids and alcohols. The formula is the referee: C4H8O2 with one degree of unsaturation is accounted for by the ester C=O. Ethyl acetate is also nail-polish remover, which helps it stick.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Test the alternative before you claim
text:
Test the alternative before you claim

Ethyl acetate and 3-hydroxybutan-2-one with their predicted NMR and IR features3-hydroxybutan-2-one is also C₄H₈O₂ with a C=O. A good claim says why it doesn’t fit: wrong integrals, wrong splitting and an O–H that isn’t there.

Try it: would a matching C=O band rescue the hydroxyketone?

Answer. No. One shared feature can’t outweigh three predictions that disagree with the data.



Real problem-solving means generating an alternative and testing it, not just confirming the first idea. The hydroxyketone’s CH3 next to CH would be a doublet; its O-bearing carbon is a CH, so 1H, not 2H; and it has an OH that the IR would show. Say it plainly: we don’t use the name of the bottle or the expected product as evidence. Ask students to name one more C4H8O2 candidate (methyl propanoate, for instance) and say which signal would rule it out.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: A high yield doesn’t prove identity
text:
A high yield doesn’t prove identity

Isolated mass against theoretical mass beside an NMR spectrum with an unexpected peak0.0100 mol × 180.16 g/mol = 1.8016 g theoretical; 1.70 g isolated is 94.4 %, if the solid is pure product. Unexpected NMR peaks challenge that “if”.

Try it: give two reasons the isolated mass could be too high.

Answer. Residual solvent or water, and unreacted starting material or a side product. One TLC (thin-layer chromatography) spot can hide a co-running impurity.



180.16 g/mol is aspirin, made from the 0.0100 mol of salicylic acid we weighed on Day 1, so this closes a loop. The yield calculation is only as good as its assumption that the mass is all product. Neither observation should be ignored: the plausible mass and the strange NMR together say “investigate”. Also mention exercise 19: dividing isolated mass by the starting-material mass (1.70 / 1.3812) gives 123 %, a reproducible number that is still chemically wrong because molar masses differ. Running the same wrong formula in R every time doesn’t make it right.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Writing a conclusion someone can check
text:
Writing a conclusion someone can check







part
for the U1 ester




claim
U1 is ethyl acetate


evidence
C₄H₈O₂; C=O, no O–H; q 2H, s 3H, t 3H


reason
O–CH₂CH₃ explains q/t; CH₃–C=O explains the singlet


alternative ruled out
hydroxyketone predicts a doublet and an O–H


limitation
simulated data, not a measured real sample


next test
measured spectra and a purity check on the isolate




Try it: why is “it’s the ester because we made the ester” not evidence?

Answer. It’s circular: it assumes the reaction worked, which is exactly what the evidence must test.



This is the Day 22 structure, now with all the chemistry filled in. Each row should be checkable by someone else. The reason row is the one students skip; insist that each observation is linked to a specific atom group. For R-based reports, the reproducibility part is that raw data and code are saved so a fresh session recreates the tables, but reproducible doesn’t mean chemically correct; both checks are needed.

Try it: you’re handed a molecule you’ve never seen. What do you do first?

Answer. Read it locally: name the functional groups and look at the atoms around each one, before thinking about any reaction.



This is the exit question from the old session, turned into a routine. The exam is built exactly like today: a molecule you may not have met, and a sequence of questions that each use one tool. Students who panic at an unfamiliar name should fall back to step 1; the name never matters, the atoms do. Encourage them to write this routine at the top of their exam paper.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Mistakes we see every year







mistake

H toward you: flip the answer

the sign of rotation is measured


dropping water from a proton transfer

trigonal planar: no stereocentre

a high yield taken as proof of purity
yield assumes identity; test it




Read each mistake aloud and ask the room why it’s wrong before revealing the fix. Every row matches an exercise from today’s set, so a student who recognises their own mistake knows which problem to redo. These are also the errors that cost the most marks on past exams.

Next: revision on Days 24–25 (spectra and calculations, final synthesis), then the exam. Practice: exercises · self-check

Close the loop: lactic acid in the blood is lactate, its configuration is S, oxidising it gives pyruvate, esterifying it gives a solvent or a plastic, and we know what a sample is only when the evidence agrees. That’s five weeks in one molecule. There’s no new lecture after this one. Days 24 and 25 are mixed revision sets in exactly this style, and the exam will ask the same kinds of linked questions. Point to the exercises: 1 to 10 are core, 11 to 16 transfer and 17 to 20 are about evidence.
